options.rationale: A markedly raised antistreptolysin O titre, sustained inflammatory response and pathological mitral regurgitation are not explained by a viral illness, and a missed diagnosis in this setting carries a lifetime of valve disease. Observation without a plan also fails a family who have travelled a long distance for assessment (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever).
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis is described as monosymptomatic when there are no daytime urinary symptoms, and it affects a substantial minority of children at school entry with spontaneous resolution at roughly 15 per cent per year. Assessment focuses on excluding daytime symptoms, constipation, an abnormal stream, neurological signs, and the polyuria of diabetes, all of which change the pathway. Constipation is the most commonly missed contributor and treating it alone resolves wetting in many children. Alarm therapy has the best sustained outcomes and works by conditioning arousal to bladder fullness, but requires a committed family and typically several weeks before dryness is achieved. Desmopressin gives faster symptomatic control and is useful for short term needs, while combination therapy is used when either alone is insufficient.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis has no daytime urinary symptoms and needs no imaging
Exclude and treat constipation before starting specific therapy
The alarm is first line with the highest sustained dry rate but takes weeks and requires family commitment
Desmopressin gives rapid short term cover and relapses commonly on cessation
Evening fluid restriction without daytime redistribution reduces functional bladder capacity
explanation.pearls: Continue an alarm until the child achieves fourteen consecutive dry nights before stopping, because ceasing at the first run of dry nights is a leading cause of relapse.

options.rationale: Desmopressin works while it is being taken but relapse after cessation is common, so it is chosen for short term cover such as a camp or when an alarm has failed or cannot be used. It also carries a hyponatraemia risk requiring evening fluid restriction (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

Anticholinergic therapy targets overactive bladder, which typically produces daytime urgency and frequency that he does not have. It is added for children with proven detrusor overactivity resistant to first line measures (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

The alarm is first line for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a school-aged child, with the highest sustained dry rate because it produces conditioned waking rather than temporary symptom suppression. Success requires a motivated family who will wake with the child, which is present here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

Restricting evening fluid without addressing his poor daytime intake reduces total intake and shrinks functional bladder capacity, making matters worse. Redistributing fluid across the school day is helpful, but as an adjunct rather than a treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, abnormal urinary stream, neurological signs or treatment failure, none of which apply to uncomplicated night time wetting. Referral first delays a treatment that most families can start immediately (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

explanation.summary: Newly arrived refugee and migrant children frequently have absent or unreliable immunisation records, and the Australian Immunisation Handbook directs that any dose without written documentation be considered not given. Repeat doses of routine childhood vaccines in an already immune child carry no additional risk beyond local reactions, whereas assuming protection that does not exist has serious consequences. Catch up schedules are calculated by age using the online calculator, with minimum intervals between doses rather than the routine intervals, and multiple vaccines are given at the same visit at separate sites. Refugee health assessment also includes screening for tuberculosis, hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus, strongyloides, schistosomiasis where relevant, and iron and vitamin D deficiency. All doses are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, which matters for childcare enrolment and family payments.
key_points: Undocumented doses are treated as not given and a full catch up schedule is started
Repeat doses of routine childhood vaccines are safe in an already immune child
Multiple vaccines may be given at the same visit at separate injection sites
Catch up schedules use minimum rather than routine intervals and are calculated by age
Serology has a limited targeted role rather than a blanket one
explanation.pearls: Use the national catch up calculator rather than the routine schedule, because it applies the shortened minimum intervals that let a child complete a multi dose course in weeks instead of months.

sources.label: Department of Health: Catch up immunisation calculator

options.rationale: Records are frequently unobtainable and waiting leaves a susceptible child unprotected while she enters group care. Documentation is used when it is available and reliable, but its absence must not delay the schedule (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Serology is not available or interpretable for all antigens, delays protection and is more expensive and distressing than vaccinating. It has a defined role for a few conditions such as hepatitis B and varicella in older children rather than as a blanket strategy (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Multiple vaccines can be safely administered at the same visit at separate sites, and spacing them out prolongs susceptibility and increases the chance the schedule is never completed. Separation is required only for specific live vaccine timing rules (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

A child without written documentation is presumed unvaccinated and started on a catch up schedule determined by age, because repeating doses already received is safe while leaving gaps is not. Doses are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, which also underpins her family assistance and childcare enrolment requirements (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
source_refs: Department of Health: Catch up immunisation calculator

options.rationale: A partial schedule leaves her unprotected against diseases with significant morbidity and relies on a return visit that often does not happen in newly arrived families. Entry requirements set a minimum administrative standard rather than a clinical target (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Short stature is assessed by plotting serial heights, calculating growth velocity, comparing with the mid parental target range and obtaining a bone age, since the pattern over time discriminates far better than any single measurement. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the commonest cause of a short prepubertal adolescent boy, characterised by a delayed bone age, a normal growth velocity, a positive family history and eventual attainment of a height within the target range. Growth failure, defined by crossing centiles downward or a velocity below the expected range, points instead to pathology such as hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, growth hormone deficiency, chronic illness or an intracranial lesion. Basic screening includes full blood examination, renal and liver function, thyroid function, coeliac serology and insulin like growth factor 1. Psychological impact is asked about explicitly because it, rather than the height itself, most often drives the decision to intervene.
key_points: Growth velocity and bone age matter more than a single height measurement
Delayed bone age with normal velocity and a family history indicates constitutional delay
Crossing centiles downward signals pathology and prompts investigation
Growth hormone is for proven deficiency or specific defined indications
A short androgen course is reserved for significant psychological distress
explanation.pearls: A bone age delayed by more than two years alongside a normal growth velocity predicts a final height within the mid parental target range, which is the specific reassurance families need rather than a general statement that he will catch up.

options.rationale: Growth hormone is indicated for proven deficiency or for specific conditions on defined criteria, and his normal insulin like growth factor 1 with a preserved growth velocity argues against deficiency. Treating a normal variant exposes him to injections and cost for no gain in final height (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

Imaging is prompted by headache, visual field loss, growth velocity failure, diabetes insipidus or a discordant clinical picture, none of which is present. His normal fields, fundi and preserved velocity make an intracranial lesion very unlikely (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

Karyotyping is indicated for dysmorphic features, disproportionate stature or a girl with unexplained short stature, and gonadotropins are hard to interpret before the pubertal window has passed. A family history of delayed puberty with delayed bone age points elsewhere (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

A short androgen course is a legitimate option when delay is causing significant psychological distress, which he does not report, and it advances puberty without increasing final height. It is offered after discussion rather than as routine management of a normal variant (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

A normal growth velocity tracking parallel to the centiles, a bone age delayed by more than two years, prepubertal testicular volume at 14 and a family history of late puberty describe constitutional delay of growth and puberty, which reaches a normal adult height without treatment. Regular review confirms the expected pubertal progression and detects the minority whose velocity falters (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

explanation.summary: Australian practice has moved away from imaging every child after a first urinary tract infection, because most abnormalities detected do not alter management and investigation carries radiation, catheterisation and incidental finding costs. An infection is classified as atypical when the child is seriously ill or septic, has poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, a non Escherichia coli organism, or fails to respond within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. Ultrasound is recommended for infants under six months with a first infection, for any atypical infection and for recurrent infection, with cortical scintigraphy and cystourethrography reserved for narrower indications. The most valuable intervention for a well infant after a typical infection is family education about testing urine early during future febrile illness. Age under three months, systemic toxicity or inability to tolerate oral therapy remain indications for intravenous treatment at the time of infection.
key_points: Typical infection means Escherichia coli with a response within 48 hours in a child who is not septic
Ultrasound is indicated under six months of age, for atypical infections and for recurrent infections
Cortical scintigraphy and cystourethrography have narrower recurrent or atypical indications
Prophylaxis is not routine after a single typical infection
Early urine testing during future febrile illness is the highest yield family advice
explanation.pearls: Collect the specimen by catheter or suprapubic aspirate in a non toilet trained child, since bag specimens have a false positive rate high enough that a positive bag culture should never be used to diagnose infection or to trigger imaging.

options.rationale: A first urinary tract infection in an infant over six months that is caused by Escherichia coli and responds within 48 hours is a typical infection, for which routine imaging is not required in Australian paediatric guidance. The family instead receives clear advice to seek early urine testing with future febrile illness, since recurrence is the trigger for imaging (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

Ultrasound is recommended for infants under six months with a first infection, for atypical infections and for recurrent infections, none of which describes her. Ordering it in a typical infection yields little and generates incidental findings and further tests (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

Cortical scintigraphy is reserved for children with recurrent or atypical infection, or where an abnormal ultrasound raises concern about scarring. Performing it after a single typical infection exposes a well infant to radiation without changing management (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

This invasive study is used for atypical or recurrent infection, an abnormal ultrasound, or a strong family history of reflux, and it requires catheterisation with radiation exposure. Identifying low grade reflux after a single typical infection does not alter outcomes (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

Prophylaxis after a single typical infection provides minimal reduction in recurrence and selects resistant organisms, and it is considered only for high grade reflux or frequent recurrences. Prompt treatment of recurrences protects the kidney better than continuous low dose therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time-critical diagnosis with two incidence peaks, in the neonatal period and around puberty, and salvage rates fall from above 90 per cent within six hours to well under half beyond twelve. The classic features are abrupt severe pain often waking the patient from sleep, nausea and vomiting, a high riding transversely lying testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, and a history of prior self-limiting episodes suggests intermittent torsion. Doppler ultrasound is useful when the picture is equivocal but must never delay exploration when the clinical suspicion is high, since preserved arterial flow can be seen in partial or early torsion. The main differentials are torsion of the appendix testis, which produces a localised upper pole tenderness with a blue dot sign, and epididymo orchitis, which develops over days with urinary symptoms. Fixation is performed bilaterally because the underlying bell clapper anatomy is usually present on both sides.
key_points: Abrupt pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis and absent cremasteric reflex indicates torsion
Salvage rates fall sharply beyond six hours of symptom onset
Doppler flow may be preserved in partial or intermittent torsion, so imaging must not delay theatre
Prior brief self-limiting episodes suggest intermittent torsion and support urgent exploration
Both testes are fixed at operation because the predisposing anatomy is usually bilateral
explanation.pearls: Manual detorsion by rotating the testis outward like opening a book can restore flow while theatre is prepared, but it relieves pain in only some patients and never replaces exploration with fixation.

options.rationale: Imaging in a case with this clinical picture only delays surgery and can be falsely reassuring in early or intermittent torsion where flow is preserved. Ultrasound is helpful when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and would not otherwise lead to exploration (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

Sudden severe pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is torsion until proven otherwise, and salvage falls sharply after about six hours of ischaemia. Exploration allows detorsion with fixation of both testes, since the anatomical predisposition is usually bilateral (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

Epididymo orchitis is rare in a prepubertal or non sexually active adolescent, develops over days with dysuria or pyuria, and is typically relieved by elevating the testis. His negative dipstick and sudden onset point away from infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Any delay of hours in a testis that has already been ischaemic for five hours converts a salvageable organ into an infarcted one. Analgesia is given while theatre is prepared, never as a reason to wait (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

Sexually transmitted infection testing is appropriate for a sexually active young man with a subacute painful epididymis, not for this presentation. Waiting for a result would waste the remaining window for testicular salvage (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for more than 95 per cent of childhood constipation and the diagnosis is clinical, resting on stool frequency, calibre, withholding behaviour and an abdominal or rectal faecal mass. Soiling in this setting is almost always overflow rather than true diarrhoea, and families and schools routinely misread it as a behavioural problem or gastroenteritis. Treatment has two distinct phases that are frequently collapsed into one: clearing the retained load, then a maintenance dose continued long enough for a stretched rectum to regain sensation. Red flags that shift the workup are delayed meconium, failure to thrive, bilious vomiting, an abnormal sacral or neurological examination and onset in the first month of life. Relapse is the norm when maintenance is stopped as soon as things improve.
key_points: Runny soiling with infrequent large stools is overflow around a retained faecal load
Disimpaction must precede maintenance or the maintenance dose appears to fail
Oral macrogol is first line for disimpaction in Australia, ahead of rectal treatment
Radiographs correlate poorly with clinical constipation and are not needed to diagnose it
Passage of meconium on day one with normal growth argues strongly against aganglionosis
explanation.pearls: Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is titrated up daily over three to seven days for disimpaction, then continued at a maintenance dose for at least two months after a soft daily stool is established, because stopping as soon as the soiling settles is the single commonest reason it comes back.

options.rationale: A radiograph adds nothing when a faecal mass is already palpable, and radiographic loading scores correlate poorly with the clinical picture, so it delivers radiation without changing the plan. Imaging is reserved for genuine diagnostic doubt or a suspected obstructive complication (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

The condition this test looks for declares itself with meconium passage beyond 48 hours, poor growth and a narrow empty rectum that decompresses explosively on examination, none of which fit a child on the 50th centile who passed meconium on day one. Overflow soiling is in fact distinctly uncommon in aganglionosis, which argues against it rather than for it (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

Runny soiling with infrequent enormous stools and a palpable faecal mass is overflow around a retained load, and no maintenance dose will work until that load is cleared, which an escalating macrogol course achieves at home over three to seven days. Pairing it with sitting on the toilet after meals treats the withholding behaviour that keeps the cycle going (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

Rectal disimpaction sits second in the Australian sequence because oral macrogol clears the same load without a rectal procedure in a child who is already withholding, and paediatric phosphate enemas can cause hyperphosphataemia with hypocalcaemia. It becomes reasonable only after an adequate oral course has failed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

A stimulant without a disimpaction phase repeats the mistake of the earlier fixed low dose trial, because driving peristalsis against an impacted rectum increases the soiling and the pain that reinforces withholding. Stimulants earn their place added to maintenance macrogol once the load has cleared (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and its reputation for delayed diagnosis rests almost entirely on referred knee pain, since roughly one in four affected children present complaining only about the knee or distal thigh. Risk factors are obesity, male sex, age around the pubertal growth spurt and endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency, and bilateral involvement occurs in about 20 to 40 per cent either at presentation or later. Anteroposterior and frog leg lateral pelvis radiographs are diagnostic, with Klein's line failing to intersect the femoral head on the affected side, and early slips can be invisible on the anteroposterior view alone. Treatment is urgent in situ screw fixation, and the single strongest determinant of outcome is whether the slip is stable at the time of surgery. Avascular necrosis and chondrolysis are the complications that produce lifelong disability.
key_points: Around a quarter of slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents as isolated knee pain
Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the key bedside finding
Anteroposterior plus frog leg lateral pelvis views are required, as early slips hide on the anteroposterior view
Non weight bearing starts on clinical suspicion, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
Normal inflammatory markers over a six week history argue against infection and transient synovitis
explanation.pearls: Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck on the anteroposterior view should intersect part of the epiphysis, and any child under about sixteen presenting with knee pain and a limp needs a hip examination before the knee is imaged.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging of a joint with a completely normal examination will be normal, and the finding that matters lies proximal to it. Referred pain along the obturator nerve means knee pain in a child of this age demands examination and imaging of the hip before the knee is investigated further (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

Ultrasound answers a different question, distinguishing transient synovitis from septic arthritis in an acutely febrile child with a hip effusion, whereas this boy has six weeks of pain, a normal temperature and normal inflammatory markers. A negative ultrasound would also not exclude the bony displacement that is actually present (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

Continued weight bearing over another four weeks risks progression from a stable to an unstable displacement, which raises the rate of avascular necrosis from under 5 per cent to as high as 50 per cent. A gradual six week history is characteristic of the condition rather than reassuring against it (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with weeks of knee pain points to displacement through the proximal femoral physis, and anteroposterior plus frog leg lateral views of the pelvis are the diagnostic test because early slips are visible only on the lateral projection. Non weight bearing is started immediately on clinical suspicion because progression to an unstable slip is the event that destroys the femoral head (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Bone and joint infection is argued against by six weeks of gradual symptoms with a normal temperature, a C reactive protein of 3 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 8 mm/h. Empirical antibiotics would also delay the imaging and weight bearing restriction that actually change his outcome (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

explanation.summary: Occult spinal dysraphism includes a tethered cord, intraspinal lipoma, dermal sinus tract, split cord malformation and thickened filum terminale, and it is frequently signalled by a cutaneous marker over the lumbosacral spine long before any neurological sign appears. Reassuring features of a simple sacral dimple are a diameter under 5 mm, a position within 25 mm of the anal verge, a visible base, a midline location within the gluteal cleft and the absence of any other skin marker. Markers that raise concern are a hair tuft, a subcutaneous lipoma, a haemangioma or other vascular lesion, a skin tag or appendage, a deviated gluteal cleft, an atypical or multiple dimple, and any discharge from the lesion, and the presence of two or more markers is a particularly strong predictor. Ultrasound is the first line investigation in the first three months while the posterior elements remain cartilaginous, with magnetic resonance imaging for abnormal or equivocal results or for older infants. Detection before symptoms matters because neurological deficits from tethering, particularly bladder dysfunction, often persist after surgical release.
key_points: Simple dimples are under 5 mm, within 25 mm of the anus, midline with a visible base and no other marker
Hair tufts, vascular lesions, lipomas, skin tags and a deviated gluteal cleft are concerning markers
Two or more cutaneous markers substantially raise the risk of dysraphism
Ultrasound is first line before three months while the posterior elements are unossified
Waiting for neurological symptoms risks deficits that do not fully reverse after release
explanation.pearls: Measure the distance from the dimple to the anal verge rather than judging it by eye, because a lesion more than 25 mm above the anus lies above the level of the sacrococcygeal segment and is far more likely to communicate with the spinal canal.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.rationale: A simple dimple that is small, sited within 25 mm of the anal verge, with a visible base and no other cutaneous marker needs no imaging, but this one is larger, higher, blind ending and accompanied by two additional skin markers. Two or more cutaneous markers substantially raise the probability of an underlying spinal cord anomaly (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the definitive study but in a neonate requires sedation or anaesthesia, and it is reserved for babies with abnormal or equivocal ultrasound findings or with neurological signs. Going straight to it exposes a well newborn to an anaesthetic that ultrasound will usually make unnecessary (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms means waiting for neurological injury, since tethering typically declares itself through leg weakness, gait abnormality or bladder dysfunction that may not fully recover after release. The point of screening is to detect the anomaly before that occurs (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.rationale: Plain films show bony vertebral anomalies but not the spinal cord, the filum terminale or an intraspinal lipoma, which are the structures that matter. It differs from ultrasound in imaging the wrong tissue while adding radiation (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.rationale: An atypical dimple with additional cutaneous markers warrants imaging, and ultrasound is the first line study because the posterior vertebral elements have not yet ossified, which allows the conus and filum to be visualised without sedation or radiation. The window closes at around three to six months as ossification progresses, after which magnetic resonance imaging becomes necessary (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

explanation.summary: Australian asthma control in children is assessed over the preceding four weeks against four questions covering daytime symptoms, reliever use, night waking and activity limitation, with more than two days a week of symptoms or reliever use marking the boundary of good control. A child with any of these features is not adequately managed on reliever alone, and low dose inhaled corticosteroid is the first line preventer for children aged six and over. Before escalating any preventer, adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure such as household smoking, and comorbid rhinitis should be reviewed, and a written asthma action plan updated. Growth is monitored because inhaled corticosteroids produce a small reduction in growth velocity in the first year of use, largely without affecting final adult height, whereas poorly controlled asthma itself suppresses growth. Response is reassessed at four to eight weeks with a view to stepping down after several months of good control.
key_points: Symptoms or reliever use on more than two days a week indicates poor control in a child
Night waking or exercise limitation each independently indicate the need for a preventer
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is first line preventer treatment from age six
Long-acting beta2 agonists are not appropriate as initial preventer therapy in this age group
Confirm technique, adherence and trigger exposure before every step up
explanation.pearls: Reassess a child four to eight weeks after starting a preventer and consider stepping down once control has been maintained for at least three months, because the commonest cause of an apparently unresponsive preventer at that review is a spacer that is never actually used at school.

options.rationale: Reliever use on three or more days a week, night waking and exercise limitation together define poor symptom control, which is precisely the trigger for adding a preventer rather than for another period of observation. His technique has already been directly observed and is correct, so there is no remediable cause to review (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

Combination therapy is the next step up if symptoms persist despite regular low dose inhaled corticosteroid, not the entry point, and long-acting beta2 agonists are not recommended as initial preventer treatment in children of this age. Starting here also makes it impossible to know whether the corticosteroid alone would have sufficed (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a second line preventer in children, less effective than inhaled corticosteroid, and carries a Therapeutic Goods Administration warning about neuropsychiatric effects including sleep disturbance and behavioural change. It is reserved for children who cannot use an inhaled corticosteroid (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

Oral corticosteroids treat acute exacerbations over three days, and a fortnight of systemic steroid for stable interval symptoms exposes him to adrenal suppression and growth effects without altering the underlying airway inflammation. Nothing in the current examination indicates an exacerbation (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

Symptoms or reliever use on more than two days per week, any night waking due to asthma, or activity limitation each independently indicate poorly controlled asthma and warrant a regular preventer, and he meets all three. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is the first line preventer for a child of this age and is delivered through the spacer he is already using correctly (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant, or beyond twenty one days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin as the first investigation, and the single question that determines urgency is whether the conjugated fraction is raised. Unconjugated prolonged jaundice is usually breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, ongoing haemolysis, urinary tract infection or Gilbert syndrome, and is investigated at a routine pace. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in this age group means biliary atresia until proven otherwise, along with choledochal cyst, neonatal hepatitis, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and metabolic disease. Biliary atresia occurs in roughly one in fifteen to twenty thousand births and its outcome depends almost entirely on the age at Kasai portoenterostomy, with native liver survival substantially better when surgery occurs before 60 days. Because affected babies feed well and gain weight normally, well appearance is not reassuring.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term baby requires a split bilirubin
A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or 20 per cent of total is always pathological
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed biliary flow
Affected infants typically thrive, so good weight gain is not reassuring
Outcomes after portoenterostomy deteriorate sharply after 60 days of age
explanation.pearls: Ask the parents to photograph a dirty nappy on their phone rather than describing the colour, because acholic stools are often reported as normal by parents who have never seen a pigmented stool and the photograph resolves the ambiguity in seconds.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice

options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or above 20 per cent of the total is never physiological and never breast milk jaundice, and pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed biliary flow that must be investigated before the surgical window closes. Outcomes after portoenterostomy fall sharply once the infant passes 60 days of age, so the referral is measured in days rather than weeks (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

Breast milk jaundice is common at this age in a thriving baby but is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normally pigmented stools, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after the conjugated fraction is confirmed normal. Pale stools and a conjugated bilirubin of 62 micromol/L exclude it outright (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water soluble isomers and does nothing for a conjugated fraction, and in cholestasis it can additionally produce the bronze baby discolouration. Repeating the total alone also misses the fraction that carries the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

Congenital hypothyroidism and galactosaemia are part of the prolonged jaundice screen but both cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and her newborn screening was normal. A week of waiting on a time-critical surgical diagnosis is the harm here (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

Ultrasound forms part of the specialist workup and may show a small or absent gallbladder or the triangular cord sign, but a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis and a routine outpatient slot loses weeks. The investigations that matter are arranged by the receiving unit rather than sequentially in the community (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice

explanation.summary: Inguinal hernia in infancy is almost always indirect and results from failure of the processus vaginalis to obliterate, so it never resolves spontaneously and always requires operative repair. Incidence is around 1 to 5 per cent of term infants and rises to 10 to 30 per cent in those born preterm, with boys affected far more often than girls. The urgency comes from incarceration, which is commonest under one year of age and carries risks of bowel ischaemia, testicular infarction from compression of the cord vessels and, in girls, strangulation of an ovary within the sac. An incarcerated hernia that cannot be reduced needs immediate surgical attention, while one reduced successfully is usually repaired on that admission after a period of settling. The umbilical hernia is managed entirely differently, closing spontaneously in the great majority and only being repaired if it persists beyond about four to five years or complicates, which is very rare.
key_points: Infant inguinal hernia never closes spontaneously and always needs repair
Incarceration risk is highest under one year and higher again after preterm birth
The diagnosis is clinical and does not require imaging when the examination is typical
Umbilical hernias close spontaneously and are observed until about four to five years
Trusses and binders have no place in paediatric hernia management
explanation.pearls: A groin swelling above and lateral to the pubic tubercle that extends towards the scrotum is a hernia, whereas one that is confined to the scrotum, transilluminates and does not extend up the cord is a hydrocele, and only the first needs a surgical appointment within days.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Paediatric surgery referral guidelines

options.rationale: Spontaneous closure is the expected course for the umbilical swelling, which is why that one is observed to school age, but the groin swelling arises through a patent processus vaginalis that does not close and can trap bowel. The umbilical rule does not apply to the groin (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

The diagnosis is clinical when a reducible swelling appears with straining above and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and imaging is reserved for an equivocal examination or for distinguishing a hydrocele of the cord. Waiting for a scan adds days of incarceration risk without changing the plan (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

Incarceration risk is highest in the first months of life and higher again in infants born preterm, running at roughly 30 per cent in the first year for this age group, so repair is arranged promptly rather than electively. Reducibility today does not lower that risk, since incarceration is an unpredictable event rather than the endpoint of a gradual process (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

Routine listing is appropriate for an older child in whom incarceration risk has fallen substantially, but a 6-week-old born at 32 weeks sits in the highest risk group. An incarcerated hernia in this age group threatens both the bowel and the testis (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

Trusses and binders have no role in children, do not prevent incarceration and can cause skin breakdown and pressure injury to the cord structures. They also give false reassurance to parents who then delay presenting when the swelling becomes irreducible (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation is the commonest elbow injury in children under five and follows sudden axial traction on a pronated forearm, classically when a child is lifted or swung by the hand. The diagnosis rests on a typical mechanism with a completely normal examination apart from refusal to use the arm, and radiographs are unnecessary when that pattern is clear because reduction is both diagnostic and therapeutic. What makes the diagnosis unsafe is any swelling, bruising, deformity or bony point tenderness, or a mechanism involving a fall, since lateral condylar and supracondylar fractures present in the same age group with a similarly held arm. Lateral condylar fractures are Salter Harris type IV injuries that cross the articular surface, are frequently subtle on the anteroposterior view and progress to non union and cubitus valgus if missed. Documented neurovascular status before and after any manipulation is part of the record in every case.
key_points: Radial head subluxation shows no swelling, bruising or bony tenderness
Any swelling or point tenderness mandates radiographs before manipulation
A fall as part of the mechanism removes the classic history
Lateral condylar fractures are intra-articular and are easily missed on one view
Reduction is diagnostic and therapeutic only when the presentation is typical
explanation.pearls: After a successful reduction a child with radial head subluxation usually begins using the arm again within five to ten minutes, and continued refusal to use the arm at thirty minutes should prompt radiographs rather than a repeat manoeuvre.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

options.rationale: Reduction is appropriate for the classic presentation, which has a clear axial traction mechanism with no swelling and no bony tenderness, and manipulating an undiagnosed fracture risks displacing it. Swelling and focal tenderness over the lateral condyle are precisely the findings that remove this option (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

Radial head subluxation produces no swelling and no bony point tenderness, so their presence together with an added fall from a slide means a lateral condylar or supracondylar fracture must be excluded before any manipulation. Lateral condylar fractures are intra-articular, are easily missed on a single view and displace if managed as a pulled elbow (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

Deferring assessment for a week risks displacement of an undiagnosed intra-articular fracture, which converts a cast into an operation. Immobilisation without imaging also leaves both the diagnosis and the neurovascular monitoring plan undefined (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

options.rationale: This is the alternative reduction technique, differing from hyperpronation only in success rate and comfort, and it carries the same objection here because the examination does not fit radial head subluxation. Splinting afterwards would also mask the failure of a manoeuvre that should not have been attempted (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

Ultrasound can demonstrate an effusion but does not characterise the fracture line, its displacement or the involvement of the articular surface, all of which determine management. Plain films answer the question that has been raised (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

explanation.summary: Nappy rash is most often an irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and faeces, and it characteristically affects the convex surfaces of the buttocks, thighs and pubic area while sparing the depths of the skin creases. Secondary candidal infection is common after about three days of any nappy rash and is recognised by bright confluent erythema that fills the creases, satellite papules and pustules outside the main area, and often coexisting oral plaques. Bacterial infection, seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, scabies and, rarely, zinc deficiency or Langerhans cell histiocytosis are the other diagnoses to hold in mind, and a rash that is eroded, ulcerated or fails to respond to appropriate treatment should prompt reconsideration. Management always includes frequent nappy changes, nappy free time, gentle cleansing without soap and a barrier preparation, with a topical imidazole added when candidal features are present. Potent corticosteroids are avoided because the nappy acts as an occlusive dressing.
key_points: Irritant dermatitis spares the skin creases while candidal infection fills them
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash indicate candida
Topical imidazole under a barrier preparation is first line treatment
Potent topical steroids are avoided because the nappy occludes and enhances absorption
Oral plaques point to a coexisting oral infection needing separate treatment
explanation.pearls: Treat the mouth at the same time as the nappy area with oral miconazole gel or nystatin, because an untreated oral reservoir passes through the gut and reinfects the nappy area within days of stopping the topical cream.

options.rationale: Involvement of the skin creases with satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash, together with adherent oral plaques, indicates candidal infection rather than the irritant dermatitis that barrier cream treats. A topical imidazole applied at each change under the barrier cream is first line, with oral treatment added for the mouth (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

Potent corticosteroids are avoided in the nappy area because occlusion under a nappy greatly increases absorption, risking skin atrophy and adrenal suppression, and they worsen an untreated fungal infection. A short course of hydrocortisone 1 per cent is the only steroid used here, and only for stubborn inflammation alongside antifungal treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

Bacterial infection of the nappy area presents with pustules, honey coloured crusting, erosions or surrounding cellulitis, none of which is present, and satellite lesions with crease involvement point elsewhere. Oral antibiotics would also further disturb the flora that allows overgrowth (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

Barrier preparations treat irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the creases because urine and faeces do not reach them, and three weeks of adequate use has already failed. Persisting adds another fortnight of discomfort without addressing the organism (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

Systemic antifungal treatment is reserved for extensive, recurrent or immunocompromised disease because topical treatment clears uncomplicated candidal nappy dermatitis, and a single dose would in any case not cover the treatment period needed. It differs from the preferred option mainly in exposing him to systemic drug effects for no added benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Abnormal head shape in infancy is usually positional in origin and follows the rise in supine sleeping, producing a flattened occiput with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced forward, giving a parallelogram when viewed from above. Craniosynostosis is far less common at about one in two thousand births and produces a characteristic shape determined by which suture has fused, with growth restricted perpendicular to the fused suture and compensatory growth parallel to it. Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single suture form and produces a long narrow skull with frontal bossing and occipital pointing, with symmetrical ear position and often a palpable ridge. Head circumference is typically normal in single suture disease because compensatory growth preserves volume, so a normal measurement is not reassuring. Multi suture and syndromic forms, including Apert and Crouzon syndromes, carry a much higher risk of raised intracranial pressure and are managed in specialist craniofacial units.
key_points: Positional moulding gives a parallelogram with the ear displaced forward on the flat side
Synostosis gives a shape determined by which suture is fused, with symmetrical ears
A palpable ridge over a suture is a key discriminating sign
Head circumference is usually normal in single suture synostosis
Endoscopic correction is generally limited to infants under about six months of age
explanation.pearls: Look at the head from directly above rather than from the front, because the parallelogram of positional moulding and the elongated boat shape of sagittal synostosis are almost indistinguishable face to face and unmistakable from the vertex view.

options.rationale: Repositioning treats deformation from external pressure, which produces a parallelogram shaped head with the ear and forehead on the flattened side pushed forward, and it cannot alter a skull constrained by a fused suture. A further three months also passes through the period of most rapid brain growth when surgical correction is most effective (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

A boat shaped skull that is long and narrow with a palpable midline ridge and symmetrical ears indicates premature fusion of the sagittal suture rather than positional moulding, and the diagnosis is confirmed and managed in a specialist unit. Referral is time critical because minimally invasive endoscopic techniques are generally restricted to infants under about six months, after which open cranial vault remodelling is required (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

Helmet therapy reshapes a skull whose sutures are all open by directing growth away from the prominent areas, and it has no capacity to release a fused suture. It differs from the correct option in treating the shape rather than the constraint that produces it (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

A palpable ridge over a suture with a skull shape that has not responded to repositioning is not a normal variant, and untreated single suture fusion can lead to raised intracranial pressure in a minority as well as a permanent cosmetic deformity. A normal head circumference is expected because compensatory growth occurs along the unfused sutures (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

Ultrasound through the fontanelle images the brain rather than defining suture fusion and would delay referral without changing the answer. Where imaging is used it is a low dose computed tomogram with three dimensional reconstruction, arranged by the receiving unit (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Craniosynostosis).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow's milk intake is its leading cause, through three separate mechanisms: displacement of iron rich foods, inhibition of absorption by calcium and casein, and occult intestinal blood loss from a milk induced enteropathy. The recommendation is to cap cow's milk at about 500 mL per day from twelve months and to avoid bottles at bedtime. The blood picture is a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a raised red cell distribution width, often a reactive thrombocytosis, and a low ferritin, though ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant so a concurrent C reactive protein is needed to interpret it. Differentials are thalassaemia trait, which has a normal ferritin and a normal red cell distribution width, lead exposure, and coeliac disease. Treatment is oral elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg per kilogram daily continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises, and failure to respond within a month usually means poor adherence, continued milk intake or an unrecognised cause of loss.
key_points: Cow's milk above about 500 mL a day is the leading cause in Australian toddlers
A low ferritin with a normal C reactive protein confirms iron deficiency
Thalassaemia trait has a normal ferritin and a normal red cell distribution width
Oral iron continues for three months after the haemoglobin normalises
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or cardiac failure
explanation.pearls: Expect the reticulocyte count to rise within three to five days and the haemoglobin to climb by around 10 g/L per fortnight, so a repeat count at four weeks that has not moved points to adherence, ongoing milk intake or the wrong diagnosis rather than to a need for a higher dose.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, cardiac failure or a haemoglobin below about 60 to 70 g/L with symptoms, and a child who is walking about with a compensated chronic anaemia does not qualify. Transfusing also carries the risk of circulatory overload in slowly developed anaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

Intravenous iron is reserved for children who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron, or who have ongoing losses outpacing replacement, and it requires a day procedure with a small risk of hypersensitivity. Nothing here suggests oral therapy will fail (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

Thalassaemia trait shares microcytosis with this picture but is distinguished by a normal or high ferritin, a normal red cell distribution width and a red cell count that is high for the haemoglobin. A ferritin of 6 mcg/L with a normal C reactive protein already establishes iron deficiency, and electrophoresis performed while iron deplete can also falsely lower the haemoglobin A2 fraction (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

Excessive cow's milk is the classic Australian cause in this age group, displacing iron rich foods, providing calcium and casein that inhibit iron absorption, and causing occult gut blood loss, so replacement fails unless the intake is capped. Oral elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg per kilogram daily with dietary change corrects the deficiency and is continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises to refill stores (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

Endoscopy is indicated when there is overt bleeding, growth failure, gastrointestinal symptoms or failure to respond to adequate oral iron, and he has normal stools, normal growth and negative coeliac serology. An anaesthetic and endoscopy before a trial of treatment inverts the sequence (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

explanation.summary: Toe walking is common in early childhood and is usually idiopathic, but the label can only be applied after a neurological examination that is entirely normal and where the child can walk with heels down when asked. The differential includes cerebral palsy with spastic diplegia, tethered cord, hereditary spastic paraplegia, autism spectrum disorder and neuromuscular disease, of which Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most time critical to identify. Boys with a dystrophinopathy present between two and five years with delayed walking, difficulty running and climbing stairs, calf pseudohypertrophy from fatty and fibrous replacement, and a positive Gower manoeuvre, and around a third have associated cognitive or language delay. Serum creatine kinase is the screening test, followed by genetic testing for dystrophin gene deletions, duplications and point mutations. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids started before significant decline prolong ambulation, and because cardiac and respiratory surveillance and genetic counselling for the family follow immediately.
key_points: Idiopathic toe walking requires a normal neurological examination and the ability to walk flat footed on request
Calf hypertrophy with proximal weakness points to a dystrophinopathy
The Gower manoeuvre demonstrates proximal weakness at the bedside
Creatine kinase is the screening test and is grossly elevated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Surgical or casting treatment before diagnosis can worsen function
explanation.pearls: Ask any boy who toe walks to stand up from sitting on the floor without using furniture, because the Gower manoeuvre takes ten seconds to elicit and converts a routine gait referral into a creatine kinase request that will usually come back above 10000 U/L.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: Serial casting treats a fixed contracture in idiopathic toe walking, which requires a normal neurological examination and no proximal weakness. Immobilising the legs of a boy with an untreated myopathy accelerates the loss of ambulation (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

Surgical lengthening treats the ankle contracture and not the weakness underneath it, and operating before the underlying diagnosis is known risks a significant functional deterioration in a child whose toe walking is compensating for weak hip and knee extensors. It differs from casting only in being irreversible (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

Toe walking with calf hypertrophy, proximal weakness demonstrated by climbing up his own legs to stand, and mild speech delay points to a dystrophinopathy, in which the creatine kinase is typically ten to a hundred times the upper limit of normal and is the cheapest and fastest screening test available. Australian mean age at diagnosis remains close to five years, and the delay is almost always because toe walking was labelled idiopathic (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

Stretching and physiotherapy form part of long term management of many causes of toe walking, but referring without a diagnosis defers the question for another six months in a boy who already has proximal weakness. A gait that has never normalised with weakness on standing is not the pattern that resolves with stretching (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

Cerebral imaging is directed at a spastic diplegia from an upper motor neurone cause, which would show increased tone, brisk reflexes and upgoing plantar responses rather than the normal tone and reflexes present here. Spinal imaging would be the relevant study if a tethered cord were suspected, which would produce back or bladder signs (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas are usually absent or minimally visible at birth, proliferate rapidly through the first three to five months, plateau, and then involute slowly over several years, which distinguishes them from vascular malformations that are present at birth and grow with the child. Most need no treatment, but a minority require systemic therapy because of their site or complications, and the window for intervention is narrow because treatment works best during proliferation. Indications for oral propranolol are obstruction of vision, the airway or the ear canal, ulceration, high output cardiac failure and lesions likely to cause permanent disfigurement, particularly on the central face. Risk factors include prematurity, low birth weight, female sex and multiple gestation, and five or more cutaneous lesions prompt abdominal ultrasound for hepatic involvement. Segmental facial lesions raise the possibility of PHACE syndrome and warrant cardiac, cerebral and ophthalmological assessment before propranolol is started.
key_points: Proliferation occurs over the first three to five months, so treatment decisions are time critical
Obstruction of the visual axis is an indication for systemic treatment
Oral propranolol is first line, started after cardiovascular assessment
Topical timolol and laser reach only superficial lesions
Five or more cutaneous lesions prompt ultrasound for liver involvement
explanation.pearls: Any periocular haemangioma large enough to touch the eyelid margin needs ophthalmology review even if the pupil looks uncovered, because pressure on the globe induces astigmatism and amblyopia without ever obstructing the visual axis.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for the majority of these lesions, which involute over several years without treatment, but a lesion obstructing the visual axis during the critical period of visual development causes deprivation amblyopia and astigmatism from pressure on the globe. Vision lost in the first year is not recovered when the lesion later involutes (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

Topical beta blocker is effective for thin superficial lesions of a few millimetres depth and is a reasonable choice where there is no functional threat. It penetrates poorly into a 22 mm lesion with a deep component and is too slow for a sight threatening problem (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

Surgery during the proliferative phase risks significant bleeding and a worse cosmetic outcome than the scar that follows involution, and it is reserved for residual fibrofatty tissue after involution or for lesions that fail medical treatment. Medical treatment shrinks the lesion faster and without a scar (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

Pulsed dye laser penetrates only about a millimetre and is used for ulcerated lesions and for residual telangiectasia after involution, not for a bulky proliferating lesion. It differs from topical treatment mainly in mechanism, sharing the same problem of reaching only the surface (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

Obstruction of the visual axis is one of the accepted indications for systemic treatment, alongside ulceration, airway involvement, disfigurement and high output cardiac failure, and oral propranolol produces measurable shrinkage within days to weeks. It is started after cardiovascular assessment with monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, ideally before the proliferative phase ends at around five months (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

explanation.summary: Head circumference is plotted at every infant health check precisely so that a change in trajectory is detected before the clinical signs of raised pressure appear, and crossing centile lines is far more significant than any single large measurement. Benign familial macrocephaly and benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces are the common benign causes and both feature a well infant with normal development, a soft fontanelle and growth along a parallel line, usually with a large parent. The findings that indicate raised intracranial pressure in an infant are a tense fontanelle when upright and settled, distended scalp veins, sunsetting eyes from pressure on the dorsal midbrain, irritability, vomiting, developmental regression and a high pitched cry. Causes include obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus, intracranial mass, chronic subdural collections including from abusive head trauma, and venous sinus thrombosis. Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle is the fastest first study in an infant, with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging following as directed by the neurosurgical team.
key_points: Crossing head circumference centiles matters more than a single large measurement
A tense fontanelle when upright and settled indicates raised pressure
Sunsetting eyes reflect pressure on the dorsal midbrain
Loss of previously acquired skills is regression and is never benign
Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle is the fastest first investigation
explanation.pearls: Always plot the parents' head circumferences before accepting benign familial macrocephaly, since the diagnosis requires a large parent as well as a well infant, and a normal sized parent converts a reassuring measurement into one that needs explaining.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Raised intracranial pressure

options.rationale: Benign familial macrocephaly runs along a large but parallel centile line in a well infant with a large parent, whereas this head has crossed three centile lines in three months in a child with a tense fontanelle, vomiting and lost skills. His father's head circumference on the 50th centile removes the familial explanation entirely (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

Rapid centile crossing with a tense fontanelle when upright, distended scalp veins, downward eye deviation and developmental regression is progressive raised intracranial pressure, and imaging with immediate neurosurgical involvement is required because untreated hydrocephalus causes irreversible visual and cognitive loss. Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle can be obtained within minutes as the first study while the referral is made (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

Abusive head trauma is an important cause of rapid head growth in infancy, but it is argued against here by the absence of bruising and of retinal haemorrhages, and by the gradual centile crossing with preserved growth elsewhere. Investigating that possibility first would delay imaging in a child with active signs of raised pressure (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

Magnetic resonance imaging gives the best anatomical detail and will be needed, but obtaining it as an outpatient in an infant who requires sedation takes weeks, and the pressure is rising now. It differs from the correct option only in timing, and timing is the whole question (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

Serial measurement is the right approach to isolated macrocephaly in a thriving infant with a soft fontanelle and normal development, none of which describes this child. Another four weeks of untreated raised pressure risks permanent optic atrophy (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate until around five months and then involute slowly over years, so most need nothing beyond explanation and review. Treatment is indicated when the lesion threatens function or life, when it ulcerates, or when it will leave significant disfigurement, and a periocular lesion obscuring the visual axis is among the clearest functional indications because deprivation amblyopia develops quickly at this age. Oral propranolol is the first line systemic therapy and produces rapid shrinkage during the proliferative phase, given after cardiovascular assessment and with feeding and hypoglycaemia advice for parents. Imaging is reserved for large segmental facial lesions or airway concern, and topical timolol is limited to small superficial lesions in non-critical sites.
key_points: Proliferation continues until about five months, which is the window where treatment works fastest
Functional threat, ulceration and disfigurement are the indications for treatment
A periocular lesion touching the visual axis risks deprivation amblyopia within weeks
Oral propranolol is first line; topical timolol suits only small superficial lesions
explanation.pearls: Ask where the haemangioma is before deciding whether it can be left alone: eyelid, nasal tip, lip, airway and perineal lesions all need same-week referral, and for one touching the visual axis oral propranolol plus ophthalmology review is urgent rather than something to revisit at the next immunisation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Infantile haemangioma

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for most of these lesions because the great majority involute without treatment, but one that obscures the visual axis can cause deprivation amblyopia within weeks at this age. Waiting until 12 months risks permanent visual loss on that side. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Topical beta blockade is useful for small superficial lesions in non-critical sites, but penetration is insufficient for a deep or bulky lesion and absorption near the eye is a further concern. It will not shrink a periocular lesion quickly enough to protect vision. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Periocular location with interference in the visual axis is one of the standard indications for systemic treatment, and oral propranolol produces visible shrinkage within days to weeks during the proliferative phase that continues to around five months. Referral includes pre-treatment cardiovascular assessment and ophthalmology involvement for amblyopia management. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Imaging is indicated for large segmental facial lesions, where associated structural anomalies of the posterior fossa, arteries, eye and sternum must be sought, or for lesions with functional airway concern. A solitary localised eyelid lesion with no other findings does not require it before treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Pulsed dye laser has a role for ulcerated lesions and for residual telangiectasia after involution, but it treats only the superficial component and does not debulk a proliferating lesion. It cannot clear the visual axis within the window that matters. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

explanation.summary: Reflex anoxic episodes are vagally mediated asystolic events in young children, triggered by a sudden fright, minor injury or unexpected pain, in which the child goes pale before losing consciousness. Brief stiffening or a few jerks from cerebral hypoxia are common and often lead to a mistaken diagnosis of epilepsy, but the sequence of trigger, then pallor, then collapse, with rapid full recovery and no postictal phase, distinguishes them. Iron deficiency is a recognised and correctable precipitant, so a full blood count and ferritin are worth checking, and an electrocardiogram is reasonable to exclude a long QT interval. Management is explanation, iron repletion when deficient, and first aid advice to lay the child flat and let the episode terminate on its own.
key_points: Pallor before the collapse, with an identifiable trigger, separates this from an epileptic seizure
Brief stiffening or jerks are hypoxic and do not indicate epilepsy
Iron deficiency is a correctable precipitant and repletion reduces episode frequency
An electrocardiogram excludes a long QT interval; further cardiac testing is rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent what colour the child went and in what order things happened: pallor that precedes the collapse after a bump or a fright is a reflex anoxic episode, and the treatment is explanation plus iron repletion if the ferritin is low, not an antiseizure medicine.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.rationale: Reflex anoxic episodes triggered by fright or minor pain, with pallor preceding collapse and rapid recovery, are benign vagally mediated events and iron deficiency is a recognised precipitant whose correction reduces their frequency. Parents need an explanation of the mechanism plus practical advice to lie the child flat and not to shake or resuscitate, since the child recovers spontaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.rationale: An antiseizure medicine is indicated for epileptic seizures, which are not preceded by pallor triggered by a fright and are usually followed by a postictal period rather than immediate normal behaviour. Treating these episodes as epilepsy exposes him to a hepatotoxic and teratogenic drug for a benign condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.rationale: An inherited arrhythmia would be suggested by episodes during exertion or swimming, a family history of sudden death, or an abnormal electrocardiogram, none of which are present with normal intervals on his tracing. Invasive electrophysiology is far beyond what a classical trigger-and-pallor history requires. (Source: RCH CPG: Syncope)

Prolonged monitoring is useful when episodes are frequent and the diagnosis genuinely remains uncertain after a careful history. Here the trigger, the pallor before collapse and the immediate recovery make the diagnosis clinically, and events triggered by fright are unlikely to occur on demand in hospital. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.rationale: Avoidance is impossible to sustain and drives restrictive parenting that harms the child's development more than the episodes themselves. Explanation with first aid advice achieves far more than attempts to eliminate every trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

explanation.summary: Midline fusion of the labia minora is common in the low oestrogen years between infancy and puberty and is usually discovered incidentally by a parent. The decision point is whether the adhesion is obstructing: a single forward stream, continence and no history of urinary infection all indicate that it is not. Asymptomatic adhesions are managed with explanation and vulval care alone, since the great majority separate spontaneously and any treatment carries a high recurrence rate before puberty. Topical oestrogen, and rarely surgical separation, are reserved for obstruction, recurrent urinary infection or persistent symptoms.
key_points: Asymptomatic labial adhesions need explanation and vulval care, not treatment
Urinary stream, continence and infection history determine whether the adhesion is obstructive
Topical oestrogen is reserved for symptomatic or obstructive adhesions and recurs commonly before puberty
White thickened plaques with fissuring and bruising point to lichen sclerosus rather than simple adhesions
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to describe the urinary stream before deciding anything about labial adhesions: a single forward stream with no post-void dribbling and no previous urinary tract infection means the adhesion is non-obstructive, and the correct plan is explanation plus soap-free vulval care with review only if symptoms appear, not a six week course of oestrogen cream.

options.rationale: Surgical separation is reserved for adhesions causing urinary obstruction, recurrent infection or symptoms that persist after topical treatment, and it carries a high recurrence rate until oestrogen levels rise at puberty. Operating on an asymptomatic girl with a patent anterior opening exposes her to anaesthesia with nothing to gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

A potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for vulval lichen sclerosus, which presents with thickened white plaques, fissuring, itch and bruise-like haemorrhage, none of which are described here. Applying it to normal vulval skin risks atrophy without addressing the fused membrane. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

Topical oestrogen does separate adhesions, but it is used for girls with obstructive symptoms, recurrent urinary infection or persistent local discomfort, and it commonly causes local pigmentation and occasionally breast budding. Starting it in an asymptomatic girl treats the parents' anxiety rather than the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Labial adhesions are an ordinary consequence of the low oestrogen state of childhood combined with local irritation, and they are not a marker of abuse; bruising, tears, bleeding or an abnormal disclosure would be. A notification made on this finding alone would be both distressing and unfounded. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Adhesions that do not obstruct urine flow need no active treatment because almost all separate spontaneously as oestrogen rises around puberty, and many resolve earlier. Explaining the mechanism, advising against soap and bubble bath, and naming the symptoms that would warrant review is complete management. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

explanation.summary: Profuse repetitive vomiting one to four hours after a food, with pallor, lethargy and hypotension but no urticaria, angioedema or respiratory signs, is the signature of food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome. Rice, oats, cow milk and egg are the usual triggers in Australian infants, and the reaction is cell mediated, so skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are typically negative and adrenaline has little role. The shock is hypovolaemic from fluid sequestration in the gut, and treatment is rapid isotonic fluid replacement with ondansetron. A previous milder episode after the same food is the historical clue that converts a presumed gastroenteritis into a recognised syndrome.
key_points: Delayed onset of one to four hours with no skin or respiratory features separates this from anaphylaxis
Treatment is 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses plus ondansetron, repeated to restore perfusion
Skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative because the mechanism is cell mediated
A repeat episode after the same food is the clue that the first was not gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: Ask what the infant ate two to four hours before the vomiting started, and whether the same food preceded a previous episode. Repetitive vomiting with pallor and shock but a normal skin and chest, twice after the same grain, is food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome: give 20 mL/kg saline boluses and ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg, not intramuscular adrenaline, and refer to a paediatric allergy service for a supervised food challenge rather than an adrenaline autoinjector.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome
ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis
RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is the treatment for immunoglobulin E mediated anaphylaxis, which is defined by acute skin or mucosal change with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise, typically within minutes of exposure. The two hour delay, quiet chest and entirely normal skin place this outside that pathway even though the child is shocked. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: This presentation is cell mediated rather than antibody mediated, and the shock comes from massive fluid shift into the gut, so the treatment is aggressive volume replacement with an antiemetic to break the vomiting cycle. Boluses are repeated until perfusion is restored, and most infants improve within hours without any adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.rationale: Sepsis is the reasonable default for a shocked lethargic infant, but the child is afebrile, the illness began abruptly two hours after a specific food, and an identical milder episode followed the only previous exposure to that food. Antibiotics can be added if the course deviates, but they do not explain a twice-repeated food-locked pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Oral rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration in gastroenteritis, but this infant is shocked with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and is vomiting repeatedly, so the oral route will fail. Shock requires intravenous or intraosseous volume regardless of the underlying trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Corticosteroids and antihistamines treat neither the volume depletion nor the underlying mechanism, and antihistamines are ineffective because histamine release is not the driver of this reaction. Relying on them would leave a shocked infant without the fluid that actually reverses the process. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

explanation.summary: Chronic lead exposure in Australian children clusters around smelter towns such as Port Pirie, Broken Hill and Mount Isa, and around disturbed pre-1970 lead paint during renovation. The presentation is deliberately non-specific: colicky abdominal pain, constipation, irritability and loss of language milestones, with a microcytic anaemia that is worsened by coexisting iron deficiency because low iron increases lead absorption. Basophilic stippling is suggestive but neither sensitive nor specific, so the diagnosis rests on a venous blood lead level. Management is source removal and iron repletion, with chelation reserved for high levels or encephalopathy, and notification thresholds follow the national guidance.
key_points: Ask about smelter towns, pre-1970 housing and recent renovation in any child with unexplained regression
Iron deficiency increases gut absorption of lead, so the two commonly coexist and each worsens the other
A venous sample is required because capillary samples are contaminated by skin lead
Source removal and iron repletion come first, with chelation reserved for very high levels or encephalopathy
