explanation.pearls: In an Australian toddler with a microcytic anaemia and lost words, the exposure history is the test-selector: a house built before 1970 that has been sanded or stripped, or an address in a smelter town, should trigger a venous blood lead level, and a level at or above 5 micrograms per decilitre is the national threshold for investigating and removing the source rather than simply treating the iron deficiency.

sources.label: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health

options.rationale: Residence near a smelter, a renovated pre-1970 house, a history of putting things in the mouth at this age, developmental regression, abdominal pain and a microcytic anaemia with stippled red cells together make lead the unifying explanation, and a venous level is the test that confirms it. Capillary samples are prone to skin contamination and a raised result on a finger prick still requires venous confirmation. (Source: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health)
source_refs: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health

options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when an anaemia is accompanied by abnormal white cells or platelets, blasts on the film, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain, and all of those are absent here. An isolated microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin is a peripheral problem, not a marrow one. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Neuroblastoma can present with irritability, anaemia and loss of milestones, but it almost always produces a mass, bone pain, periorbital bruising or hepatomegaly, none of which are found. The environmental history and basophilic stippling point away from malignancy. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

Electrophoresis is the right test when a microcytosis is disproportionate to the anaemia and iron stores are normal, whereas this child's ferritin of 9 micrograms/L already shows genuine iron deficiency. Neither result would account for the language regression or the stippled film. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Coeliac disease is a fair explanation for iron deficiency with abdominal pain, but it does not cause loss of acquired speech, and it produces loose stools or faltering growth rather than constipation with centile-stable growth. It remains a reasonable second line test if lead is not the answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

explanation.summary: Scalp dermatophyte infection is distinguished from other scaly scalp conditions by hairs broken close to the skin and by regional lymphadenopathy, which are absent in psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis. Because the organism lives within the hair shaft, topical antifungals cannot cure it, and six weeks of a topical cream that has failed is itself part of the pattern. Oral therapy with griseofulvin or terbinafine is started on clinical grounds while culture is pending, with an antifungal shampoo added to reduce shedding and household spread. Untreated infection can progress to a boggy inflammatory mass with permanent scarring alopecia.
key_points: Hairs broken at the scalp surface plus occipital lymph nodes are the clinical signature of scalp dermatophytosis
Topical antifungals fail because the organism is inside the hair shaft
Start oral therapy on clinical grounds; culture refines the agent and duration later
Antifungal shampoo is an adjunct to reduce spore shedding, never the sole treatment
explanation.pearls: Feel for occipital nodes whenever you assess a scaly scalp in a child: their presence alongside hairs broken a few millimetres above the skin makes dermatophyte infection likely enough to start oral griseofulvin the same day, typically for six to eight weeks and given with a fatty meal, rather than waiting the three to four weeks that culture takes.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Fungal infection of the scalp involves the hair shaft and follicle, which topical agents cannot penetrate, so oral therapy is required and treatment is started before culture returns when the clinical picture is characteristic. Griseofulvin with a fatty meal to aid absorption remains a standard first line oral agent for this infection in children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

Antifungal shampoo reduces surface spore shedding and is a useful adjunct that limits spread to classmates and siblings, but it does not reach the fungus inside the hair shaft and will not cure the infection. Using it alone repeats the error of the last six weeks with a different bottle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

Antibiotics would be needed for a boggy pustular inflammatory mass with secondary bacterial infection, but there is no fluctuance, no pus and no systemic upset here. Treating a dermatophyte with cefalexin lets the scarring alopecia progress untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: A corticosteroid would be the treatment if this were scalp psoriasis or discoid eczema, but those do not break hairs off at the scalp or produce regional lymphadenopathy. Steroid applied to an untreated dermatophyte suppresses the inflammation while the fungus spreads. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

Culture takes up to four weeks and guides the choice of agent and duration, but withholding treatment during that wait allows further hair loss and ongoing transmission. Australian practice is to treat on the clinical picture and adjust once the organism is known, and exclusion from school is not required once treatment has begun. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

explanation.summary: Crusted scabies is the hyperinfested form seen in immune suppression, and itch is minimal or absent, so the appearance is mistaken for eczema or psoriasis. Thick fissured plaques on palms, soles and scalp in a child on prednisolone, with classic burrow rash in other household members, is the recognisable pattern. Because the crust shelters an extremely high mite burden, single-agent treatment fails: the regimen combines a keratolytic to soften scale, topical permethrin, and repeated doses of oral ivermectin, with simultaneous treatment of all contacts. In northern and central Australia this is also a public health matter, since the associated streptococcal skin infection drives acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and acute rheumatic fever.
key_points: Minimal itch does not exclude scabies and is characteristic of the crusted form
Thick crusts shelter mites from topical agents, so keratolytic softening is part of treatment
Repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide is the standard combination for crusted disease
Treat every household contact at the same time or reinfestation is immediate
explanation.pearls: When a child on immunosuppression has thick crusted plaques and does not scratch, ask what rash the other children in the house have: classic finger web itch in contacts alongside minimal itch in the index case is crusted scabies, and it needs a keratolytic plus topical permethrin plus a multi-dose oral ivermectin schedule with same-day treatment of the whole household.

sources.label: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections

options.rationale: Two doses is the regimen for ordinary scabies, but a heavily crusted infestation carries millions of mites and requires multiple ivermectin doses combined with a topical agent and keratolytic therapy. Treating only the index child also leaves the household reservoir untouched. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies)

Permethrin alone cannot penetrate crusts that are millimetres thick, so mites survive in the deeper layers and the child relapses. It remains part of the regimen, but only alongside keratolytic softening and repeated oral ivermectin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Scabies)

Crusted infestation is treated as a combination protocol because the crust shelters an enormous mite burden: a keratolytic such as urea or salicylic acid softens the scale, topical scabicide is applied to the softened skin, and oral ivermectin is repeated on a schedule determined by severity. Simultaneous treatment of every household contact prevents the immediate reinfestation that otherwise follows. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies)

Antibiotics are added when there is impetigo or cellulitis complicating the infestation, and that matters in this setting because of the risk of subsequent acute rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. There is no pus or cellulitis described, and antibiotics do nothing about the mite burden. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections)
source_refs: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections

options.rationale: Immune suppression is the reason the infestation became crusted and the steroid dose should be reviewed with her nephrology team, but abrupt cessation risks adrenal insufficiency and relapse of the underlying renal disease. The infestation is treated now, not after a week of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

explanation.summary: Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis is the commonest periodic fever syndrome of early childhood and is defined clinically by its regularity. The three features that make the diagnosis are clockwork recurrence, complete wellness between episodes, and entirely normal growth. Negative throat swabs and a normal interval blood count exclude the alternatives that would otherwise need treatment. A single dose of prednisolone at fever onset usually aborts the attack within hours, which both treats the episode and confirms the diagnosis, although families should be warned that episodes may then recur sooner.
key_points: Calendar regularity with complete wellness between episodes is the diagnostic hallmark
Normal growth and a normal interval blood count argue against malignancy and immunodeficiency
A single dose of prednisolone at fever onset usually aborts the episode within hours
Steroid may shorten the interval between attacks; tonsillectomy is a later option for disabling disease
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to bring the calendar or phone diary: fevers that fall every three to six weeks to the day, each lasting three to five days with mouth ulcers and a sore throat, with a completely well child in between and a normal growth chart, is periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and adenitis, and a single prednisolone dose at onset that aborts the fever within hours seals the diagnosis without any genetic test.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis

options.rationale: Penicillin treats streptococcal pharyngitis, which would produce positive swabs and a course that does not recur on a monthly timetable. Repeated antibiotic courses for this pattern expose the child without altering the interval. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis

options.rationale: Monogenic periodic fever syndromes are considered when episodes involve serositis, rash, arthritis or amyloidosis, or when there is a suggestive ethnic and family history, and their attacks are not calendar-regular. Testing is reasonable if the course deviates, but it should not delay a therapeutic step that is also diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

Malignancy is the concern behind recurrent fever, but it produces progressive illness, faltering growth, cytopenias or organomegaly rather than eight months of complete wellness between identical four-day episodes. Invasive investigation is not justified by this pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Fever without focus)

A single corticosteroid dose given as the fever starts typically aborts the episode within hours in this syndrome, which makes it both the treatment and a strong diagnostic confirmation. Families are counselled that steroid may shorten the interval between episodes, and that the condition is self-limiting over years with normal growth throughout. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

Tonsillectomy does resolve this syndrome in many children and is a recognised option, but it is a second line consideration for frequent disabling episodes after the diagnosis has been established and the natural resolution explained. Proceeding to surgery before a steroid trial skips the least invasive confirmatory step. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

explanation.summary: Protection of infants against respiratory syncytial virus in their first winter now runs along two alternative routes: maternal vaccination in the third trimester, or a long-acting monoclonal antibody given directly to the infant. When the mother was not vaccinated during pregnancy the infant route applies, and nirsevimab is given as a single dose before or early in the season to cover roughly five months. Preterm birth increases the risk of severe bronchiolitis and strengthens the indication, while immunisation itself follows chronological rather than corrected age. Influenza vaccine remains part of the winter plan from 6 months of age, with household cocooning until then.
key_points: Either maternal third trimester vaccination or infant monoclonal antibody protects the first season, not both routes by default
Maternal vaccine given after delivery does not protect the infant, since the mechanism is transplacental antibody
Scheduled vaccines for preterm infants follow chronological age, not corrected age
Influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, with two doses in the first year of vaccination
explanation.pearls: For any infant facing their first winter, ask one question first: did the mother receive a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine in the third trimester? If not, the infant needs a single dose of nirsevimab before or early in the season, and the dose is scheduled by chronological age even in a baby born at 32 weeks.

sources.label: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus
Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants

options.rationale: Monthly injections are burdensome and this product has largely been replaced in Australian programs by a single dose long-acting monoclonal antibody covering a whole season. Monthly dosing also restricted eligibility to the most severe chronic lung and cardiac disease, which this infant does not have. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.rationale: Protection against respiratory syncytial virus in the first season comes either from maternal vaccination in pregnancy or from a long-acting monoclonal antibody given to the infant, and this mother received neither, so the infant needs the antibody. A single dose before or early in the season covers approximately five months, and prematurity places him in the group that benefits most. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.rationale: Influenza vaccine is recommended from 6 months of age, with two doses in the first year of vaccination, so it is a real part of this family's winter plan but cannot be given at 3 months. Cocooning by vaccinating the household is the interim measure at this age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Influenza)

Correcting for prematurity is right for developmental milestones but wrong for immunisation, which follows chronological age, and deferral would leave him unprotected through the very season in question. Preterm infants are at higher risk of severe bronchiolitis, not lower. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants

options.rationale: Maternal vaccination works by transferring antibody across the placenta in the third trimester, so giving it after birth does not protect an infant already born. Breast milk carries some protection but not the specific antibody titre this strategy relies on. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Hip displacement in cerebral palsy is progressive, painless in its early stages, and closely related to gross motor function, which is why Australian practice uses scheduled radiographic surveillance rather than waiting for symptoms. The measurement that drives decisions is the migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to the lateral margin of the acetabulum. Referral to orthopaedics is triggered by a migration percentage above 30 per cent or a rise of more than 10 percentage points between annual films, and this child meets both. Tone management with baclofen or botulinum toxin supports comfort and care but does not reverse established displacement.
key_points: Surveillance frequency is set by gross motor function level, and non-ambulant children carry the highest risk
Migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral even in a pain free child
A rise of more than 10 percentage points in a year is itself a referral trigger
Tone reduction improves comfort and care but does not prevent progressive displacement
explanation.pearls: Compare the migration percentage with the previous film rather than reading it in isolation: in a non-ambulant child with cerebral palsy, either crossing 30 per cent or gaining more than 10 percentage points in a year warrants orthopaedic referral that day, because these hips are painless until they are already subluxed.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Annual imaging is the correct interval for a stable hip in a child at this functional level, but a migration percentage that has risen by 14 points in a year and crossed 30 per cent has already breached the threshold for referral. Continuing to watch risks silent progression to dislocation and later pain. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Tone reduction is a useful adjunct that can improve comfort and ease of care, but no medical therapy reverses established femoral head displacement. Relying on baclofen would let the migration percentage keep climbing while the window for simpler surgery closes. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Displacement in this population is characteristically painless until the hip is subluxed or dislocated, which is precisely why radiographic surveillance exists rather than symptom-triggered imaging. Waiting for pain means intervening after the deformity is established. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent, or a rise of more than 10 percentage points in a year, is the trigger for orthopaedic referral regardless of symptoms, and both criteria are met here. Early referral allows soft tissue surgery or preventive reconstruction before the head displaces far enough to require salvage procedures. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Botulinum toxin can improve adductor tone and sitting comfort and may be used alongside surgical planning, but it has not been shown to prevent progressive displacement on its own. Offering it as the definitive answer substitutes a temporary tone measure for the structural assessment the imaging demands. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

explanation.summary: Painless discharge through a perforation persisting beyond six weeks defines chronic suppurative otitis media, which carries a high burden in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and is a leading cause of preventable childhood hearing loss in Australia. The treatment that changes outcomes is mechanical: dry mopping the canal so that topical antibiotic actually reaches the middle ear, using a quinolone because aminoglycoside drops risk cochlear toxicity through an open drum. Systemic antibiotics have a limited role unless there are signs of complication such as mastoiditis or facial palsy. Audiology referral is an essential part of the plan, since the conductive loss affects language and schooling and may need amplification or classroom sound field support.
key_points: Discharge through a perforation beyond six weeks is chronic, not acute, otitis media
Dry mopping before drops is what allows topical therapy to reach the middle ear
Use quinolone drops rather than aminoglycoside preparations when the drum is perforated
Every child with chronic discharge needs audiology and educational support, not antibiotics alone
explanation.pearls: Treat the hearing as seriously as the discharge: a child with a chronically discharging ear who does not answer when called across a classroom needs formal audiology and school based amplification alongside dry mopping and ciprofloxacin drops, because the conductive loss rather than the infection is what costs them their reading.

sources.label: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin is the treatment for acute otitis media with an intact drum and systemic symptoms, a picture that includes pain and fever rather than three painless months of discharge. Once a perforation is chronically discharging, oral therapy alone rarely dries the ear because the biofilm sits in the middle ear cleft. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.rationale: This combination is used for infection of the canal skin where the drum is intact, and the aminoglycoside component is avoided when the middle ear is open because of the risk of inner ear toxicity. The non-tender pinna and normal canal skin indicate the problem is not an outer ear infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Otitis media)

Urgent imaging and admission are for suspected intracranial or mastoid complications, signalled by fever, postauricular swelling, facial nerve palsy, severe headache or vertigo, and none of these are present. Transferring a systemically well child out of community for a chronic problem delays the treatment that actually helps. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.rationale: A ventilation tube is used for persistent middle ear fluid behind an intact drum, and the right ear is already ventilated by the perforation itself, so a tube adds nothing there. Surgical repair of the drum is considered only after the ear has been dry for a prolonged period and the child is older. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.rationale: Discharge through a perforation lasting beyond six weeks is treated by regular cleaning of the canal so that drops reach the middle ear, together with a quinolone preparation that is not toxic to the inner ear when the drum is open. Audiology is mandatory rather than optional because the hearing loss is driving the classroom difficulty and needs measurement and amplification planning. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

explanation.summary: The discriminating finding in adolescent gynaecomastia is testicular volume interpreted against the stage of pubic hair. Physiological pubertal gynaecomastia occurs when the testes are already 10 mL or larger and settles within about two years, whereas testes of 4 mL with advanced pubic hair indicates that androgen is coming from the adrenal while the testis has failed. A raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone localises the problem to the gonad, and the combination with tall stature, long limbs and learning difficulties is characteristic of an additional X chromosome. Karyotype confirms the diagnosis, after which management involves paediatric endocrinology, testosterone replacement, educational support and early counselling about fertility.
key_points: Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer before attributing gynaecomastia to puberty
Raised gonadotropins localise the defect to the testis rather than the pituitary
Tall stature with long limbs and learning difficulty alongside small firm testes suggests an extra X chromosome
Suppressed gonadotropins with small testes would instead suggest exogenous androgen use
explanation.pearls: Gynaecomastia plus testes under 6 mL in a boy with well developed pubic hair is never physiological: check morning testosterone with luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone, and if the gonadotropins are high, send a karyotype rather than scheduling a six month review.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Delayed puberty and hypogonadism

options.rationale: A hormonally active testicular tumour is the concern when gynaecomastia is accompanied by a palpable testicular mass or a raised beta human chorionic gonadotropin, and both are absent here. Bilateral small firm testes point to failure of the gonad rather than a tumour within it. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

A pituitary lesion causing hypogonadism would suppress rather than elevate the gonadotropins, so the raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone place the lesion below the pituitary. Imaging the pituitary here would be normal and would delay the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Watchful waiting is correct for physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, which occurs at mid puberty with normally enlarging testes of 10 mL or more and resolves within two years. Testes of 4 mL alongside advanced pubic hair is a mismatch that excludes the physiological pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Exogenous androgen use suppresses the gonadotropins and shrinks the testes, so it belongs in the differential of small testes with gynaecomastia, but the raised gonadotropins here point the other way. The history of no supplement or anabolic use is consistent with that biochemistry. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Small firm testes with a raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone identify primary testicular failure, and in a tall adolescent with disproportionately long limbs, breast development and learning difficulty the explanation is an additional X chromosome. Karyotype confirms it and opens the discussion about testosterone replacement and fertility preservation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood; the coronary arteries are the principal target and untreated disease carries a 25% risk of aneurysm formation, falling to under 5% with timely IVIG. RCH and the American Heart Association both treat presentations beyond day 10 with IVIG plus aspirin when systemic inflammation persists (CRP raised, ESR raised, platelets rising, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria) or when the echocardiogram shows coronary changes. Aspirin is used at anti-inflammatory dose while febrile then reduced to antiplatelet dose for six to eight weeks or until inflammatory markers normalise. Follow-up echocardiography at two and six weeks catches late aneurysm development.
key_points: Four of five principal criteria plus fever meet clinical Kawasaki diagnosis; incomplete Kawasaki uses a supplementary lab algorithm.
IVIG 2 g/kg reduces coronary aneurysm risk from roughly 25% to under 5%.
Late-presenting Kawasaki (after day 10) still receives IVIG if CRP raised or coronaries abnormal.
IVIG resistance (fever >36 hours after infusion) is the trigger for adjunctive steroids or infliximab.
Aspirin is used at anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet dose and is one of the paediatric exceptions to the Reye syndrome caution.
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria plus a strawberry tongue plus a platelet count above 450 x10^9/L in a persistently febrile toddler flips the differential from viral exanthem toward Kawasaki disease before the classic extremity peeling appears.

sources.label: American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

options.rationale: Fulfilment of four principal criteria with persistent inflammation (CRP 158, platelets 612, hyponatraemia, hypoalbuminaemia) meets the AHA definition of Kawasaki disease presenting late. IVIG is still indicated beyond day 10 when inflammatory markers are elevated OR coronary changes are present, because it lowers aneurysm risk even in the sub-acute phase. Withholding therapy exposes the child to progressive coronary injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Discharge on a non-steroidal without immunomodulation abandons the disease-modifying window entirely. Ibuprofen does not treat vasculitis and worsens the risk profile if aspirin is later required. Inpatient IVIG plus aspirin is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

The clinical pattern is not bacterial sepsis nor EBV (no exudative pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, negative cultures at 24 hours). Antibiotic escalation delays IVIG. Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis and infectious workup should not defer treatment when criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Corticosteroids in Kawasaki disease are adjunctive for predicted IVIG resistance or for genuine IVIG failure (persistent fever 36 hours after first infusion), not as a first-line replacement for IVIG. Steroid monotherapy leaves the coronary risk unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

This child fulfils four of the five principal criteria (rash, conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, extremity changes, cervical adenopathy >1.5 cm) with persistent fever and strongly elevated inflammatory markers past day 10; RCH and AHA both recommend IVIG plus aspirin in the sub-acute phase provided CRP or coronary artery changes remain. Serial echocardiography detects late aneurysm formation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

explanation.summary: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is managed on a stepped pathway that keeps the mother-baby dyad together where possible. RCH defines a target of at least 2.6 mmol/L pre-feed from 2 hours of age in at-risk infants: infants of diabetic mothers, small or large for gestational age, preterm 35-37 weeks, and those with perinatal stress. Asymptomatic first low readings are treated with buccal 40% dextrose gel at 200 mg/kg plus a supported breastfeed, with recheck 30 minutes after the feed. Failure of two gel-and-feed cycles, symptomatic hypoglycaemia, or a glucose under 1.5 mmol/L escalates to IV dextrose and special-care admission with a target glucose infusion rate that keeps the infant euglycaemic.
key_points: At-risk infants (IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm, perinatal stress) get pre-feed BSL at 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours.
First-line treatment for asymptomatic BSL <2.6 mmol/L is 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) of 40% dextrose gel plus a feed.
Recheck BSL 30 minutes after the feed; if still low, repeat gel plus feed once before IV dextrose.
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL <1.5 mmol/L bypasses gel and goes straight to IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg then infusion.
Persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours or GIR >8 mg/kg/min triggers a hyperinsulinism screen.
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dosed at 200 mg/kg keeps the mother and baby together and reduces NICU admission for hypoglycaemia by about 40% in the Sugar Babies trial - remember 0.5 mL/kg of 40% gel.

sources.label: Sugar Babies (Harris 2013) buccal dextrose gel trial

options.rationale: IV dextrose bolus is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia OR persistently low glucose despite oral or buccal glucose gel measures. An asymptomatic first low reading at 1.9 mmol/L is treated first with oral 40% glucose gel and a feed, per RCH and Australasian pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

A hyperinsulinism screen is triggered by hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 hours, requiring glucose infusion rates above 8 mg/kg/min, or occurring outside a recognised risk category. It is not the first response to a single mildly low reading in an infant of a diabetic mother. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

A 30 mL/kg formula bolus at 2 hours of life is a supra-physiological volume and undermines breastfeeding without addressing the immediate metabolic risk any better than gel plus feed. Testing intervals are pre-feed at 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours for infants of diabetic mothers, not at a six-hour gap. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

The physiological glucose nadir in healthy term babies is around 1 hour of life; a value of 1.9 mmol/L at 2 hours in an infant of a diabetic mother is below the RCH intervention threshold of 2.6 mmol/L and requires active management, not observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

The Sugar Babies/HYPO protocol adopted by RCH treats asymptomatic hypoglycaemia below 2.6 mmol/L in at-risk infants with 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) of 40% buccal dextrose gel plus a supported feed, then rechecks the level 30 minutes after the feed. This avoids unnecessary separation and preserves breastfeeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: Sugar Babies (Harris 2013) buccal dextrose gel trial

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is the commonest paediatric anaemia in Australia, peaking between nine months and three years when rapid growth outstrips a milk-heavy diet with limited iron intake. Excess cow's milk (>500 mL/day) both displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss through non-IgE cow's milk protein enteropathy in some children. Assessment includes an iron panel with ferritin (an acute phase reactant that may be falsely normal), coeliac serology, and dietary counselling. Oral ferrous sulfate 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron is first line; expect a haemoglobin rise of about 10 g/L per fortnight and a reticulocyte response within a week. Continue treatment for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation to replenish stores.
key_points: Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day in toddlers to prevent iron deficiency.
First-line oral iron dose is 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron; ferrous sulfate 30 mg = 6 mg elemental.
Co-order coeliac serology because coeliac disease is a common cause of refractory iron deficiency.
Expect Hb rise of about 10 g/L per fortnight; failure to respond triggers investigation for malabsorption or loss.
Continue oral iron for three months after Hb normalises to refill stores.
explanation.pearls: In a well-appearing toddler with dietary iron deficiency, transferrin saturation below 16% and ferritin below 15 microg/L confirm the diagnosis; a rise in reticulocyte count within seven days of starting ferrous sulfate proves the therapy is working before the haemoglobin has moved.

options.rationale: The clinical picture (excess milk intake, meat refusal, microcytic hypochromic anaemia without haemolysis or bleeding) is classic dietary iron deficiency. RCH treats with 3-6 mg/kg elemental iron daily and reduces cow's milk to below 500 mL/day. Coeliac serology (transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA) is co-ordered because coeliac disease is a common co-cause of iron deficiency in toddlers. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Bone marrow biopsy is reserved for suspected marrow failure, refractory anaemia after adequate iron replacement, or when the blood film and history do not fit a common cause. Dietary iron deficiency in an otherwise well toddler does not warrant an invasive procedure as a first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

IV iron in children under five is reserved for oral iron intolerance, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD), or ongoing losses that outstrip oral replacement. A well toddler with dietary iron deficiency will respond to oral iron; ferric carboxymaltose is not licensed under one year and is second line under five. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

The presentation strongly favours iron deficiency (dietary history, low MCH, high red cell distribution width, no family history of haemoglobinopathy). Iron replacement should not be delayed pending electrophoresis, though electrophoresis is legitimate if the response to iron is inadequate at eight weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

A multivitamin containing 4 mg of iron delivers approximately one-fifth of the therapeutic dose required and will not correct clinical anaemia in a reasonable timeframe. Six-month review of a haemoglobin of 82 g/L delays diagnosis of the roughly 20% of iron-deficient toddlers who have an underlying malabsorptive cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: The mantra 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise' captures the epidemiology: bruising in an infant who cannot yet mobilise (roll, cruise, walk) is exceptional in accidental injury and highly predictive of inflicted trauma. The TEN-4 FACESp decision rule flags bruising to the Trunk, Ear, Neck in any child under four years, Face, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid or Subconjunctivae, or Patterned bruising, and any bruise in a pre-cruiser as a sentinel injury requiring evaluation. Standard RCH workup includes full skeletal survey (repeated at 2 weeks for equivocal findings), MRI brain, dilated fundoscopy, coagulation and full blood count, and same-day involvement of the paediatric child protection team. Mandatory reporting to the statutory child protection agency is triggered by reasonable belief of harm, not diagnostic certainty.
key_points: Pre-mobile infant bruising is a sentinel injury for abusive head trauma and occult fracture.
TEN-4 FACESp flags Torso, Ear, Neck (under 4 years); Face, Angle jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Subconjunctivae; Patterned; and pre-cruisers.
Full skeletal survey (21 views) not a limited two-view study; consider a repeat at 2 weeks.
MRI brain is preferred over CT for abusive head trauma; dilated fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages.
Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable belief, not certainty; runs in parallel with medical workup.
explanation.pearls: A bruise on the ear or the cheek of an infant under 4 months old carries a positive predictive value for inflicted injury above 90% in TEN-4 FACESp derivation cohorts; a full skeletal survey plus MRI brain the same day is standard of care regardless of the explanation offered.

sources.label: TEN-4 FACESp bruising clinical decision rule

options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant carries a strong statistical association with inflicted injury regardless of the explanation offered, because the mechanisms available to an infant who cannot roll are extremely limited. Discharge without a full skeletal survey and child protection referral misses occult fractures and abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Any bruise in a non-mobile infant is a sentinel injury: TEN-4 FACESp screening puts this in the highest concern category (face and ear bruising, under 4 months). RCH mandates full skeletal survey, neuroimaging for abusive head trauma, ophthalmology fundoscopy, and same-day involvement of the hospital child protection team plus a mandatory report to statutory services. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
source_refs: TEN-4 FACESp bruising clinical decision rule

options.rationale: Bleeding disorders should be excluded but do not replace child protection assessment. Coagulation screening runs in parallel with skeletal survey, neuroimaging and social work involvement, not instead of them. Sequential single-track workup delays safeguarding decisions. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Photodocumentation is important but not sufficient. Discharging a pre-mobile infant with unexplained bruising home before completing the skeletal survey and safeguarding pathway exposes the child to further injury; the child health nurse cannot substitute for the paediatric child protection team. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

A limited two-view series misses the classic metaphyseal lesions, posterior rib fractures, and healing fractures that a full 21-view skeletal survey detects. Statutory notification is mandatory for reasonable suspicion regardless of imaging results in every Australian jurisdiction. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Any jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days in a preterm) must have a split bilirubin done. A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L, or above 20% of the total, is always pathological. The differential includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, neonatal hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis, TORCH infection, metabolic disorders and parenteral nutrition associated cholestasis. Biliary atresia is the not-to-miss diagnosis because Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 60 days of life gives the best native-liver survival; every week of delay after that meaningfully worsens outcomes. Standard workup pairs ultrasound (looking for the 'triangular cord sign' and absent gallbladder) with hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA) after phenobarbital priming and, when indicated, liver biopsy plus intraoperative cholangiogram.
key_points: Split bilirubin is mandatory for jaundice persisting beyond 14 days (21 days preterm).
Conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is pathological.
Pale stool plus dark urine is biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life optimises native-liver survival.
Phototherapy has no role and can cause bronze baby syndrome when conjugated fraction is high.
explanation.pearls: Any breastfed baby still jaundiced at two weeks needs a split bilirubin; a direct fraction of 68 micromol/L with pale stools mandates same-week ultrasound and hepatology referral because Kasai portoenterostomy done inside the 60-day window doubles the 10-year native-liver survival.

sources.label: GESA and Liver Foundation Australia biliary atresia pathway

options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is UNCONJUGATED. A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L (or above 20% of total) is always pathological in infancy and cannot be attributed to breastfeeding. Delayed workup misses the Kasai-portoenterostomy window for biliary atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers; it does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and can cause bronze baby syndrome in the presence of a significant direct fraction. It also anchors decision-making on the wrong pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L with pale stool and dark urine in an infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 60 days of life gives the best long-term native-liver survival, so admit, involve paediatric hepatology, and expedite the triple workup of ultrasound, HIDA and liver biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: GESA and Liver Foundation Australia biliary atresia pathway

options.rationale: A milk-swap trial is only relevant to distinguishing breast milk unconjugated jaundice; it has no role once the conjugated fraction is elevated. Two weeks of delay in biliary atresia crosses the critical 60-day surgical window. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

UTI and hypothyroidism are recognised causes of prolonged UNCONJUGATED jaundice. Neither typically produces a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L with pale stools. Sequential ruling out of these before hepatology referral delays the surgical window for biliary atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Hemiplegic migraine is a rare familial migraine subtype defined by aura that includes reversible motor weakness lasting minutes to days, typically alongside visual, sensory or aphasic aura. Paediatric ischaemic stroke is the critical mimic and is missed on non-contrast CT in roughly half of cases at presentation. Diffusion-weighted MRI with MRA is the diagnostic investigation of choice: normal DWI in the presence of hemiparesis strongly supports migraine, while restricted diffusion drives stroke pathways (paediatric-adapted thrombolysis or thrombectomy in select centres). Once stroke and other structural mimics are excluded, hemiplegic migraine attacks are managed with anti-nausea therapy, hydration, analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen, avoiding triptans and ergots) and paediatric neurology follow-up for preventive strategy.
key_points: Hemiplegic migraine causes fully reversible motor aura; diagnosis requires exclusion of stroke.
Non-contrast CT is insensitive for paediatric ischaemic stroke; DWI-MRI plus MRA is the investigation of choice.
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine and while stroke is on the differential.
Familial hemiplegic migraine is autosomal dominant with mutations in CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A.
Attack treatment is supportive: hydration, antiemetic, non-triptan analgesia.
explanation.pearls: In a child under 12 with focal neurological deficit and a normal non-contrast CT, arrange MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging within 60 minutes: the absence of restricted diffusion strongly supports hemiplegic migraine over stroke, while its presence opens the paediatric acute stroke pathway.

sources.label: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.rationale: Paediatric acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis is not routinely offered in Australia and requires confirmed arterial occlusion on MRI/MRA, exclusion of stroke mimics, and specialist involvement. Empirical thrombolysis of a probable hemiplegic migraine attack carries substantial haemorrhage risk without benefit. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

Non-contrast CT is insensitive for early paediatric ischaemic stroke and cannot exclude arterial dissection or basilar occlusion. Diffusion-weighted MRI with MRA is the definitive investigation, distinguishes hemiplegic migraine (typically normal DWI) from ischaemic stroke (restricted diffusion), and drives all subsequent treatment decisions. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)
source_refs: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.rationale: Triptans are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine because of vasoconstrictive potential in the presence of neurological deficit and until stroke is definitively excluded. Family history is supportive but not diagnostic while a fixed hemiparesis is present. (Source: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus)
source_refs: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.rationale: Phenytoin loading is a status epilepticus treatment; there is no witnessed seizure and no evidence of ongoing epileptiform activity. Waiting six hours for CT changes squanders diagnostic time and risks a genuine stroke going untreated. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

Empirical dual antiplatelet therapy for undifferentiated paediatric neurological deficit is not supported by evidence and carries bleeding risk if imaging reveals intracranial haemorrhage or dissection with an intramural haematoma. Advanced imaging precedes treatment selection. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

explanation.summary: Recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula complicates 5-15% of primary oesophageal atresia repairs, usually presenting between four weeks and six months with feed-triggered coughing, cyanotic spells, recurrent right lower lobe aspiration and failure to thrive. The tube oesophagogram may show a linear air column above the anastomosis but is diagnostically insensitive; rigid bronchoscopy with instillation of methylene blue into the oesophagus, watching for dye appearance on the tracheal side, is the reference standard and simultaneously localises the fistula for repair. Alternative diagnoses include anastomotic stricture (progressive dysphagia rather than aspiration), gastro-oesophageal reflux, laryngeal cleft, and vocal cord dysfunction from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. VACTERL association carries a higher rate of postoperative complications and demands coordinated multidisciplinary follow-up.
key_points: Recurrent TOF classically presents with feed-triggered cyanosis and right lower lobe aspiration.
Tube oesophagogram is insensitive; rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue is the reference standard.
Anastomotic stricture presents with progressive dysphagia and food bolus impaction, not aspiration.
VACTERL infants require coordinated cardiac, renal, orthopaedic, spinal and airway follow-up.
Repair of recurrent TOF may need pleural or pericardial interposition to prevent second recurrence.
explanation.pearls: In an oesophageal atresia infant with new feed-related cyanosis and right lower lobe pneumonia after day 21, ask theatre for rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue down the upper pouch: dye on the tracheal side confirms recurrent TOF and localises it for corrective surgery.

options.rationale: The combination of feed-related cyanosis, recurrent right lower lobe pneumonia and a persistent anterior air column above the anastomosis on tube oesophagogram is classic for a recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula. Rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue instilled into the oesophagus and observed on the tracheal side is the reference standard test; it also localises the fistula for the corrective operation. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

Gastro-oesophageal reflux is common after oesophageal atresia repair and can contribute to aspiration, but MII-pH testing does not detect recurrent fistula and is not the first investigation when the barium study shows a suspicious air column. Reflux workup follows exclusion of a mechanical airway to oesophagus connection. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

HIDA scintigraphy assesses biliary tract patency, not tracheo-oesophageal communication, and has no role in evaluating recurrent aspiration after oesophageal atresia repair. The imaging modalities of value are contrast oesophagogram and rigid bronchoscopy. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

Videofluoroscopy assesses oro-pharyngeal swallow safety; it cannot distinguish aspiration from swallow incoordination from aspiration via a recurrent fistula and delays definitive endoscopic diagnosis in a systemically unwell infant with witnessed apnoea and consolidation. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

Anastomotic stricture typically presents with progressive dysphagia and food impaction, not feed-triggered cyanosis and pneumonia. Dilating a suspected recurrent fistula site risks converting a small communication into a large one and forces contamination of the mediastinum. Diagnosis precedes intervention. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

explanation.summary: Adolescent iron deficiency anaemia is common in menstruating girls and is compounded by vegetarian diet and tannin-rich beverages that block non-haem iron absorption.
key_points: Alternate-day oral iron gives better absorption per dose and fewer gastrointestinal effects than daily dosing.
Vitamin C taken with iron improves non-haem iron absorption; tea, milk, calcium and PPIs reduce it.
IV iron reserved for oral intolerance, malabsorption, or losses exceeding oral replacement capacity.
explanation.pearls: Each oral iron dose raises hepcidin, which blocks absorption of a dose taken the next day, so alternate-day dosing gives higher absorption per dose than daily dosing.

options.rationale: Alternate-day oral iron in confirmed iron deficiency (ferritin 6, transferrin saturation 8%) gives better absorption per dose with fewer gastrointestinal effects, vitamin C aids absorption, and the heavy menstrual loss driving the deficit needs its own review. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency; RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Daily dosing produces a hepcidin rise that reduces absorption of the next day's dose, so alternate-day dosing gives more absorbed iron per dose, and this plan leaves the heavy menstrual loss unaddressed. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency)

IV iron in adolescents is reserved for oral intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing loss exceeding oral replacement, or failure of an adequate oral trial; none applies before oral iron has been tried. (Source: AMH: Iron replacement)

Endoscopy is considered in adolescents with iron deficiency when menstrual and dietary causes do not explain it or oral iron fails; here heavy periods and a vegetarian diet account for the deficit. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Twice-daily dosing worsens hepcidin-driven absorption blockade, meals reduce iron uptake, and proton pump inhibitors reduce the gastric acid that non-haem iron absorption depends on. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Australian bronchiolitis pathways use a stepped escalation model: room air where possible, then low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min targeting SpO2 90% and above, then high-flow nasal cannula when low flow fails after 2 hours.
key_points: SpO2 target for bronchiolitis is 90% and above (not 92-94% as in some older guidelines).
Low-flow ceiling is 2 L/min in infants; escalate to HFNC 2 L/kg/min after a 2-hour trial fails.
Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not routine in Australian bronchiolitis care.
explanation.pearls: In Australian ED bronchiolitis care, escalate to high-flow nasal cannula 2 L/kg/min after 2 hours of failed low-flow (SpO2 <90% or worsening work of breathing).

options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prongs deliver an unreliable FiO2 above 2 L/min and there is a ceiling effect around 2 L/min in infants. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Australian bronchiolitis guidance moves to high flow when saturations stay below 90% with no improvement in respiratory state after 2 hours of low-flow oxygen, which describes this infant. RCH targets an SpO2 of 90% or above unless there is underlying cardiopulmonary disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Salbutamol is not recommended for bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months because there is no consistent evidence of benefit, and it delays effective respiratory support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Hypertonic saline is not recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways for emergency department infants because the evidence does not show a clinically important benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

CPAP is reserved for infants who fail high-flow nasal cannula, or who have impending respiratory failure with hypercapnia and apnoeas; this alert infant has not yet had a high-flow trial. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management in Australia uses gestational-age and postnatal-age nomograms with lower thresholds when haemolysis risk factors are present (positive DAT, isoimmunisation or other haemolysis).
key_points: Positive DAT with ABO incompatibility lowers the phototherapy and exchange thresholds.
Intensive phototherapy is first-line above the phototherapy line, with recheck at 4-6 hours.
Exchange transfusion for continued rise despite phototherapy or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
explanation.pearls: In ABO incompatibility with positive DAT at 54 hours, a bilirubin above the phototherapy line needs intensive phototherapy now and a repeat serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours to confirm it is falling.

options.rationale: Positive DAT with ABO incompatibility lowers the phototherapy threshold on Australasian nomograms because ongoing haemolysis can raise the bilirubin quickly, and waiting 24 hours at this level is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin approaches the exchange line despite intensive phototherapy, or where there are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; neither applies here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

At 54 hours of age, 320 micromol/L in the presence of a haemolysis risk factor (positive DAT with ABO incompatibility) exceeds the phototherapy threshold, so intensive phototherapy starts now with a repeat serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; ANZCOR)
Interrupting breastfeeding is not the primary intervention here and does not address haemolysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

IVIG is an adjunct in haemolytic disease of the newborn (isoimmune) with rising bilirubin despite intensive phototherapy; it is given alongside phototherapy, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: RCH diagnoses complete Kawasaki disease with fever for 4 days or more and at least 4 of the 5 principal features: conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes, rash, changes in the hands and feet, and cervical lymphadenopathy. This boy has four of them (conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and the node), so normal hands and feet do not stop him meeting the criteria. Incomplete Kawasaki disease, with fewer than 4 features, needs abnormal investigations or echo findings to support it. A large single node with fever is often treated first as bacterial adenitis, and failure to respond without an abscess on ultrasound should prompt a search for the other features.
key_points: Complete Kawasaki disease: fever for 4 days or more with at least 4 of the 5 principal clinical features.
Incomplete Kawasaki disease: fewer than 4 features, supported by abnormal investigations or echo findings.
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is first-line; do not wait for coronary changes on echo.
Cervical adenitis unresponsive to antibiotics, without abscess on ultrasound, plus supportive labs, should raise Kawasaki disease.
explanation.pearls: RCH gives aspirin 5 mg/kg orally daily alongside IVIG and continues it until cardiology review at about 6 weeks.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: The picture does not fit staphylococcal or streptococcal cervical lymphadenitis: no abscess on ultrasound, no response to antibiotics, and conjunctivitis, oral changes and rash alongside the node. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Persisting with the bacterial adenitis pathway ignores four principal Kawasaki features after 6 days of fever: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a truncal rash and cervical lymphadenopathy. IV flucloxacillin with a repeat scan suits a node that is fluctuant or has an abscess forming on ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Corticosteroids are added to IVIG, not given instead of it, and only in children at high risk of coronary artery aneurysms, such as infants 6 months or younger or those with coronary artery dilatation on echo. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Six days of fever with conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash and an antibiotic-unresponsive node without abscess, supported by raised CRP, thrombocytosis, raised ALT, low albumin and sterile pyuria, is Kawasaki disease: give IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin and obtain an echo. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease; AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Atypical mycobacterial cervical adenitis is usually indolent and non-tender, in preschool children with violaceous overlying skin and without high fever or systemic inflammation. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; the feared diagnosis is malrotation with midgut volvulus, which can produce bowel necrosis within hours.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until surgically proven otherwise.
Shocked infant with bilious vomiting: resuscitate and phone surgery, do NOT go to radiology first.
NGT on free drainage decompresses the stomach and reduces vomiting risk.
explanation.pearls: A shocked infant with green vomit goes to theatre for Ladd's procedure, not to the contrast suite; upper GI series is only for the stable, uncertain case.

options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in an infant with shock is malrotation with midgut volvulus until surgically excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting)
Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)
Oral rehydration is contraindicated in a shocked drowsy infant with a surgical abdomen and bilious vomiting; aspiration risk is high and it delays surgical review. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Sepsis is on the differential, but bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency, and a lumbar puncture in a shocked infant is unsafe and delays surgical review. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

Bilious vomiting plus shock in an infant is midgut volvulus complicating malrotation until proven otherwise, and the priority is resuscitation, gastric decompression and immediate surgical referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting)

explanation.summary: Bruising in an infant who is not yet cruising is one of the strongest single features of inflicted injury.
key_points: Bruises in a pre-mobile infant are inflicted injury until otherwise explained.
TEN-4-FACES-p flags bruises requiring NAI workup: torso, ear, neck, or any in under-4-month-olds.
Structured workup: skeletal survey, fundoscopy, coagulation, CT head as indicated, social review.
explanation.pearls: The rule 'if they don't cruise, they don't bruise' means any bruise in an infant under 4 months mandates a full non-accidental injury workup plus notification to child protection.

options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, with an inconsistent mechanism from a non-parent carer, meets criteria for a full NAI workup and a report under mandatory reporting obligations. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Bruising in a non-mobile infant carries a high probability of inflicted injury (TEN-4 rule: any bruise in an infant 4 months or younger), so reassurance leaves her at risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
A normal coagulation screen does not rule out inflicted injury; it forms one part of the NAI workup alongside skeletal survey, fundoscopy and head imaging as indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
Confrontation is not the doctor's role and may compromise the safety of the mother, the child, and staff. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
Discharging on a second-hand confirmation of the mechanism does not add clinical information and does not meet the doctor's mandatory reporting obligation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates 0.5 to 1% of paediatric DKA episodes and carries around 20% mortality, with survivors often left with cognitive impairment.
key_points: Cushing response (bradycardia plus rising BP) plus GCS drop in DKA equals cerebral oedema until proven otherwise.
Give hyperosmolar therapy first (3% saline or mannitol); CT after stabilisation.
Reduce the IV fluid rate by one-third at the same time.
explanation.pearls: Hyperosmolar therapy (3% saline or mannitol) is given for suspected paediatric DKA cerebral oedema as soon as rising BP with falling pulse and a GCS drop appear, without waiting for imaging.

options.rationale: Adding glucose is appropriate once glucose falls to 15 mmol/L or below, but it does not treat the cerebral oedema that is the immediate threat. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (Cushing response), headache, vomiting, incontinence and GCS drop during DKA treatment indicate cerebral oedema: give hyperosmolar therapy and reduce fluids without waiting for imaging. RCH gives 3% sodium chloride 3 mL/kg IV over 15 minutes (or 20% mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 20 minutes) and reduces the fluid rate by one-third. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ISPAD DKA guideline)

Interrupting insulin will halt ketolysis and worsen acidosis; potassium can be replaced through fluids while insulin continues, and neither step treats cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Additional saline bolus can worsen cerebral oedema by continuing free-water accumulation intracellularly during rapid osmolar shifts; fluids are reduced, not increased. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)
Insulin escalation would accelerate glucose fall, worsening osmolar shift and cerebral oedema, and is not indicated while cerebral oedema is being treated. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Neonates with duct-dependent left-sided obstructions (critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, hypoplastic left heart, critical aortic stenosis) can pass 24-hour saturation screening and present with collapse when the duct closes in the following days.
key_points: A ductal-arch obstruction can pass the 24-hour saturation screen; collapse comes days later.
Pre- to post-ductal SpO2 gradient greater than 3% with weak femorals equals duct-dependent CHD.
Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) reopens the ductus; ANMF starts at 10 nanogram/kg/min (range 5 to 50).
explanation.pearls: In a collapsed neonate under 2 weeks with pre-post-ductal saturation difference over 3% and weak femorals, start a prostaglandin E1 infusion immediately.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant

options.rationale: Volume in a duct-dependent left-sided obstruction (likely coarctation or interrupted aortic arch here) can worsen pulmonary oedema and does not reopen the duct. (Source: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant

options.rationale: High FiO2 in duct-dependent left-sided obstruction is harmful because oxygen constricts the ductus and worsens systemic perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant

options.rationale: Collapse in the first two weeks of life with weak femoral pulses, a pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient greater than 3% and hepatomegaly means duct-dependent circulation: start prostaglandin E1 now and be ready to ventilate for apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant; ANMF: Alprostadil)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are reasonable while workup proceeds because sepsis is a differential, but delaying prostaglandin allows further deterioration as the duct closes. (Source: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Recognition of the seriously unwell neonate and young infant

options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of tension pneumothorax or anaphylaxis; the picture fits duct-dependent circulation. (Source: ANZCOR: Neonatal)

explanation.summary: This infant meets RCH criteria for oxygen with SpO2 at 89% at rest and 88% with feeds despite airway clearance. The RCH pathway starts oxygen at low flow via nasal prongs 1-2 L/min with a saturation target of 90%. HFNC is reserved for failure of low flow after two hours, not as an initial device. Neither salbutamol nor systemic corticosteroids alter the natural history of viral bronchiolitis and neither addresses hypoxia.
key_points: SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90%, not 92-94%
First line oxygen is low flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min
HFNC is second line after failed low flow, not first
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: The PARIS trial showed early HFNC does not reduce PICU admission compared with rescue HFNC after low flow failure - low flow first is both cheaper and evidence based.

options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids do not shorten bronchiolitis and are not part of the RCH pathway; the immediate issue is hypoxia which needs oxygen, not steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

The AU PARIS trial and RCH pathway both make HFNC a second line device after failed low flow rather than the first oxygen chosen; jumping straight to HFNC has not been shown to reduce PICU admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months as there is no consistent benefit on admission length, oxygen need or work of breathing; salbutamol is not the answer to falling saturations. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; AAP Clinical Practice Guideline 2014)

RCH bronchiolitis guidance identifies low flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min as the first line escalation for infants dropping below the SpO2 target of 90%; humidification and heating are not required at these flow rates. HFNC is reserved for failure of low flow after two hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Persistent SpO2 at 89% at rest is below the RCH target of 90% and mandates oxygen now rather than a further period of observation on room air; ongoing hypoxia risks feed failure and apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: This child has moderate croup on the RCH scoring - stridor at rest that settles when calm with mild recession and no cyanosis or agitation. Both mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; the 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe presentations. Adrenaline is added only to severe or life threatening croup and always with dexamethasone cover. RCH observes for four hours after steroids or three hours after nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral single dose
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline
Nebulised adrenaline dose is flat 5 mL of 1:1000, not per kg
Observe for 3 hours after last adrenaline before discharge
explanation.pearls: The 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone dose is often used reflexively - RCH specifies 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup, which covers most emergency presentations.

options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is second line to oral dexamethasone when a child cannot tolerate an oral dose; there is no vomiting or refusal here so the oral route is preferred and cheaper. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved by RCH for severe croup with stridor and marked recession at rest that does not settle, or with agitation or exhaustion; using it for moderate croup gives no added benefit over 0.15 mg/kg. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

RCH croup guidance uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose for mild and moderate croup, giving effective symptom relief with the lower dose. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. Stridor at rest that settles when calm is moderate. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Oral prednisolone has weaker evidence than dexamethasone with a shorter duration of action requiring a multiday course, and re-presentation rates in AU emergency data are higher; dexamethasone is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, and a steroid must still be given because adrenaline effect wears off in 90-120 minutes; adrenaline alone risks rebound stridor without underlying anti-inflammatory cover. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: This child has 5-6% dehydration with failed oral trial after ondansetron. RCH pathway makes NGT rehydration the next step - it has equivalent efficacy to IV in AU trials with fewer complications, no need for cannulation and shorter time to full rehydration. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure. Antimotility agents like loperamide are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line when oral fails in mild to moderate dehydration
IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure
Ondansetron dose is banded by weight: 2 mg for under 15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg
Loperamide is contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: The AGREE trial (Melbourne) showed NGT rehydration was non-inferior to IV with fewer complications - AU practice has shifted decisively toward NGT first.

options.rationale: The AU ondansetron dose for a child under 15 kg is 2 mg not 4 mg, and repeat dosing is not recommended in the emergency department pathway; further oral only has already failed once. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure; in mild to moderate dehydration NGT is preferred and has lower cannulation failure and complication rates in AU emergency populations. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

RCH gastroenteritis pathway makes nasogastric rehydration first line when oral trial fails in mild to moderate dehydration (5-10%); it avoids IV access, has fewer complications and equal efficacy in AU trials. Rate is 25 mL/kg in the first hour then continue over 4-6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Continued oral trial without route change ignores the failure of the first oral attempt with antiemetic cover, and diluted juice has an inappropriate electrolyte content and osmolality compared with oral rehydration solution. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Antimotility agents are contraindicated in children with acute infective gastroenteritis due to the risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged infection; they are not part of the AU pathway. (Source: AMH: Antidiarrhoeals)

explanation.summary: The AU approach to uncomplicated AOM in a well child over 6 months is analgesia with delayed antibiotics. Immediate antibiotics are indicated for children under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children (higher risk of chronic suppurative otitis media), systemically unwell children or a perforated ear. When antibiotics are indicated, amoxicillin is first line at 15 mg/kg/dose three times daily for five days; augmentin is reserved for treatment failure.
key_points: Delayed antibiotic script is first line for well non-Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children over 6 months
Immediate antibiotics: under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, unwell, perforated
Amoxicillin is first line; augmentin only after 48-72 h treatment failure
Ciprofloxacin drops are for otitis externa or chronic suppurative OM with perforation
explanation.pearls: The AU rationale for immediate antibiotics in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children is the substantially higher rate of chronic suppurative otitis media and its consequences for hearing and schooling.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48-72 hours on amoxicillin, or where there is a high concern for beta lactamase producing organisms; it is never first line in uncomplicated paediatric AOM in the AU pathway. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

Immediate antibiotics are indicated for children under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, systemically unwell children or perforated AOM; a well 22-month-old with unilateral AOM does not meet criteria and gains little from immediate treatment. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

RCH and eTG endorse analgesia with delayed antibiotic in non Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children over 6 months without perforation who are systemically well; most cases resolve without antibiotics and delayed scripts reduce use without increasing complications. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media; eTG: Acute otitis media)

Ciprofloxacin ear drops are used for otitis externa or for chronic suppurative otitis media with a perforation; they cannot cross an intact tympanic membrane and have no role in acute otitis media with an intact drum. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

IV antibiotics are reserved for suspected mastoiditis, meningitis or a systemically unwell child not tolerating oral therapy; this child is systemically well with a normal neurological examination and does not need admission. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Any infant with jaundice beyond 14 days needs a split (conjugated and unconjugated) bilirubin. A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is always pathological and mandates urgent hepatology assessment for biliary atresia. Pale stools, dark urine and a firm liver support this. The Kasai portoenterostomy has a much higher rate of biliary drainage restoration if performed under 60 days of age, and each week of delay reduces success. Do not send this child home on watchful waiting.
key_points: Conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is always pathological
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes fall sharply after 60 days of age
Phototherapy has no role in conjugated jaundice
Pale stools and dark urine are red flags for biliary obstruction
explanation.pearls: The stool colour chart in the RCH resources should be given to every family with prolonged neonatal jaundice - parents can catch progression to biliary atresia earlier than any single blood test.

options.rationale: Empirical ursodeoxycholic acid without a diagnosis delays surgical treatment of biliary atresia; UDCA has a role after diagnosis of specific cholestatic disorders but is never a substitute for urgent structural workup. (Source: NASPGHAN 2017)

Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and cannot explain a conjugated fraction of 42 micromol/L or pale stools; labelling this as breast milk jaundice delays workup for biliary atresia beyond the 60 day Kasai window and worsens outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to a water soluble form; it has no effect on conjugated bilirubin and can cause bronze baby syndrome in cholestatic infants. This infant has cholestasis, not unconjugated jaundice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total in an infant over 2 weeks mandates urgent hepatology workup for biliary atresia; the Kasai portoenterostomy has a much higher success rate if done before 60 days of life. Pale stools plus dark urine with a firm liver make biliary atresia the leading concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN 2017)

An ultrasound is a helpful adjunct but a normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia and a one month delay would push definitive surgery past the 60 day Kasai window when outcomes fall sharply; urgent referral is required regardless of the ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when there are five or more days of fever with only two or three classical features plus supportive laboratory findings.
