This child has bilateral non exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips and extremity oedema plus six supportive lab features. Under the AHA algorithm this warrants IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin. Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply after day 10 of illness so treatment cannot wait for classical criteria. Echocardiography is done at diagnosis and repeated at 1-2 weeks and 4-6 weeks.
key_points: AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria: fever with 2-3 features plus supportive labs
Supportive labs: albumin below 30, sodium below 135, sterile pyuria, anaemia, raised platelets, raised ALT, raised WCC
Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin without waiting for full features
Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply beyond day 10 of illness
explanation.pearls: Infants under 12 months present most often with incomplete Kawasaki and have the highest coronary aneurysm rate - a low threshold for IVIG in this group is life saving.

options.rationale: Six days of fever plus two of five classical features and multiple supportive laboratory findings (albumin below 30, sodium below 135, platelets rising, sterile pyuria, anaemia, raised ALT) meets the AHA algorithm for incomplete Kawasaki disease with more than three lab criteria. Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin without waiting for full classical criteria to prevent coronary aneurysms. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Delaying treatment beyond day 10 of illness sharply increases the risk of coronary aneurysm; empirical antibiotics without response and negative cultures should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, not further watchful waiting. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

Corticosteroids are added to IVIG only for high risk patients (Kobayashi score high risk, under 12 months in Japanese cohorts) or for IVIG resistance; monotherapy corticosteroids are not first line and IVIG is still required. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

There is no seizure, focal neurology or altered consciousness to raise concern for HSV encephalitis, and the clinical and laboratory picture fits incomplete Kawasaki; empirical aciclovir does not address the coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

A miserable infant with six days of unremitting fever, incomplete Kawasaki features and rising markers cannot be discharged; missed Kawasaki disease can cause life threatening coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends observation for a minimum of four hours after the last adrenaline dose for children who required more than one dose, had persistent or protracted symptoms, or had features suggesting a biphasic reaction. This child had two doses and needs a further 3.5 hours of observation. On discharge every child needs an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan, a prescription for a weight banded adrenaline autoinjector (EpiPen Jr 150 microgram for 10-20 kg, EpiPen 300 microgram for 20 kg or more) and referral to a paediatric immunology or allergy service.
key_points: Observe a minimum of 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose if 2 or more doses needed
EpiPen Jr 150 mcg for 10-20 kg; EpiPen 300 mcg for 20 kg or more
Oral prednisolone does not reduce biphasic reactions
First anaphylaxis warrants immunology referral to identify the trigger
explanation.pearls: Antihistamines and steroids have never been shown to reduce biphasic anaphylaxis - they treat urticaria but do not replace observation time or adrenaline.

options.rationale: Deliberate re-exposure to the trigger after an anaphylactic reaction is contraindicated and would not be done as an inpatient challenge; if food challenge is needed it is done later in a supervised immunology setting after negative testing. (Source: ASCIA food allergy guidelines)

ASCIA specifies a minimum observation of four hours after the last adrenaline dose in a child needing more than one dose; discharging at 30 minutes exposes the child to a missed biphasic reaction without adrenaline access at hospital. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

A 24 hour admission is not required after a first anaphylaxis that has responded well; oral prednisolone does not reduce biphasic reactions and is not recommended in ASCIA guidance. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

ASCIA guidance requires a minimum of four hours observation after the last adrenaline dose in a child who had more than one dose or persistent symptoms; the 30 minute mark from the second dose is short of that. Immunology referral is standard for a first anaphylactic reaction to identify the trigger. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

This child weighs 18 kg so the correct device is EpiPen Jr 150 microgram (10-20 kg band); EpiPen 300 microgram is for children 20 kg and above. Antihistamines relieve urticaria but have no role in the immediate anaphylaxis pathway. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

explanation.summary: Clinical cerebral oedema complicates 0.5-1% of paediatric DKA episodes and has a mortality of about 20% with major morbidity in survivors. Risk factors present here include age under 12, new onset, severe acidosis on admission and a rapid rise in corrected sodium. The Muir criteria triad of headache, vomiting and altered conscious state with Cushing response (hypertension and relative bradycardia) mandates immediate hyperosmolar therapy - hypertonic saline 2.7% at 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg - alongside head elevation, halving the fluid rate and PICU escalation. Do not delay for imaging.
key_points: Diagnose cerebral oedema clinically, treat before imaging
Hyperosmolar therapy: 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce fluid rate to two thirds maintenance, head up 30 degrees
Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except for life threatening hyperkalaemia
explanation.pearls: The classic warning is a rise in blood pressure with a fall in heart rate during DKA resuscitation - it is a Cushing response and not a sign the child is recovering.

options.rationale: Increasing insulin and giving further boluses worsen cerebral oedema by lowering osmolality and dropping glucose too fast; the presenting problem is not persistent acidosis but neurological deterioration during resuscitation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Drowsiness, headache, vomiting, hypertension with relative bradycardia (Cushing response) four hours into DKA fluids in a child under 12 with severe presentation defines clinical cerebral oedema; treatment is hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg 2.7% or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), head elevation, fluid restriction to 2/3 maintenance and immediate PICU involvement. (Source: BSPED/ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline 2020; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk and is contraindicated except for life threatening hyperkalaemia; it will not reverse the neurological deterioration and may worsen it. (Source: ISPAD 2022; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Clinical cerebral oedema is a treat first diagnosis - CT is often normal early and delays hyperosmolar therapy; the child should be treated on clinical grounds and imaged only if she stabilises or the diagnosis is unclear. (Source: BSPED/ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline 2020)

Reducing insulin without addressing the raised intracranial pressure does not treat the cerebral oedema, and stopping dextrose risks rebound ketosis; the priority is hyperosmolar therapy and PICU escalation, not a tweak to insulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: In a child aged 6 to 24 months who has a first typical urinary tract infection with rapid clinical response and documented normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound, dimercaptosuccinic acid or micturating cystourethrogram. Ultrasound during the acute illness is reserved for features of atypical infection, and the dimercaptosuccinic acid and micturating cystourethrogram cascade is NICE, not RCH. Safety netting for recurrent fever and prompt clean catch urine at re-presentation is the appropriate plan. Documented antenatal monitoring and prompt clinical response together carry weight.
key_points: Atypical urinary tract infection triggers ultrasound during illness: poor response at 48 hours, non-Escherichia coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine.
Dimercaptosuccinic acid and micturating cystourethrogram are NOT in the RCH cascade after a first typical infection.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for demonstrated high grade vesicoureteric reflux or recurrence, not routine first infection.
explanation.pearls: For an 18-month-old girl with a first Escherichia coli urinary tract infection that responds within 48 hours and normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH advises safety net advice with no routine imaging.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Paediatric urinary tract infection

options.rationale: For a first typical urinary tract infection in a child aged 6 to 24 months who responds to antibiotics within 48 hours, has documented normal antenatal kidney imaging and no risk features for atypical infection, RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound; safety netting for recurrence is the appropriate plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection: poor response after 48 hours of antibiotics, non-Escherichia coli organism, sepsis, abdominal or bladder mass, or raised creatinine. None of those apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

The dimercaptosuccinic acid renal cortical scan is a NICE pathway construct, not part of the RCH imaging cascade. RCH does not use routine dimercaptosuccinic acid to assess scarring in a typical first infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Micturating cystourethrogram is invasive, carries a radiation and infection risk, and is not part of the RCH cascade after a first typical urinary tract infection in this age group. Reserve for recurrent infection or a hydronephrotic kidney on ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Long term antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a first typical infection in a child of this age without demonstrated high grade vesicoureteric reflux or an abnormal urinary tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: RCH recommends low flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min titrated to an SpO2 target of 90% as the first line for hypoxic bronchiolitis, with review at 60 to 120 minutes. High flow is not the first line and is reserved for children who deteriorate or do not improve on low flow after 2 hours. Salbutamol, hypertonic saline and steroids are not routinely recommended under 12 months. Oxygen is the primary supportive treatment; hydration by nasogastric or intravenous route is added as feeding deteriorates.
key_points: First line oxygen in bronchiolitis is nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, target SpO2 90% under RCH.
High flow nasal cannula is a rescue after failure of low flow at 2 hours, not the initial setting.
Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline and steroids are not routinely used in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: For a 7-month-old with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis and SpO2 87%, start low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min to a target 90%; do not open with high flow.

options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants who fail low flow after 2 hours; starting straight on high flow is not the RCH first line and can commit an infant to a higher acuity area unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

First line oxygen for bronchiolitis is low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, titrated to SpO2 target 90% (not 92 to 94%); escalation to high flow is considered if low flow fails after 2 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Nebulised bronchodilators are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and delay appropriate oxygen and feeding assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway and has no reliable short stay benefit; it does not address the immediate hypoxia. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Isolated tachypnoea in an infant who is not exhausted, apnoeic or unresponsive is not an indication for intubation; escalate through low flow then high flow first. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis fluid management uses an initial 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus only if perfusion demands, then maintenance plus a capped 5 to 7 percent deficit spread evenly over 48 hours with isotonic fluid containing 40 mmol/L potassium once serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L and urine output is established. Insulin runs at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour, started at least 1 hour after fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk. Dextrose is added when blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L rather than dropping the insulin rate first. The disconfirming feature that kills the more aggressive options is the drowsy state on presentation, which raises baseline cerebral oedema risk.
key_points: Deficit is capped at 5 to 7 percent and replaced over 48 hours to minimise cerebral oedema.
Insulin starts 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Add dextrose when blood glucose falls under 15 mmol/L; do not reduce insulin first.
explanation.pearls: For a 28 kg child with pH 7.05, use isotonic fluid at maintenance plus 5 to 7 percent deficit over 48 hours, potassium 40 mmol/L once safe, insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour started 1 hour later.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus 2022: DKA and hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state

options.rationale: The maintenance plus deficit approach is right but the deficit is capped at 5 to 7 percent regardless of clinical estimate and must be replaced over 48 hours using isotonic fluid with potassium; insulin should be at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour and started at least 1 hour after fluids. Adding 20 mmol/L potassium is only appropriate once serum potassium is known to be <5.5 mmol/L and urine output confirmed; this option is close but misses the potassium detail and the insulin dose caveat that the 40 mmol/L potassium, 0.05 units/kg/hour option addresses. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Aggressive fluid boluses beyond an initial 10 mL/kg (repeated only for persistent shock) increase the risk of cerebral oedema. Insulin should not be started immediately as it worsens fluid shifts and cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

RCH and ISPAD advise capped deficit of 5 to 7 percent regardless of estimate, replaced over 48 hours using isotonic fluid with 40 mmol/L potassium once serum potassium is <5.5 mmol/L and urine output established, insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour started 1 hour after fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Half normal saline as initial fluid and replacement over 24 hours are associated with rapid corrected sodium change and higher risk of cerebral oedema; RCH uses isotonic fluid, spread rehydration over 48 hours, and adds dextrose only once blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Running fluids at 2 times maintenance during initial rehydration exceeds RCH capped rates, increases the risk of cerebral oedema, and starting insulin simultaneously worsens osmotic shift. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: A 6-week-old with fever >=38.0 degC needs a full septic screen and empirical intravenous antibiotics regardless of how well or unwell they look, because clinical assessment poorly discriminates serious bacterial infection under 3 months. RCH recommends lumbar puncture with cefotaxime plus ampicillin/amoxicillin (for Listeria) plus aciclovir until herpes simplex encephalitis is excluded. Waiting for biomarkers to trend or discharging on oral antibiotics both risk missing bacterial meningitis or bacteraemia. This pathway is stricter than that used in older children where a source-driven approach is acceptable.
key_points: Fever under 3 months: full septic screen including lumbar puncture where safe.
Empirical cover: IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus aciclovir until herpes simplex encephalitis excluded.
Clinical wellness and normal C reactive protein do not exclude serious bacterial infection in this age.
explanation.pearls: A 6-week-old with a documented temperature of 38.4 degC gets lumbar puncture plus IV cefotaxime, amoxicillin and aciclovir even if he brightens briefly on the parent's lap.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in neonates and infants

options.rationale: Any infant under 3 months with a temperature >=38.0 degC requires a full septic screen and empirical antibiotics; discharge without treatment carries an unacceptable meningitis and bacteraemia miss rate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

Oral antibiotics do not achieve reliable central nervous system penetration for bacterial meningitis and deferring lumbar puncture undertreats a serious bacterial infection risk in a 6-week-old. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

C reactive protein trends do not exclude bacterial meningitis in this age group; deferring the lumbar puncture to observe biomarkers is not the RCH pathway for an under 3-month-old with fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

For any infant under 3 months with fever, RCH advises full septic screen including a lumbar puncture where safe, followed by empirical IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover under 1 month; broadly used to under 2 to 3 months in some pathways) plus IV aciclovir until herpes simplex is excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

The child is not shocked or hypoxic and does not need high flow or a fluid bolus; the immediate priority is the septic screen and empirical antibiotics, not paediatric intensive care unit transfer. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup as a single dose, escalating to 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup with stridor at rest, respiratory distress or agitation. Nebulised adrenaline is added for moderate to severe cases and needs 3 hours minimum observation after the last nebule. The stridor is present only when upset and the child settles on his father's lap, which places him in the mild category and rules out the higher dose. Prednisolone is a fallback where dexamethasone is unavailable.
key_points: Mild/moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose.
Severe croup with stridor at rest: 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000, observe 3 hours.
Nebulised budesonide is a fallback when oral steroid cannot be given.
explanation.pearls: Stridor only when upset with normal air entry and no recession at rest is mild croup; give 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone, not 0.6 mg/kg.

options.rationale: Prednisolone is used in some services but dexamethasone is preferred for its longer half life and lower recurrence of symptoms in the following 24 hours; RCH lists dexamethasone first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised budesonide is a second line option when oral dexamethasone is not tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred as first line where available. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest; steroid should be given in mild and moderate cases and this child qualifies for oral dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

0.6 mg/kg is only indicated for severe croup with stridor at rest and increased work of breathing; this child is mild with stridor only when upset and does not need tertiary retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; escalate to 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup with stridor at rest. Observation for 30 minutes is standard before discharge if he remains well. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines use a banded weight table for intramuscular adrenaline: 150 microg for children 10 to 20 kg (equivalent to an EpiPen Junior), 300 microg for 20 kg and over, and 500 microg for large adolescents and adults. Doses are drawn from 1:1000 ampoule (or delivered by autoinjector) and given into the mid anterolateral thigh. Repeat every 5 minutes if the patient has not improved. 1:10,000 adrenaline is reserved for intravenous or intraosseous rescue and 10 microg/kg arithmetic is not the AU standard because banded dosing is faster and safer under stress.
key_points: ASCIA banded intramuscular adrenaline: 10 to 20 kg = 150 microg; 20 kg and over = 300 microg.
Intramuscular route into anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes.
1:10,000 preparation is for intravenous or intraosseous administration only, not intramuscular.
explanation.pearls: A 16 kg child in anaphylaxis gets 150 microg (0.15 mL of 1:1000) intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh - the banded ASCIA dose, not 10 microg/kg arithmetic.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: ASCIA uses a banded weight table with 150 microg (0.15 mL 1:1000) for children 10 to 20 kg, given intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeatable every 5 minutes as required. This is the AU standard rather than the 10 microg/kg arithmetic approach. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: 300 microg (EpiPen dose) is the banded dose for children 20 kg and over; this child is 16 kg and falls into the 10 to 20 kg band, so the 150 microg dose is correct. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: 10 microg/kg arithmetic is not the AU banded standard, the 1:10,000 preparation is for intravenous or intraosseous rescue only, and the deltoid site is inferior to the anterolateral thigh in emergency doses. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after intramuscular doses have failed, given in a monitored high dependency or paediatric intensive care setting. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis; hydrocortisone is second line and not the first drug. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: A shocked 3-year-old with a potassium of 2.4 mmol/L is at high risk of arrhythmia and arrest, particularly under catecholamine infusion. The Australian paediatric sepsis pathway prioritises antibiotics within the hour, up to 60 mL/kg fluid in aliquots and early vasopressor via peripheral or intraosseous route; once refractory, the next competing priorities are correcting severe electrolyte disturbance and moving from peripheral adrenaline to noradrenaline via central access. Rapid potassium bolus is unsafe; instead a monitored infusion of 0.5 mmol/kg/hour balances speed and safety. Steroid, ventilation and renal replacement each have narrower roles and do not address the immediate arrhythmia risk.
key_points: Severe hypokalaemia in septic shock is arrhythmogenic and must be corrected by infusion, not bolus.
Standard paediatric potassium replacement is up to 0.5 mmol/kg/hour with continuous cardiac monitoring.
Central noradrenaline is preferred to escalating peripheral adrenaline once catecholamine resistance emerges.
explanation.pearls: In a shocked child with potassium 2.4 mmol/L, run a monitored potassium infusion at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour and prepare to switch to central noradrenaline; do not bolus potassium or push more crystalloid.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Paediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock

options.rationale: Further crystalloid beyond 60 mL/kg without addressing severe hypokalaemia risks hyperchloraemic acidosis and pulmonary oedema and does not treat the arrhythmogenic potassium; further volume before correcting potassium is not the appropriate step. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

Severe hypokalaemia at 2.4 mmol/L in a shocked child is arrhythmogenic and precipitates cardiac arrest particularly during catecholamine therapy; the correct step is to begin controlled potassium replacement at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour under continuous monitoring while maintaining current inotropic support until central access allows noradrenaline. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

Rapid potassium bolus is contraindicated because of high arrhythmia risk; the recommended rate is 0.5 mmol/kg/hour via continuous infusion with cardiac monitoring, not a bolus. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

Hydrocortisone is reasonable in catecholamine resistant shock but is not the pre eminent step here; ignoring an arrhythmogenic potassium of 2.4 mmol/L exposes the child to sudden arrest and it should be corrected in parallel or ahead of steroid consideration. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

Intubation and renal replacement are not indicated at present given adequate oxygenation and moderate lactate; both delay the immediate correction of the arrhythmogenic hypokalaemia and could precipitate arrest during induction. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

explanation.summary: d-transposition of the great arteries places the pulmonary and systemic circulations in parallel; adequate mixing depends on the atrial septum, ventricular septum or ductus arteriosus. When the ventricular septum is intact and the atrial communication is restrictive, oxygenation cannot improve with prostaglandin E1 alone because there is minimal ductal mixing available. Emergency balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) under echocardiographic guidance enlarges the interatrial communication, increases mixing and buys time for the arterial switch operation. Prostaglandin continues but is not the answer to persistent cyanosis in this specific anatomy.
key_points: d-transposition: systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel; oxygenation depends on mixing.
Restrictive atrial communication in d-transposition demands balloon atrial septostomy, not more prostaglandin.
Arterial switch is the surgical goal; septostomy is the temporising manoeuvre.
explanation.pearls: For d-transposition of the great arteries with intact ventricular septum and restrictive atrial communication and persistent cyanosis on prostaglandin E1, the temporising manoeuvre is a balloon atrial septostomy.

sources.label: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook
AAP/RCPCH neonatal cyanotic congenital heart disease review

options.rationale: In d-transposition with a restrictive atrial septum, further ductal opening does not improve mixing because the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel; nitric oxide can worsen the mismatch. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.rationale: Cessation of prostaglandin E1 removes a small source of mixing at the duct; inotrope alone does not treat the parallel circulation and induced hypothermia is not the immediate step for a duct dependent lesion. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.rationale: In d-transposition of the great arteries with an intact ventricular septum and restrictive atrial communication, cyanosis is due to inadequate mixing at atrial level; a balloon atrial septostomy performed under echocardiographic guidance improves mixing and is a temporising manoeuvre before the arterial switch. Prostaglandin alone is insufficient when the atrial septum is restrictive. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.rationale: Hyperventilation and hyperoxia in a parallel circulation do not increase mixing and can be harmful; the driver of hypoxia here is inadequate atrial mixing not pulmonary vascular resistance. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.rationale: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is not a peripheral bedside procedure in a regional nursery and does not address the anatomical problem; balloon atrial septostomy under echocardiographic guidance is the standard temporising step. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

explanation.summary: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a school-aged child is treated after conservative measures (reward chart, fluid timing, constipation exclusion, sleep disordered breathing exclusion) fail. Two first line active therapies are enuresis alarm (highest sustained cure rate but 8 to 12 weeks to work) and desmopressin (rapid response, useful for camps or sleepovers, but relapse on cessation is common). A specific short deadline favours desmopressin cover with a plan for the alarm afterwards. Anticholinergics are reserved for detrusor overactivity or combined therapy after first line failure.
key_points: Enuresis alarm is the highest sustained cure rate therapy but needs 8 to 12 weeks to work.
Desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer (or 200 microg tablet) at bedtime is preferred for short term cover such as camps.
Anticholinergics are reserved for detrusor overactivity or combination therapy after first line failure.
explanation.pearls: For a 6 week camp deadline: desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer at bedtime with strict evening fluid restriction; plan an enuresis alarm as durable therapy after the camp.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis
International Children's Continence Society standardisation on monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis

options.rationale: Reward charts alone have already failed after a 3 month trial; escalation to an active therapy is indicated with a defined event in 6 weeks. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.rationale: Enuresis alarms are the most effective first line therapy for durable cure (evidence-based number needed to treat around 2) but need at least 8 weeks and are not suited to a 6 week camp deadline. Explain benefits and offer as durable therapy after the camp. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.rationale: Anticholinergics are used in enuresis with detrusor overactivity or when desmopressin plus alarm have failed; they are not first line for primary monosymptomatic enuresis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.rationale: In primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis at age 7 with a specific short term social need (camp in 6 weeks), desmopressin sublingual wafer 120 microg (or 200 microg tablet) at bedtime with strict evening fluid restriction is the recommended short term option; the durable therapy is an enuresis alarm and should be planned once the deadline passes. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.rationale: Urodynamics is not indicated in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis with a normal examination and negative urinalysis; workup can be entirely non-invasive. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

explanation.summary: Neonatal testicular torsion often occurs prenatally or perinatally; the testis at birth is typically necrotic and non salvageable. The critical clinical decision is not testicular salvage but protection of the contralateral testis by fixation at the same operation. Bell clapper anatomy predisposes to bilateral torsion and metachronous loss. Ultrasound with Doppler helps confirm loss of flow but does not delay operative planning. Post operatively, parents require counselling about fertility, testosterone monitoring at puberty and consideration of testicular prosthesis at adolescence.
key_points: Neonatal torsion at birth is almost always non salvageable prenatal torsion.
Contralateral orchidopexy at the same operation is the critical intervention because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral.
Repeat imaging delays care and does not change the plan of urgent exploration and fixation.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal firm blue hemiscrotum with absent Doppler flow: urgent scrotal exploration; left orchidectomy plus right orchidopexy to protect the contralateral testis from metachronous torsion.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline
American Urological Association guideline on testicular torsion in the neonate

options.rationale: Manual detorsion is not appropriate in the neonate; the neonatal scrotum requires operative exploration. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.rationale: Observation risks loss of the contralateral testis if bell clapper anatomy is present; contralateral fixation is prioritised. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.rationale: Neonatal torsion presenting at birth with a firm discoloured testis and absent Doppler flow is almost always non salvageable prenatal or perinatal torsion. Contralateral orchidopexy at the same operation is essential because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral, risking metachronous torsion of the only remaining testis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.rationale: Contralateral orchidopexy is essential because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral; failing to fix the right testis risks metachronous torsion. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.rationale: Serial imaging delays care; the plan is defined by the clinical finding of a firm, discoloured neonatal testis and absent Doppler flow. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

explanation.summary: Acute otitis externa is diagnosed clinically by canal inflammation and tragal or pinna tenderness. First line therapy in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines is aural toilet plus a topical antimicrobial with a corticosteroid such as ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops, with pool avoidance until symptoms resolve. Systemic antibiotics are added for cellulitis spread beyond the canal. Necrotising otitis externa is suspected in diabetics or immunocompromised patients with severe pain, granulation tissue at the bony cartilaginous junction, or cranial nerve palsy; it needs urgent ear nose throat specialist review, imaging and intravenous ciprofloxacin. If the tympanic membrane is perforated or grommets are present, an aminoglycoside containing drop is avoided.
key_points: First line: aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops for 7 days.
Oral antibiotics only if cellulitis extends beyond the canal or in immunocompromise.
Avoid aminoglycoside drops with perforated tympanic membrane or grommets.
explanation.pearls: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane: aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone 5 drops twice daily for 7 days, plus pool avoidance until symptoms resolve.

sources.label: American Academy of Otolaryngology Clinical Practice Guideline on Acute Otitis Externa

options.rationale: Systemic antibiotics are not first line for uncomplicated otitis externa; topical therapy achieves higher local concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

First line therapy for acute otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines is aural toilet (wick or microsuction) plus topical ciprofloxacin 0.3 percent plus dexamethasone 0.1 percent 5 drops twice daily for 7 days, with pool avoidance until symptoms resolve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
Aluminium acetate has some effect but topical antimicrobial therapy is more effective; it is not first line monotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
Irrigation risks worsening the canal maceration; aural toilet by trained personnel plus topical antibiotic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

Oral ciprofloxacin is reserved for otitis externa with cellulitis extending beyond the canal, malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, or refractory disease; it is not first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

explanation.summary: Metformin is a recommended adjunct to intensified lifestyle intervention in adolescents (10 years or older) with obesity and impaired glucose regulation, defined as impaired fasting glucose 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L, impaired glucose tolerance (2 hour 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L), or haemoglobin A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent, when lifestyle alone is inadequate. Standard titration is extended release 500 mg daily up to 2 g daily over 4 weeks. Liraglutide 3 mg is TGA registered from age 12 for adolescent obesity but is not first line for dysglycaemia. Bariatric surgery is reserved for body mass index over 40 or over 35 with severe comorbidity after failed intensive therapy. Screen for polycystic ovary syndrome, non alcoholic fatty liver disease and obstructive sleep apnoea.
key_points: Metformin is first line pharmacotherapy in adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation after failed lifestyle intervention.
Titrate extended release 500 mg daily up to 2 g daily over 4 weeks.
Bariatric surgery: body mass index >=40 or >=35 with severe comorbidity after failed intensive medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: Adolescent obesity with impaired glucose tolerance after failed 6 month lifestyle program: add metformin extended release 500 mg daily titrated to 2 g daily over 4 weeks alongside continued lifestyle intervention.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Obesity in Children Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after failure of intensified pharmacological and lifestyle programs and typically at body mass index >=40 or >=35 with severe comorbidity; not first line here. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Orlistat is not first line pharmacotherapy for adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation; metformin is preferred when dysglycaemia is present. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Liraglutide 3 mg is TGA registered for adolescent obesity from age 12 but is not first line for impaired glucose regulation and access via the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme is limited. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Insulin is inappropriate for impaired glucose regulation without established diabetes; metformin is the recommended first line pharmacotherapy. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Metformin is a recommended adjunct to lifestyle intervention in adolescents 10 years and older with obesity and impaired glucose regulation (impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, or haemoglobin A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent) when lifestyle alone is inadequate. Titration from 500 mg daily to 2 g daily over 4 weeks is standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Frequently relapsing steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome is defined as at least 2 relapses in 6 months or at least 4 in 12 months, and steroid dependent as relapse during steroid taper or within 2 weeks of stopping. Both are indications for a steroid sparing agent alongside a fresh steroid induction, particularly if steroid toxicity is established. First line steroid sparing options in KDIGO are oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg), levamisole where available, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil. Rituximab is reserved for complicated cases after failure of a conventional steroid sparing agent. Renal biopsy is not required before a steroid sparing trial in typical steroid sensitive disease.
key_points: Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome: >=2 relapses in 6 months or >=4 in 12 months.
Steroid sparing options include cyclophosphamide, levamisole, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil.
Rituximab reserved for complicated disease after conventional agents fail.
explanation.pearls: Fourth relapse with steroid toxicity: prednisolone induction and taper alongside cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg) as the steroid sparing agent.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Nephrotic Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Rituximab is reserved for complicated frequently relapsing or steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome that has failed a conventional steroid sparing oral agent; it is not first line here. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.rationale: Continued repeated steroid courses without a sparing agent worsen the established steroid toxicity; a steroid sparing agent is indicated. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.rationale: Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome with prompt response does not require biopsy before a steroid sparing trial; biopsy is considered if steroid resistant or atypical features are present. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.rationale: Frequently relapsing (>=2 relapses in 6 months or >=4 in 12 months) or steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome with steroid toxicity is an indication for a steroid sparing agent alongside a fresh steroid induction. Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg) is a standard KDIGO first line steroid sparing option; levamisole (where available), calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil are alternatives. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are antiproteinuric adjuncts, not induction therapy for active nephrotic relapse; induction plus steroid sparing is required. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

explanation.summary: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children is defined by fever, laboratory evidence of inflammation, evidence of multiorgan involvement (cardiac, renal, respiratory, haematological, gastrointestinal, dermatological or neurological), recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or seropositivity, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses. It typically presents in older children (median 8 to 10 years) with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, lymphopenia, elevated ferritin and troponin, and myocardial dysfunction. Kawasaki disease occurs mainly in children under 5, with normal or elevated platelet count and coronary artery aneurysm as the classic cardiac lesion. Initial management shares intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg but multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children also uses methylprednisolone and consideration of anakinra or infliximab in refractory cases.
key_points: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children: older age, prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, elevated troponin, myocardial dysfunction.
Kawasaki disease: median age under 5, normal or elevated platelets, coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiogram.
Both treated with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg; multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children adds methylprednisolone.
explanation.pearls: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children differentiators: older age (median 8 to 10 years), prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, elevated troponin, myocardial dysfunction rather than coronary aneurysm, plus recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or IgG positivity.

sources.label: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children
American College of Rheumatology Clinical Guidance for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.rationale: Bilateral non purulent conjunctivitis is a classic feature of both conditions and does not discriminate. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.rationale: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children typically presents in older children (median 8 to 10 years), with prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia early, myocardial dysfunction with elevated troponin, and a recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or seropositivity. Classic Kawasaki disease is a disease of children under 5 with a normal or elevated platelet count and coronary artery aneurysm rather than global left ventricular dysfunction as the cardiac lesion. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.rationale: Fever and rash are shared features; they do not discriminate. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.rationale: Cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm and mucous membrane changes are shared features of both conditions, so they do not separate them. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.rationale: Extremity oedema and rash are classic Kawasaki disease features and do not discriminate multisystem inflammatory syndrome. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

explanation.summary: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia presents with severe isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well neonate of a mother with a normal platelet count, most commonly due to maternal antibody against fetal HPA-1a inherited from the father. Intracranial haemorrhage risk is 10 to 20 percent, often in utero, and can occur despite in utero intravenous immunoglobulin. Treatment of severe thrombocytopenia (<30 x10^9/L) is human platelet antigen matched (HPA-1a negative) platelet transfusion plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg. Maternal washed and irradiated apheresis platelets are a backup. Antenatal management of subsequent pregnancies with weekly maternal intravenous immunoglobulin from 20 to 26 weeks is standard.
key_points: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: severe isolated thrombocytopenia in a well neonate with a maternal normal platelet count.
Treatment: HPA-1a negative platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg.
Intracranial haemorrhage risk is 10 to 20 percent, often in utero, mandating urgent transfusion at platelets below 30 x10^9/L.
explanation.pearls: Severe neonatal thrombocytopenia (platelets 15) with a well mother and no maternal platelet drop is neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: HPA-1a negative platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg immediately.

sources.label: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia
International Collaboration on Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia recommendations

options.rationale: Suspected neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia with severe thrombocytopenia (<30 x10^9/L) is treated with human platelet antigen matched platelet transfusion (HPA-1a negative if the antigen is unknown, since HPA-1a is the most common alloantigen in Caucasian populations), plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg to reduce further platelet destruction and prolong response duration. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.rationale: Random donor platelets are consumed by the maternal antibody within hours; the response is transient and poor. Human platelet antigen matched platelets are preferred. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.rationale: Maternal platelets require apheresis, washing to remove antibody and irradiation to prevent graft versus host disease; they take time and are used if human platelet antigen matched platelets are unavailable. Corticosteroids have limited evidence in the neonate. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.rationale: Severe thrombocytopenia in a neonate with intracranial haemorrhage risk requires urgent transfusion regardless of clinical bleeding; the intracranial haemorrhage risk (10 to 20 percent, often in utero) mandates prompt correction. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma does not correct platelet count and is not appropriate treatment for immune thrombocytopenia. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Severe combined immunodeficiency is a paediatric emergency with mortality close to 100 percent by age 2 without haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Live vaccines including rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella and measles-mumps-rubella can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease and must be avoided. Diagnosis is confirmed by absent T cell receptor excision circles and profoundly low CD3 (and often CD19 and natural killer) counts. Management is immediate protective isolation, Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, treatment of opportunistic infections, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative cellular blood products, and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Family counselling is essential for future pregnancies; T cell receptor excision circle newborn screening is now standard in several AU jurisdictions.
key_points: Severe combined immunodeficiency requires urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant; untreated mortality is close to 100 percent by 2 years.
All cellular blood products must be irradiated and cytomegalovirus negative.
All live vaccines (rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella, measles-mumps-rubella) are contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: Severe combined immunodeficiency (absent T cell receptor excision circles, CD3 <0.05, and vaccine strain rotavirus enteritis): protective isolation, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative blood products, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant workup.

sources.label: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Primary Immunodeficiency Guideline

options.rationale: Treating opportunistic infections alone without immediate immunology and transplant referral misses the diagnosis window; severe combined immunodeficiency mortality without haematopoietic stem cell transplant is 100 percent by 2 years. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.rationale: Home discharge is unsafe with severe combined immunodeficiency and active Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus and vaccine strain rotavirus enteritis; specialist inpatient management with isolation is essential. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.rationale: Severe combined immunodeficiency confirmed by absent T cell receptor excision circles and profoundly low CD3, CD19 and natural killer cells requires immediate protective isolation, use of irradiated cytomegalovirus negative cellular blood products (to prevent transfusion associated graft versus host disease), Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, avoidance of all live vaccines and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant workup because untreated mortality is close to 100 percent by 2 years. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.rationale: Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe combined immunodeficiency; live rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella and measles-mumps-rubella vaccines can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.rationale: Corticosteroids in undiagnosed severe combined immunodeficiency will worsen opportunistic infections; the priority is diagnosis and transplant referral. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is managed supportively with feeding support and oxygen. Low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min is the first line respiratory support, titrated to SpO2 of at least 90 percent. High flow nasal cannula is a second line intervention for infants failing low flow after 1 to 2 hours, not a first choice. Bronchodilators, adrenaline, corticosteroids and antibiotics have no routine role.
key_points: Low flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min is first line; target SpO2 at or above 90 percent.
High flow nasal cannula is second line after failure of low flow.
Bronchodilators, nebulised adrenaline and corticosteroids do not change outcomes in viral bronchiolitis.
explanation.pearls: SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent on room air; start low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min and reassess before escalating to high flow.

options.rationale: Bronchiolitis with SpO2 below 90 percent and moderate work of breathing needs low flow nasal oxygen first line, titrated to a target SpO2 of at least 90 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

High flow is reserved for infants who fail a trial of low flow oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min after at least 1 to 2 hours; it is not the first respiratory step in ward level bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Nebulised salbutamol and adrenaline are not recommended in viral bronchiolitis under 12 months; they do not change length of stay or oxygen requirement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Corticosteroids have no role in acute viral bronchiolitis; delaying oxygen when SpO2 is already 89 percent is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
He is alert with only moderate recession and no apnoea; escalation should begin with the least invasive effective option, which is low flow oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Viral croup severity is graded by stridor and recession at rest. Mild and moderate croup are both treated with a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. The higher dose of 0.6 mg/kg with nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, defined by stridor and marked recession at rest with agitation or exhaustion. Observation for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline is required before discharge; a shorter period is acceptable after oral steroid alone.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
Observe for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline before considering discharge.
explanation.pearls: Stridor only on agitation with moderate recession is moderate croup: give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and observe for a few hours before discharge.

options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone plus nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession or exhaustion, not moderate croup that settles when calm. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Moderate croup is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; observation for a few hours is appropriate if there was no nebulised adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg is an alternative if dexamethasone is not available, but a single dose is used, not a 3 day course; observation before discharge is still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Humidified air alone does not improve viral croup and there is no evidence that dexamethasone increases bacterial tracheitis; steroid is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
There is no drooling, tripod posture or toxic appearance; empirical ceftriaxone and nasoendoscopy are not indicated for classic viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Any infant less than 3 months old with a documented temperature of at least 38 degC needs a full septic workup regardless of general appearance because the risk of serious bacterial infection is high and clinical assessment is unreliable at this age. Investigations include blood culture, urine by catheter or suprapubic aspirate and lumbar puncture, with empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin in Australia. Bag urine is not sent as a definitive specimen. Watching without investigation is unsafe.
key_points: Infant under 3 months with fever at or above 38 degC: full septic workup regardless of appearance.
Catheter or suprapubic urine, blood culture and lumbar puncture are all needed.
Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the standard neonatal regimen.
explanation.pearls: A well looking infant under 3 months with fever still needs a full septic screen and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; do not send bag urine alone or defer the lumbar puncture.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in Neonates

options.rationale: Well appearance in an infant under 3 months does not exclude serious bacterial infection; discharging without workup is unsafe at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

Under 3 months of age with fever, the required investigations include blood culture and lumbar puncture as well as urine; bag urine is unreliable and cannot be sent as the only investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

A rectal temperature of 38 degC or higher in an infant less than 3 months is a full septic workup indication irrespective of appearance, with empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

Lumbar puncture should not be deferred pending markers in an infant less than 6 weeks with fever unless there is a contraindication; ceftriaxone monotherapy is also not the preferred neonatal regimen. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)
Watchful waiting without investigation in an infant under 3 months with documented fever is unsafe and misses early treatable bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

explanation.summary: Severe acute asthma in a child needs immediate salbutamol delivered by spacer (12 puffs for over 6 years) every 20 minutes for the first hour, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg or intravenous methylprednisolone if oral not tolerated) and titrated oxygen to SpO2 above 94 percent. Ipratropium 8 puffs is added by spacer if the response is inadequate. Second line therapy is intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes for life threatening or non responding exacerbations, then intravenous salbutamol or aminophylline. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is pneumonia.
key_points: First hour: 12 puffs salbutamol via spacer every 20 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, titrated oxygen.
Add ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer if inadequate response in the first hour.
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg is second line for severe or non responding cases.
explanation.pearls: Severe childhood asthma first hour: back to back inhaled salbutamol 12 puffs every 20 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, titrated oxygen and add ipratropium for poor response.

options.rationale: Intravenous salbutamol is reserved for life threatening asthma failing inhaled therapy; inhaled salbutamol via spacer is first line even in severe cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

Intravenous magnesium sulfate is second line, reserved for severe or life threatening asthma not responding to initial salbutamol, prednisolone and ipratropium in the first hour. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

Nebulised adrenaline is not first line in asthma; dexamethasone is not the preferred oral corticosteroid; empirical antibiotics are not indicated for asthma exacerbations without pneumonia. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

In severe childhood asthma, first hour treatment is back to back salbutamol via spacer (or nebulised if unable), oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg and titrated oxygen; ipratropium is added if response is poor. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)
Inhaled corticosteroids are not effective for acute exacerbations; systemic corticosteroid is given in the first hour to reduce admission and relapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in infants presents with paroxysmal crying, drawing up the legs, vomiting and blood stained mucus in the nappy. Ultrasound target sign is diagnostic. Provided there is no peritonism, perforation on imaging, or refractory shock, first line treatment in Australia is air (pneumatic) enema reduction in interventional radiology after intravenous fluid resuscitation, blood cross match and antibiotic cover, with paediatric surgery on standby. Barium is avoided because of chemical peritonitis risk if perforation occurs. Surgery is reserved for peritonism, perforation, failed enema or a lead point.
key_points: Diagnosis by ultrasound target sign; look for signs of ischaemia and perforation before deciding.
Air enema is first line if no peritonism, perforation or refractory shock; resuscitate and give antibiotics first.
Surgery indications: peritonism, perforation, failed enema reduction or identified lead point.
explanation.pearls: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonism goes to air enema reduction after fluids, cross match and antibiotics; barium is not used because of chemical peritonitis risk.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Journal of Surgery Intussusception Position Statement

options.rationale: Barium is not used in AU centres because of chemical peritonitis risk if perforation occurs; pre procedure resuscitation and cross match are standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Bile stained vomiting alone is not a contraindication to air enema; without peritonism, perforation or shock, enema reduction is attempted first with surgical backup. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Osmotic laxatives are not used to reduce intussusception; observation alone risks progression to ischaemia and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Confirmed intussusception on ultrasound requires urgent reduction and admission; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Ileocolic intussusception without peritonism, perforation or shock is managed by air enema reduction after resuscitation, cross match and antibiotic cover, with surgery on standby. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management is guided by hour specific bilirubin nomograms with separate phototherapy and exchange transfusion thresholds and by risk factors including haemolytic pattern, prematurity and clinical instability. A positive direct antiglobulin test suggests ABO or rhesus haemolysis and lowers the treatment threshold. When bilirubin rises despite single surface phototherapy, the next step is intensive multiple surface phototherapy plus attention to hydration and feeding, with blood cross match in preparation for exchange. Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered if intensive phototherapy fails in immune haemolytic disease. Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin exceeds the exchange line or acute bilirubin encephalopathy develops.
key_points: Escalate to intensive phototherapy before considering exchange when bilirubin rises above threshold.
Positive direct antiglobulin test lowers thresholds and warrants cross match early.
Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg is second line after intensive phototherapy in immune haemolysis.
explanation.pearls: Rising serum bilirubin above threshold on single phototherapy with positive direct antiglobulin test: escalate to intensive multiple surface phototherapy, cross match blood and consider intravenous immunoglobulin before exchange.

options.rationale: Intensive multiple surface phototherapy is escalated first; exchange is reserved for failure to respond, or bilirubin above the exchange line, or acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

Bilirubin rising above the phototherapy line with a positive direct antiglobulin test in a haemolytic pattern needs intensive phototherapy and blood cross match while awaiting the response; exchange is not yet mandatory. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)
Stopping phototherapy in a haemolytic pattern with rising bilirubin above threshold risks progression to acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered in rhesus or ABO haemolytic disease not responding to intensive phototherapy, not before intensive phototherapy has been tried. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)
Single surface phototherapy has already failed to control the rise; delaying escalation for 12 hours risks bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Secondary prophylaxis after acute rheumatic fever prevents recurrent group A streptococcal infection and progression to rheumatic heart disease. In Australia the first line agent is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days. Duration is stratified by the episode and outcome: at least 10 years after the last episode or until age 21 (whichever is longer) for acute rheumatic fever without carditis; longer in the presence of persistent or worsening rheumatic heart disease. Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin twice daily is reserved for patients who cannot receive intramuscular therapy. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from high risk communities have a high recurrence risk that justifies the longer duration.
key_points: First line: intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days.
Duration for acute rheumatic fever without carditis: at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin twice daily is second line for those unable to have intramuscular therapy.
explanation.pearls: Australian secondary prophylaxis for acute rheumatic fever is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer; longer if carditis or rheumatic heart disease is present.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Azithromycin is not the preferred agent in AU; duration is not 3 years and echocardiography is not used to decide when to stop. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)
Oral penicillin is second line only if intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin cannot be given; a 5 year fixed duration is not the AU standard. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

In Australia, secondary prophylaxis for acute rheumatic fever without carditis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer, especially in a high risk community. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)
Absence of carditis does not remove the need for prophylaxis; recurrent episodes are common and cause carditis on subsequent presentations. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)
The correct dosing interval is 28 days (or 21 days in special situations), not 12 weeks; prednisolone is not used for prevention. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis and often develops during the first 4 to 12 hours of treatment. Diagnostic clues include a falling Glasgow Coma Score, new headache, incontinence, bradycardia with rising blood pressure (Cushing response) and cranial nerve palsies. Australian paediatric guidelines require immediate osmotherapy with 3 percent hypertonic saline 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes or 20 percent mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg, reduction of intravenous fluid rate by around a third, head up positioning and urgent neurosurgical retrieval. Bicarbonate, further fluid boluses and rapid glucose falls are risk factors and should be avoided. Imaging must not delay osmotherapy when clinical criteria are met.
key_points: Cushing response and falling Glasgow Coma Score in DKA meet clinical criteria for cerebral oedema.
Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 2 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg immediately and reduce fluid rate.
Bicarbonate use, aggressive volume and rapid glucose fall are recognised risk factors.
explanation.pearls: New headache with falling Glasgow Coma Score and bradycardia and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment is cerebral oedema: give hypertonic 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 g/kg immediately, cut the fluid rate by a third and call retrieval.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and Hyperglycaemic Hyperosmolar State

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is not first line for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA; imaging must not delay osmotherapy when clinical criteria are met. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)
The clinical picture is Cushing response with intracranial hypertension, not hypovolaemia; further crystalloid bolus and higher rates worsen cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)
Bicarbonate is a recognised risk factor for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA and is not recommended; higher insulin does not treat cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

Falling Glasgow Coma Score, new headache and rising blood pressure with bradycardia meet AU paediatric DKA criteria for cerebral oedema; hypertonic saline (or 20 percent mannitol), fluid reduction and neurosurgical retrieval are first line. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)
Observation without acting on falling Glasgow Coma Score and Cushing response allows brainstem herniation; osmotherapy must not be delayed. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is managed with supportive care alone; bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated in the Australian guideline. Admission criteria in AU tertiary paediatric emergency departments include persistent room air SpO2 below 92 percent, feeding less than 50 to 75 percent of normal, moderate to severe work of breathing, apnoeas, dehydration, or clinician concern in a family without safe follow up. Low flow nasal cannula oxygen (up to 2 L per minute) is the first line respiratory support; high flow is reserved for those failing low flow, and continuous positive airway pressure or transfer to a paediatric intensive care unit is considered next. Feeding is often the earliest and most sensitive marker of severity.
key_points: AU admission triggers: SpO2 below 92% persistently, feeds less than 50 to 75% of normal, moderate to severe work of breathing.
Low flow nasal cannula oxygen is the first line respiratory support before high flow.
Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: Feeding under 50 to 75 percent of normal intake in a bronchiolitis infant is an admission trigger in its own right in the AU pathway even if the SpO2 is 92 percent or above.

options.rationale: Persistent SpO2 below 92 percent on room air in a bronchiolitis infant meets AU admission criteria; feeding below 50 to 75 percent of normal is a further indication and low flow oxygen with feed review is standard ward care. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Salbutamol trials are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and response is not a validated admission criterion in the AU pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated in acute viral bronchiolitis under 12 months and do not alter disposition. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Discharge is not safe with SpO2 below 92 percent and reduced feeding under 75 percent; both are AU admission triggers regardless of proximity to hospital. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

High flow is reserved for infants failing standard low flow oxygen or with moderate to severe work of breathing; escalation before a trial of low flow is not the AU first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Australian non-Aboriginal children under 2 years with bilateral disease or associated fever above 38 degC is a specific indication for immediate amoxicillin rather than observation with a delayed script. Unilateral disease in an older well child without fever can be managed with analgesia and a delayed prescription filled at 48 hours if symptoms persist. Amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days is first line; amoxicillin plus clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have a lower threshold for immediate antibiotics and longer courses because of higher rates of chronic suppurative otitis media.
key_points: Bilateral acute otitis media under 2 years or fever above 38 degC: immediate amoxicillin.
Unilateral acute otitis media in a well child over 2 years: delayed script at 48 hours is reasonable.
Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is second line for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours, not first line.
explanation.pearls: Immediate amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days is the AU first line for any child with bilateral acute otitis media under 2 years, not the delayed script offered in older well children.

options.rationale: Cephalosporins are not first line for uncomplicated acute otitis media in AU and add resistance risk without benefit over amoxicillin. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years or with fever above 38 degC is a specific AU indication for immediate amoxicillin rather than a delayed script or observation. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

Delayed prescription is offered for unilateral acute otitis media without fever in a well older child; bilateral disease under 2 years with fever needs immediate treatment. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)
Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48 to 72 hours of amoxicillin, not first line for a second episode months apart. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)
Tympanocentesis is reserved for treatment failure, immunocompromise or suppurative complications; it is not needed in an uncomplicated first presentation. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

explanation.summary: Australian law and Royal Australian College of General Practitioners guidance recognise Gillick competence for adolescents consenting to health care. A minor under 16 years assessed as understanding the nature, purpose and consequences of a treatment may consent without parental involvement. Mandatory reporting is triggered by exploitation, coercion, a significant age gap or a partner in a position of power, not by consensual activity between similarly aged 15-year-olds. Long-acting reversible contraception is the most effective option and should be offered at the same visit even when a specific method is requested. Confidentiality is central to adolescent engagement; disclosure without consent is only justified for a safeguarding risk.
key_points: Gillick competence allows minors under 16 to consent to their own health care in Australia.
Consensual sexual activity between similarly aged 15-year-olds is not automatically a mandatory report.
Offer long-acting reversible contraception at the same visit even when a specific method is requested.
explanation.pearls: A Gillick competent 15-year-old with no contraindications may be prescribed combined oral contraception confidentially in Australia; mandatory reporting only follows exploitation or a significant age gap, not similarly aged consensual sex.

sources.label: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework

options.rationale: Australian law recognises Gillick competence for consent to health care in minors; a 15-year-old assessed competent may consent without parental involvement. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

Breaching confidentiality without her consent is not lawful and undermines therapeutic engagement; disclosure is only mandated for a mandatory reporting risk. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)
