She meets Gillick competence with no contraindications; AU guidance actively promotes discussion of long-acting reversible contraception alongside prescribing the requested method. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

Condoms alone give inferior pregnancy protection and denying hormonal contraception to a competent adolescent is neither guideline concordant nor legally required. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

Consensual sexual activity between similarly aged 15-year-olds without exploitation is not a mandatory report in Victoria; a report here would breach confidentiality without cause. (Source: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework)
source_refs: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice in the first week is common; the Australian consensus phototherapy nomogram plots total serum bilirubin against age in hours and gestation. Values below the phototherapy line but within about 50 micromol/L of it, especially in the first 48 hours, warrant repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours because bilirubin can continue to rise. Direct antiglobulin negativity and maternal group compatibility make isolated ABO or rhesus haemolytic disease unlikely, but ongoing tracking is still required until levels plateau. Breastfeeding support, adequate hydration and follow up review are the mainstays; formula top ups are not first line in a well feeding baby with normal weight loss and urine output. Early discharge without a repeat bilirubin risks missing a crossing trajectory.
key_points: Values within about 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy line under 48 hours need repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours.
The AU consensus nomogram is plotted by age in hours and gestation.
Support breastfeeding; formula top ups are not first line in a well feeding baby with normal weight loss.
explanation.pearls: A term breastfed newborn with a bilirubin within 50 micromol/L of the AU phototherapy line under 48 hours needs a repeat serum bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours to plot the trajectory, not immediate phototherapy or discharge.

options.rationale: Her serum bilirubin sits below the phototherapy line and there is no evidence of severe or rapidly rising haemolytic jaundice to warrant intensive phototherapy or exchange preparation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Formula top ups are not first line in a well established breastfed baby with normal weight loss and normal urine output; repeat bilirubin remains needed to check trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

A bilirubin within 40 to 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy line at under 48 hours needs repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours; discharge without follow up risks missing a crossing trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

AU practice for a bilirubin within about 50 micromol/L of the line under 48 hours is to continue feeding, support breastfeeding and repeat in 12 to 24 hours to track the trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

There are no clinical features of sepsis in this well feeding afebrile baby; a septic screen and empiric antibiotics are not indicated for isolated jaundice within the safe zone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child with 5 or more days of fever and 2 or 3 principal clinical criteria plus supporting laboratory features because 15 to 20 percent of cases present incompletely. Supporting labs include C reactive protein above 30 mg/L or erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/hr, and 3 or more of hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase, thrombocytosis after day 7, leucocytosis and sterile pyuria. Baseline echocardiography looks for coronary artery abnormalities, but treatment should not wait for it if the diagnosis is otherwise clear. Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin (3 to 5 mg per kg daily until markers normalise and echocardiography is clear at 6 to 8 weeks) is first line. High risk patients may receive adjunctive corticosteroid.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: 5 or more days of fever, 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory features.
Supportive labs: CRP above 30, ESR above 40, plus 3 or more of low albumin, anaemia, ALT high, platelets high, WCC high, sterile pyuria.
First line: intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg plus low dose aspirin with baseline echocardiography.
explanation.pearls: Perineal desquamation and sterile pyuria are two supportive features that often clinch an incomplete Kawasaki diagnosis when the mucocutaneous criteria are incomplete; treat within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk.

options.rationale: Waiting for the classical 5 criteria misses the treatment window; supportive laboratory features with 2 criteria and fever above 5 days meet AU incomplete Kawasaki pathway thresholds. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Cultures are negative, viral panel negative and the picture (perineal desquamation, sterile pyuria, hepatitis, hyponatraemia, thrombocytosis) fits incomplete Kawasaki rather than a bacterial focus. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Intravenous immunoglobulin is first line in Kawasaki disease and should not be replaced by pulse steroid alone; steroid is added to high risk patients or given as rescue. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Delaying decision by a week risks coronary artery aneurysm; the syndrome fits incomplete Kawasaki now and IVIG is time critical within 10 days of fever onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Fever 5 or more days with 2 clinical criteria plus supportive labs (CRP above 30, ESR above 40, plus 3 or more of albumin low, anaemia, ALT elevated, platelets high, WCC high, sterile pyuria) meets AU incomplete Kawasaki criteria for IVIG and low dose aspirin with baseline echocardiography. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schoenlein purpura) is the commonest paediatric small vessel vasculitis and usually self limits. Renal involvement affects around a third of children in the first 6 months and is the main determinant of long term prognosis. All children with IgA vasculitis should have weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, fortnightly for 2 months, then monthly to 6 months. Persistent proteinuria above 100 mg per mmol for 4 or more weeks or any nephrotic range proteinuria (above 250 mg per mmol) triggers urgent nephrology referral and consideration of renal biopsy. Corticosteroids reduce joint and abdominal symptoms but do not prevent nephritis.
key_points: All IgA vasculitis children need urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for at least 6 months.
Protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol or persistent above 100 for 4 weeks triggers urgent nephrology referral.
Corticosteroids do not prevent nephritis; they reduce joint and abdominal symptoms only.
explanation.pearls: Nephrotic range proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol) with red cell casts in new IgA vasculitis is an AU trigger for urgent paediatric nephrology referral, not for empirical prednisolone alone.

options.rationale: Protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol (nephrotic range) or persistent above 100 for 4 or more weeks in IgA vasculitis is an AU trigger for urgent nephrology referral and biopsy consideration. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

Corticosteroids reduce arthralgia and abdominal pain but do not prevent renal disease; commencing empirically without nephrology input in nephrotic range proteinuria is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

Nephrotic range proteinuria with red cell casts is not benign and needs urgent specialist review; the standard weekly then monthly surveillance schedule assumes normal or trace urine findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

Angiotensin blockade is not first line in acute paediatric nephrotic range proteinuria without a diagnosis; nephrology guides use and biopsy comes first. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

Pulse steroid is a nephrology decision after biopsy in crescentic disease; discharge without nephrology input for nephrotic range proteinuria is unsafe. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

explanation.summary: Paediatric foreign body aspiration classically presents in a toddler with a witnessed choking episode followed by cough, wheeze or stridor. Peanuts, seeds and small toys are the commonest culprits. A normal supine inspiratory chest radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis; 20 percent of early films are normal. Expiratory films or lateral decubitus views may show unilateral air trapping. When history plus any of persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry are present, rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not wait for advanced imaging. Delayed diagnosis risks obstructive pneumonia, atelectasis and bronchiectasis.
key_points: Witnessed choking with persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry mandates rigid bronchoscopy.
A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude foreign body aspiration.
Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and comes before computed tomography.
explanation.pearls: In a toddler with a witnessed choke and a focal wheeze, rigid bronchoscopy is indicated even with a normal chest radiograph; up to 20 percent of early films are read normal in confirmed foreign body aspiration.

options.rationale: A witnessed peanut aspiration with a focal wheeze is a strong clinical indication for bronchoscopy regardless of a normal saturation and an initially normal radiograph; early chest films are normal in around 20 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

A history of witnessed choking with any of persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry meets AU indications for rigid bronchoscopy even with a normal radiograph. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

Expiratory or decubitus views can support the diagnosis but a normal series does not exclude foreign body; clinical history plus focal signs still mandates bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)
A witnessed choke and focal wheeze is not viral wheeze; bronchodilators and steroids risk masking the picture and delay definitive bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

Radiation is not first line when the pretest probability is high; bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and does not need to await computed tomography. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

explanation.summary: Critical coarctation of the aorta presents in the first weeks of life with shock as the arterial duct closes and lower body perfusion collapses. An upper to lower limb blood pressure gradient of 20 mmHg or greater, weak or absent femoral pulses and a pre to post ductal saturation gradient (arm minus foot) of 3 percent or more are the pathognomonic triad. Initial management is intravenous prostaglandin E1 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute to reopen the duct, cautious fluid resuscitation (5 to 10 mL per kg boluses reassessed), preservation of spontaneous ventilation and avoidance of high inspired oxygen which closes the duct and worsens the left to right pulmonary steal. Complications of prostaglandin include apnoea, fever, flushing and hypotension; be ready to intubate. Definitive treatment is surgical or catheter based repair after transfer to a paediatric cardiac centre.
key_points: Pre to post ductal saturation gradient of 3% or more (upper minus lower) is pathognomonic for duct dependent systemic obstruction.
Prostaglandin E1 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute reopens the arterial duct and restores lower body perfusion.
Avoid high FiO2 (closes duct) and large fluid boluses (worsens pulmonary oedema in duct dependent systemic circulation).
explanation.pearls: In a shocked neonate with a pre to post ductal saturation gap and weak femorals, start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms per kg per minute before any large fluid bolus or high FiO2 and prepare for apnoea within 60 minutes of commencement.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease
RCH CPG: Duct Dependent Congenital Heart Disease

options.rationale: Aggressive fluid boluses can precipitate pulmonary oedema in duct dependent systemic circulation; small measured boluses (5 to 10 mL per kg) with reassessment are preferred and prostaglandin is the priority. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.rationale: Intubation may drop the arterial CO2 and worsen the left to right shunt and pulmonary steal; ventilation targets must protect ductal flow; inotrope alone without prostaglandin is not first line. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.rationale: Prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute reopens the arterial duct and restores lower body perfusion in duct dependent systemic circulation; apnoea and hypotension are the two main early adverse effects. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.rationale: The picture is upper to lower limb pressure gradient with weak femorals and post ductal desaturation, not hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; beta blockade will worsen shock. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.rationale: High inspired oxygen closes the arterial duct and worsens duct dependent systemic perfusion; target saturations are 75 to 85 percent in single ventricle physiology and around 85 to 92 percent in coarctation while duct is preserved. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

explanation.summary: Paediatric iron overdose progresses in five phases starting with gastrointestinal irritation within 6 hours, then a latent phase, followed by shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity and finally gastric outlet obstruction. Ingested elemental iron above 20 mg/kg produces symptoms, above 60 mg/kg is potentially toxic, and above 150 mg/kg is potentially lethal. Assessment includes abdominal radiograph looking for radiopaque tablets and a serum iron level at 4 to 6 hours post ingestion. Deferoxamine 15 mg per kg per hour is indicated for serum iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, acidosis or altered conscious state. Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol is considered if the radiograph shows visible tablets.
key_points: Assessment: abdominal radiograph and serum iron level 4 to 6 hours after ingestion.
Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/h for shock, coma, acidosis or iron level above 90 micromol/L.
Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron; consider whole bowel irrigation if tablets are visible on abdominal radiograph.
explanation.pearls: Paediatric iron ingestion above 60 mg/kg elemental requires abdominal radiograph and serum iron at 4 to 6 hours; deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour intravenous if level above 90 micromol/L or shock.

options.rationale: Ingested elemental iron above 60 mg/kg is potentially toxic; abdominal radiograph may show radiopaque tablets and a 4 to 6 hour post ingestion serum iron guides chelation. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron and gastric lavage is not routinely recommended; whole bowel irrigation is considered if radiopaque tablets are visible. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Empirical deferoxamine is reserved for severe symptoms or shock; peak level at 4 to 6 hours guides use rather than routine empirical therapy. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Symptomatic ingestion with tachycardia, pallor and vomiting requires observation and iron level; discharge at 1 hour misses the delayed toxic phase. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
N acetylcysteine is used for paracetamol not iron toxicity; there is no role in acute iron overdose beyond compassionate use. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction defined by acute onset of skin or mucosal involvement plus either respiratory compromise or hypotension. Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the single first line intervention and delaying it increases mortality. The ASCIA banded weight table sets dose by weight class: 7.5 to 10 kg receives 150 microgram, 10 to 20 kg receives 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr), 20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (EpiPen), above 50 kg receives 300 to 500 microgram. Adjuncts include supine positioning, high flow oxygen, intravenous fluid bolus 20 mL/kg for hypotension and nebulised salbutamol for wheeze. Antihistamines and corticosteroids treat associated urticaria but neither prevents nor treats anaphylaxis.
key_points: IM adrenaline anterolateral thigh is first line; ASCIA banded weight table dosing.
20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) IM; repeat every 5 minutes if needed.
Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjuncts and never replace adrenaline in anaphylaxis.
explanation.pearls: For paediatric anaphylaxis 20 to 50 kg give intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids and bronchodilators do not treat anaphylaxis; delaying intramuscular adrenaline increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Adrenaline intramuscular by ASCIA banded weight table is first line; 20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (EpiPen), repeat every 5 min if needed. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis in a monitored setting; first line is intramuscular for a child not in arrest. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Oral antihistamine treats urticaria but not airway compromise or hypotension; anaphylaxis mandates intramuscular adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
150 microgram dose is for 10 to 20 kg; a 24 kg child receives 300 microgram, and thigh (vastus lateralis) is preferred over deltoid. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary:
Infants are obligate nose breathers, so nasal secretions in bronchiolitis interrupt feeding out of proportion to the lower airway disease. Where secretions are clearly limiting intake, saline drops with superficial suction before feeds is the supported measure. Routine or deep suction is avoided because it causes bradycardia, apnoea and mucosal injury without changing the course. If intake remains inadequate despite this, the next step is nasogastric feeding rather than a pharmacological agent.

In context: bronchiolitis care is a short list of things that help and a long list of things that do not. Oxygen for hypoxaemia, feeding support by nasogastric tube when intake falls, and minimal handling make up almost the whole of it. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, antibiotics and decongestants are all outside the Australasian guideline.
key_points: Infants are obligate nose breathers, so nasal blockage limits feeding
Superficial suction with saline drops before feeds is supported when intake is poor
Deep nasopharyngeal suction risks bradycardia and apnoea
Nasogastric feeding is the next step if intake stays inadequate
explanation.pearls: The commonest reversible reason a bronchiolitic infant will not feed is a blocked nose, not the lower airway disease.

options.rationale: The PREDICT guideline supports superficial nasal suction, with saline drops, where secretions are limiting feeding in an infant who is otherwise stable, while discouraging it as a routine measure. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline; RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Deep suction is not recommended; it provokes vagal bradycardia, apnoea and mucosal trauma, and is used only to clear the airway of an intubated or peri-arrest infant. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline)

Hypertonic saline does not shorten admission or reduce escalation in Australian practice and is confined to trial settings or to other conditions such as cystic fibrosis. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline)

Bronchodilators are not recommended under 12 months because the wheeze comes from airway plugging rather than smooth muscle; they would be appropriate for an older child with asthma. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Topical decongestants are not used in infants because of systemic absorption and rebound congestion; they have a limited role in older children and adults. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is defined by acute onset with skin or mucosal involvement plus airway compromise or hypotension. ASCIA is the Australian authority for acute management and specifies IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh using a banded weight table rather than mg/kg arithmetic. Second-line therapies include IV fluids for hypotension, nebulised adrenaline for stridor, and salbutamol for bronchospasm; steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only and never delay adrenaline. Observation for 4 hours after resolution is required because of biphasic reactions.
key_points: Adrenaline 150 mcg IM (EpiPen Jr band) for 10 to 20 kg
Adrenaline 300 mcg IM (EpiPen band) for 20 kg or more
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if no response
IV bolus adrenaline is a critical care rescue only
Observe 4 hours after resolution for biphasic reaction
explanation.pearls: For a child under 10 kg the ASCIA table gives adrenaline 0.1 mg (100 mcg) IM; below infants there is no branded autoinjector and 0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000 drawn from an ampoule is used.

options.rationale: IV bolus adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis and arrest under critical care supervision; first-line remains IM into the thigh and IV bolus risks fatal arrhythmia (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).
The 300 mcg EpiPen band starts at 20 kg; his weight of 17 kg puts him in the 150 mcg band and 300 mcg risks tachyarrhythmia (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

The ASCIA AU standard for prescribing anaphylaxis adrenaline uses a banded weight table rather than 10 mcg/kg arithmetic; per-kg dosing is not the AU field practice (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

ASCIA bands EpiPen Jr 150 mcg IM for a child 10 to 20 kg; his 17 kg falls in this band and the correct route is IM into the anterolateral thigh with repeat at 5 minutes (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically but is not systemic anaphylaxis therapy; IM adrenaline is the first-line for anaphylaxis with hypotension (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis, usually parainfluenza, that peaks between 6 months and 3 years. RCH grades it as mild (stridor with agitation only), moderate (stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession), or severe (stridor at rest with marked recession, agitation or lethargy). Steroids reduce need for adrenaline and admission; oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is standard for mild to moderate, with 0.6 mg/kg reserved for severe. Nebulised adrenaline (a flat 5 mL of 1:1000) buys hours in severe cases and mandates a 3 hour observation after the last dose because of rebound.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is standard for mild or moderate croup
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally is reserved for severe croup
Nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1:1000) is severe-only
Observation for 3 hours after last adrenaline is required
Do not perform pharyngeal examination in suspected epiglottitis
explanation.pearls: In AU practice single-dose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg PO reaches peak effect at 2 to 4 hours with duration up to 72 hours, covering the typical resolution window.

options.rationale: Prednisolone is inferior to single-dose dexamethasone in croup because its shorter half-life increases relapse; a 3 day course is not standard (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup at RCH; using it here overtreats a moderate presentation and observation after single-dose steroid without adrenaline is 3 hours (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).
Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession; using it here is escalation beyond the presentation and does not replace steroid (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Nebulised budesonide is an alternative only when the child cannot tolerate oral steroid; oral dexamethasone is preferred in AU because of ease, better absorption and lower cost (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

RCH gives dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild to moderate croup as a single dose; the higher 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: Serious bacterial infection in infants under 3 months cannot be reliably excluded clinically; the risk is highest under 28 days and remains substantial from 4 to 12 weeks. RCH pathways require a full septic workup (blood culture, urine catheter, LP) and empirical parenteral antibiotics whenever the infant is unwell or under 4 weeks. The AU empirical combination is cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover early gram negatives, group B streptococcus and Listeria; ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonate because of biliary sludging and displacement of bilirubin. Blood culture and urine alone miss meningitis which shifts management from days of treatment to weeks.
key_points: Unwell infant under 3 months with fever requires full septic workup
AU empirical antibiotics: cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
Avoid ceftriaxone in the neonate because of bilirubin displacement
LP is not optional even with normal inflammatory markers
Group B streptococcus and Listeria coverage is age-specific
explanation.pearls: Group B streptococcus late-onset disease presents at 7 days to 3 months, most often as meningitis; early-onset disease presents in the first 6 days and is largely septicaemia. Benzylpenicillin covers both windows.

options.rationale: Any unwell infant under 3 months with fever requires admission with parenteral empirical antibiotics after septic workup; discharge on oral therapy is unsafe (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

Omitting LP under 3 months misses meningitis which cannot be excluded clinically at this age; ceftriaxone is also relatively contraindicated in the neonatal period because of hyperbilirubinaemia risk (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

In infants under 3 months with fever without source and features of sepsis, RCH mandates a full septic workup including LP plus empirical cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin to cover group B streptococcus and Listeria; his mother had no intrapartum prophylaxis (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Monotherapy does not cover the gram negative and Listeria spectrum required under 3 months and blood cultures alone miss urinary tract and CNS sources (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Delaying antibiotics for biomarkers in an unwell infant under 3 months breaches the sepsis hour and normal inflammatory markers do not exclude meningitis in the neonate (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA carries a risk of cerebral oedema that is uncommon in adults and drives most morbidity. APEG and RCH pathways use a smaller resuscitation bolus (10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride) than the general paediatric shock volume, reassess before repeating, and delay insulin for at least 60 minutes after fluid is started. Insulin is 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h and is never bolused. Bicarbonate is not used because it worsens neurologic outcomes. Recognise the high-risk features: age under 5 years, new onset, pH under 7.1, initial urea rise, and rapid osmolar shifts.
key_points: AU paediatric DKA bolus is 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride, not 20
Delay insulin for at least 60 minutes after fluid is started
Insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, never bolus
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA
Watch for cerebral oedema in the first 12 to 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Suspect cerebral oedema at any deterioration in Glasgow Coma Scale, bradycardia with hypertension (Cushing's response), or new headache; give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3 percent 5 mL/kg while imaging.

options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is standard paediatric shock volume but in DKA it is now avoided as first-line because of higher cerebral oedema risk shown in observational data (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

Australasian paediatric DKA protocols use 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 30 minutes for shock or poor perfusion rather than 20 mL/kg to minimise cerebral oedema risk; reassessment before further fluid is required (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).
Fluid should precede insulin by at least an hour to reduce cerebral oedema and rebound hypoglycaemia risk; insulin without fluid is not APEG standard (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).
Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA and is associated with worse neurologic outcomes and paradoxical CNS acidosis (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

Balanced crystalloid can be used later but the first-line resuscitation in AU paediatric DKA is a 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus and insulin is started at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h after 1 hour of fluid (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

explanation.summary: Therapeutic hypothermia is the only proven neuroprotective intervention for moderate to severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy and must start within 6 hours of birth to be effective. Australian eligibility requires gestational age at least 35 weeks, evidence of intrapartum asphyxia (Apgar under 5 at 10 min, ongoing resuscitation at 10 min, cord pH under 7.0, or base deficit at least 12), and moderate or severe encephalopathy on modified Sarnat. Passive cooling during retrieval is acceptable when servo controlled cooling is not immediately available; target core temperature is 33.5 degrees Celsius for 72 hours followed by slow rewarming. Antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated but continuous amplitude EEG guides treatment.
key_points: Therapeutic hypothermia window closes at 6 hours from birth
Target core temperature 33.5 degrees Celsius for 72 hours
Eligibility needs asphyxia evidence plus moderate to severe encephalopathy
Passive cooling acceptable during retrieval
Never actively warm above 37 degrees Celsius in HIE
explanation.pearls: Modified Sarnat encephalopathy grading combines level of consciousness, spontaneous activity, posture, tone, primitive reflexes, and autonomic system; two features in moderate or severe columns qualify for cooling.

options.rationale: Active warming above 37 degrees Celsius in HIE worsens neurologic outcomes; missing the 6 hour cooling window forfeits therapeutic hypothermia neuroprotection (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement).

He meets AU therapeutic hypothermia criteria (term, cord pH under 7.0 with base deficit at least 12, moderate to severe encephalopathy on modified Sarnat) and the 6 hour therapeutic window requires cooling to begin now with passive cooling during transfer (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement; RCH CPG: Neonatal encephalopathy).

Prophylactic phenobarbital does not improve outcomes in HIE and is reserved for observed or amplitude-EEG confirmed seizures; the immediate priority is cooling (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement).
His glucose is within normal range and glucose bolus in HIE can worsen neurologic outcomes through cerebral hyperperfusion (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement).

There is no blood pressure or ongoing arrest indication documented and further adrenaline risks tachyarrhythmia and cerebral hyperperfusion; the therapeutic priority is cooling (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation).

explanation.summary: Neonatal urea cycle disorders classically present after an initial well period as feeding declines, with vomiting, hypothermia, tachypnoea and encephalopathy; the tachypnoea produces a distinctive respiratory alkalosis. Ammonia over 200 micromol/L is neurotoxic and over 400 mandates extracorporeal removal (haemodialysis is more efficient than exchange transfusion). Protein must be stopped and endogenous catabolism reversed with high-rate glucose (with insulin as needed) to reduce ongoing nitrogen liberation. Definitive diagnosis needs plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid and organic acids; ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate) are added under metabolic team guidance.
key_points: Well after birth then decompensates with vomiting suggests IEM
Respiratory alkalosis with high ammonia is the urea cycle pattern
Ammonia over 400 micromol/L needs haemodialysis
Stop protein and give anabolic glucose immediately
Send plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid and organic acids
explanation.pearls: Organic acidaemias also decompensate in the neonate but produce metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap and positive ketones; the biochemical fingerprint separates them from urea cycle disorders.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.rationale: Protein must be withheld until the diagnosis is confirmed and ammonia is controlled; further nitrogen load worsens hyperammonaemia in a urea cycle defect (Source: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.rationale: Cultures are pending but the absent acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, normal CRP and profound hyperammonaemia point to metabolic disease; sepsis rarely produces ammonia over 400 (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus).
Phenobarbital treats seizures but does not lower ammonia; hyperammonaemia over 200 micromol/L directly injures the brain and requires urgent ammonia removal (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus).
The blood gas shows alkalosis rather than acidosis; bicarbonate worsens the alkalaemia and does nothing for the hyperammonaemia (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus).

Respiratory alkalosis with absent acidosis, absent ketones and ammonia over 400 micromol/L in a term neonate suggests a urea cycle disorder; RACP metabolic guidance advises stopping protein, giving anabolic glucose and starting haemodialysis for ammonia over 400 (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus; Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

explanation.summary: Typical RSV bronchiolitis with hypoxia below 90% and moderate work of breathing. Australian practice starts low flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to a 90% target. HFNC and non-invasive ventilation are reserved for failure of low flow. Bronchodilators are not routine in this age group.
key_points: RCH threshold to start oxygen is SpO2 persistently below 90%.
Low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min is first line, not HFNC.
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: For under 12 month bronchiolitis at RCH, low flow oxygen to a SpO2 target of 90% precedes any HFNC trial.

options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance escalates in a stepwise fashion beginning with low flow nasal prong oxygen when SpO2 persistently drops below 90%; titration to a target of 90% avoids the harms of over oxygenation and prolonged admission (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow oxygen after an adequate trial or for infants with severe work of breathing; PARIS 1 showed no benefit as first line over standard oxygen (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

Nebulised bronchodilators are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months because there is no sustained clinical benefit and they can worsen ventilation perfusion mismatch (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

Non-invasive ventilation is a PICU level intervention considered after low flow and high flow trials fail with rising pCO2 or exhaustion; his gas and mental state do not yet warrant it (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).
SpO2 persistently at 88% in room air with moderate recession meets the RCH threshold to commence supplemental oxygen; watchful waiting risks prolonged hypoxia (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: Stridor at rest with only mild recession fits the RCH mild to moderate croup band. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is standard; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe cases. Nebulised budesonide is a route substitute, not a preferred first agent. Prednisolone courses are inferior to single dose dexamethasone.
key_points: Dose 0.15 mg/kg for mild to moderate croup at RCH.
Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup (marked recession, hypoxia, agitation).
Oral dexamethasone is preferred over nebulised budesonide when tolerated.
explanation.pearls: The RCH severity to dose rule is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild to moderate croup and 0.6 mg/kg only for severe.

sources.label: Bjornson et al. Cochrane review: Nebulised epinephrine for croup

options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with marked recession, hypoxia, agitation, or exhaustion; using it routinely in mild to moderate croup adds no efficacy and needless steroid exposure (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).
RCH classifies stridor at rest with only mild recession as mild to moderate croup, for which 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone as a single dose is the recommended regimen (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).
Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children who cannot tolerate the oral route; an alert 2-year-old drinking water in the cubicle should receive oral dexamethasone (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

RCH and the CDC croup evidence base favour a single dose of dexamethasone over a prednisolone course because relapse rates are higher and duration of steroid exposure is longer (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).
Stridor at rest is the threshold to give dexamethasone; delaying treatment prolongs symptoms and extends emergency length of stay (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: A well thriving 14-month-old with a first typical UTI, normal antenatal scans, and prompt defervescence needs no routine imaging under the RCH cascade. Imaging is reserved for atypical or recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not part of the RCH pathway.
key_points: RCH does not recommend routine ultrasound after a single typical UTI over 6 months old.
Atypical features (poor response after 48 hours, non E coli, sepsis, mass, raised creatinine) trigger imaging.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH first UTI cascade.
explanation.pearls: Under RCH, a single typical UTI in a well child over 6 months of age with normal antenatal scans requires no routine imaging.

options.rationale: DMSA scanning is not part of the RCH cascade for a first typical UTI and adds radiation without changing management for a well thriving child (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

RCH does not recommend routine ultrasound after a first typical UTI in a child older than 6 months with normal antenatal imaging; this is a NICE style pathway not adopted by RCH (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

RCH restricts routine ultrasound to atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without documented normal antenatal scans; a typical single UTI in a well infant older than 6 months does not require imaging (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

MCUG is invasive and is not first line for a single typical UTI in an older infant; RCH reserves it for selected atypical or recurrent cases after ultrasound findings (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).
Antibiotic prophylaxis after a first typical UTI has minimal benefit in preventing scarring and RCH does not recommend it routinely for a well child (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

explanation.summary: This child has mild to moderate dehydration with failed oral rehydration despite a single dose of ondansetron. RCH prefers nasogastric rehydration next, at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours, before intravenous fluids. IV therapy is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line after failed oral rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration.
Ondansetron dose in this age group is a single dose only.
IV rehydration is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.
explanation.pearls: For mild to moderate paediatric dehydration that fails oral rehydration, the RCH next step is nasogastric rehydration at 25 mL/kg/hour, not intravenous fluids.

options.rationale: Ad libitum sipping in a child who repeatedly vomits does not correct the estimated 8% deficit in a defined time and lengthens admission (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).
Intravenous rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or failure of nasogastric rehydration; this child is not shocked and has not yet had an NGT trial (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).
A single ondansetron dose is the RCH recommended maximum; repeat oral dosing has no evidence and delays effective rehydration in a child already failing the oral route (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

For mild to moderate dehydration where oral rehydration has failed, RCH prefers nasogastric rehydration ahead of intravenous fluids because it corrects deficit safely and avoids cannulation morbidity (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

Metoclopramide is not first line for paediatric gastroenteritis vomiting in Australia because of extrapyramidal risk; ondansetron is preferred but NGT is the escalation when it fails (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

explanation.summary: An unwell febrile infant under 3 months needs a full septic workup, including lumbar puncture, and empirical intravenous cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria in the neonatal age band. Ceftriaxone is avoided at this age because of bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation risk. Outpatient oral antibiotics, biomarker guided deferral of the CSF sample, and pure observation all delay definitive treatment in a window where mortality rises hour by hour.
key_points: Under 3 months: full septic screen including CSF for any unwell appearance.
Cover Listeria with benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime under 4 to 6 weeks.
Avoid ceftriaxone in the neonatal period.
explanation.pearls: For an unwell febrile infant under 3 months, RCH gives cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin, not ceftriaxone, alongside a full septic screen including lumbar puncture.

options.rationale: An unwell appearing febrile infant under 3 months requires empirical antibiotics within the first hour after cultures; observation alone would delay life saving treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).
Outpatient oral antibiotics are inappropriate for a febrile infant under 3 months, and an unwell appearance mandates admission with intravenous therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

Under 3 months, biomarker guided deferral of lumbar puncture is not recommended by RCH; occult meningitis has been missed with a strategy that waits for inflammatory markers (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

Ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonatal period because of ceftriaxone calcium precipitation and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia risks; cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin is preferred (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

For a febrile infant under 3 months, particularly one who is unwell appearing, RCH mandates full septic screening including CSF and empirical intravenous cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: This child meets anaphylaxis criteria with airway involvement, wheeze, and borderline blood pressure. ASCIA uses banded weight based intramuscular adrenaline dosing; 150 microgram is the correct dose for the 10 to 20 kg band. The 300 microgram dose is reserved for 20 kg and above. IV bolus adrenaline is not first line.
key_points: ASCIA bands: EpiPen Junior 150 microgram for 10 to 20 kg; EpiPen 300 microgram for 20 kg and above.
IM anterolateral thigh is the correct route; subcutaneous is inadequate.
IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases in a monitored setting.
explanation.pearls: Weight 16 kg puts a child in the 10 to 20 kg ASCIA band, which is EpiPen Junior 150 microgram IM.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: ASCIA and the RCH anaphylaxis guideline use banded weight based intramuscular dosing; EpiPen Junior 150 microgram is the correct autoinjector for a child in the 10 to 20 kg band (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: The 300 microgram EpiPen is reserved for children 20 kg and above; giving it to a 16 kg child overshoots the ASCIA banded dose (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: ASCIA reserves intravenous adrenaline infusions for refractory anaphylaxis in a monitored setting and does not use bolus 10 microgram/kg IV as first line; IM is the correct starting route (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline may be considered adjunctively for upper airway oedema but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in a child with anaphylaxis (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline is not recommended in anaphylaxis because peripheral vasoconstriction delays absorption; the intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the standard site (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: This is severe DKA with an intact conscious state and modest hypovolaemia rather than frank shock. Australian ISPAD aligned practice gives a cautious 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, reassesses, then plans deficit fluid over 48 hours. Insulin infusion is delayed by at least an hour and dextrose is added only when serum glucose falls to about 14 to 17 mmol/L to minimise cerebral oedema risk.
key_points: Initial fluid in paediatric DKA is 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 30 to 60 minutes unless shocked.
Insulin is delayed by at least 1 hour to reduce cerebral oedema risk.
Dextrose is added when glucose falls to 14 to 17 mmol/L, not upfront.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA at RCH, the first fluid is 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 30 to 60 minutes; insulin waits at least 1 hour.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and HHS

options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is reserved for genuine shock in paediatric DKA and rapid resuscitation increases the risk of cerebral oedema in the alert child (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

Australian ISPAD aligned protocols give a cautious 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes in the alert dehydrated child, then reassess before deficit rehydration to avoid cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

Dextrose containing fluid is not used in the initial resuscitation bolus; dextrose is added once serum glucose falls to about 14 to 17 mmol/L during ongoing insulin (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

Hartmann is not a substitute for 0.9% saline in the initial DKA bolus in Australian paediatric practice; the lactate is not the reason to change the first fluid and adds no acidosis correction advantage (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

Insulin is deliberately started after the initial fluid, at least 1 hour later in most Australian protocols, because early insulin worsens the fluid shift risk of cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: This is meningococcal type paediatric sepsis with cold shock. The RCH pathway is IV or IO access, blood cultures, antibiotic within the hour, then rapid crystalloid boluses of 20 mL/kg titrated up to 40 to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes come after fluid resuscitation, not before.
key_points: Access, cultures, antibiotic within 60 minutes.
20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes; repeat to 40 to 60 mL/kg.
Inotropes come after fluid not before.
explanation.pearls: At RCH the paediatric sepsis order is access, cultures, antibiotic within the hour, then 20 mL/kg saline boluses; inotropes follow the fluids.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
ANZICS Paediatric Study Group sepsis pathway

options.rationale: Antibiotics must not be delayed for definitive culture results; the first empirical dose is given within the first hour after the culture is drawn (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Adrenaline follows fluid resuscitation up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in Australian paediatric sepsis pathways; giving it first delays antibiotics and cultures without addressing hypovolaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway prioritises timely access, cultures, and antibiotics inside 60 minutes, with rapid 20 mL/kg boluses; inotropes come after fluids not before (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: CT brain is not required before empirical antibiotics or fluid in a child with clinical sepsis and no focal neurology; imaging must not delay antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: A child with mottling, drowsiness, tachycardia, hypotension for age, and a non blanching rash needs immediate resuscitation, not antipyresis alone (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: This is a term baby with focal motor seizures, normal glucose and ionised calcium, and a cranial ultrasound consistent with perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke. Metabolic causes are effectively excluded so antiepileptic loading with phenobarbital is next, alongside urgent transfer for aEEG and MRI. Levetiracetam is inferior in the neonatal window and cooling is not indicated outside HIE criteria.
key_points: First line neonatal antiepileptic in Australia is phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV, not levetiracetam.
Normal glucose and ionised calcium exclude common reversible causes.
Cooling is only for HIE meeting entry criteria within 6 hours.
explanation.pearls: In focal neonatal seizures with normal glucose and calcium and stroke on cranial ultrasound, load phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV and transfer for aEEG rather than trialling levetiracetam.

options.rationale: Therapeutic hypothermia is only supported for moderate to severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy meeting entry criteria within 6 hours; it is not indicated for perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke and this baby is well perfused (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal cooling guideline).

The NEOLEV2 trial showed levetiracetam is inferior to phenobarbital at controlling neonatal seizures, and phenobarbital remains the first line antiepileptic in Australian neonatal practice (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

Glucose and ionised calcium are both within the neonatal reference range so metabolic replacement is not the mechanism; the stroke on cranial ultrasound redirects therapy to antiepileptic loading (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

In neonatal seizures with corrected metabolic causes, the first line antiepileptic in Australian NICUs is intravenous phenobarbital 20 mg/kg, alongside continuous aEEG monitoring at a tertiary centre to guide further therapy and treat electrographic only seizures (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

Delaying antiepileptic loading in ongoing neonatal seizures risks secondary brain injury; treat the seizures now and pursue metabolic screen in parallel (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation follows sudden longitudinal traction on a pronated extended arm and results from the annular ligament slipping over the radial head. The child holds the limb pronated and slightly flexed, refuses to use it, and is characteristically comfortable at rest with no swelling, no bruising and no bony tenderness anywhere along the limb. Pain reproduced only on attempted supination is the discriminating finding and separates it from a fracture. Reduction is attempted on clinical grounds alone, with hyperpronation preferred over supination flexion because it succeeds more often and hurts less. Radiographs belong to children with focal tenderness, swelling, deformity, an inconsistent history, or failure of two reduction attempts.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated arm is the mechanism, most often between one and four years
Absence of swelling, bruising and bony tenderness argues strongly against fracture
Hyperpronation has a higher success rate and causes less pain than supination flexion
Arm use usually returns within thirty minutes of successful reduction
Image only for atypical history, focal bony signs, or two failed attempts
explanation.pearls: Distract the child with a sticker or toy held at the midline after the manoeuvre, because spontaneous reach across with the affected hand within thirty minutes is the most reliable confirmation of success, and warn parents that recurrence happens in about a quarter of children before the annular ligament strengthens at around five years.

options.rationale: A history of axial traction with the arm held pronated, no bony tenderness and pain only on supination is a bedside diagnosis, and reduction is attempted without imaging. Hyperpronation succeeds more often than supination flexion and is less painful, with arm use typically returning within thirty minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

Radiographs are reserved for an atypical history, focal bony tenderness, swelling or deformity, or failure of two reduction attempts, none of which are present. Films in this setting are usually normal and delay a manoeuvre that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

Immobilisation treats a fracture, and this presentation has no bony tenderness, swelling or deformity to support one. A week in a sling leaves a readily reducible annular ligament entrapment untreated and prolongs the disuse. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

The mechanism given accounts fully for the presentation and matches the child's stage of development, so this is not an unexplained injury. Traction on an extended arm is the ordinary cause and a survey exposes the child to radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Spontaneous resolution does occur but is unpredictable and leaves the child in pain and functionally one handed meanwhile. Analgesia is reasonable adjunctive care yet it is not the treatment when a simple manoeuvre resolves the problem in minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

explanation.summary: Granulation tissue at the umbilicus is common after cord separation and presents as a small pink moist stalk that weeps serous fluid onto clothing. The critical distinction is from an umbilical polyp, which is a remnant of the vitellointestinal duct or urachus lined by intestinal or urothelial mucosa, and from a patent urachus or vitelline duct, which discharge urine or faecal material. A polyp is typically firmer, brighter red and does not shrink with cautery, and it needs surgical referral and imaging. Omphalitis is a separate and urgent diagnosis marked by periumbilical erythema, induration and systemic illness in a neonate. Simple granulation tissue is treated with silver nitrate applied to the lesion with the surrounding skin protected, usually with resolution after one or two applications.
key_points: Granulation tissue is soft, pink and shrinks with silver nitrate; a polyp is firm, bright red and does not
Urine or faecal discharge points to a patent urachus or vitellointestinal duct and needs imaging
Periumbilical erythema and induration in a neonate indicates omphalitis and warrants urgent assessment
Protect surrounding skin during cautery because silver nitrate burns normal epidermis
Persistent lesion after adequate cautery earns a surgical opinion
explanation.pearls: Failure of a supposed granuloma to shrink after two silver nitrate applications is the practical trigger to refer, because an umbilical polyp of retained vitellointestinal mucosa will not respond to cautery and may sit above a persistent duct that requires excision.

options.rationale: Topical salt has been described and is sometimes used, but it is slower and less reliable than cautery performed in the clinic and depends heavily on parental technique. It is a reasonable fallback where cautery is unavailable rather than the first choice. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

A small pink moist stalk of granulation tissue persisting after cord separation in an otherwise well infant responds to chemical cautery, and one or two applications are usually sufficient. Surrounding skin is protected with a barrier because silver nitrate causes chemical burns to normal epidermis. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, induration, tenderness and systemic upset, none of which are present here. Treating a bloodless granulation stalk with antibiotics exposes the infant to adverse effects without addressing the tissue that is weeping. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

Imaging is indicated when the discharge is urinary or faecal, when the lesion is large or firm and bright red, or when granulation fails to settle after cautery, since those suggest a patent urachus or vitellointestinal remnant. Scanning every moist umbilicus adds cost and delay without altering the usual outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

Surgical excision is held back for lesions that persist after adequate chemical cautery or that prove to be an umbilical polyp of intestinal or urothelial mucosa. Committing a well 5-week-old to general anaesthesia ahead of a bedside treatment is disproportionate. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis is the commonest cause of a fixed head tilt in early infancy and is associated with difficult or instrumental delivery and intrauterine crowding. The head tilts towards the affected sternocleidomastoid and the chin rotates away from it, and a firm fusiform mass within the muscle is present in a proportion of infants. Restriction of passive rotation is what separates it from a simple positional preference and from ocular torticollis, in which passive range is full. Management is physiotherapy with a stretching and positioning program, and outcomes are best when this starts within the first few months. Imaging and specialist referral are for atypical features, neurological signs, failure to improve, or a tilt of later onset.
key_points: Head tilts towards the affected muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Restricted passive rotation distinguishes muscular from positional or ocular torticollis
Early physiotherapy resolves the large majority; late referral has poorer outcomes
Examine the hips, since developmental dysplasia coexists in a meaningful minority
Later onset tilt, vomiting or abnormal tone shifts the differential towards neuroimaging
explanation.pearls: Always examine the hips in an infant with congenital muscular torticollis, because developmental dysplasia of the hip coexists in roughly one in five and both conditions share the crowded intrauterine mechanism, so a normal neonatal hip check does not remove the need to reassess.

options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for torticollis with neurological signs, abnormal tone, vomiting or a tilt appearing after a period of normal head control. This infant has an identifiable muscular cause and a normal neurological examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Watchful waiting without stretching risks progressive muscle shortening, secondary skull asymmetry and facial deformity, and children referred late have worse outcomes. Reassurance alone is appropriate only for positional preference without restriction or a mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Restricted passive rotation with a firm mass within the sternocleidomastoid after an instrumental birth is the typical picture, and early physiotherapy with stretching and positioning resolves the great majority when started in the first months. Earlier referral gives better outcomes, so the program begins now rather than after further investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Ultrasound is used when the mass has atypical features or the diagnosis is unclear, and radiographs when a bony anomaly of the cervical spine is suspected. A firm mass confined to the sternocleidomastoid with the classic tilt and rotation pattern needs neither before starting stretches. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Ocular torticollis from a superior oblique palsy is a genuine cause of head tilt but produces no neck mass and no restriction of passive rotation. It also tends to appear once fixation matures rather than in the first weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Positional plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was adopted and is compounded by prolonged time in capsules and rockers. The characteristic shape is a parallelogram: occipital flattening with the ipsilateral ear displaced forwards and ipsilateral frontal bossing, with open sutures and normal head growth. Lambdoid craniosynostosis, the important mimic, produces a trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced backwards, a palpable ridge over the fused suture and often a compensatory mastoid bulge. Management of the positional form is repositioning, supervised tummy time while awake, and treatment of any coexisting torticollis, with review to confirm improvement. Helmet therapy is reserved for moderate or severe deformity that has not improved with these measures, and safe supine sleep is never traded away for head shape.
key_points: Parallelogram shape with the ear forwards on the flat side indicates a positional cause
Trapezoid shape with the ear backwards and a palpable ridge suggests lambdoid synostosis
Repositioning and supervised tummy time are first line and are effective in most infants
Helmets are for moderate to severe deformity persisting despite repositioning
Supine sleep is maintained regardless of head shape concerns
explanation.pearls: Check passive neck rotation in every infant with occipital flattening, because untreated congenital muscular torticollis keeps the head resting on the same point and repositioning advice will fail until the tight sternocleidomastoid is being stretched by a physiotherapy program.

options.rationale: Surgery addresses true craniosynostosis, in which the fused suture ridges and the head shape is trapezoid with the ear pulled backwards on the affected side. The pattern here is the opposite and open sutures exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Helmet therapy is considered for moderate to severe deformity that fails to improve with repositioning, usually from around six months. Fitting one before a trial of conservative measures commits the family to cost and daily wear that most infants never need. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Non supine sleep raises the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy and is never advised to manage head shape. Pressure relief is achieved during waking hours and by alternating the head position within supine sleep. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

A parallelogram head shape with the ear and forehead displaced forwards on the flattened side, open sutures and normal head growth is positional in origin and responds to repositioning and increased time off the occiput. Review confirms improvement and identifies the minority who need a helmet or further assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Skull imaging is directed at suspected premature suture fusion, signalled by a palpable ridge, a trapezoid rather than parallelogram shape or abnormal head growth. Scanning a typical positional deformity delivers ionising radiation to an infant brain for no change in management. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: A hydrocele in an infant reflects fluid tracking down a patent processus vaginalis and characteristically transilluminates, is painless and varies in size across the day. The critical bedside distinction from an inguinal hernia is whether the upper border can be defined with a normal cord above and whether the swelling reduces, since a hernia extends into the inguinal canal, does not transilluminate reliably and can be reduced. Most communicating hydroceles resolve as the processus closes during the first two years, so observation is standard. Surgical referral follows persistence beyond two years, progressive enlargement, or the appearance of an inguinal component. Aspiration has no role in children because fluid simply reaccumulates and bowel may be injured.
key_points: Transillumination and a palpable upper border with normal cord identify a hydrocele
Failure to get above the swelling or a reducible mass indicates an inguinal hernia
Most communicating hydroceles resolve spontaneously by two years of age
Hernia in infancy is repaired promptly because of incarceration risk
Aspiration is not used in children; ligation of the processus is the operation when needed
explanation.pearls: A hydrocele that appears for the first time after infancy, or one that becomes tense and tender in an older boy, should prompt scrotal ultrasound rather than reassurance, since a reactive hydrocele can be the presenting sign of an underlying testicular tumour or of torsion of an appendix testis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.rationale: Incarceration risk belongs to an inguinal hernia, which presents as a reducible inguinal swelling that does not transilluminate and in which the upper border cannot be defined. Early operation is the rule for hernia and the exception for hydrocele. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

Ultrasound is used when the testis cannot be palpated, when the swelling is solid or does not transilluminate, or when torsion or a tumour is a concern. Here both testes are palpable and normal and the physical signs already define the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.rationale: Aspiration of a paediatric hydrocele is not performed because the fluid reaccumulates through the patent processus and the needle risks injuring bowel within a coexisting hernia. Definitive treatment when needed is ligation of the processus vaginalis. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.rationale: Torsion presents with sudden severe pain, a tender high riding testis and an unwell child, and has a course of hours rather than eleven months. A painless swelling of this duration does not fit and urgent exploration is not warranted. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.rationale: A transilluminating scrotal swelling with a normal cord above it and no inguinal component is a communicating hydrocele, and the processus vaginalis closes spontaneously in most boys during the first two years. Referral is made if it persists beyond that age, enlarges progressively, or an inguinal component appears. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

explanation.summary: Balanoposthitis is inflammation of the glans and prepuce and is common in uncircumcised boys, frequently precipitated by forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin. Presentation is with local redness, swelling, discharge and pain on voiding, and the child is usually afebrile and systemically well. The essential differential is paraphimosis, where a retracted foreskin has become trapped behind the corona and constricts the glans, which is a urological emergency requiring reduction. Treatment of uncomplicated balanoposthitis is saline bathing and a topical agent, together with the crucial advice to stop forcible retraction, since the prepuce separates spontaneously over childhood. Systemic antibiotics and referral are reserved for spreading cellulitis, systemic illness, or recurrent disease with pathological scarring.
key_points: Forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin is the usual precipitant
Paraphimosis is the emergency mimic and is identified by a foreskin trapped behind the corona
Saline bathing plus a topical agent treats most first episodes at home
Fever, systemic upset or spreading cellulitis moves treatment to systemic antibiotics
Circumcision is for recurrent disease or pathological scarring, not a single episode
explanation.pearls: Distinguish physiological non retractility, which is normal in most boys until well into school age, from true pathological phimosis with a pale scarred fibrous ring at the tip, because only the latter is an indication for topical corticosteroid or surgical referral.

options.rationale: Localised balanoposthitis in an afebrile boy with a normal urinary stream is treated with saline baths and a topical agent, and the forced retraction that caused the microtrauma is stopped. Physiological adhesions separate on their own and forcible retraction is the usual precipitant. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

Reduction manoeuvres treat paraphimosis, in which a retracted foreskin traps behind the corona and constricts the glans. This foreskin sits in its normal position and returns freely, so there is nothing to reduce. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

Urinary infection is suggested by fever, systemic upset, loin tenderness or an abnormal stream, none of which are present, and local inflammation readily explains the pain on voiding. Contamination from the inflamed prepuce also makes a sample unreliable at this moment. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Circumcision is considered for recurrent balanoposthitis or for pathological scarring of the prepuce, not for a first uncomplicated episode. Most boys have no further trouble once retraction stops and the physiological adhesions are left alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

Parenteral antibiotics are for a child who is febrile or systemically unwell or who has spreading cellulitis of the shaft. An afebrile boy with localised preputial inflammation is managed at home with local measures. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection producing firm dome shaped umbilicated papules, most often in preschool and primary school children and frequently spread by direct contact and shared towels. Lesions are self-limiting, usually clearing over six to eighteen months, and treatment is not required in immunocompetent children. Two phenomena worry families unnecessarily: an eczematous halo around lesions, which is an immune response and is treated with a topical corticosteroid, and the so called beginning of the end inflammation, in which lesions become red and angry shortly before resolving. Children are not excluded from school or swimming, though covering lesions and avoiding shared towels is sensible. Destructive treatments are painful and risk scarring and are reserved for selected situations.
key_points: Central umbilication of firm dome shaped papules is the diagnostic morphology
Spontaneous resolution over six to eighteen months is the natural history
An eczematous halo is an immune reaction and is treated with topical corticosteroid
No exclusion from school or swimming; cover lesions and avoid sharing towels
Very extensive or persistent disease prompts consideration of underlying immunodeficiency
explanation.pearls: Warn parents in advance that individual lesions often turn red, swollen and tender in the weeks before they disappear, because this beginning of the end reaction is regularly mistaken for bacterial infection and leads to unnecessary courses of oral antibiotics.

options.rationale: Immune workup is considered for very extensive or unusually persistent disease, especially with other infections or failure to thrive. Around twenty lesions over three months in a thriving child with mild atopic dermatitis is ordinary. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

Molluscum contagiosum in a well immunocompetent child is self-limiting over months to a couple of years, and no exclusion from school or swimming is required. The itchy eczematous halo around individual lesions responds to a topical corticosteroid and emollient, which also reduces scratching and spread. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

Bacterial superinfection is suggested by honey coloured crust, pustulation, warmth and tenderness rather than by a dry itchy halo. The inflammation described is eczematous and antibiotics would not address it. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

Physical destruction is painful, risks scarring and dyspigmentation, and is generally avoided in young children given spontaneous resolution. Exclusion from school and swimming is not recommended and adds social cost without controlling transmission. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

Scabies is treated this way and presents with intensely itchy burrows in web spaces, wrists and axillae with affected household members, not with discrete umbilicated papules. The morphology described does not fit a mite infestation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: In-toeing has three levels of origin and the prone rotational examination localises which one applies. Metatarsus adductus lies in the foot and gives a curved lateral border with a medial midfoot crease, internal tibial torsion lies in the leg and gives an inwardly directed thigh foot angle, and excess femoral anteversion lies in the hip and gives internal rotation greatly exceeding external rotation with a W sitting preference. Internal tibial torsion typically appears when walking begins and remodels through the preschool years, while femoral anteversion peaks around age five and also improves. Reassurance is the treatment, since braces, special footwear and exercises do not change the natural history. Referral is prompted by pain, asymmetry, limp, functional limitation, deterioration or neurological abnormality.
key_points: Prone rotational examination localises in-toeing to foot, tibia or femur
Straight lateral foot border excludes metatarsus adductus as the cause
Symmetrical hip rotation argues against excess femoral anteversion
Internal tibial torsion appears with early walking and remodels spontaneously
Pain, asymmetry, limp or neurological signs are the referral triggers
explanation.pearls: Asymmetrical in-toeing deserves a different level of attention from symmetrical in-toeing, because unilateral rotational change with a subtle limp can be the presenting sign of a spastic hemiplegia or of hip pathology, and both are missed if the finding is filed as normal variation.

options.rationale: Serial casting treats metatarsus adductus, in which the forefoot deviates inwards giving a curved lateral border and a medial midfoot crease, and only when it is rigid. The foot borders are straight here so the deformity is not in the foot. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

Rotational alignment of the tibia is determined by bone shape rather than muscle balance, so strengthening does not change it. Physiotherapy has a role where there is genuine neuromuscular abnormality, which the normal examination excludes. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

Symmetrical in-toeing from internal tibial torsion in a painless child with symmetrical hip rotation and straight foot borders is a normal stage of lower limb development that remodels through early childhood. Referral is triggered by pain, asymmetry, limp, regression of gait or an abnormal neurological examination. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

Night braces and torsion bars do not alter the natural history and burden the child and family with equipment. They persist in family lore because spontaneous remodelling occurs regardless of what is worn. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

Imaging is not used to assess rotational profile in a well child, since the diagnosis is made from the prone rotational examination at the bedside. Excess femoral anteversion also gives internal rotation far exceeding external rotation, which is not the pattern here. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral or oblique fracture of the tibial shaft in a child roughly between nine months and three years, produced by a low energy twisting force with the foot fixed. Initial radiographs are often normal or show only a subtle lucency in one plane, so a negative film does not exclude the injury and the diagnosis rests on the history and on focal pain reproduced by gentle torsion of the tibia. Management is immobilisation with orthopaedic review, and periosteal reaction on films at one to two weeks confirms the diagnosis retrospectively when needed. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis are the important alternatives and are suggested by fever, systemic upset, raised inflammatory markers and pain on passive joint movement. A fracture of this kind in a child who is not yet independently mobile carries an entirely different significance and requires child protection assessment.
key_points: Low energy twist with a fixed foot in a toddler is the classic mechanism
Normal initial radiographs do not exclude the fracture; up to a third are occult
Focal pain on gentle tibial torsion with painless joint movement localises to bone
Immobilise and review; repeat films at one to two weeks show periosteal reaction
The same fracture in a pre-ambulant infant demands child protection assessment
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child has been walking independently before accepting a toddler fracture as innocent, because a spiral tibial fracture in a child who has never cruised or walked has no plausible self generated mechanism and moves the presentation directly into a child protection pathway.

options.rationale: Septic arthritis presents with fever, systemic upset, raised inflammatory markers and pain through passive hip movement, and this child is afebrile with a normal C-reactive protein and painless hip movement. Aspiration is invasive and the clinical picture points to bone rather than joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Acutely limping child)
