The mechanism was witnessed, is developmentally plausible for a walking toddler and matches the injury pattern, so this is not an unexplained fracture. Concern would rise sharply if the same injury were found in a child not yet walking. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Bone scanning is sensitive but delivers a significant radiation dose and is reserved for a limping child in whom the site of pathology genuinely cannot be localised. Here the pain localises to the tibia and empirical immobilisation achieves the same end. (Source: RCH CPG: Acutely limping child)

An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft in a toddler is frequently invisible on initial films and is a clinical diagnosis based on refusal to weight bear with focal pain on tibial torsion after a low energy twist. Immobilisation and review is standard, and repeat films at one to two weeks show periosteal reaction if confirmation is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler fracture)

Initial radiographs miss a substantial proportion of these fractures because the spiral lucency is undisplaced and may be visible in only one plane. Treating a normal film as an exclusion sends home a child with a genuine fracture and no protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler fracture)

explanation.summary: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent athlete is usually benign and most often traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity or patellofemoral pain, both of which improve with relative rest and loading programs. The features that break this pattern are pain that wakes the child at night, pain that worsens despite rest, systemic features such as weight loss, and any palpable deep mass, and osteosarcoma has a peak incidence in the adolescent growth spurt with the distal femur the commonest site. A raised alkaline phosphatase in this setting is supportive but not diagnostic and is not required to act. Plain radiography is the correct first investigation and typically demonstrates an aggressive periosteal reaction and abnormal matrix, after which magnetic resonance imaging stages the lesion locally. The biopsy must be arranged by the sarcoma service, since an inappropriately placed tract can compromise limb salvage.
key_points: Night pain and pain worsening despite rest are the cardinal red flags in adolescent bone pain
Tenderness above rather than at the tibial tuberosity moves the diagnosis away from apophysitis
Distal femur is the commonest osteosarcoma site and the peak is the adolescent growth spurt
Plain radiograph is the first imaging test; magnetic resonance imaging then stages locally
Biopsy is planned and performed by the sarcoma unit, never locally
explanation.pearls: A previous benign label such as growing pain or apophysitis is one of the strongest contributors to delayed sarcoma diagnosis, so treat failure to improve after six weeks of genuine rest as an indication to image rather than as a reason to reinforce the original advice.

options.rationale: This is the management of traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity, where tenderness sits over the bony prominence below the kneecap and pain settles with relative rest. Tenderness above the kneecap and deterioration despite six weeks off sport contradict that diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

Magnetic resonance imaging is essential for local staging but follows the plain radiograph, which characterises the aggressive periosteal reaction and matrix that establish suspicion. Ordering a scan limited to the knee also risks missing a lesion centred in the femoral metaphysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

Subacute osteomyelitis can mimic bone tumour and cause night pain, but a firm palpable soft tissue mass with weight loss is not explained by it, and treating blind delays a time-critical diagnosis. Antibiotics before imaging and tissue diagnosis also confound interpretation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

Biopsy of a suspected primary bone sarcoma is planned and performed by the unit that will carry out the definitive resection, because a poorly placed tract contaminates compartments and can convert a limb sparing operation into an amputation. Speed matters but so does who holds the scalpel. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

Night pain, pain persisting despite rest, weight loss and a firm deep mass over the distal femur are red flags for primary bone malignancy, and plain radiography is the first imaging test and is highly informative in osteosarcoma. Referral runs in parallel because biopsy must be planned by the treating sarcoma unit rather than performed locally. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors and halts red cell production for roughly a week, which is clinically silent in a child with a normal red cell lifespan but catastrophic when the lifespan is already shortened by hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia or sickle cell disease. The signature is severe anaemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, and bilirubin often falls rather than rises because haemolysis is not increased. This inverted pattern distinguishes it from a haemolytic crisis, splenic sequestration or autoimmune haemolysis, all of which drive reticulocytosis. Treatment is supportive with transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, and marrow recovery follows within one to two weeks. Confirming parvovirus also triggers contact advice, since infection in pregnancy risks fetal hydrops and infection in other children with haemolytic disorders risks the same crisis.
key_points: Anaemia with a suppressed reticulocyte count after a viral exanthem indicates red cell aplasia
Bilirubin falls in aplastic crisis because haemolysis is not increased
Rising reticulocytes point instead to haemolysis, sequestration or bleeding
Management is supportive with transfusion; the marrow recovers in one to two weeks
Confirmation drives contact tracing for pregnant women and other haemolytic patients
explanation.pearls: The child is most infectious in the week before the facial rash appears and is generally no longer infectious once the rash is visible, so exclusion at rash onset achieves little, while a pregnant household contact who was exposed in the preceding week needs parvovirus serology and fetal surveillance arranged.

options.rationale: A slapped cheek illness followed by profound anaemia with a suppressed reticulocyte count in a child with chronic haemolysis is transient aplastic crisis, in which parvovirus B19 arrests erythroid precursors for about a week. Serology plus nucleic acid testing confirms it, and testing matters because it identifies the household infection risk to pregnant contacts and to other children with haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Autoimmune haemolysis raises the reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates and typically gives a positive antiglobulin test with rising bilirubin. Here the reticulocytes are suppressed, bilirubin is low and the antiglobulin test is already negative. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Marrow infiltration usually depresses more than one lineage and is accompanied by bruising, bone pain, lymphadenopathy or an abnormal white cell picture. A normal white cell and platelet count with an isolated red cell arrest after a viral exanthem does not warrant an invasive marrow test. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Splenic sequestration causes a rapidly enlarging spleen with a falling haemoglobin and a high reticulocyte count as the marrow responds. This spleen is unchanged from the clinic record and the reticulocyte count has collapsed. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Iron deficiency develops over months with microcytosis and does not produce a fall to this level within a week. Chronic haemolysis also tends towards iron loading rather than depletion once transfusions begin. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

explanation.summary: Lower limb alignment follows a predictable arc, with physiological varus at the start of walking correcting towards neutral by about two years and passing through a valgus phase before settling near adult alignment by about seven years. Departures from that arc are what matter, and the concerning features are asymmetry, progression rather than improvement, an intercondylar distance beyond about 6 cm, short stature, bone pain and a lateral thrust of the knee during stance. Infantile tibia vara affects the medial proximal tibial physis, is strongly associated with high body mass and early walking, and produces exactly this asymmetrical progressive picture. Nutritional rickets is the main metabolic alternative and is screened for with calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D, which are normal here. Standing long leg radiographs with orthopaedic referral is the correct pathway once the presentation leaves the physiological arc.
key_points: Physiological varus corrects by around two years and is symmetrical and painless
Asymmetry, progression and a lateral knee thrust indicate a physeal growth disturbance
High body mass and early walking are the recognised associations of infantile tibia vara
Normal calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D exclude nutritional rickets
Standing long leg alignment films are the imaging of choice, not knee views alone
explanation.pearls: Measure the intercondylar distance with the medial malleoli touching and record it in the notes at each visit, because a gap that is widening across two visits after the second birthday is a more reliable trigger for radiographs than any single measurement, and the metaphyseal diaphyseal angle can then be calculated from a standing film to separate tibia vara from persistent physiological varus.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Night splinting has no role in either physiological varus or in a progressive physeal deformity, and the abnormal gait is a consequence of the bony alignment rather than a learned pattern. Bracing that is used for infantile tibia vara is a specific daytime knee ankle foot orthosis prescribed after imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Bowing that is asymmetrical, worsening after the age at which physiological varus should be correcting, and accompanied by a lateral thrust in a heavy child points to a growth disturbance of the proximal tibial physis rather than a normal variant. Standing alignment films quantify the deformity and allow the metaphyseal diaphyseal angle to be measured, and orthopaedic input is needed because bracing or osteotomy may be required. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Physiological varus is symmetrical and is correcting by around two years towards neutral and then valgus, so worsening asymmetrical bowing at three years falls outside that pattern. Waiting a further year allows a progressive physeal deformity to become harder to correct. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Nutritional rickets is excluded by a normal corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D level together with the absence of wrist widening or costochondral swelling. Supplementing a replete child treats no deficiency and delays the correct assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

A skeletal dysplasia is suggested by short stature with a height well below the expected range for the family and by disproportionate limb segments. This child's height is on the 50th centile, which makes a generalised dysplasia unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia is common and most infants with a visible frenulum feed perfectly well, so the decision to divide rests on function rather than appearance. The threshold combines an anatomically restrictive frenulum, demonstrated by limited tongue elevation and extension with notching of the tip, and a feeding problem such as persistent nipple pain and damage, clicking, prolonged feeds and inadequate weight gain. Crucially, skilled lactation assessment must come first, since positioning and attachment correction resolves the majority of nipple pain without any procedure. Where support has been delivered and the problem persists, frenotomy is a quick low risk office procedure that improves maternal nipple pain most consistently, and lactation follow up afterwards is essential. Division of the upper lip frenulum is not supported and posterior tongue tie remains a contested entity.
key_points: Appearance alone never justifies frenotomy; function plus anatomy does
Skilled lactation support must be delivered and shown to fail first
Restricted elevation and extension with tip notching define an anatomical restriction
Maternal nipple pain is the outcome that improves most consistently after division
Upper lip frenulum division is not recommended for breastfeeding difficulty
explanation.pearls: Weight against birth weight is the objective anchor in these consultations: an infant who has not regained birth weight by day fourteen has a feeding problem requiring action regardless of the frenulum, while a thriving infant with an obvious tongue tie and comfortable feeding needs no procedure at all.

options.rationale: Candidal nipple pain classically begins after a period of comfortable feeding and is burning pain persisting between feeds, often with a shiny areola. Pain present from the outset with clicking and poor transfer points to a mechanical problem instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Evidence for division of the upper lip frenulum to improve breastfeeding is weak and the practice is not recommended in Australian paediatric guidance. Adding an unproven procedure and a therapy program delays the intervention with the best evidence. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

Frenotomy is offered when an anatomically restrictive frenulum is coupled with a demonstrated feeding problem that has not responded to skilled lactation support, which is exactly this pair after two days of hands on work. The procedure is quick and low risk in a young infant, and continued lactation support afterwards is what converts the anatomical change into improved transfer. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

Skilled support is the correct first step and has already been delivered across two days without change, while the infant remains below birth weight at twelve days. Repeating an intervention that has failed risks established low supply and early weaning. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

Full transfer to expressed feeding is a reasonable temporary rescue for severe damage but does not address the restriction and commonly ends direct breastfeeding altogether. It also adds a substantial expressing burden without treating the cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult presentation in both distribution and treatment. Infants characteristically have palmar and plantar involvement with pustules, nodules in the axillae and groin, and involvement of the scalp, face and neck, all sites that are typically spared in adults. Diagnosis is clinical, strongly supported by an intensely itchy household contact with the classic nocturnal itch, and burrows are the pathognomonic lesion. Permethrin 5 percent is the Australian first line agent and can be used in young infants under medical supervision, applied to the entire body surface including the scalp and face in this age group, with all household and close contacts treated on the same day regardless of symptoms. Itch persists for two to four weeks after successful eradication, and this post scabetic itch should be treated symptomatically rather than being read as treatment failure.
key_points: Infantile scabies involves palms, soles, scalp and face, unlike the adult distribution
Permethrin 5 percent is first line and covers the whole body including the scalp in infants
All household and close contacts are treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms
Oral ivermectin is avoided below 15 kg and is reserved for crusted disease or failure
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and is not evidence of treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Reserve a second permethrin application for seven days after the first, since the agent is not fully ovicidal and a repeat treatment kills mites hatching from surviving eggs, while treating persistent itch at three weeks with repeated scabicide instead of an emollient and a short corticosteroid course causes irritant dermatitis that is then mistaken for continuing infestation.

options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is an alternative scabicide but causes marked stinging and irritant dermatitis and requires dilution in young children, so it is not the preferred first agent in infancy. Restricting application to below the neck also misses the scalp and face, which are involved at this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Corticosteroid suppresses the itch and the inflammatory response while the mites continue to multiply, producing the modified and often widespread picture sometimes called incognito scabies. It has a place only after scabicidal treatment for the residual post scabetic itch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Pustules in infantile scabies are usually sterile and part of the infestation rather than bacterial superinfection, which would show honey coloured crusting, warmth or cellulitis. Antibiotics are added only when those secondary features are present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Palmoplantar pustules, burrows and axillary nodules with an itchy household contact is scabies, and permethrin 5 percent is the preferred agent in Australia and may be used from the neonatal period under medical supervision. Infants differ from adults in that the scalp, face, neck, palms and soles must all be treated, and simultaneous treatment of every household contact prevents immediate reinfestation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Oral ivermectin is not used in infants below 15 kg because safety at low body weight has not been established, and it is reserved for crusted scabies, outbreaks and treatment failure. The weight here is far below that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Zinc deficiency in an exclusively breastfed infant arises either from an inherited defect of intestinal zinc absorption or, distinctively, from a maternal defect in the mammary zinc transporter that produces breast milk of abnormally low zinc content in an entirely well mother. Preterm infants are at particular risk because most zinc is accrued in the third trimester and their requirements per kilogram are high. The clinical signature is a sharply marginated erosive eruption in periorificial and acral distribution that fails antifungal and barrier treatment, together with diarrhoea, irritability, developmental regression, faltering growth and sparse depigmenting hair. A low serum alkaline phosphatase is a useful supporting clue because the enzyme requires zinc, and serum zinc should be interpreted alongside albumin since zinc is largely protein bound and hypoalbuminaemia lowers the measured value. Supplementation is started empirically because the dermatological response within days is both therapeutic and diagnostic.
key_points: Periorificial plus acral erosions failing antifungal therapy is the pattern to recognise
Preterm infants have low zinc stores because accrual is a third trimester event
A well mother can produce zinc deficient milk through a mammary transporter defect
Low alkaline phosphatase supports the diagnosis because the enzyme is zinc dependent
Interpret serum zinc alongside albumin and treat empirically rather than waiting
explanation.pearls: Measure zinc in the mother's breast milk rather than her serum when an exclusively breastfed infant responds to supplementation, because a maternal SLC30A2 mammary transporter defect leaves her own serum zinc and her health entirely normal, and identifying it changes counselling for any subsequent infant she breastfeeds.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.rationale: Candidal nappy rash involves the skin folds with satellite pustules and responds to antifungal treatment, neither of which fits a rash that has failed two weeks of therapy and extends to the mouth, fingertips and heels. Adding a corticosteroid treats inflammation without correcting the underlying deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash)

Immunobullous disease in infancy is rare and presents with tense blisters and erosions in a distribution not confined to periorificial and acral sites, without the systemic triad seen here. Biopsy delays a treatment that would produce a visible response within days. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

Cow milk protein allergy in an exclusively breastfed infant is managed by maternal dietary exclusion rather than formula, and it does not produce sharply marginated acral erosions or hair depigmentation. The rash distribution is the finding that does not fit an allergic enteropathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis can present with a zinc responsive rash through malabsorption and deserves consideration, but newborn screening covers the great majority of Australian infants and the rash still requires zinc replacement whatever the cause. Testing without treating leaves a rapidly correctable deficiency unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

An acral and periorificial erosive eruption resistant to antifungals, with diarrhoea, sparse lightening hair, developmental regression and faltering growth, is the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and hair change that defines zinc deficiency, and the low alkaline phosphatase is a supportive clue because that enzyme is zinc dependent. Treatment is started before the level returns because the clinical response within days is itself confirmatory and the deficiency is rapidly reversible. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

explanation.summary: A hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation is the position of maximum capsular volume and is the joint's way of minimising pressure from an effusion. The Kocher predictors were derived to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis, and the probability of infection climbs steeply as predictors accumulate rather than at any single cut-off. Ultrasound reliably detects an effusion but cannot characterise it, so the fluid must be sampled. Untreated septic arthritis of the hip destroys articular cartilage within days and can infarct the femoral head, which is why this sits alongside testicular torsion as a same-day surgical problem.
key_points: The four predictors are non-weight bearing, fever above 38.5 C, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L
Ultrasound confirms an effusion but never tells you whether it is infected
Blood cultures and joint fluid go before the first antibiotic dose wherever the delay is minutes rather than hours
Transient synovitis follows a viral illness, the child is afebrile and inflammatory markers are normal or marginal
Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism beyond the neonatal period in Australia
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is the leading cause of septic arthritis between 6 months and 4 years and grows poorly on solid media, so joint fluid should be inoculated directly into a paediatric blood culture bottle at the bedside rather than sent dry.

options.rationale: He meets four of the four predictors used in Australian practice: non-weight bearing, temperature above 38.5 C, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L. Aspiration of the effusion under orthopaedic care secures the microbiological diagnosis, and taking it before antibiotics preserves culture yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

Magnetic resonance imaging answers a different question: it is used when osteomyelitis is suspected alongside or instead of joint infection, or when the effusion is not accessible. Here ultrasound has already shown drainable fluid and imaging only delays the diagnostic tap. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

Antibiotics before aspiration reduce the chance of isolating an organism from joint fluid, which matters because treatment runs for weeks and may need narrowing. Give the first dose immediately after the sample is taken, not before it. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

Serial ultrasound cannot distinguish infected from reactive fluid, so a repeat scan will not change the decision it is being used to defer. Observation is reasonable only when the predictor count is low and the child is afebrile. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

This is the pathway for transient synovitis, which is afebrile with normal or near-normal inflammatory markers. A temperature of 38.9 C with a C-reactive protein of 78 mg/L places him in the high-probability band and a 48 hour delay risks irreversible cartilage damage. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a spectrum from mild acetabular shallowness to fixed dislocation, and the physical signs change as the child grows. In the newborn the unstable hip can be provoked in and out of the socket, which is what the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres detect; once the hip sits dislocated and the soft tissues contract, those tests fall silent and asymmetric abduction becomes the most sensitive sign. Breech presentation, female sex and a positive family history are the three risk factors that trigger imaging in Australia even when the examination is normal. A normal newborn check never excludes the diagnosis, because dysplasia can develop after birth.
key_points: Ultrasound is the modality under 4.5 months; the plain pelvic radiograph takes over after that
Limited abduction and apparent femoral shortening are the signs of an established dislocation
Negative Ortolani and Barlow in an older infant is reassuring only if abduction is full and symmetric
Breech presentation at or after 36 weeks, female sex and a first-degree family history warrant imaging regardless of examination
Later diagnosis means a higher chance of open reduction, femoral osteotomy and early degenerative disease
explanation.pearls: A Pavlik harness is effective up to about 6 months of age and carries a failure rate above 50% once the hip is dislocated and irreducible, which is why the Australian newborn risk-factor ultrasound is booked at 6 weeks rather than left to the routine checks.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Ultrasound is the correct modality under 4.5 months, when the femoral head is still cartilaginous and acoustically transparent. At 6 months the ossific nucleus casts an acoustic shadow over the medial acetabulum and the study becomes unreliable. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantial gonadal radiation dose to an infant and adds nothing to a plain film at the diagnostic stage. It has a narrow role in complex revision surgical planning. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for assessing reduction after closed or open surgical treatment, not for making the initial diagnosis. It requires sedation or anaesthesia in this age group for no diagnostic gain over a plain film. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Beyond about 4.5 months the femoral head ossifies and the cartilaginous landmarks that ultrasound depends on are obscured, so the plain radiograph becomes the investigation of choice. Acetabular index and the relationship of the ossific nucleus to Perkin's and Hilgenreiner's lines are assessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Limited abduction with apparent femoral shortening after 3 months is the presentation of an established dislocation, and Ortolani and Barlow become negative precisely because the hip is no longer reducible. Waiting six months converts a closed reduction into an open one. (Source: RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and less commonly Streptococcus pyogenes, and the two cannot be separated clinically. The management decision is driven almost entirely by extent rather than by organism, because topical therapy cannot reliably cover widespread disease and oral therapy is unnecessary for a few lesions. Crust is a reservoir of organisms and a barrier to topical penetration, so soaking it off with a warm damp cloth before each application materially improves cure. The public health dimension matters in Australian practice because untreated streptococcal skin infection is a driver of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and contributes to the rheumatic heart disease burden in some communities.
key_points: Localised disease is treated topically; oral antibiotics are for multiple sites, extensive lesions or systemic symptoms
Remove crust by soaking before each topical application
Fusidic acid is avoided in Australia because of resistance rates
Children may return to school 24 hours after treatment starts if lesions are covered
Recurrent or extensive impetigo warrants a scabies examination and household screening
explanation.pearls: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows skin infection by 3 to 6 weeks rather than the 1 to 2 weeks that follows pharyngitis, so a child with cola-coloured urine one month after impetigo needs a blood pressure and urinalysis, not a throat swab.

options.rationale: Fusidic acid resistance in Australian Staphylococcus aureus isolates is high enough that it is no longer preferred, and exclusion runs only until 24 hours of treatment with lesions covered, not until healing. Both halves of this option are wrong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Australian guidance reserves oral antibiotics for widespread or multiple-site disease, systemic symptoms or outbreak settings, and treats localised impetigo topically. Soaking and removing crust first is part of the treatment because it lets the ointment reach the colonised skin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This is the regimen used in remote Australian communities where impetigo is often extensive and where methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common, and it is an oral agent for the same reason that oral cefalexin is wrong here. The deciding factor is the burden of disease, not the organism. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

Oral therapy is indicated when lesions are numerous, spread across multiple body regions, or the child is systemically unwell, none of which applies here. Using it for three localised lesions adds gastrointestinal side effects and selection pressure without improving cure rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antiseptic creams are an option in some overseas guidance for very limited disease but are not the Australian recommendation, and evidence for cure is weaker than for topical antibiotics. They have a role in decolonisation adjuncts rather than as primary treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Universal newborn hearing screening in Australia uses automated auditory brainstem response or otoacoustic emissions to sort infants into pass and refer, and a refer result is a screening flag rather than a diagnosis. The purpose of the program is captured in the 1-3-6 framework: screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months and start intervention by 6 months, because receptive and expressive language outcomes track closely with the age at which amplification begins. Unilateral loss still matters, producing difficulty with sound localisation and with speech discrimination in noisy classrooms. Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest non-genetic cause and is only diagnosable from a sample taken in the first three weeks, after which a positive result cannot be distinguished from postnatal acquisition.
key_points: A refer result on the repeat screen leads to diagnostic audiology, not to another screen
The Australian benchmark is diagnosis by 3 months and intervention by 6 months
A startle response does not exclude significant hearing loss
Congenital cytomegalovirus testing must be collected within the first 3 weeks of life
Unilateral loss requires follow-up because of localisation and speech-in-noise difficulty
explanation.pearls: Congenital cytomegalovirus hearing loss can be progressive and late onset, so an infant with a positive urine polymerase chain reaction needs audiological review every 6 months to at least 3 years even if the initial diagnostic assessment shows normal thresholds.

options.rationale: Tympanometry is unreliable in the first few months because the infant ear canal is compliant, and there is no otoscopic abnormality to suction. Surgical referral follows the audiological diagnosis rather than preceding it. (Source: RCH CPG: Hearing Loss)

Rescreening has already been done and failed, so repeating the same test answers nothing and consumes the diagnostic window. A behavioural startle to a loud noise is a brainstem reflex that is preserved in unilateral and in moderate bilateral loss. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)

A refer result that persists on the repeat screen triggers diagnostic audiological assessment, and the Australian benchmark is diagnosis by 3 months with intervention started by 6 months. Diagnostic auditory brainstem response gives ear-specific and frequency-specific thresholds that the automated screen cannot. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)

Urine polymerase chain reaction for cytomegalovirus is genuinely time-critical and should be collected within the first 3 weeks, so it is done in parallel rather than instead of audiology. Sequencing it ahead of the hearing assessment delays both. (Source: RCH CPG: Hearing Loss)

Waiting for speech delay to declare itself is the historical pathway that universal newborn screening was built to replace, since language outcomes deteriorate sharply once amplification starts after 6 months. Surveillance supplements audiology but cannot substitute for it. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)

explanation.summary: Strabismus in infancy is common enough that the clinical task is separating a true deviation from the far more frequent pseudostrabismus produced by a broad nasal bridge and epicanthic folds. Two bedside tests settle it: the corneal light reflex should sit symmetrically just nasal to the centre of each pupil, and the cover test should produce no movement in the uncovered eye if both eyes are already fixing. Intermittent deviation before 3 to 4 months can be physiological as binocular control matures, but a constant deviation at any age and any deviation beyond 4 months is pathological. The clinical stake is amblyopia, where the cortex suppresses input from the deviating eye and visual development is permanently curtailed if not treated within the sensitive period.
key_points: Symmetric corneal light reflexes plus a normal cover test defines pseudostrabismus
A refixation movement on cover testing means a true manifest deviation
Any constant squint, or any squint after 4 months of age, needs ophthalmology referral
Always check the red reflex, because leukocoria may signal retinoblastoma or cataract
Amblyopia treatment is far more effective before 7 years of age
explanation.pearls: Accommodative esotropia typically appears between 2 and 3 years in a hypermetropic child and can be fully corrected by glasses alone, so cycloplegic refraction precedes any discussion of squint surgery.

options.rationale: An abnormal cover test with a refixation movement confirms a manifest deviation and excludes pseudostrabismus, whatever the epicanthic folds suggest. Any constant squint beyond 3 to 4 months of age needs specialist assessment because amblyopia develops rapidly in the sensitive period. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once refraction and visual acuity have been measured and the deviation characterised, and the amount of patching is titrated to those findings. Starting it in general practice risks treating the wrong eye or over-occluding. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric Vision Screening)

Squint can be the presenting sign of retinoblastoma, but the screening test for that is the red reflex, which is present and symmetric here. Ordering imaging ahead of an ophthalmological examination inverts the assessment sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

Cycloplegic refraction is an essential part of the workup because accommodative esotropia responds to hypermetropic correction, but an infant with a constant deviation needs the full orthoptic and ophthalmological assessment that includes it. This option covers only one component. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric Vision Screening)

Pseudostrabismus is the correct label only when the corneal light reflexes are symmetric and the cover test shows no refixation movement, because the folds merely obscure nasal sclera. Here both tests are abnormal, so the appearance is real. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis complicates juvenile idiopathic arthritis in a pattern almost perfectly inverse to the joint disease: the children with the fewest joints involved and the mildest arthritis carry the highest ocular risk. The inflammation runs entirely independently of joint activity, so a child whose arthritis is in remission is not thereby protected and screening continues regardless. Because the eye remains white and the child never complains, the diagnosis is made only by planned slit lamp examination, and the complications that follow missed disease are posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma and permanent vision loss. Risk stratification in Australian practice is built from antinuclear antibody status, arthritis subtype and age at onset, and it sets the screening interval rather than whether screening happens at all.
key_points: Highest risk is antinuclear antibody positive, oligoarticular onset, young and female
Screening for the high-risk group is 3-monthly slit lamp examination
The uveitis is painless with a white eye and normal acuity until late
Ocular inflammation is independent of joint disease activity and of treatment response
Systemic onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis carries the lowest uveitis risk
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate reduces the incidence of uveitis flares in juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and adalimumab added to methotrexate is the escalation for refractory disease, but neither alters the screening interval while the child remains in the high-risk category.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: Antinuclear antibody positivity, oligoarticular subtype, female sex and onset under 7 years together define the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, which is screened 3-monthly. The interval is short because the inflammation is asymptomatic and white-eyed until structural damage has occurred. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: This inverts the central fact about this complication: the uveitis of oligoarticular arthritis is characteristically painless and the eye stays white, unlike the acute anterior uveitis of the spondyloarthropathies. Symptom-triggered review means presentation at the stage of band keratopathy or cataract. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

The pathology is in the anterior chamber, which direct fundoscopy does not visualise, and the problem is the instrument rather than the interval. Screening must be done on a slit lamp by someone trained to grade anterior chamber activity. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

Acuity is preserved until the anterior chamber inflammation has caused posterior synechiae, cataract or glaucoma, so it is a late and insensitive marker. Only the slit lamp detects the cells and flare that define active disease. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: Annual screening is the interval used for the low-risk groups, such as antinuclear antibody negative children with polyarticular disease or those with systemic onset arthritis. Applying it to this risk profile misses the window in which silent inflammation can be caught. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

explanation.summary: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children seeds the metaphysis, where sluggish flow in the vascular loops adjacent to the physis favours bacterial lodgement, and it is therefore metaphyseal tenderness rather than joint signs that localises the disease. The adjacent joint is normal, so a limp with fever can be wrongly attributed to a musculoskeletal strain when the radiograph comes back clear. Staphylococcus aureus dominates, and empirical therapy in Australia is high-dose intravenous flucloxacillin with the duration guided by clinical and C-reactive protein response before an oral switch. Surgery is required when there is a subperiosteal or intraosseous collection, when the child fails to respond to antibiotics, or when there is an adjacent septic joint.
key_points: Plain radiographs remain normal for 10 to 14 days and cannot exclude early osteomyelitis
Magnetic resonance imaging shows marrow oedema early and identifies drainable collections
Metaphyseal tenderness with a normal adjacent joint is the characteristic localising sign
Staphylococcus aureus is the dominant pathogen beyond the neonatal period
Blood cultures are positive in a substantial minority and may be the only microbiological yield
explanation.pearls: In the hip, shoulder and elbow the metaphysis lies inside the joint capsule, so metaphyseal osteomyelitis at those three sites can decompress directly into the joint and produce a concurrent septic arthritis that changes the operation required.

options.rationale: Serial films will eventually become positive, which is exactly the problem: waiting for radiographic change means treating a 2-week-old infection that has had time to form sequestrum. The test is specific but far too slow for this decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

Computed tomography shows cortical destruction and sequestrum well, which makes it useful in chronic osteomyelitis, but it is relatively insensitive to the marrow oedema of early disease. Computed tomography images mineral, while magnetic resonance imaging images marrow water. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

Bone scintigraphy is sensitive early and retains a role when the site is unclear or multifocal disease is suspected, but it gives poor anatomical resolution and cannot show a drainable collection. It is the fallback when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable or the child cannot be scanned. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

Ultrasound can demonstrate subperiosteal pus and periosteal elevation once those have developed, and it is useful for guiding aspiration, but a negative study does not exclude intramedullary infection. It cannot see into the marrow, which is where the disease starts. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

Plain films stay normal for 10 to 14 days because roughly a third of bone mineral must be lost before lysis is visible, so a normal radiograph at day 5 carries no reassurance. Magnetic resonance imaging detects the marrow oedema of early infection and defines any subperiosteal or intraosseous collection that would need surgical drainage. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty is defined in Australian practice as secondary sexual development before 8 years in girls and before 9 years in boys, and the first branch point is whether the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis has switched on early or whether sex steroids are arriving from an autonomous peripheral source. Central disease is gonadotrophin dependent and follows the normal sequence of puberty, whereas peripheral causes such as an ovarian cyst, an adrenal tumour or McCune-Albright syndrome produce a disordered sequence with suppressed gonadotrophins. Bone age advancement matters because premature epiphyseal fusion is what costs final adult height, and it is the main reason to treat. Isolated premature thelarche without growth acceleration or bone age advance is a benign non-progressive variant that needs observation rather than a workup of this depth.
key_points: Central precocious puberty is gonadotrophin dependent and confirmed by a pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation
Peripheral precocity has suppressed gonadotrophins and a disordered pubertal sequence
Bone age advancement and growth acceleration separate progressive disease from benign thelarche
Brain imaging follows confirmation of central disease and has a higher yield the younger the child
Treatment of central disease is with a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist to preserve adult height
explanation.pearls: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist such as leuprorelin paradoxically suppresses the axis by continuous rather than pulsatile receptor stimulation, and treatment is generally continued until around 11 years of bone age to maximise the adult height gained.

options.rationale: A pubertal luteinising hormone rise after stimulation proves that the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis has been reactivated, which is the definition of central precocious puberty and the trigger for brain imaging and for treatment. An equivocal basal level cannot make that distinction, which is why the dynamic test exists. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

Pelvic ultrasound is a useful adjunct that shows oestrogen exposure and can reveal an autonomous ovarian cyst or tumour, but uterine changes reflect oestrogen from any source. It describes the downstream effect rather than identifying whether the drive is central. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

Brain imaging is the right next step once central precocious puberty has been confirmed, particularly in a girl this young where the yield for hypothalamic hamartoma and other lesions is meaningful. Ordering it before the axis has been characterised images children whose problem is peripheral. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

Germ cell tumour markers matter in boys with peripheral precocity, where beta human chorionic gonadotrophin can drive testicular testosterone production, and have little role in an isolated female thelarche. They are a reasonable adjunct but will not answer the central versus peripheral question. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

This panel investigates adrenal androgen excess, which produces pubic and axillary hair, acne and clitoromegaly rather than breast development. The isolated thelarche with Tanner stage 1 pubic hair points away from an adrenal source. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

explanation.summary: The commonest avoidable error in coeliac diagnosis is testing a patient who has already started a gluten free diet, because both the serological and the histological abnormalities are consequences of ongoing gluten exposure and both resolve without it. An adequate challenge means a meaningful daily gluten intake for at least six weeks in children before serology is repeated, and longer if biopsy is planned. Securing the diagnosis matters more than the symptom response suggests, because it drives long-term surveillance for iron and bone mineral deficiency, first-degree relative screening, and the distinction from non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, which needs no lifelong restriction. Human leucocyte antigen typing sits outside the diet problem entirely and is best used when a challenge is refused or poorly tolerated, since a negative result closes the question permanently.
key_points: Coeliac serology and duodenal histology both normalise on a gluten free diet
A gluten challenge of at least six weeks is needed before repeat testing in a child
Total IgA must accompany tissue transglutaminase IgA because selective IgA deficiency causes false negatives
HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing is diet independent and useful for its negative predictive value only
Confirming the diagnosis triggers family screening and long-term nutritional surveillance
explanation.pearls: Selective IgA deficiency is about ten times more common in coeliac disease than in the general population, so an undetectable tissue transglutaminase IgA with a low total IgA should be followed by an IgG-based assay rather than read as a negative result.

options.rationale: The serology was taken under conditions that make a negative result uninformative rather than reassuring. Committing a child to a lifelong restrictive diet without a diagnosis also removes her access to follow-up, bone density surveillance and family screening. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

Human leucocyte antigen typing is valuable only for its negative predictive value, because a negative result effectively excludes coeliac disease for life, and it is unaffected by diet. A positive result is shared by roughly a third of the population and confirms nothing. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

Deamidated gliadin peptide testing is genuinely useful when total IgA is deficient, since it is an IgG-based assay, but total IgA is normal here. It is subject to exactly the same normalisation on a gluten free diet as tissue transglutaminase, so it does not solve the problem. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet just as serology does, so biopsies taken now risk a false negative and an unnecessary anaesthetic. Endoscopy has a place after the challenge if the repeat serology is positive or discordant. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

Coeliac serology measures an immune response to ingested gluten and normalises within weeks to months of withdrawal, so a negative result on a gluten-restricted diet cannot exclude the diagnosis. An adequate gluten challenge before retesting is the only way to make the result interpretable. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

explanation.summary: Crusted scabies represents a failed host response to Sarcoptes scabiei, with mite numbers in the thousands to millions rather than the ten or so carried in ordinary infestation, and it is correspondingly far more contagious. It is classically associated with immunosuppression but occurs in people with no identifiable immune defect, and in Australia it is concentrated in remote communities where it drives ongoing transmission, recurrent skin infection and the downstream burden of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic heart disease. Grading by crusting distribution, thickness and skin condition determines how many ivermectin doses are given. Because the index case seeds the household and the wider community, treating contacts simultaneously is part of the treatment rather than an optional public health add-on.
key_points: Crusted scabies carries a vastly higher mite burden and is far more transmissible than ordinary scabies
Hyperkeratotic crust blocks topical penetration, so combined oral and topical therapy is required
Keratolytic treatment softens crust and lets the scabicide reach the mites
Ivermectin dose number is set by disease grade rather than being fixed
Simultaneous treatment of household and close contacts prevents immediate reinfestation
explanation.pearls: Itch persists for 2 to 4 weeks after successful scabies treatment because it is a hypersensitivity response to retained mite antigen, so ongoing scratching in that window should prompt a moisturiser and a topical corticosteroid rather than a third course of scabicide.

options.rationale: Bacterial superinfection is a genuine and serious complication of this condition, but he is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers and no cellulitic margin, so there is nothing to treat today. Deferring definitive scabicide until discharge leaves the mite burden untouched. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

Two applications of permethrin a week apart treat ordinary scabies, and this has already failed twice because the cream cannot penetrate hyperkeratotic crust to reach the mites beneath it. Treating the household remains essential but is not sufficient for the index case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

The crusted form carries a mite burden orders of magnitude above ordinary scabies, and the hyperkeratosis physically shields mites from topical agents, so neither modality succeeds alone. Australian guidance combines repeated oral ivermectin with topical scabicide and a keratolytic to break down the crust, with the number of doses set by disease grade. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

Benzyl benzoate is an alternative scabicide but is irritant on fissured skin and remains a topical agent facing the same penetration barrier. Antihistamines address the symptom of itch without reducing the mite load that is driving it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A single dose does not cover eggs that hatch after treatment, and in the crusted form even the standard two-dose schedule is inadequate. It also lacks the topical and keratolytic components. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

explanation.summary: Murmurs are audible in a large proportion of healthy children at some point, and the clinical skill is applying the criteria that define an innocent murmur rather than relying on the absence of symptoms. Innocent murmurs are soft, systolic, short, sited over a small area, unaccompanied by a thrill, and vary with posture, with normal heart sounds and normal pulses. Diastolic timing sits outside that framework entirely: it reflects either regurgitation through a semilunar valve or turbulent flow across an atrioventricular valve, both of which are structural. In an athletic pre-participation context the decision carries additional weight because clearing a child with an undiagnosed structural lesion for competitive sport transfers the risk to an unsupervised setting.
key_points: Every diastolic murmur is pathological and requires echocardiography
Innocent murmur criteria apply only to systolic murmurs
A Still's murmur is vibratory, mid-systolic, at the lower left sternal edge and softens on standing
A venous hum is continuous, loudest above the clavicle, and abolished by lying flat
Absent or delayed femoral pulses point to coarctation and need four-limb blood pressures
explanation.pearls: In Australian children an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation or a mid-diastolic mitral murmur should prompt consideration of rheumatic heart disease, which remains a leading cause of acquired valve disease in young people in northern and central Australia and is diagnosed echocardiographically.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Guideline for Rheumatic Heart Disease

options.rationale: Four-limb blood pressures are aimed at coarctation of the aorta, which produces radiofemoral delay and diminished femoral pulses, and his femoral pulses are present and synchronous. This investigates a different lesion from the one the auscultatory findings indicate. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

A Still's murmur is a low-pitched vibratory mid-systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that softens on standing, and it is the commonest innocent murmur at this age. Timing separates them: Still's is systolic, and this murmur is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

A venous hum is continuous rather than confined to diastole, is loudest in the neck and infraclavicular area, and characteristically disappears when the child lies flat or the neck veins are compressed. None of those features is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

Both tests are insensitive for the valve lesions that produce a diastolic murmur, and a normal electrocardiogram with a normal chest film would not exclude aortic regurgitation. Using them as a gate to referral risks a falsely reassuring result. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

Any diastolic murmur is pathological regardless of how soft it is or how well the child appears, because normal flow across normal valves does not generate diastolic turbulence. Innocent murmur criteria apply only to systolic murmurs, so no combination of reassuring features rescues this one. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

explanation.summary: Hip pathology refers pain along the obturator nerve distribution to the medial thigh and knee, so a child presenting with knee pain and a normal knee examination has a hip problem until proven otherwise. Slipped upper femoral epiphysis occurs during the adolescent growth spurt when shear forces across a widened physis exceed its strength, and obesity is the dominant risk factor in Australian practice. The physical sign that gives it away is obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed, produced by the posteriorly displaced epiphysis. The stakes are set by two complications, avascular necrosis and chondrolysis, both of which rise sharply if a stable slip is allowed to become unstable, which is why non-weight bearing begins before the confirmatory image is obtained rather than after it.
key_points: Knee pain with a normal knee examination requires a full hip assessment
The anteroposterior view alone can miss early posterior slippage; a lateral view is mandatory
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the characteristic mechanical sign
Make the child non-weight bearing immediately, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
Avascular necrosis risk is much higher in unstable than in stable slips
explanation.pearls: Around one in five slips is bilateral at presentation and a further proportion of the remainder slip on the other side within 18 months, so both hips are imaged at diagnosis and the contralateral side is reviewed at every follow-up until the physes close.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Early slippage displaces the femoral epiphysis posteriorly, which an anteroposterior projection can miss entirely while the lateral view shows it clearly, so a normal single-view film does not exclude the diagnosis. Weight bearing risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one, which carries a far higher rate of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: The knee examination is entirely normal and the abnormal findings are all at the hip, so imaging the symptomatic site rather than the pathological one is the classic error in this presentation. Allowing him to walk for two weeks meanwhile is the more serious half of the mistake. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: He is afebrile with a C-reactive protein of 3 mg/L and a normal white cell count, which makes septic arthritis very unlikely, and the six-week history is wrong for it. Ultrasound may show a small effusion in this condition but does not visualise the epiphyseal displacement that defines it. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation is a specific mechanical sign that cannot be explained by growth-related knee pain. Progression during a month of continued weight bearing is what turns a pinning operation into a salvage one. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

Endocrinopathy including hypothyroidism and renal osteodystrophy is a genuine association worth screening for, particularly in atypical age groups or bilateral disease, but it is a parallel investigation rather than a prerequisite. Sequencing it first delays the imaging that determines today's management. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents with musculoskeletal complaints in a significant minority of children, and a proportion of those are initially labelled as juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The features that should redirect the diagnosis are bone pain that is disproportionate to the joint findings, pain located away from joints, severe night pain that wakes the child, and any cytopenia, particularly when the white cell count is normal or low rather than high. A normal white cell count is not reassuring because blasts may not yet have spilled into the peripheral blood, and the blood film can be unremarkable in early disease. Giving corticosteroids before the marrow is examined is a well-recognised harm: it can induce a partial remission that delays diagnosis, makes the marrow uninterpretable, and is associated with worse outcomes.
key_points: Bone pain away from joints and severe night pain point to marrow disease rather than arthritis
Cytopenia in two or more lines is not a feature of oligoarticular or polyarticular arthritis
A normal white cell count and a bland blood film do not exclude acute leukaemia
Never give corticosteroids for presumed arthritis before excluding leukaemia when red flags are present
Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid rise with high cell turnover and support the suspicion
explanation.pearls: In children with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting as arthritis, the combination of a platelet count below 150 x10^9/L with a normal or low white cell count and a history of night pain has been shown to discriminate leukaemia from juvenile idiopathic arthritis with high specificity, and any one of those three should stop a steroid prescription.

options.rationale: This is the specific error the presentation is built around, because a partial response to steroid is common in marrow disease and provides false reassurance. Systemic onset arthritis also typically raises rather than lowers the white cell count and platelet count. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

A non-steroidal agent is a reasonable holding treatment in uncomplicated arthritis and avoids the steroid problem, but a two-week delay is unacceptable when the counts already show bicytopenia. The safety of the drug does not compensate for the delay in diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukaemia)

Two or more reduced cell lines with severe non-articular bone pain and a raised lactate dehydrogenase point away from arthritis and towards marrow infiltration, which can present with joint swelling and normal or low white cell counts. Corticosteroids given first partially treat leukaemia, obscure the marrow and worsen risk stratification and outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukaemia)

Macrophage activation syndrome is a genuine cause of cytopenias in a child with arthritis and fever, and this panel is the right way to look for it, but it complicates established systemic arthritis rather than presenting at onset. The severe night bone pain and raised lactate dehydrogenase fit marrow infiltration better. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

Imaging may show marrow signal change but cannot distinguish leukaemic infiltration from chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis or from reactive change, so it does not yield a diagnosis. It also takes longer to organise than the definitive test. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukaemia)

explanation.summary: Mumps remains in circulation in the Pacific and in under-immunised Australian communities, and breakthrough disease in twice-vaccinated children is well described. The public health response rests on three actions: laboratory confirmation by buccal swab polymerase chain reaction, exclusion from school or childcare, and notification so that contacts can be traced and vaccinated. Complications worth specifically examining for are orchitis in post-pubertal males, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis and sensorineural hearing loss. Serology is a poor confirmatory test in the vaccinated because the immunoglobulin M response is often absent.
key_points: Exclusion is 5 days from onset of parotid swelling, not from fever onset and not until resolution
Mumps is notifiable in all Australian jurisdictions; notify on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for the swab result
Two vaccine doses give roughly 80 to 90 per cent protection, so breakthrough infection does not exclude the diagnosis
Buccal swab polymerase chain reaction is the confirmatory test of choice; immunoglobulin M serology is unreliable after vaccination
explanation.pearls: Collect the buccal swab within 3 days of parotid swelling onset if possible, since polymerase chain reaction sensitivity falls sharply beyond day 5 of swelling.

sources.label: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps
NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

options.rationale: Resolution of swelling can take 10 days or more and is not the criterion used in Australia; exclusion is tied to a fixed interval from swelling onset, not to clinical resolution. Notification is correct but the exclusion advice is not. (Source: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps)
source_refs: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps

options.rationale: Australian public health guidance sets exclusion at 5 days after the onset of parotid swelling, which covers the period of greatest viral shedding, and mumps is a notifiable condition in every state and territory. Two documented vaccine doses reduce but do not remove the risk of infection and transmission, so the exclusion period still applies. (Source: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps)
source_refs: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps
NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

options.rationale: Nine days reflects older international guidance based on the full duration of viral shedding; current Australian guidance shortened this to 5 days because transmission after that point is uncommon. (Source: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps)
source_refs: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps

options.rationale: Vaccine effectiveness against mumps after two doses is around 80 to 90 per cent and breakthrough cases shed virus, so vaccination status does not waive exclusion. An immunisation record is not proof of non-infectivity. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Mumps)

Four days from fever onset is the measles exclusion rule applied to the wrong illness; the mumps clock starts at parotid swelling, which often begins after the prodromal fever. (Source: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services)
source_refs: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the epidermis that resolves spontaneously, usually within 18 months, and the Australian paediatric position is to avoid destructive treatment in well children. Children with atopic dermatitis develop more numerous and more widespread lesions because barrier dysfunction and scratching spread the virus. A halo of dermatitis around lesions, sometimes called molluscum dermatitis, is common and responds to topical corticosteroid. Crusting, redness and swelling of individual lesions frequently signal the immune response that precedes resolution rather than bacterial infection. There is no requirement to exclude an affected child from childcare or school.
key_points: Lesions clear spontaneously over 6 to 18 months; destructive treatment adds pain and scarring without changing that course
Treating the surrounding eczema reduces scratching and therefore autoinoculation and spread
Inflamed crusted lesions usually herald immune-mediated resolution, not bacterial superinfection
No childcare or school exclusion is required in Australia; covering lesions under clothing is sufficient
Immune workup is reserved for hundreds of lesions, confluent facial disease or other infection red flags
explanation.pearls: The beginning-of-the-end sign is an individual molluscum becoming red, swollen and tender over about a week; it predicts clearance of that lesion and should not trigger antibiotics.

sources.label: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

options.rationale: Curettage under general anaesthesia exposes a well child to anaesthetic risk and scarring for a self-limiting condition, and new lesions commonly appear afterwards from subclinical infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

Cryotherapy is painful, poorly tolerated in preschoolers and risks post-inflammatory pigment change or scarring in a condition that resolves without treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

There is no cellulitis or systemic illness, so antibiotics are not indicated; the crusting reflects the inflammatory host response rather than bacterial superinfection. Molluscum also carries no exclusion requirement in Australian childcare guidance. (Source: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services)
source_refs: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

options.rationale: Thirty lesions is within the ordinary range for a child with atopic dermatitis, whose impaired skin barrier allows wider spread; immune investigation is reserved for hundreds of lesions, facial confluence or other infection red flags, none of which are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

Molluscum is self-limiting over 6 to 18 months, and the itch driving scratching and autoinoculation comes from the surrounding dermatitis, so controlling that eczema with a topical corticosteroid reduces spread and secondary infection. Active destruction adds pain and scarring without shortening the natural history. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

explanation.summary: Joint bleeding is the dominant cause of long-term disability in severe haemophilia, and the Australian treatment principle is that suspicion of a bleed is itself the indication for factor replacement. Children learn to recognise a prodromal aura of tingling or fullness before pain or swelling appears, and that report should be believed and acted on. Every haemophilia treatment centre issues families with an emergency plan directing that factor is given first and assessment follows. For a target joint or an established bleed, factor VIII is typically dosed to raise the plasma level to around 50 per cent, with repeat dosing guided by the treating centre. Inhibitor development changes the whole approach, which is why the inhibitor status is checked regularly.
key_points: Suspected bleed equals treat: factor replacement precedes imaging, orthopaedic review and analgesia decisions
Early haemarthrosis presents as tingling or fullness with loss of terminal range before any visible swelling
Desmopressin works only where residual endogenous factor VIII exists, so it has no role in severe haemophilia A
Tranexamic acid is an adjunct for mucosal bleeding, never monotherapy for a joint bleed
Contact the haemophilia treatment centre early, since dosing and repeat scheduling are centre-directed
explanation.pearls: Aim for a factor VIII level of about 50 per cent for a joint bleed and give the first dose within an hour of symptom onset; the roughly 12-hour half-life of factor VIII means repeat dosing is planned in 12-hourly cycles.

sources.label: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia
World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia

options.rationale: The tingling, full sensation with loss of terminal extension is the earliest symptom of a joint bleed, and factor replacement must precede imaging or specialist review because every hour of delay increases the bleed volume and the risk of long-term arthropathy. Absence of visible swelling is expected this early and does not argue against a bleed. (Source: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia)
source_refs: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia
World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia

options.rationale: Desmopressin releases stored factor VIII from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, which requires residual endogenous factor and therefore works only in mild haemophilia A or von Willebrand disease; a child with severe disease has no store to release. Severe haemophilia A needs factor VIII concentrate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Rest, ice, compression and elevation are useful adjuncts but never a substitute for factor replacement, and a 24-hour delay in a severe phenotype allows a substantial haemarthrosis to accumulate. (Source: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia)
source_refs: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia

options.rationale: Tranexamic acid stabilises clot that has already formed and has a genuine role in mucosal and dental bleeding, but it cannot generate thrombin in the absence of factor VIII and is not adequate monotherapy for a joint bleed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Plain radiographs do not show early haemarthrosis and cannot exclude one, so imaging that gates treatment simply delays it; a fracture can be excluded after factor has been given. (Source: World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia)
source_refs: World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia

explanation.summary: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the commonest cause of short stature with delayed maturation in adolescent boys and is a diagnosis supported by positive findings rather than one of pure exclusion. The three supportive findings are a height tracking parallel to a centile line with a normal growth velocity, a bone age delayed relative to chronological age, and a family history of late maturation in a parent or sibling. Testicular volume is the single most informative examination finding: 4 mL or more means the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis has activated. The delayed bone age is reassuring because it represents growth potential still in hand. Psychosocial distress is real and deserves acknowledgement, follow-up and, where severe, endocrine referral for consideration of short-course testosterone priming.
key_points: Testicular volume of 4 mL or more confirms that puberty has started, whatever the height centile
Normal growth velocity with a height tracking along a centile line points away from chronic disease
A bone age delayed relative to chronological age represents retained growth potential and predicts a later but adequate spurt
Red flags that change the approach are anosmia, headache, visual field defect, falling velocity and weight loss
Serial six-monthly growth measurement is both the investigation and the management in constitutional delay
explanation.pearls: A growth velocity below 4 cm per year in mid-childhood is the threshold that should trigger investigation rather than observation, irrespective of how short the child is on the centile chart.

options.rationale: Gonadotrophin and karyotype testing is indicated when puberty has not started by age 14 in a boy; here a testicular volume of 5 mL confirms that the axis has already activated, so these tests will simply return pubertal values. (Source: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty)

Screening for occult chronic disease is appropriate where growth velocity has fallen or weight has crossed centiles downwards; his velocity of 5 cm per year with stable centiles and a normal appetite argues against it. (Source: RCH CPG: Short stature)

Testicular volume of 5 mL means puberty has begun, a bone age delayed by about 20 months predicts continued growth after peers have finished, and the paternal history of a late growth spurt completes the picture of constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Serial growth measurement is both the diagnostic test and the management. (Source: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty)

Pituitary imaging is warranted with headache, visual field loss, anosmia suggesting Kallmann syndrome, or a falling growth velocity with absent pubertal signs; none of those features is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty)

Low-dose testosterone priming is reserved for boys with significant psychosocial distress whose puberty has not yet started, and giving it once puberty is established risks accelerating bone age and reducing final adult height. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Contact tracing around a smear positive index case is coordinated by the state tuberculosis control unit, and children under 5 are the highest priority group because their risk of progression to severe disease is greatest. The sequence is always the same: exclude active disease clinically and radiologically first, because treating active tuberculosis with a single drug generates resistance, then treat latent infection. Tuberculin skin test cut-offs in Australia are 5 mm for the immunosuppressed and for contacts in some jurisdictions, and 10 mm for most other groups. Prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination in infancy causes only modest and waning induration and should not be used to dismiss a strongly positive test in a close contact. Children under 5 who are close contacts may be started on preventive therapy even when the initial test is negative, then reassessed at 8 to 12 weeks.
key_points: Exclude active disease with history, examination and chest radiograph before starting single-drug preventive therapy
Daily isoniazid for 9 months is a standard Australian paediatric latent infection regimen; 3 months of rifampicin with isoniazid is the shorter alternative
A positive tuberculin skin test in a close contact should not be attributed to infant bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination
Children under 5 carry the highest risk of progression to miliary disease and tuberculous meningitis
Notification and contact management are led by the state or territory tuberculosis control unit
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine is not routinely needed with isoniazid in well-nourished Australian children, but should be added for exclusively breastfed infants, malnourished children and adolescents on other neuropathic drugs.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection
