National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Position statement on interferon gamma release assays

options.rationale: She is a close household contact of a smear positive case with a tuberculin skin test above the 10 mm threshold and active disease excluded clinically and radiologically, which is the definition of latent infection requiring preventive therapy. Nine months of daily isoniazid is a standard Australian regimen in young children, in whom the risk of progression to disseminated or meningeal disease is highest. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.rationale: Combination regimens for latent infection run for 3 months, not 6, and a 6-month two-drug course is neither a preventive regimen nor adequate treatment for active disease. Three months of daily rifampicin with isoniazid is an accepted alternative when a shorter course improves completion. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.rationale: Repeat testing at 8 weeks applies to a contact whose initial test was negative and who is within the window period; a test already at 12 mm needs no repetition and waiting exposes a 3-year-old to the period of greatest progression risk. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.rationale: An interferon gamma release assay is most useful for resolving whether a positive tuberculin skin test reflects prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination, but a 12 mm reading in a household contact of a smear positive case already exceeds the treatment threshold whatever the assay shows. Vaccination given in infancy rarely produces induration of this size a decade later. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Position statement on interferon gamma release assays)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Position statement on interferon gamma release assays

options.rationale: Observation alone accepts a risk of progression that is around 5 to 10 per cent lifetime overall but front-loaded and much higher in the first 2 years for a child of this age, in whom disseminated disease and tuberculous meningitis are the feared outcomes. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

explanation.summary: Brain tumours are the commonest solid malignancy of childhood and the majority in this age group sit in the posterior fossa, where they obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and raise intracranial pressure. The diagnostic delay in Australian series is measured in months, most often because episodic headache with vomiting is attributed to migraine. Distinguishing features are headache that is present or worst on waking, vomiting that relieves the headache, and any new neurological sign. A persistent head tilt in a child is an ominous sign that may reflect a fourth nerve palsy or tonsillar herniation rather than a musculoskeletal problem. Papilloedema is a late sign, so its absence never excludes the diagnosis.
key_points: Morning headache relieved by vomiting, plus any new neurological sign, mandates urgent intracranial imaging
A new persistent head tilt in a child is a posterior fossa red flag, not torticollis
Magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred modality for the posterior fossa; computed tomography is the rapid substitute
Lumbar puncture before imaging in a child with papilloedema risks herniation
Absent papilloedema does not exclude a tumour, since it appears late in the course
explanation.pearls: Migraine essentially never begins with headaches that consistently wake a child before dawn; a fixed early morning pattern over more than 4 weeks should trigger imaging rather than prophylaxis.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Signs and symptoms of brain cancer in children

options.rationale: Prophylaxis treats a diagnosis that the absent aura, absent photophobia, absent family history and the new neurological signs all argue against, and it delays recognition of a mass lesion by another 6 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Confirming papilloedema does not change the need for urgent intracranial imaging, and a 2-week wait is unacceptable when the combination of morning vomiting, head tilt and ataxia already points to a posterior fossa process. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Lumbar puncture in the presence of papilloedema from an unconfirmed cause risks fatal tonsillar herniation if a posterior fossa mass is present; imaging must come first. It would be the right test only once a mass and hydrocephalus have been excluded and idiopathic intracranial hypertension is the working diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Raised intracranial pressure)

Headache on waking that is relieved by vomiting, a new head tilt and an ataxic tandem gait with bilateral papilloedema is the classic posterior fossa syndrome and requires same day imaging with neurosurgical involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging is preferred because it images the posterior fossa without the beam-hardening artefact that limits computed tomography there. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Signs and symptoms of brain cancer in children

options.rationale: The timeframe is too slow for papilloedema with focal signs, and computed tomography is the weaker modality for the posterior fossa, although it remains the right first test when magnetic resonance imaging is not available quickly or the child is deteriorating. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Hip displacement affects around a third of children with cerebral palsy and the risk rises steeply with Gross Motor Function Classification System level, reaching about 90 per cent at level V. Australian hip surveillance programs were built on this relationship: they set radiograph frequency by motor level and age, and use the migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to Perkin's line, as the trigger for action. Referral is indicated at a migration percentage above 30 per cent or with progression of more than 10 percentage points per year. A dislocated hip in a non-ambulant child causes pain, difficulty with perineal care, seating problems and scoliosis, and salvage surgery at that stage is far less satisfactory than earlier reconstruction. Pain is a late and unreliable marker, which is exactly why radiographic surveillance exists.
key_points: Migration percentage above 30 per cent, or progression over 10 points in a year, triggers orthopaedic referral
Surveillance frequency is set by Gross Motor Function Classification System level; level V children need annual or six-monthly radiographs from 2 years of age
Absence of hip pain does not justify delay, since pain appears once displacement is advanced
Botulinum toxin, baclofen and bracing address tone and comfort but do not prevent progressive displacement
Late salvage surgery for a dislocated hip gives poorer outcomes than timely reconstruction
explanation.pearls: Migration percentage is measured from a standardised anteroposterior pelvis film with the legs in neutral rotation; a rotated film falsely alters the value, so check positioning before acting on a borderline reading around 30 per cent.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Six-monthly radiographs are the surveillance interval for a level V child whose migration percentage sits below 30 per cent; once the threshold is crossed, surveillance is no longer the answer and referral is. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral under the Australian hip surveillance guidelines, and a value of 42 per cent rising 16 points in a year indicates progressive displacement that usually needs bony reconstruction rather than soft tissue measures alone. Absence of pain is expected at this stage and is not a reason to wait, because the aim of surveillance is to intervene before the hip becomes painful and dislocated. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Botulinum toxin reduces adductor tone and may improve seating comfort, but it does not reverse established displacement and there is no evidence it prevents progression once the migration percentage exceeds 30 per cent. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Abduction bracing has not been shown to prevent progressive hip displacement in cerebral palsy and is frequently poorly tolerated; it is a comfort and positioning measure, not a structural one. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Higher baclofen doses reduce tone and may help care and comfort but do not alter the mechanical course of hip displacement, and a level V child has no independent standing program to modify. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis typically presents between 10 and 16 years, is more common in boys and strongly associated with obesity, and around a quarter of cases present with knee or thigh pain alone because of referral through the obturator nerve. Delay is the single biggest determinant of outcome: a stable slip, in which the child can still weight bear, has a low risk of avascular necrosis, whereas an unstable slip carries a risk in the order of 20 to 50 per cent. Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most reliable bedside sign. Around 20 per cent of cases are bilateral at presentation and more become so later, so both hips are imaged and the contralateral hip is monitored. Endocrine screening is considered where the child is younger than 10, underweight or unusually short, since hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and renal osteodystrophy are recognised associations.
key_points: Any adolescent with knee pain and a limp needs the hip examined and imaged
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the key bedside sign
Request anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvis views; early slips are invisible on the anteroposterior view alone
Make the child non-weight-bearing immediately, since progression to an unstable slip sharply raises the risk of avascular necrosis
Image both hips, as around 20 per cent are bilateral at presentation
explanation.pearls: On the anteroposterior film, draw Klein's line along the superior femoral neck: in a normal hip it intersects part of the femoral head, and failure to do so indicates a slip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: The knee examination is entirely normal, so imaging it will be unrevealing; hip pathology refers pain to the knee, so the hip is the joint to image. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Ultrasound is the right first test for suspected transient synovitis or septic arthritis in a younger child, but a normal C-reactive protein and afebrile state make infection unlikely and ultrasound cannot show the bony slip. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Treating this as a soft tissue overuse problem allows continued weight bearing, and further slip during that period converts a stable presentation into an unstable one with a markedly higher risk of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Aspiration is the investigation for suspected septic arthritis, which a 5-week history, normal temperature, normal white cell count and normal C-reactive protein together make very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with weeks of knee pain and a limp is the classic presentation of a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and radiographs must include a frog-leg lateral because early slips are missed on the anteroposterior view alone. Immediate non-weight-bearing and orthopaedic referral prevent progression to an unstable slip. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: Oesophageal atresia occurs in about 1 in 3500 births and is frequently signalled antenatally by polyhydramnios with a small or absent stomach bubble, although these findings have low positive predictive value on their own. The postnatal hallmark is excessive frothy oral secretions with choking on the first feed, and the bedside test is the inability to pass a firm tube beyond about 10 cm. Holding management aims entirely at protecting the airway from two sources of soiling: saliva pooling in the blind upper pouch, and gastric acid refluxing up a distal fistula. Associated anomalies occur in around half of cases, so echocardiography, renal ultrasound and careful examination of the anus and limbs are performed before or soon after surgery. Definitive repair is undertaken at a paediatric surgical centre.
key_points: Frothy secretions with choking on the first feed plus a tube that will not pass beyond about 10 cm is the clinical diagnosis
A replogle tube on continuous low suction with head-up nursing and nil by mouth is the holding management
Contrast studies risk aspiration pneumonitis; a plain radiograph with the tube in situ is the safe confirmatory image
Avoid elective positive pressure ventilation where a distal fistula may be present, because of gastric distension
Screen for associated cardiac, renal, vertebral, anorectal and limb anomalies before repair
explanation.pearls: Gas in the stomach and bowel on the plain film means a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula is present, whereas a gasless abdomen indicates pure atresia and predicts a long gap needing delayed repair.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network clinical practice resources

options.rationale: A double lumen replogle tube on continuous low suction empties the blind upper pouch and is the single measure that prevents ongoing aspiration of pooled saliva during the hours before transfer and surgery. Keeping the baby nil by mouth and nursing head-up completes the holding management. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network clinical practice resources

options.rationale: Contrast in a blind upper pouch spills into the airway and causes chemical pneumonitis; a plain chest and abdominal radiograph with a firm tube in situ answers the anatomical question safely. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation can preferentially inflate the stomach through a distal fistula, causing gastric distension, splinting of the diaphragm and even perforation; intubation is reserved for babies who genuinely need it for respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

options.rationale: The baby is afebrile with normal perfusion and the secretions have a mechanical explanation, so empirical sepsis therapy addresses the wrong problem; antibiotics may be started later if aspiration pneumonitis develops. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal sepsis)

Feeding cannot be delivered through a tube that will not pass, and nursing flat increases the risk of reflux of gastric contents up through a distal fistula into the trachea. Head-up positioning is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

explanation.summary: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and results from expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Because a maternal premutation expands to a full mutation when transmitted, the family history often shows affected males in the maternal line alongside premutation carriers with their own distinct phenotypes. Two of those carrier phenotypes are diagnostically valuable: fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency in women, and fragile X-associated tremor and ataxia syndrome in older carriers of either sex. The physical features in the child, a long face, prominent ears, macrocephaly and joint hypermobility, are supportive but often subtle before puberty. A diagnosis has direct implications for reproductive counselling across the extended family, which is why cascade testing through a clinical genetics service follows confirmation.
key_points: Chromosomal microarray plus FMR1 repeat analysis is the first line pair for unexplained global developmental delay in Australia
Premature ovarian insufficiency and late-onset tremor with ataxia in the maternal line are premutation carrier signatures
Repeat expansion occurs on maternal transmission, so affected males cluster in the maternal line
Exome sequencing is a second tier test arranged through clinical genetics after first line testing is negative
A confirmed diagnosis triggers cascade testing and reproductive counselling for the wider family
explanation.pearls: FMR1 repeat sizes matter: under 45 is normal, 45 to 54 is intermediate, 55 to 200 is a premutation carrying ovarian insufficiency and tremor-ataxia risk, and over 200 is the full mutation causing fragile X syndrome.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

options.rationale: Karyotype resolves only rearrangements larger than about 5 to 10 megabases and has been superseded as a first line test by microarray, which detects far smaller copy number changes across the whole genome. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

Targeted methylation testing is appropriate when the phenotype fits, which would require neonatal hypotonia and hyperphagia, or the ataxic gait with a happy demeanour and severe speech absence of Angelman syndrome; neither matches this boy. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

Australian practice pairs chromosomal microarray with FMR1 repeat analysis as the first line for unexplained global developmental delay, and the pedigree here of an affected maternal uncle, premature ovarian insufficiency in the grandmother and her late-onset tremor with ataxia is the recognisable X-linked signature of an expanding FMR1 repeat across generations. Microarray is still done in parallel because copy number variants remain the commonest single yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

options.rationale: Classic Rett syndrome affects girls and features developmental regression with loss of purposeful hand use and acquired microcephaly, none of which fits a boy with a head circumference on the 90th centile. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

Exome sequencing has a real place in Australian practice but sits at the second tier, undertaken through a clinical genetics service after microarray and FMR1 testing are non-diagnostic. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

explanation.summary: An abdominal mass in a preschool child is a malignancy until proven otherwise, and the two dominant diagnoses are nephroblastoma and neuroblastoma. Distinguishing them at the bedside rests on whether the mass crosses the midline, whether the child looks systemically well, and whether there are marrow or bone features. Hypertension and haematuria point towards a renal origin. The management pathway diverges sharply from adult oncology practice in one respect: percutaneous biopsy of a suspected nephroblastoma is avoided because tumour spill upstages the disease and adds radiotherapy to the treatment. North American and European protocols differ, with upfront nephrectomy favoured in one and preoperative chemotherapy in the other, and Australian centres follow a defined protocol, which is another reason the child must reach a paediatric oncology centre before anyone takes tissue.
key_points: Ultrasound with Doppler of the renal vein and inferior vena cava is the first imaging study for a suspected renal tumour
Percutaneous biopsy upstages nephroblastoma through tumour spill and should not be arranged outside a paediatric oncology centre
A mass that crosses the midline in an unwell child with bone pain or periorbital bruising suggests neuroblastoma instead
Hypertension with haematuria in a child with a flank mass points to a renal origin
Refer immediately to a paediatric oncology centre, which coordinates staging imaging and definitive tissue diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Tumour thrombus reaches the inferior vena cava in around 4 to 10 per cent of nephroblastomas and occasionally extends to the right atrium; finding it before surgery is what changes the operative plan and the need for cardiac bypass.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a renal tumour spills tumour cells into the retroperitoneum and upstages the disease to stage III under Children's Oncology Group criteria, committing the child to abdominal radiotherapy she might otherwise avoid. The scheduling outside a paediatric oncology centre compounds the error. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.rationale: Marrow sampling and catecholamines are the right workup for a neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and is accompanied by bone pain, periorbital bruising or marrow failure; none of those is present and a mass confined to one flank points elsewhere. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.rationale: Treating the hypertension in isolation ignores its cause, which in a child with a renal mass is usually renin secretion by the tumour or renal artery compression, and a 2-week delay is unjustifiable for an undiagnosed abdominal mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

Ultrasound with Doppler is the correct first imaging step because it establishes the renal origin of the mass and, critically, looks for tumour thrombus extending into the renal vein and inferior vena cava, which changes the surgical approach and must be known before any operation. Referral to a paediatric oncology centre follows immediately, and tissue diagnosis is made by the treating surgical team rather than by percutaneous biopsy. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.rationale: Cross-sectional chest and abdominal imaging is needed for staging, but it follows ultrasound rather than replacing it, and it neither answers the venous thrombus question as reliably nor avoids the radiation burden in a preschool child when the first question is simply whether the mass is renal. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

explanation.summary: A receding chin with a cleft of the soft palate in a newborn with airway obstruction describes Pierre Robin sequence, in which a small mandible displaces the tongue base backwards and obstructs the pharynx. Management follows a stepwise ladder: prone or side positioning first, then a nasopharyngeal airway, then continuous positive airway pressure or tongue-lip adhesion, then mandibular distraction osteogenesis, with tracheostomy reserved for failure of all of these. Feeding difficulty runs alongside the airway problem because the cleft prevents an effective seal, and specialised soft compressible bottles with assisted delivery, or nasogastric supplementation, are commonly required. Objective assessment with overnight oximetry or polysomnography guides escalation better than daytime observation, since obstruction is worst during sleep. About half of affected babies have an associated syndrome, most often Stickler syndrome, so genetic and ophthalmological review is arranged.
key_points: The escalation ladder runs positioning, then nasopharyngeal airway, then continuous positive airway pressure or tongue-lip adhesion, then mandibular distraction, with tracheostomy last
Failure of positioning is defined by ongoing sleep desaturation or rising carbon dioxide while already prone
Sleep is when obstruction is worst, so overnight oximetry or polysomnography guides escalation, not daytime observation
Feeding support with specialised teats or nasogastric supplementation addresses the separate problem of poor seal across the cleft
Around half have an associated syndrome, most commonly Stickler syndrome, warranting genetics and ophthalmology review
explanation.pearls: Size the nasopharyngeal airway to reach from the nostril to the tragus and pass it about 1 cm beyond the tongue base; too short a tube fails to relieve the obstruction and is a common reason for apparent treatment failure.

sources.label: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

options.rationale: Prone positioning is the correct first measure but it has now been tried and has failed, as shown by repeated sleep desaturations and a rising carbon dioxide while already prone; continuing it accepts ongoing intermittent hypoxaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)

A nasopharyngeal airway stents the airway past the tongue base and is the standard next step in the Australian escalation ladder when positioning alone fails, and it can be managed in a special care nursery and maintained during transfer. The mildly raised carbon dioxide with a normal bicarbonate indicates obstruction that is real but not yet chronic, which is the window in which a nasopharyngeal airway works well. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)
source_refs: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

options.rationale: Intubation in this anatomy is technically difficult and commits an otherwise stable baby to sedation, ventilation and its complications, when a less invasive measure has not yet been tried. It becomes the right answer only if a nasopharyngeal airway fails or the baby develops respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)

Nasogastric feeding addresses the feeding-related events and the weight loss, and will very likely be needed, but it leaves the sleep obstruction untreated and is therefore an incomplete answer to a problem that is primarily one of airway patency. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)

Mandibular distraction is a surgical option for babies who fail non-surgical airway measures, so it sits several rungs further up the ladder and is decided by the craniofacial team after a sleep study, not selected at 36 hours of age. (Source: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

explanation.summary: Nipple pain in the early weeks is far more often a problem of attachment and positioning than of anatomy, and the two are commonly conflated because a visible frenulum invites a mechanical explanation. Assessment of ankyloglossia is functional rather than anatomical: what matters is whether the tongue can elevate and lateralise enough to draw the nipple deep into the mouth, not whether a membrane is visible. A structured feed observation by a skilled practitioner is the investigation, and it frequently identifies a correctable hold. Frenotomy rates have risen internationally well beyond what the evidence supports, and an unnecessary procedure exposes a neonate to bleeding and to the false reassurance that the feeding problem has been addressed. Adequate output and a weight tracking up from the physiological nadir mean there is time to do this properly.
key_points: Tongue elevation to mid-mouth with bilateral lateralisation indicates mild restriction unlikely to be the cause of feeding failure
A full feed observed by a lactation practitioner is the assessment that decides whether a frenulum is functionally significant
Pain that settles with repositioning points to attachment rather than anatomy
Weight regained above the day-4 nadir with six or more heavy nappies daily indicates adequate transfer
Upper labial frenulum division has no established breastfeeding benefit
explanation.pearls: Physiological weight loss bottoms out around day 4 at up to 10 per cent of birth weight and birth weight should be regained by day 14; a baby already climbing from the nadir does not need top-ups while attachment is being corrected.

options.rationale: Tongue elevation to mid-mouth with bilateral lateralisation and a membrane inserting behind the gum ridge is a mild restriction, and the observed pain resolved with repositioning, so the feeding problem is attachment rather than the frenulum. Weight has been regained above the nadir with adequate output, which buys time for hands-on lactation review before any procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

Frenotomy is reserved for restriction that demonstrably impairs feeding after skilled lactation assessment, and here the assessment identified a positional cause that responded to repositioning. Frenotomy would be correct if pain and transfer failed to improve with optimised attachment. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

Weight is tracking up from the nadir with six heavy nappies daily, so intake is adequate and routine top-ups risk reducing maternal supply. Top-ups would be correct if weight were still falling or below the birth weight by day 14. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

Nipple and oral candidiasis causes persistent burning pain that does not change with repositioning, and there is no oral plaque or nipple appearance described here. Antifungal treatment would be correct if pain persisted after attachment was optimised and typical signs were present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Upper lip tie division has no established feeding benefit and the restriction described here is lingual, not labial. General anaesthesia is never the default route for a neonatal frenulum in any case, since frenotomy is an awake bedside procedure. (Source: RACGP: Tongue tie and breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation happens when the annular ligament slips over the radial head during axial traction on an extended, pronated arm, and it is one of the few paediatric musculoskeletal presentations diagnosed and cured within a single consultation. The classic picture is a child under 5 who simply stops using the arm rather than complaining of a specific painful point, which is why the absence of swelling and focal tenderness is as important as the mechanism. Reduction by supination with elbow flexion, or by hyperpronation, restores use within minutes and often produces a palpable click. Failure to regain use after two attempts is the trigger to image, because an undisplaced fracture can mimic the presentation. Recurrence is common until about age 5 and parents should be warned against lifting the child by the hands.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated, extended arm is the mechanism; a fall or direct blow points elsewhere
The child refuses to use the arm rather than localising pain, and the arm is held pronated and slightly flexed
Absence of swelling, deformity and bony point tenderness makes imaging unnecessary before reduction
Supination with flexion or hyperpronation both work and often produce a palpable click
Image after two failed reduction attempts, because an occult fracture can present identically
explanation.pearls: Return of spontaneous arm use within about 15 minutes of a single supination and flexion manoeuvre confirms the diagnosis retrospectively; if the child is still not using the arm after two attempts, radiograph rather than repeat the manoeuvre a third time.

options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in radial head subluxation and delay a manoeuvre that restores function within minutes. Imaging would be correct if there were swelling, deformity, bony point tenderness or a mechanism involving a fall or direct blow. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

A longitudinal traction mechanism with a pronated arm, absent swelling and no point tenderness over any bony landmark is a clinical diagnosis of radial head subluxation, and the management is immediate bedside reduction. Imaging before reduction is not required when the history and examination are typical and there is no localised bony tenderness. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Immobilisation treats a fracture that has not been demonstrated and leaves a reducible subluxation unreduced for days. A backslab would be correct for a confirmed undisplaced supracondylar or forearm fracture, which would show swelling or focal tenderness. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

The mechanism is consistent, developmentally plausible and matches the injury, and there is no bruising or injury pattern raising concern. A skeletal survey would be correct where the history is absent, changes, or does not fit the injury, particularly in a child under 2 years. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Ultrasound is not part of the assessment pathway for a pulled elbow and an effusion is not the lesion in radial head subluxation. Ultrasound would be correct in suspected septic arthritis of the hip, where an effusion guides aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Middle ear effusion after acute otitis media is extremely common and the great majority clears without intervention within 3 months, which is why the default is observation rather than treatment. The decision to operate turns on three things together: bilateral persistence beyond that window, the degree of hearing loss, and whether that loss is translating into a developmental or educational cost. A child with a 35 dB bilateral loss is missing conversational speech at a distance, and the speech pathology report converts an audiological number into a functional argument for intervention. Ventilation tubes restore hearing promptly and are usually extruded within 9 to 15 months. Antibiotics, steroids and decongestants have all been studied and none produces durable clearance, so offering them mainly delays the referral.
key_points: Observe for 3 months first: most effusions resolve spontaneously after acute otitis media
Refer when bilateral effusion persists beyond 3 months with hearing loss and a functional impact
A flat tympanogram with a retracted dull drum and fluid level confirms effusion rather than acute infection
Antibiotics, intranasal steroids and decongestants do not durably clear middle ear effusion
Document the developmental cost, since it is what converts an audiogram into an operative indication
explanation.pearls: A bilateral conductive loss averaging 25 dB or worse persisting past 3 months is the audiological trigger for ear, nose and throat referral; below that threshold, hearing is usually adequate for language acquisition and observation continues.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion
NICE: Otitis media with effusion in under 12s

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is the correct approach for the first 3 months because most effusions resolve spontaneously, but that window has already passed and language is now measurably affected. Further observation would be correct if hearing were better than 25 dB and language were age-appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Prolonged antibiotics do not produce durable resolution of a sterile middle ear effusion and expose the child to resistance and adverse effects. Amoxicillin would be correct for acute otitis media with a bulging erythematous drum and systemic symptoms, which are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Bilateral effusion persisting beyond 3 months with a hearing loss of this degree and a documented language impact meets the threshold for surgical referral rather than further observation. The 4-month-old note establishes persistence, which is the element that converts watchful waiting into referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroids have not been shown to clear middle ear effusion or improve hearing outcomes in children. They would be correct for allergic rhinitis causing nasal obstruction, which is a separate problem and is not described here. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Autoinflation offers a small short-term benefit and is a reasonable adjunct during the observation window, but it does not substitute for referral once persistence and language impact are established. It would be correct as an interim measure in the first 3 months of a newly detected effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

explanation.summary: Food protein induced allergic proctocolitis presents in the first months of life as blood-streaked mucousy stools in an otherwise well infant, and it is a delayed, non-IgE process, so allergy testing has no role in diagnosis. Management is a stepped elimination: an extensively hydrolysed formula first, which resolves the problem in roughly 90 per cent of cases, and an amino acid formula for the remainder who still react to residual peptides. The pattern of partial improvement followed by relapse on a hydrolysate is characteristic of that residual peptide load rather than of treatment failure through non-adherence. Faltering growth changes the urgency because it signals that intake and absorption are both being affected. Most infants tolerate cow milk protein again by 12 months, so a planned reintroduction under supervision belongs in the longer term plan.
key_points: Blood-streaked mucousy stools in a well infant suggest non-IgE food protein induced proctocolitis
Skin prick and specific IgE testing are negative in non-IgE disease and do not exclude it
Extensively hydrolysed formula is first-line and resolves about 90 per cent of cases
Amino acid formula is the next step when symptoms persist or relapse on a hydrolysate
Soy formula is unsuitable under 6 months because of frequent co-reactivity
explanation.pearls: Expect symptoms to settle within 2 to 4 weeks of starting an appropriate elimination formula; relapse after an initial week of improvement on an extensively hydrolysed feed is the signal to escalate to amino acid based formula rather than to question adherence.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention
RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.rationale: A substantial proportion of infants with non-IgE cow milk proteinopathy react to soy as well, so soy is not a reliable next step under 6 months of age. Soy formula would be reasonable in an older infant with isolated IgE-mediated cow milk allergy and confirmed soy tolerance. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Skin prick testing detects IgE sensitisation and is negative in the non-IgE delayed pattern described here, so a normal result would wrongly reassure. Testing would be correct if reactions occurred within minutes with urticaria, angioedema or wheeze. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: The reaction is to intact or partly hydrolysed cow milk protein, and a lactose free formula retains that protein while removing a sugar that is not the problem. Lactose free formula would be correct for transient secondary lactose intolerance after a proven gastroenteritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.rationale: Persistent blood-streaked stools and centile fall despite 4 weeks of an extensively hydrolysed formula identify the minority of infants whose residual peptide load still drives the reaction, and the next step up the ladder is an amino acid based formula. Dietetic involvement is needed because faltering growth on an elimination diet requires energy and nutrient adequacy to be checked. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Endoscopy is not required to diagnose food protein induced proctocolitis in a well infant, where response to elimination is the diagnostic test. Colonoscopy would be correct if bleeding persisted on an amino acid formula or if there were systemic features suggesting inflammatory bowel disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

explanation.summary: Positional plagiocephaly became substantially more common after supine sleeping was adopted to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy, and it is benign, but it is frequently confused with craniosynostosis. Geometry rather than severity separates them: positional flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, producing a parallelogram viewed from above, while lambdoid synostosis restricts growth and pulls the ipsilateral ear backward into a trapezoid with a palpable ridge. Congenital muscular torticollis underlies a large share of positional cases and is the reason the deformity recurs if only repositioning is advised. Head circumference crossing centiles or a ridged suture are the findings that should prompt craniofacial referral. Most positional asymmetry improves substantially once the infant becomes mobile and spends less time lying against a surface.
key_points: Parallelogram head with the ipsilateral ear displaced anteriorly indicates positional deformity
Trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly plus a palpable ridge indicates lambdoid synostosis
Normal head circumference tracking along a centile argues against synostosis
Treat the associated sternocleidomastoid restriction or the head shape will recur
Never advise prone sleeping to offload a flattened occiput
explanation.pearls: Check passive neck rotation in every infant with an asymmetric head: congenital muscular torticollis drives the positional preference, and physiotherapy started before 6 months resolves the great majority without a helmet.

options.rationale: Lambdoid synostosis produces a trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly and a palpable ridge, which is the opposite ear displacement to the parallelogram described here. Referral would be correct if the ear sat posteriorly, a ridge were palpable, or head circumference were crossing centiles. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Positional plagiocephaly is a clinical diagnosis and computed tomography delivers ionising radiation to an infant brain for no management gain. It would be correct where examination genuinely suggests synostosis and a craniofacial service requests it to plan surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Helmet therapy is a second-line option considered from around 6 months when conservative measures have failed, and it does nothing for the underlying neck restriction. It would be correct for severe persisting asymmetry after an adequate trial of physiotherapy and repositioning. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Prone sleeping is a major modifiable risk factor for sudden unexpected death in infancy and must never be advised to improve head shape. Repositioning is achieved by alternating head orientation while supine and by waking tummy time under supervision. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

A parallelogram head shape with the ipsilateral ear displaced anteriorly, a normal head circumference and no sutural ridge is positional deformity driven by a restricted sternocleidomastoid, and the treatment is physiotherapy for the torticollis plus repositioning. Treating the neck restriction is the element that prevents recurrence, because the head shape follows the preferred head position. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas follow a predictable course: a herald patch in the first weeks, rapid proliferation to about 5 months, then slow involution over years. Because the natural history is benign for most lesions, the clinical skill lies in recognising the minority that need treatment, which are those threatening vision, the airway, feeding or permanent disfigurement, and those that ulcerate. Periocular lesions can induce astigmatism and deprivation amblyopia even without covering the pupil, so ophthalmology review is part of the assessment rather than a substitute for treatment. A large segmental facial lesion also raises the question of PHACE association, which warrants cerebrovascular and cardiac imaging before beta blockade lowers perfusion pressure. Timing matters more here than in most paediatric dermatology, because a lesion allowed to complete proliferation leaves fibrofatty residue that no drug reverses.
key_points: Proliferation runs to roughly 5 months, so treatment decisions cannot wait for a routine review interval
Treat lesions threatening vision, airway, feeding, or causing ulceration or permanent disfigurement
Oral propranolol is first-line; corticosteroid is now second-line for failure or contraindication
Topical timolol is limited to thin superficial lesions of small size
Large segmental facial lesions raise the possibility of PHACE association warranting imaging
explanation.pearls: A periocular haemangioma can cause amblyopia through astigmatism from lid pressure without ever covering the pupil, so a clear visual axis does not make observation safe.

options.rationale: A large segmental facial lesion involving the eyelid margin and lip that is still proliferating at 7 weeks carries a high risk of functional and cosmetic complication, and systemic propranolol is first-line treatment. The proliferative phase runs to roughly 5 months, so starting now captures the window in which treatment alters the trajectory rather than merely accelerating involution. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Most small truncal lesions can be observed safely, but a periocular and perioral segmental lesion can cause deprivation amblyopia and permanent lip distortion before involution begins. Observation would be correct for the 6 mm shoulder papule, which threatens no structure. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Topical beta blockade has useful effect only on thin superficial lesions of limited size and would not control a 45 mm segmental plaque. Timolol would be correct for the small flat shoulder papule or a superficial lesion under about 10 mm. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Pulsed dye laser penetrates only the superficial dermis and is used mainly for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulcerated lesions. It would be correct once the lesion has involuted and left surface vessels, not as proliferative-phase control. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Systemic corticosteroid was the former first-line agent but propranolol is more effective and better tolerated, so steroid is now reserved for propranolol failure or contraindication. Prednisolone would be correct where beta blockade is contraindicated, such as in significant reactive airways disease. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: The toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft produced by a low-energy twisting force in a child in the first years of independent walking, and its defining feature is that the initial radiograph is often normal. The periosteum is thick and intact in this age group, so the fracture is stable and the injury is far less dramatic than the refusal to weight bear suggests. The diagnostic task is really one of exclusion: a normal hip examination, normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever separate it from septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, which are the diagnoses that cannot be missed. Treating on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for radiographic proof is the accepted approach, and a repeat film at 10 to 14 days shows periosteal new bone that confirms it retrospectively. Healing is reliable and long-term sequelae are rare.
key_points: Low-energy twisting in a child aged roughly 9 months to 3 years is the characteristic mechanism
Initial radiographs are frequently normal because the fracture is undisplaced and spiral
Focal pain on gentle tibial torsion localises the injury and separates it from hip pathology
Normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever argue against osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
Immobilise on clinical suspicion; periosteal reaction confirms the diagnosis on later imaging
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone appears on repeat radiographs at about 10 to 14 days, so a film taken at the 1 to 2 week orthopaedic review confirms the fracture that the presentation film missed.

options.rationale: A normal radiograph does not exclude this fracture, and leaving an unstable tibia unsupported causes ongoing pain and refusal to weight bear. Discharge without immobilisation would be correct if tibial torsion were painless and the refusal to weight bear were unexplained by a focal sign. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

A low-energy twisting injury in a newly walking toddler with focal distal tibial tenderness and a normal radiograph is an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture, which is radiographically occult in a substantial proportion of cases at presentation. Immobilisation on clinical grounds is the standard approach, with review when periosteal reaction makes the fracture visible. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

Hip movements are full and painless and the tenderness is over the distal tibia, so the hip is not the source and an effusion is not expected. Hip ultrasound would be correct for a limping child with restricted or painful hip rotation where septic arthritis or transient synovitis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Bone scanning delivers a significant radiation dose and is reserved for a limping child with no localising sign after clinical and radiographic assessment. It would be correct where the site of pathology genuinely cannot be localised, which is not the case with focal tibial torsional pain. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Osteomyelitis is the important alternative but requires fever or elevated inflammatory markers, both of which are normal here, and a clear traumatic mechanism argues against it. Antibiotics and magnetic resonance imaging would be correct if the child were febrile with a raised C-reactive protein and no convincing injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between 4 and 10 years and is confirmed by the combination of brief behavioural arrest without postictal confusion, ready provocation by hyperventilation, and generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background. Frequent brief absences are often mistaken for inattention or daydreaming, and a slipping school performance is commonly the presenting complaint rather than the seizures themselves. The comparative trial evidence is unusually clear for a paediatric epilepsy: ethosuximide and valproate control seizures equally, but valproate impairs attention more, and ethosuximide therefore wins on the outcome that matters to a child in the classroom. The important caveat is that ethosuximide has no efficacy against generalised tonic-clonic seizures, so a history of any convulsion changes the choice. Prognosis is good, with most children entering remission by adolescence.
key_points: Hyperventilation for 3 minutes provokes an absence in most untreated children and is a bedside diagnostic test
Generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background is the electroencephalographic signature
Ethosuximide and valproate are equally effective, but ethosuximide preserves attention better
Ethosuximide does not protect against generalised tonic-clonic seizures
Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine aggravate generalised absence seizures
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about any lifetime generalised convulsion before choosing ethosuximide: it has no efficacy against tonic-clonic seizures, and their presence moves the choice to valproate or lamotrigine despite the attentional and teratogenic trade-offs.

sources.label: Epilepsy Action Australia: Childhood absence epilepsy

options.rationale: Valproate controls absence seizures effectively but carries dose-related teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harm, so it is avoided in females of childbearing potential when an equally effective alternative exists. It would be the choice if generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexisted, since ethosuximide does not protect against them. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Lamotrigine is less effective than either ethosuximide or valproate for absence seizures and its mandatory slow titration delays control in a child having 20 events daily. It would be reasonable as third-line therapy or where both first-line agents have failed or are not tolerated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

In typical childhood absence epilepsy without generalised convulsions, ethosuximide gives seizure freedom rates equal to valproate with significantly less attentional impairment, which matters directly given the reported decline in reading. It is preferred over valproate in a girl because it avoids the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks that accompany long-term valproate exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Sodium channel blockers aggravate generalised absence and myoclonic seizures and can precipitate absence status, so carbamazepine is contraindicated here. It would be appropriate for focal epilepsy, where the discharge is localised rather than generalised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Levetiracetam has weaker evidence in absence epilepsy than the established first-line agents and was inferior in comparative trials. It is widely used in other generalised epilepsies and would be considered where first-line options have failed or behavioural monitoring is acceptable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Dog bites deliver a mixed inoculum of aerobes and anaerobes deep into tissue, and the two management decisions that matter are which antibiotic and whether to close. Amoxicillin with clavulanate is the Australian agent of choice because it is the only widely used oral option covering Pasteurella multocida alongside staphylococci, streptococci and anaerobes. Facial bites occupy a special position: the cosmetic stakes push toward early closure and the excellent facial blood supply makes it safer than elsewhere, but that latitude closes once the wound is several hours old and inflamed. Australia's rabies-free status means lyssavirus prophylaxis turns on bat contact or overseas acquisition rather than on the bite itself, which is a frequent source of unnecessary anxiety. Bites near the eyelid margin, over joints, or involving the hand warrant a lower threshold for specialist involvement.
key_points: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is first-line because it covers Pasteurella multocida plus anaerobes
Prophylaxis is indicated for bites to the face, hands, feet, over joints, and in immunocompromised children
Primary closure is limited to early, clean, well-irrigated wounds; inflamed or late wounds are left open
Australian domestic dogs pose no classical rabies risk; bats are the local lyssavirus reservoir
Tetanus immunoglobulin is for incomplete or unknown immunisation, not for every bite
explanation.pearls: In penicillin-allergic children the Australian bite alternative is trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole plus metronidazole, because cefalexin and clindamycin each leave Pasteurella multocida uncovered.

options.rationale: Primary closure of a bite presenting at 14 hours with established local inflammation traps inoculated organisms and raises the risk of deep infection. Primary closure would be correct for a clean facial bite irrigated and closed within roughly 8 hours with no signs of inflammation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cefalexin has unreliable activity against Pasteurella multocida and no anaerobic cover, so it is not adequate for a bite wound despite being a standard skin infection agent. It would be appropriate for uncomplicated non-bite cellulitis caused by streptococci and staphylococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Immunoglobulin is reserved for tetanus-prone wounds in people who are incompletely immunised or whose status is unknown, and this child has four documented vaccine doses. Immunoglobulin would be correct if fewer than three doses were documented or the history were unavailable. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Amoxicillin with clavulanate covers Pasteurella multocida and the oral anaerobes that make dog bites infect, and prophylaxis is indicated for facial bites regardless of appearance. Beyond about 8 hours with established oedema and erythema the wound is left open for delayed closure or revision rather than sutured primarily. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Australia is free of classical rabies and the only local lyssavirus reservoir is bats, so a domestic dog with no overseas travel poses no lyssavirus risk. Post-exposure prophylaxis would be correct after a bat bite or scratch in Australia, or a dog bite acquired overseas. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is frequently diagnosed late because the earliest presentation is developmental rather than obviously neuromuscular, with speech delay and difficulty keeping up being common first complaints. A creatine kinase discovered incidentally is often the moment the diagnosis becomes apparent, and the characteristic value is in the thousands to tens of thousands rather than the modest elevation seen with exercise or trauma. Raised aminotransferases often mislead, because alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are both released from damaged muscle and boys are not uncommonly investigated for liver disease before anyone measures a creatine kinase. Early molecular diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started before substantial function is lost prolongs ambulation, and because exon-skipping therapies depend on knowing the precise variant. Genetic confirmation also enables carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the mother and wider family.
key_points: Speech and global developmental delay are common presenting complaints before weakness is recognised
Gowers manoeuvre plus calf hypertrophy plus creatine kinase in the thousands is the diagnostic triad
Raised alanine and aspartate aminotransferase come from muscle; a normal bilirubin points away from liver
Deletion and duplication analysis is first-line and detects roughly 70 per cent of variants
Muscle biopsy is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative
explanation.pearls: Measure creatine kinase in any boy with unexplained developmental delay who is not yet walking by 18 months or who has isolated aminotransferase elevation with a normal bilirubin and gamma-glutamyl transferase.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: The raised aminotransferases originate from muscle rather than liver, which the normal bilirubin and grossly elevated creatine kinase indicate, so a hepatic workup pursues an artefact. Hepatology referral would be correct if gamma-glutamyl transferase were also raised and creatine kinase were normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

Central imaging does not explain a creatine kinase of this magnitude, which is a muscle-specific finding, and reflexes and plantar responses are normal. Brain imaging would be correct for global delay with upper motor neuron signs, microcephaly or regression. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

Biopsy is invasive and is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative but clinical suspicion persists. It would be correct after deletion, duplication and sequence analysis all return negative in a boy with this phenotype. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

Electrophysiology confirms a myopathic pattern but does not identify the cause and adds a distressing procedure when a blood test gives the diagnosis. It would be useful where a neuropathy or a neuromuscular junction disorder is suspected and creatine kinase is normal or only mildly raised. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

Proximal weakness with a Gowers manoeuvre, calf hypertrophy and a creatine kinase in the thousands in a boy of this age is dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and genetic testing has replaced muscle biopsy as the first-line confirmatory test. Deletion and duplication analysis detects around 70 per cent of causative variants, with sequencing for the remainder. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Salicylate poisoning produces a characteristic mixed picture of respiratory alkalosis from direct respiratory centre stimulation superimposed on a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The initial gas here shows the alkalotic phase, and the transition to acidaemia marks the point at which the patient is decompensating rather than improving. That transition is dangerous out of proportion to the numbers, because salicylate is a weak acid whose non-ionised fraction rises as pH falls, allowing it to cross the blood-brain barrier and cause cerebral oedema, seizures and death. Urinary alkalinisation works by trapping ionised salicylate in the tubule and is the mainstay of moderate poisoning, but once it has been optimised and concentrations still rise, only extracorporeal removal will clear the drug. Salicylate concentrations should be repeated every 2 hours until falling, because delayed and erratic absorption from tablet concretions means a single value never excludes serious toxicity.
key_points: Expect mixed respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap metabolic acidosis; a falling pH signals decompensation
Acidaemia increases the non-ionised fraction that crosses into the brain, so pH matters more than concentration alone
Haemodialysis is indicated for concentrations above roughly 700 mg/L, acidaemia, altered mental state, or renal failure
Intubation is high risk because loss of compensatory hyperventilation can precipitate arrest
Repeat concentrations every 2 hours until clearly falling, because absorption is delayed and erratic
explanation.pearls: If intubation becomes unavoidable in salicylate poisoning, match the ventilator to the patient's own pre-intubation minute ventilation, often above 30 breaths per minute, rather than to conventional lung-protective settings.

options.rationale: A rising concentration above 700 mg/L together with a falling arterial pH despite adequate urinary alkalinisation meets the criteria for extracorporeal removal, and each feature independently would justify it. The fall in pH is the critical change, because acidaemia shifts salicylate into the non-ionised form that crosses into the brain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Alkalinisation has already been delivered to a urine pH of 7.6 and the concentration is still climbing while the arterial pH falls, so persisting without escalation allows deterioration. Continued alkalinisation alone would be correct if the concentration were falling and the arterial pH were stable or rising. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Multiple dose charcoal can limit ongoing absorption from a concretion but does not remove salicylate already distributed to tissue, and it carries aspiration risk in a vomiting, agitated patient. It would be a useful adjunct earlier in a protected, non-vomiting patient with a rising concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Intubation in salicylate poisoning is hazardous because any drop in minute ventilation during the apnoeic period worsens acidaemia and can precipitate cardiac arrest. It would be necessary only for airway failure or exhaustion, and then with ventilation matched to the pre-intubation respiratory rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity by replenishing glutathione and has no role against salicylate, which causes oxidative phosphorylation uncoupling rather than a reactive metabolite injury. It would be indicated if a co-ingested paracetamol concentration sat above the treatment line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Childhood lead exposure in Australia clusters around older housing with deteriorating pre-1970 paint, mining and smelting communities, and take-home contamination on parental work clothing, all three of which are present in this family. There is no threshold below which lead is known to be safe, and the cognitive effects are subclinical at the levels most children present with, so the absence of symptoms is expected rather than reassuring. The counterintuitive part of management is that chelation is not the answer for most elevated levels: it lowers the measured blood concentration without demonstrated cognitive benefit at moderate levels, and the level rebounds from bone stores once treatment stops. Source removal is the only intervention that changes long-term body burden, which is why notification and an environmental health assessment do more than any drug. Iron deficiency deserves specific attention because it both increases gastrointestinal lead absorption and independently harms development, so the two problems compound each other.
key_points: Blood lead of 5 micrograms/dL or above is notifiable in Australia and triggers environmental investigation
Source removal and correction of iron deficiency are the interventions that lower body burden at moderate levels
Oral chelation is generally considered from about 45 micrograms/dL; parenteral therapy for encephalopathy or 70 micrograms/dL and above
Chelation at moderate levels lowers the blood concentration without demonstrated cognitive benefit and is followed by rebound from bone
Take-home exposure on parental work clothing is a recognised route in smelting and mining communities
explanation.pearls: Iron deficiency increases lead absorption through the shared divalent metal transporter 1 in the duodenum, so replacing iron in a lead-exposed child lowers the level independently of any chelating agent.

sources.label: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.rationale: Parenteral chelation is reserved for encephalopathy or levels at or above 70 micrograms/dL, and this child is asymptomatic at 28 micrograms/dL. It would be correct for a child with seizures, altered consciousness or a level in that range. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.rationale: Below the chelation threshold the interventions that lower a blood lead level are removal of the source and correction of iron deficiency, because iron deficiency upregulates the divalent metal transporter that absorbs lead from the gut. A level of 5 micrograms/dL or above is notifiable in Australian jurisdictions and triggers the environmental investigation that addresses both the paint and the take-home occupational exposure. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.rationale: Oral chelation is generally considered from about 45 micrograms/dL, and trials at lower levels showed no cognitive benefit while the level rebounded once the drug stopped. Succimer would be appropriate for a symptomatic child or one in that higher band with the source already removed. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.rationale: Adequate dietary calcium modestly reduces lead absorption and is part of general advice, but supplementation alone does not lower an established level while exposure continues. It would be a reasonable adjunct once the environmental source had been identified and controlled. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.rationale: Bowel irrigation is used to clear ingested radio-opaque lead objects or paint chips seen on imaging, and this radiograph shows none. It would be correct where a retained lead foreign body such as a swallowed sinker or fragment were visible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Vesicoureteric reflux was historically treated aggressively on the assumption that reflux caused scarring and that preventing infection would prevent renal failure, but randomised trials substantially narrowed the indications for both prophylaxis and surgery. The current position is that prophylaxis provides a modest absolute reduction in recurrence concentrated in children with dilating grades III to V reflux and recurrent febrile infection, while conferring little benefit at lower grades and selecting for resistant organisms in everyone. This child sits squarely in the group where the evidence still supports treatment. Australian practice reserves the micturating cystourethrogram for atypical or recurrent infection rather than performing it routinely, and its findings here directly determine management. Most reflux resolves spontaneously as the child grows and the intravesical ureteric tunnel lengthens, so prophylaxis is a holding measure rather than a permanent commitment, and bladder and bowel dysfunction should be addressed once the child is toilet trained.
key_points: Prophylaxis benefit concentrates in dilating grade III to V reflux with recurrent febrile infection
Trimethoprim at a quarter of the treatment dose nightly is the standard Australian prophylactic agent
Amoxicillin is unsuitable for prophylaxis beyond the neonatal period because of resistance selection
Surgery follows breakthrough febrile infection on prophylaxis or progressive scarring, not initial diagnosis
Most reflux resolves spontaneously with growth, so prophylaxis is an interim measure
explanation.pearls: Breakthrough febrile urinary infection while adherent to nightly trimethoprim is the specific trigger that converts medical management into a surgical referral, so document adherence before attributing a recurrence to prophylaxis failure.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is supported for low grade reflux and for a single infection, but this child has had two febrile infections with grade IV reflux, where recurrence risk and renal scarring risk are both substantially higher. No prophylaxis would be appropriate for grade I or II reflux after a single infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Surgery is reserved for breakthrough febrile infection on prophylaxis, progressive scarring, or reflux persisting beyond early childhood, because most reflux resolves as the intravesical ureteric tunnel lengthens with growth. Reimplantation would be correct after failure of medical management. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Recurrent febrile infection combined with high grade dilating reflux is the subgroup in which prophylaxis reduces recurrence, even though trials show no benefit for low grade reflux or a single infection. Trimethoprim is the standard Australian agent at a quarter of the treatment dose, given nightly while the reflux is expected to resolve spontaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Amoxicillin achieves poor urinary concentrations relative to resistance rates in Escherichia coli and rapidly selects resistant organisms, so it is not used for urinary prophylaxis beyond the neonatal period. It is the preferred prophylactic agent only in infants under about 6 weeks, where trimethoprim is avoided. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A cortical scan documents established scarring but does not alter the decision to start prophylaxis in a child who already has proven high grade reflux and recurrent febrile infection. It would be useful later to establish a baseline of renal parenchymal damage for long-term follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Foot deformity in the newborn splits into positional deformity, which is supple and self-correcting, and structural talipes equinovarus, which is rigid and needs treatment. The three findings that mark the structural form are failure to correct the equinus passively, deep medial and posterior skin creases, and wasting of the calf, all of which reflect a genuinely short and abnormal posteromedial soft tissue complex. The Ponseti method uses weekly manipulation and above-knee casting, usually followed by a percutaneous tendo-Achilles tenotomy, and then a foot abduction orthosis worn for several years. Treatment started in the first weeks of life needs fewer casts and achieves better long-term function than treatment deferred to later infancy. Untreated clubfoot leads to weight bearing on the lateral border of the foot with callus, pain and disability.
key_points: Rigidity, creases and calf wasting separate structural talipes from positional deformity
Ponseti casting should begin in the first weeks of life, not after a period of observation
Imaging of the foot does not guide the decision to cast
Bracing belongs to the maintenance phase after casting has corrected the deformity
Examine the hips in every infant with a foot deformity, but a normal hip examination does not delay foot referral
explanation.pearls: The Ponseti maintenance orthosis is worn 23 hours a day for the first 3 months after casting and then at night until about age 4; non-adherence to the brace is the single largest driver of recurrence.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
BMJ Best Practice: Congenital talipes equinovarus

options.rationale: Rigid equinovarus that will not correct past plantarflexion, with a deep medial crease and calf wasting, is structural talipes equinovarus rather than a positional deformity. Ponseti casting is most effective when started in the first weeks of life while the ligaments are still highly responsive to maternal relaxin, so referral is made before discharge rather than deferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

Passive stretching is the treatment for positional talipes, which is soft and fully correctable to a neutral dorsiflexed position at the cot side. These feet are fixed in equinus with skin creases and calf wasting, and six weeks of stretching would waste the window in which casting works best. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

Talipes equinovarus is a clinical diagnosis made on rigidity and the classic crease and calf findings, and imaging of the foot does not change the decision to cast. Imaging is reserved for atypical or syndromic feet being planned for surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

Bracing has a role only after the deformity has been corrected by casting, as the Ponseti maintenance phase with a foot abduction orthosis. Splinting an uncorrected rigid foot achieves nothing and a three month delay materially worsens the number of casts needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

Hip imaging is the right reflex when a foot deformity coexists with risk factors or an abnormal hip examination, but abduction here is full and symmetrical with negative Ortolani and Barlow testing. Deferring the foot referral to the hip scan appointment delays the time-critical intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Catch-up schedules turn on a small number of interval rules rather than on the individual vaccine. Inactivated vaccines can be co-administered with anything and have no minimum spacing from other vaccines, so the Haemophilus influenzae type b dose proceeds today. Two parenteral live vaccines interact through a transient interferon response, so they are given on the same day or separated by at least 4 weeks; if the interval is breached the second dose is invalid and must be repeated. Live oral vaccines such as rotavirus are exempt from this rule. Children under 10 years presenting for catch-up can complete a full schedule relatively quickly because most remaining antigens are inactivated.
key_points: Two parenteral live vaccines: same day, or at least 4 weeks apart
A dose given inside the 4 week window is invalid and must be repeated
Inactivated vaccines have no minimum interval from other vaccines
Pre-vaccination serology is not routine in catch-up of a well child
Live oral vaccines are not subject to the 4 week parenteral live vaccine rule
explanation.pearls: Tuberculin skin testing is suppressed by measles containing vaccine: do the skin test on the same day as the vaccine or wait at least 4 weeks, otherwise a false negative is likely.

options.rationale: Two parenteral live vaccines must be given either on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart, and 10 days falls inside that window. Giving it today risks interferon mediated blunting of the varicella response, which would then require a repeat dose. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Where two parenteral live vaccines are not given on the same day, the minimum interval is 4 weeks, so the varicella dose is scheduled for at least 28 days after the measles containing vaccine. The Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine is inactivated and can be given today without waiting. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)
