Serological testing is not required before catch-up vaccination in a well child with no documented disease, and vaccinating a person who is already immune is safe. Pre-vaccination serology is reserved for specific groups such as some hepatitis B and varicella exposures in adults. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

One week still falls short of the 4 week minimum interval between two parenteral live vaccines. Routine prophylactic paracetamol is also not recommended because it can reduce antibody responses and is reserved for specific meningococcal B schedules. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

The measles containing dose 10 days ago was valid and counts towards her schedule, so repeating it adds no benefit. Three months is the interval used after an immunoglobulin or blood product exposure, which she has not had. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult disease in both distribution and treatment. Infants characteristically involve the scalp, face, palms and soles, sites that are deliberately spared when treating adults, so the application instructions change with age. Permethrin 5 per cent is the Australian first-line agent from 2 months onward, and sulfur preparations fill the gap below that age. Treatment fails far more often because contacts were not treated simultaneously than because the drug was wrong, so every household member and any regular carer is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms. Itch persists for 2 to 4 weeks after successful treatment and is not by itself evidence of failure.
key_points: Permethrin 5 per cent is first line from 2 months of age; below that use sulfur in white soft paraffin
In infants apply the scabicide to scalp, face, palms and soles as well as the body
Treat every household member on the same day, symptomatic or not
Oral ivermectin is avoided under 15 kg and is reserved for crusted scabies or failure
Post-scabetic itch lasting 2 to 4 weeks does not mean treatment failed
explanation.pearls: Wash bedding and clothing in hot water on the day of treatment; items that cannot be washed are sealed in a plastic bag for 72 hours, which exceeds the time a mite survives off human skin.

options.rationale: Permethrin 5 per cent is the standard Australian first-line scabicide but is not recommended below 2 months of age, and this infant is 6 weeks old. It is the right agent for the mother and sister, who should be treated on the same day. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

Benzyl benzoate is highly irritant on infant skin and at full strength risks a severe chemical dermatitis, so it is not used in this age group. It is a second-line agent for older children and adults when permethrin has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Sulfur in white soft paraffin is the preferred scabicide below 2 months of age, applied to the whole body including scalp, face, palms and soles for three consecutive nights. Simultaneous treatment of every household member on the same day is what prevents the cycle of reinfestation from the untreated mother and sister. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

Oral ivermectin is not used under 15 kg because safety data in small infants are lacking, and it is reserved for crusted scabies, outbreaks or treatment failure. It would be a reasonable adjunct for adult contacts in a crusted scabies scenario, which this is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Topical corticosteroid treats the eczematous reaction but leaves the mite alive, and used alone it can produce the poorly inflamed, widely disseminated picture of scabies incognito. Steroid has a place only alongside a scabicide for persistent post-scabetic itch. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

explanation.summary: Breath-holding spells affect up to 5 per cent of young children and divide into a cyanotic type, provoked by anger or frustration, and a pallid type, provoked by pain or fright and mediated by vagal asystole. The diagnosis rests on the stereotyped sequence of provocation, cry, colour change and brief loss of tone with rapid recovery, and investigations are directed at the two things that genuinely change management: iron deficiency and, in atypical or pallid cases, a cardiac conduction abnormality. Iron deficiency is present in a large proportion of affected children and correcting it reduces spell frequency, which is the only pharmacological intervention with a reasonable evidence base. Parents are taught to lay the child flat on their side and let the event end on its own, avoiding shaking, mouth-to-mouth or cold water. The condition resolves spontaneously by school age and does not increase the risk of epilepsy.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical: a provocation, a prolonged cry, then colour change and loss of tone with rapid recovery
Check a full blood count and ferritin in every child with breath-holding spells
Iron replacement reduces spell frequency and is the only drug treatment with useful evidence
Reserve electroencephalography for events without a trigger, during sleep, or with prolonged recovery
Consider an electrocardiogram for pallid spells or a family history of sudden death
explanation.pearls: Cow milk intake above 500 mL per day in a toddler is itself a cause of iron deficiency through occult gut blood loss and calcium mediated inhibition of iron absorption; capping milk at 500 mL is part of the treatment, not an afterthought.

options.rationale: Every episode has been preceded by a prolonged cry with an identifiable provocation, which is the hallmark of a breath-holding spell rather than a seizure. Electroencephalography would be indicated if events occurred without a trigger, during sleep, or with a prolonged postictal phase, none of which applies here. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

Structural heart disease is suggested by events at rest or on exertion, a murmur or abnormal pulses, and cardiovascular examination and femoral pulses are normal. Echocardiography is the wrong test for a child whose episodes are reliably provoked by crying. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

Antiseizure medication has no role in breath-holding spells because the events are reflex in origin rather than epileptic. Valproate would additionally be a poor first choice in any young child given its hepatic and metabolic risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Microcytic anaemia with a ferritin of 7 microgram/L confirms iron deficiency, driven here by an intake of about a litre of cow milk daily, and treating it reduces both the frequency and severity of breath-holding spells. Iron is given for at least 3 months to refill stores, with parental reassurance about the benign natural history and first aid positioning. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

An electrocardiogram is a reasonable screen when spells are of the pallid type, occur without a preceding cry, or there is a family history of sudden death, and it can be done in parallel rather than as a reason to withhold iron. Here the cyanotic phenotype with a consistent crying trigger makes a primary arrhythmia a remote possibility. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

explanation.summary: Murmurs are heard in a large minority of children at some point, and most are innocent, but the prior probability of structural disease is far higher in the first year of life than later in childhood. The newborn examination misses lesions whose murmur depends on a pressure gradient that only develops as pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first weeks, so a ventricular septal defect or an atrioventricular septal defect commonly declares itself at the 6 week check rather than at birth. Features that would prompt urgent rather than routine referral include poor feeding with sweating or tachypnoea, faltering growth, a diastolic murmur, a thrill, absent or delayed femoral pulses, cyanosis or an abnormal second heart sound. Echocardiography is the investigation of choice; chest radiography and electrocardiography lack the sensitivity to exclude significant disease. In an older child with a classic Still murmur, normal pulses and no symptoms, reassurance without imaging is entirely reasonable.
key_points: A murmur first heard under 1 year of age warrants specialist assessment with echocardiography
A normal newborn check does not exclude a shunt lesion that becomes audible weeks later
Chest radiography and electrocardiography are not sensitive enough to exclude structural disease
Red flags for urgent referral include feeding difficulty, faltering growth, diastolic murmur, thrill, weak femoral pulses or cyanosis
Bedside criteria for an innocent murmur are reliable in older children, not in infants
explanation.pearls: A ventricular septal defect murmur is loudest when the defect is small: as the defect gets larger the gradient falls, so a quiet murmur with a loud pulmonary second sound and tachypnoea is more worrying than a loud isolated murmur.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of paediatric heart murmurs

options.rationale: The features that allow a murmur to be called innocent at the bedside, such as a vibratory Still murmur that softens on standing, are not reliably assessable in early infancy. A murmur appearing after a documented normal newborn examination is exactly the pattern seen when a ventricular septal defect becomes audible as pulmonary vascular resistance falls. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

Chest radiography and electrocardiography are insensitive for the defects that present this way and a normal pair of tests does not exclude a significant lesion. Echocardiography has superseded both as the investigation that settles the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

Four limb pressures screen for coarctation, and the equal volume femoral pulses already make that diagnosis unlikely, so a normal result would not explain the murmur. Excluding one lesion is not the same as characterising the murmur. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

Watchful waiting is appropriate for an asymptomatic murmur with clearly innocent characteristics in an older child, not for a new murmur under 1 year of age. A left-to-right shunt can drive heart failure and faltering growth well within a three month window. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

Any murmur first detected under 1 year of age warrants specialist assessment with echocardiography, because a substantial proportion represent structural disease and bedside criteria for innocence do not perform well at this age. She is well and growing, so the referral is timely rather than emergency, and the family can be told that many such murmurs prove to be small defects or normal flow. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

explanation.summary: A slipped upper femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and is missed most often because roughly a quarter of children present with knee or distal thigh pain and no hip complaint at all. The peak age is 10 to 16 years, obesity is the dominant risk factor, and bilateral disease eventually occurs in about a fifth of cases. The single most useful bedside sign is obligate external rotation: as the hip is flexed the thigh rotates outward because the metaphysis has displaced anteriorly relative to the epiphysis. Radiographs must include a frog-leg lateral view, since an early slip can look normal on the anteroposterior film alone. Management is in situ screw fixation, and the key determinant of outcome is whether the slip remains stable, so any child with a suspected slip is made non-weight bearing immediately.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain and a normal knee
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with loss of internal rotation is the hallmark sign
Order anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs, not knee films
Make the child non-weight bearing from the moment the diagnosis is suspected
Obesity is the leading risk factor and about 20 per cent eventually slip on the other side
explanation.pearls: On the anteroposterior pelvis, Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck should intersect part of the epiphysis; if it passes entirely above the epiphysis the slip is present even when the femoral head still looks round.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Imaging the knee answers the wrong question, because the knee examination is entirely normal and the pain is referred along the obturator nerve from the hip. Loading the joint through a strengthening program before the hip is imaged risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.rationale: Activity modification is the treatment for Osgood-Schlatter disease, which produces tenderness localised to the tibial tuberosity that is absent here. A six week delay in a slipped upper femoral epiphysis substantially increases the risk of slip progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation in an overweight adolescent is the classic sign of a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which needs anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs and surgical fixation. Non-weight bearing from the moment of suspicion is the intervention that protects the epiphyseal blood supply while transfer is arranged. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.rationale: Aspiration is the right move for a suspected septic joint, which presents with fever, an effusion and pain through a restricted arc, none of which is present over a seven week history. Ultrasound of a clinically normal knee will not identify the proximal femoral pathology. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee would be reasonable for mechanical knee symptoms such as locking or giving way with a normal radiograph, but the knee here is normal on examination. The delay inherent in outpatient magnetic resonance imaging is also unacceptable when the hip is the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis complicates up to a fifth of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and is the main cause of preventable visual loss in this population. Risk is stratified by three variables: subtype, age at onset and antinuclear antibody status, with young antinuclear antibody positive girls with oligoarticular disease at the top of the risk table and screened three monthly. The inflammation is silent, so the child gives no warning and the first sign may be an irregular pupil from posterior synechiae or a reduced red reflex from cataract. Screening intervals lengthen with time since diagnosis and with increasing age, but surveillance continues for years and is not stopped when the joints settle. Established uveitis is treated with topical corticosteroid and mydriatics, escalating to methotrexate and then adalimumab if control is not achieved.
key_points: Risk stratification uses subtype, age at onset and antinuclear antibody status
Antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular disease with onset under 7 years is screened three monthly
The uveitis is asymptomatic, so symptom-triggered review is unsafe
Slit lamp examination is required; acuity testing and fundoscopy both miss it
Eye and joint disease activity are independent, so screening continues in joint remission
explanation.pearls: Adalimumab combined with methotrexate outperforms methotrexate alone for refractory juvenile idiopathic arthritis associated uveitis; etanercept is the anti-tumour necrosis factor agent that does not work for the eye disease despite controlling the joints.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: The uveitis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is characteristically chronic, anterior and completely asymptomatic, so waiting for a red or sore eye means waiting for a complication. Symptom-triggered review is appropriate in the acute anterior uveitis of an older human leucocyte antigen B27 positive child, which is painful and photophobic. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Visual acuity is preserved until posterior synechiae, band keratopathy or cataract have already formed, so acuity testing detects the disease too late. The eye also needs magnified examination of the anterior chamber, which an acuity chart cannot provide. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Twelve monthly screening is the interval used for the lowest risk groups, such as older children with rheumatoid factor positive polyarticular disease or systemic onset disease. Applying it to a young antinuclear antibody positive girl leaves a year in which silent inflammation can scar the anterior chamber. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment, whereas this disease inflames the anterior chamber, where cells and flare are only visible on slit lamp examination. A normal fundus therefore provides false reassurance. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Onset under 7 years with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody defines the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, and three monthly slit lamp screening is the recommended interval for the first several years. Screening continues on this schedule even when the arthritis is in remission, because eye and joint activity are not correlated. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

explanation.summary: Leukocoria is an abnormal white pupillary reflex and is the presenting sign in roughly 60 per cent of retinoblastomas, with squint accounting for a further 20 per cent. Other causes include congenital cataract, persistent fetal vasculature, Coats disease, toxocariasis and retinopathy of prematurity, and all of them warrant prompt ophthalmological assessment because visual development is time critical. Parents commonly notice the abnormality in photographs before any clinician does, and a parental report of a white reflex should be believed even if the reflex looks normal in a brightly lit consulting room. Examination under anaesthesia with full mydriasis and scleral indentation is the definitive assessment, since a struggling toddler cannot be adequately examined awake. Retinoblastoma is heritable in about 40 per cent of cases, so genetic counselling and examination of siblings follow the diagnosis.
key_points: Compare the red reflexes of both eyes in the same view; asymmetry is the abnormal finding
Leukocoria and new squint are the two commonest presentations of retinoblastoma
Believe a parental report of a white reflex in photographs even if your examination looks normal
Definitive assessment is dilated examination under anaesthesia at a tertiary centre within days
Never patch an eye for presumed amblyopia before a structural cause has been excluded
explanation.pearls: Around 40 per cent of retinoblastoma is heritable through a germline RB1 mutation, and those children need lifelong surveillance for second primary cancers, particularly osteosarcoma, which is why genetic testing is arranged at diagnosis rather than later.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: An asymmetric white reflex with a new squint in a toddler demands dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia at a tertiary centre within days, because retinoblastoma is the diagnosis that must be excluded first and survival and eye salvage both fall sharply with delay. Squint developing in the second year is a recognised second presentation of the same disease once central vision has been lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: Treating this as an isolated squint ignores the abnormal red reflex, which is the finding that changes the differential entirely. Routine orthoptic referral would be right for a comitant squint with symmetrical bright red reflexes and normal visual behaviour. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate an intraocular mass with calcification but it neither excludes small tumours nor stages the eye, and a month of waiting is unacceptable. Imaging is arranged by the ophthalmology service alongside examination under anaesthesia, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: A pseudoleukocoria from off-axis flash is symmetrical or varies between photographs, whereas this is reproducibly unilateral across four images and is confirmed by a dull red reflex on examination. Reassurance in this setting is the commonest route to a delayed diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once a structural cause of reduced vision has been excluded, and patching the better eye here would leave a child functionally blind while a tumour goes untreated. Amblyopia therapy follows the fundus examination, never precedes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome follows in utero exposure to opioids and presents with central nervous system irritability, autonomic overactivity and gastrointestinal dysfunction, typically within 24 to 72 hours for heroin and later, up to 5 to 7 days, for methadone because of its longer half-life. Scoring systems such as the modified Finnegan tool exist to make the decision to treat reproducible rather than impressionistic, and the standard triggers are three consecutive scores of 8 or more or two consecutive scores of 12 or more. Non-pharmacological care, meaning rooming in, minimal handling, a quiet dim environment, swaddling and frequent small feeds, reduces the proportion of babies who need drug treatment and is never abandoned when medication starts. Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal, weaned by protocol once scores have been controlled for 24 to 48 hours. Breastfeeding is actively encouraged for mothers stable on methadone or buprenorphine, and babies exposed to methadone need observation for at least 5 days before discharge.
key_points: Treat when three consecutive modified Finnegan scores are 8 or more, or two are 12 or more
Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal; phenobarbital is for sedative or polysubstance exposure
Non-pharmacological care continues alongside drug treatment, it is not replaced by it
Breastfeeding is encouraged on stable methadone or buprenorphine and shortens withdrawal
Methadone exposed babies are observed for at least 5 days because onset is delayed
explanation.pearls: Naloxone is contraindicated at the birth of an opioid exposed baby even when the baby is apnoeic, because it precipitates acute withdrawal and seizures; ventilate instead and let the exposure wear off.

options.rationale: Phenobarbital is the agent of choice when the withdrawal is from a non-opioid sedative or when polysubstance exposure is documented, and it is added as a second agent if morphine alone fails. Using it first for pure methadone withdrawal treats the wrong receptor and brings unnecessary sedation. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

Three consecutive modified Finnegan scores of 8 or more is the trigger for pharmacological treatment, and oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal because it replaces the same receptor activity and is weaned predictably. Breastfeeding continues because methadone transfers into milk in very small quantities and reduces both the severity and duration of withdrawal. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

Optimised non-pharmacological care is the foundation of management and is already in place, but it has not held the scores below threshold across three consecutive assessments. Persisting with it alone risks poor feeding, weight loss and seizures. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

Clonidine is an adjunct used to reduce total opioid exposure or when morphine weaning stalls, not a first-line single agent. Its hypotensive and bradycardic effects also require closer monitoring than a postnatal ward usually provides. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

Separating mother and baby worsens withdrawal scores and removes the single most effective non-pharmacological intervention, and stopping breastfeeding removes the small protective opioid transfer through milk. Formula feeding is advised for maternal human immunodeficiency virus infection or ongoing unsanctioned drug use, neither of which applies here. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

explanation.summary: A parapneumonic effusion complicates a significant minority of childhood bacterial pneumonias and progresses through an exudative phase, a fibrinopurulent phase with septation, and finally an organising phase with a fibrous peel. The decision point is not the presence of fluid but whether the child is failing treatment, judged by persistent fever beyond 48 hours, rising inflammatory markers, an increasing oxygen requirement or a rising respiratory rate. Ultrasound is the first imaging test because it distinguishes free fluid from septated collections, estimates volume and marks a safe drainage site, all without radiation. Small bore pigtail drainage with intrapleural fibrinolysis is the standard first intervention in Australian paediatric centres, with video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery reserved for failure. Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the commonest organism but Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are over-represented in empyema, so antibiotic cover is broadened at the time of drainage.
key_points: Failure at 48 hours means persistent fever, rising markers or a rising oxygen requirement
Ultrasound is the imaging of choice; computed tomography is reserved for complications
Small bore drain plus intrapleural fibrinolytic is the standard first intervention
Broadening antibiotics alone does not treat a loculated collection
Cover Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes once empyema is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Long-term lung function after paediatric empyema is essentially normal even when the radiograph remains abnormal for months, so persistent opacification at discharge is not a reason to extend antibiotics or re-drain.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parapneumonic effusion and empyema

options.rationale: Persistent fever, rising inflammatory markers and a rising oxygen requirement at 48 hours define antibiotic failure, and a loculated collection will not resolve with more of the same therapy. Continued observation alone is reasonable only for a small free-flowing effusion in a child who is improving. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

Computed tomography adds radiation without changing the initial drainage decision and is reserved for suspected necrotising pneumonia, bronchopleural fistula or failure of chest drainage. Ultrasound answers the question of loculation better and with no ionising radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

A diagnostic tap without a drain leaves the collection in place, and a child on supplemental oxygen with a rising C-reactive protein is not dischargeable. Simple aspiration alone is an option only for a small, free-flowing, non-purulent effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

Ultrasound is the imaging of choice to size the collection and demonstrate septations, and a large loculated empyema in a child failing antibiotics is drained with a small bore catheter plus intrapleural urokinase or alteplase. This combination shortens hospital stay and has outcomes equivalent to primary video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery at lower cost. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

Broadening antibiotic cover does not address the mechanical problem of a loculated collection that antibiotics penetrate poorly, though cover is usually widened to include Staphylococcus aureus at the time of drainage. Blood cultures are positive in only a minority of paediatric empyema and repeating them daily will not guide management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Premature thelarche is isolated breast development, usually appearing between 6 months and 3 years, driven by transient follicular activity in a minipubertal ovary rather than by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. It is distinguished from true precocious puberty by what is absent as much as by what is present: no pubic or axillary hair, no acne or adult body odour, no growth acceleration and no bone age advance. Bone age is the single most informative investigation because oestrogen exposure sufficient to develop breast tissue over months would also advance the skeleton. Serial observation over 6 months is diagnostic, since thelarche stays static or regresses while true precocity progresses through the Tanner stages. Referral thresholds are breast development before 8 years in girls or testicular enlargement before 9 years in boys when accompanied by growth acceleration or bone age advance.
key_points: Premature thelarche is isolated breast tissue with no other secondary sexual characteristics
Normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age are the reassuring findings
Serial staging and height velocity over 6 months is the diagnostic test
Investigate when there is pubic hair, acne, growth acceleration, bleeding or virilisation
Brain imaging follows biochemical confirmation of central activation, not clinical suspicion alone
explanation.pearls: Areolar enlargement and pigmentation, rather than the size of the breast bud itself, is the physical sign that most reliably marks genuine oestrogen exposure and should prompt investigation even when the bone age is only mildly advanced.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Puberty disorders

options.rationale: Stimulation testing is used to confirm central activation when the clinical picture already suggests true precocious puberty, meaning progressive staging with accelerated growth and an advanced bone age. Testing a child whose skeletal age matches her chronological age generates cost, distress and false positives without altering management. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

Central nervous system imaging is indicated once central precocious puberty has been biochemically confirmed, and the yield is highest in girls under 6 years and in all boys. Imaging a child with no evidence of gonadotrophin activation would require sedation for no diagnostic gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

Agonist therapy is reserved for confirmed central precocious puberty where rapid progression threatens final adult height or causes psychosocial harm. Suppressing an axis that has not been activated exposes the child to injections and side effects with no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

Ultrasound and androgen measurement search for a peripheral oestrogen or androgen source such as an ovarian cyst, a McCune-Albright lesion or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, all of which produce virilisation, rapid progression or bleeding. The absence of pubic hair, clitoromegaly, acne and growth acceleration argues strongly against a peripheral source. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

Isolated waxing and waning breast tissue in a toddler with no other secondary sexual characteristics, a normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age is premature thelarche, a benign self-limiting variant. Serial review of height velocity and staging is the investigation, because progression over 6 months is what separates thelarche from true precocity. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

explanation.summary: Egg allergy has been progressively removed as a barrier to vaccination as ovalbumin content in manufactured vaccines has fallen. Influenza vaccines registered in Australia contain ovalbumin at concentrations far below the threshold associated with reactions, and large studies including children with previous anaphylaxis have found no excess of severe reactions. Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture rather than egg and has never been contraindicated by egg allergy. The two vaccines that do contain clinically relevant quantities of egg protein are yellow fever and Q fever vaccine, and those require allergist assessment before administration. Every vaccinee, allergic or not, is observed for 15 minutes in a setting able to recognise and treat anaphylaxis.
key_points: Egg allergy, including previous anaphylaxis, is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination
Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is cultured in chick fibroblasts and is safe in egg allergy
Yellow fever and Q fever vaccines do contain relevant egg protein and need specialist assessment
Split or graded dosing has been abandoned and is not a licensed administration method
Specialist referral is for anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the same vaccine or its components
explanation.pearls: Gelatin, not egg, is the component most often responsible for genuine anaphylaxis to measles, mumps and rubella or varicella vaccine, so a child who reacts to those vaccines should be assessed for gelatin allergy rather than re-tested to egg.

sources.label: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

options.rationale: Egg allergy of any severity, including previous anaphylaxis, is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in Australia, because the ovalbumin content of registered vaccines is below the threshold that triggers reactions. Vaccination proceeds in any setting equipped to manage anaphylaxis, with the same standard 15 minute observation applied to every vaccinee. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Specialist immunisation clinic referral is reserved for a documented anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the vaccine itself or to one of its other components such as gelatin or neomycin. Referring for egg allergy alone creates a delay in which the child may miss the season altogether. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Graded or split dosing was historical practice abandoned once studies showed no excess reactions with full single doses in egg allergic children. Splitting the dose risks giving an incomplete antigen load and is not a licensed method of administration. (Source: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child)
source_refs: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

options.rationale: Cocooning through household vaccination is an adjunct for infants under 6 months who cannot be vaccinated, not a substitute for a child who is eligible. Withholding leaves a preschool child, a group with high influenza hospitalisation rates, unprotected on the basis of a contraindication that does not exist. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Skin testing with vaccine is not predictive of clinical reaction and generates irritant false positives that lead to unnecessary withholding. It has a limited role only in evaluating a suspected reaction to a previous dose of the same vaccine. (Source: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child)
source_refs: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

explanation.summary: Total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage returns oxygenated pulmonary venous blood to the right atrium rather than the left, so survival depends on an atrial communication and the clinical picture is set by whether the anomalous channel is obstructed. The infracardiac form, which descends through the diaphragm to the portal system, is the one most often obstructed, and it presents in the first days with profound cyanosis, severe respiratory distress and a chest radiograph showing pulmonary venous congestion over a heart of normal size. That combination of a small heart with wet lungs is the radiological signature and is the reason the lesion is repeatedly mistaken for respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia or persistent pulmonary hypertension. The crucial management point is that the usual neonatal cardiac rescues make it worse: prostaglandin and nitric oxide both increase flow into a circuit that cannot drain, and extracorporeal support is not a substitute for relieving the obstruction. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical reimplantation of the pulmonary venous confluence into the left atrium.
key_points: A small heart with diffuse pulmonary venous congestion in a cyanosed term baby is the radiological signature
The hyperoxia test fails, but the obstruction is downstream of the lungs, not duct dependent
Prostaglandin and nitric oxide can both worsen obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
Hepatomegaly with a quiet precordium and no murmur is typical rather than reassuring
Definitive treatment is emergency surgery, so retrieval is arranged without waiting for stability
explanation.pearls: In obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage the murmur is usually absent because there is no turbulent flow across a valve or septal defect, so a silent precordium in a deeply cyanosed term baby should raise suspicion rather than lower it.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network: Neonatal retrieval guidance
BMJ Best Practice: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection

options.rationale: Prostaglandin rescues lesions in which systemic or pulmonary blood flow depends on the duct, and it is the reflex answer to a failed hyperoxia test. Here the obstruction lies downstream of the lungs in the pulmonary venous pathway, so opening the duct increases pulmonary blood flow into an already congested circuit and can worsen the pulmonary oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Nitric oxide is the treatment for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, which usually follows meconium aspiration, sepsis or asphyxia and is supported by a pre-ductal to post-ductal saturation gradient. Given into an obstructed pulmonary venous pathway it increases transpulmonary flow against a fixed obstruction and precipitates frank pulmonary oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: The granular radiographic appearance genuinely mimics surfactant deficiency, which is why this lesion is so often missed, but respiratory distress syndrome is a disease of prematurity and this baby is 39 weeks with no risk factors. Surfactant deficiency also responds to oxygen, whereas the hyperoxia test here failed outright. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: A term baby with a failed hyperoxia test, hepatomegaly, a quiet precordium and a normal sized heart with diffuse pulmonary venous congestion has obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, in which no medical therapy relieves the obstruction. Intubation with positive pressure ventilation buys oxygenation and reduces the work of breathing while emergency surgical relief of the obstruction is arranged, and this is one of the few true surgical emergencies in neonatal cardiology. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are appropriate alongside any neonatal deterioration and cultures should be taken, but sepsis does not explain a hyperoxia test that fails to lift the arterial oxygen tension above 100 mmHg. Treating this as sepsis alone delays the only intervention that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia results from galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency and presents in the first two weeks once milk feeding has begun, with vomiting, poor feeding, jaundice that becomes conjugated, hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and renal tubular dysfunction. Its most characteristic association is Escherichia coli sepsis, which occurs because accumulated galactose-1-phosphate impairs neutrophil function, and a Gram negative septicaemia in a jaundiced neonate should always prompt the question. The bedside clue is a positive urinary reducing substance test alongside a negative glucose oxidase dipstick, since the dipstick is glucose specific while the reducing substance test detects galactose as well. Newborn screening includes galactosaemia in Australian programs but the result may not be available fast enough for a baby who is already unwell, so treatment is started on clinical suspicion. Lifelong lactose restriction prevents the acute liver and renal disease, although ovarian insufficiency and learning difficulties can still occur despite good dietary control.
key_points: Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose dipstick indicates a non-glucose reducing sugar
Escherichia coli sepsis in a jaundiced neonate is the classic association of galactosaemia
Withdraw lactose immediately on clinical suspicion; do not wait for the screening result
Extensively hydrolysed formulas usually still contain lactose, so soy based formula is used
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with coagulopathy in a neonate is always pathological
explanation.pearls: Soy formula is used in galactosaemia even though soy is otherwise avoided in infancy, because the galactose in soy is bound as raffinose and stachyose, which human infants cannot hydrolyse and therefore cannot absorb.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Newborn bloodspot screening

options.rationale: Breast milk is the richest dietary source of lactose, and every further feed delivers the galactose that is driving the liver injury, the renal tubular dysfunction and the hypoglycaemia. Continuing to feed while treating only the infection leaves the underlying substrate load untouched. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate

options.rationale: Extensive hydrolysis alters the protein fraction to reduce allergenicity but most hydrolysed formulas still contain lactose, so the galactose exposure continues. The formula that treats cow milk protein allergy is not the formula that treats a galactose disorder. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate

options.rationale: Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose specific dipstick means a non-glucose reducing sugar, and galactosaemia presenting with conjugated jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and Escherichia coli sepsis fits precisely. Lactose is withdrawn immediately and replaced with a soy based formula while confirmatory galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase assay and the newborn screening result are chased, because the biochemical injury reverses within days of removing the substrate. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate

options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid is used for cholestasis of other causes such as biliary atresia awaiting surgery or parenteral nutrition associated liver disease, and it does nothing about an accumulating toxic metabolite. Treating the cholestasis symptomatically does nothing while the cause continues to be fed. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Phenobarbital induces hepatic enzymes and was historically used in hyperbilirubinaemia of other causes, and it is not a treatment for conjugated jaundice with coagulopathy. It would also sedate an already encephalopathic infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation accounts for a large share of upper limb presentations in children under five and is diagnosed on the combination of a longitudinal traction mechanism, a pronated arm held still, and the absence of swelling, bruising or focal bone tenderness. The differential that matters is a supracondylar or forearm fracture, which follows a fall rather than a pull and almost always produces swelling or point tenderness. Reduction is performed at the bedside without analgesia in most children, and a child who resumes using the arm within fifteen minutes needs no imaging and no follow up. Recurrence is common until about five years of age, so parents should be warned against lifting the child by the hands. Persistent non use after two attempts should prompt radiographs, because an occult fracture has then become the likely explanation.
key_points: The mechanism is axial traction on an extended, pronated arm, not a fall
Absence of swelling, bruising and focal bone tenderness effectively excludes fracture in this age group
Supination with flexion and hyperpronation are both acceptable reduction techniques
Return of spontaneous arm use within fifteen minutes confirms the diagnosis retrospectively
Radiographs are indicated only after failed reduction or when examination raises fracture concern
explanation.pearls: Hyperpronation reduces radial head subluxation on the first attempt slightly more often than supination and flexion and is reported by children as less painful, so it is a reasonable first technique in a distressed toddler.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: Axial traction on a pronated forearm with a limb that is non-tender and free of swelling is the classic radial head subluxation, which is a clinical diagnosis treated by reduction without imaging. Supination with flexion, or hyperpronation, restores spontaneous use within minutes in most children. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

A sling treats the pain but leaves the annular ligament entrapped, so the child continues not to use the arm for days. Slings belong to undisplaced fractures, where the diagnosis has already been made radiologically. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Backslab immobilisation with delayed imaging is the pathway for a suspected occult fracture, which requires focal bone tenderness or a fall onto the outstretched hand. Neither feature is present here. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: Ultrasound can show a displaced annular ligament but adds cost and delay to a diagnosis already secure on history and examination. It is reserved for children whose arm use does not return after two reduction attempts. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: Radiographs are reserved for an atypical mechanism, visible swelling or deformity, or focal bone tenderness, none of which are present. Imaging a classic traction injury delays a manoeuvre that usually restores function within minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood, often called toddler diarrhoea, is the commonest cause of persistent loose stools between one and five years of age and is a positive diagnosis rather than one of exclusion. It is driven by a combination of excessive fluid intake, high fructose and sorbitol loads from juice and cordial, a low fat intake, and excess fibre, all of which shorten intestinal transit. The features that permit a confident diagnosis are preserved growth, absence of nocturnal stools, absence of blood, and undigested food fragments in the stool. Correcting the dietary pattern resolves symptoms within weeks in most children, and the condition remits spontaneously by school age. Failure to improve after genuine dietary change, or the emergence of growth faltering, nocturnal symptoms or blood, should trigger referral rather than a longer dietary trial.
key_points: Preserved growth and absent nocturnal stools are the two most reassuring features
Fruit juice, cordial and low fat intake are the modifiable drivers
Undigested vegetable matter in the stool reflects rapid transit, not malabsorption
Coeliac serology requires a total immunoglobulin A alongside it to be interpretable
A normal faecal calprotectin makes inflammatory bowel disease highly unlikely in this age group
explanation.pearls: Capping total juice at about 120 mL per day and lifting fat to roughly 35 to 40 per cent of energy intake will resolve most toddler diarrhoea within two to four weeks, which is why a six week review is long enough to judge the response.

options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy causing loose stools presents in infancy with blood or mucus, faltering growth or atopy, and rarely begins at this age in a thriving child. Elimination diets in a 2-year-old risk calcium and energy shortfall without addressing the osmotic load. (Source: RCH CPG: Chronic diarrhoea)

Persistent infection such as giardiasis is worth excluding when there is weight loss, overseas travel, or a childcare outbreak, none of which are described. Four months of stable growth with a normal calprotectin argues strongly against an infective or inflammatory cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Probiotics and bulking agents have at best a marginal effect on this condition and leave the driving dietary factors untouched. They also risk framing a benign functional pattern as a disease requiring medication. (Source: RCH CPG: Chronic diarrhoea)

Endoscopy is warranted for growth failure, blood in the stool, nocturnal symptoms or a raised calprotectin, and none are present. Submitting a thriving toddler to anaesthesia for a dietary problem is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Normal growth, daytime only symptoms, undigested food in the stool and a high osmotic fluid load with a low fat intake define chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood, which responds to correcting these four dietary factors. Reducing the sorbitol and fructose load slows transit enough for the stool to reform. (Source: RCH CPG: Chronic diarrhoea)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pains affect up to a third of primary school-aged children and are characterised by bilateral, deep, poorly localised pain in the calves, shins or behind the knees, occurring in the evening or first part of the night and absent by morning. The diagnosis rests on a completely normal examination and normal growth, and it is not a diagnosis of exclusion requiring blood tests. The features that should redirect the assessment are unilateral pain, pain that persists or recurs during the day, limp or refusal to weight bear, localised bone tenderness, fever, weight loss, night sweats, bruising or organomegaly. Leukaemia and bone tumours in children characteristically produce persistent, progressive, often unilateral pain with systemic features rather than a stereotyped nightly pattern that vanishes by breakfast. Naming the red flags to the family explicitly converts reassurance into a shared safety net.
key_points: Bilateral, evening or night only pain with complete resolution by morning is the defining pattern
Examination and growth must be entirely normal for the diagnosis to stand
Unilateral pain, limp, bone tenderness or systemic features mandate a full blood count and film
Morning stiffness suggests inflammatory arthritis rather than benign limb pains
Explicit safety netting is more valuable than a normal blood test for parental reassurance
explanation.pearls: Pain that reliably wakes a child in the second half of the night and is relieved within twenty minutes of ibuprofen should raise osteoid osteoma, which is the one benign bone lesion that mimics growing pains but is almost always unilateral and fixed to a single site.

options.rationale: Scheduled anti-inflammatory therapy exposes a well child to gastric and renal risk for pains that resolve within half an hour without drugs. Regular dosing also obscures the diagnostic value of any future pain pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

Bilateral pain confined to the evening and night, resolving completely by morning, with a normal examination and normal growth, is benign nocturnal limb pain, for which explanation and safety netting are the treatment. Naming the red flags that would change the plan is what makes this safe rather than dismissive. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

Blood tests are indicated when pain is unilateral, persists into the day, wakes the child in the second half of the night, or is accompanied by systemic features, none of which are present. Investigating a textbook benign pattern medicalises it and a normal result rarely reassures an already frightened parent. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

An osteoid osteoma causes persistent localised night pain at one site that is strikingly relieved by a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, whereas this pain is bilateral, migratory and settles with rubbing. Bilateral symmetrical pain effectively excludes a solitary bone lesion. (Source: RACGP: Musculoskeletal pain in children)

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis requires objective joint swelling or restriction persisting at least six weeks, and morning stiffness rather than night pain is its hallmark. This child is stiffness free and examination is normal. (Source: RACGP: Musculoskeletal pain in children)

explanation.summary: Functional abdominal pain disorders account for the large majority of chronic abdominal pain in school-aged children and are defined by symptom criteria rather than by the absence of every alternative. Alarm features that shift the assessment include involuntary weight loss or centile crossing, growth deceleration, pain that wakes the child from sleep, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, gastrointestinal blood loss, unexplained fever, arthritis, perianal disease and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease. Pain that clusters around school mornings, improves at weekends and is associated with anxiety or a recent transition is characteristic, and school avoidance rapidly becomes self-reinforcing. Effective management combines an explicit positive explanation of gut and brain signalling, a graded return to school, and psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy or gut directed hypnotherapy. Continued investigation in the absence of alarm features prolongs disability and strengthens illness beliefs.
key_points: A functional disorder is diagnosed positively on symptom pattern, not by exclusion alone
Normal growth and a normal faecal calprotectin carry most of the reassurance value
Pain waking a child from sleep is an alarm feature, unlike pain on waking in the morning
School avoidance compounds disability and needs an explicit graded return plan
Cognitive behavioural therapy and gut directed hypnotherapy have the strongest evidence in children
explanation.pearls: Tenderness that vanishes when the child is distracted during palpation, sometimes elicited by re-palpating with the stethoscope, is a useful bedside sign favouring a functional disorder over an inflammatory abdominal process.

options.rationale: A low fermentable oligosaccharide diet has some evidence in irritable bowel syndrome with prominent bloating and altered stools, which this child does not have. Restrictive diets in school-aged children also carry a real risk of disordered eating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Serial normal tests in a child who is growing normally and has no red flags add nothing and reinforce the family's belief that an undetected disease is present. Repeat testing is warranted only if new alarm features emerge. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal pain, chronic)

Endoscopy is indicated for dysphagia, persistent vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, growth faltering or a raised calprotectin, and none are present here. A general anaesthetic for a functional disorder carries risk without diagnostic yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal pain, chronic)

Six months of periumbilical pain without alarm features, with normal growth and normal screening tests, meets the criteria for a functional abdominal pain disorder, which is diagnosed positively rather than by exhaustion of tests. Restoring school attendance and addressing the anxiety are the interventions that change the trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal pain, chronic)

Acid suppression helps epigastric pain with reflux or dyspeptic features, not periumbilical pain unrelated to meals. Using a drug trial as a diagnostic test also risks attributing natural fluctuation to the medication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Capillary malformations, often called port wine stains, are present at birth, grow only in proportion to the child, and persist for life, in contrast to infantile haemangiomas which appear after birth, proliferate, then involute. The clinical significance of a facial capillary malformation depends on its distribution, and involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, particularly the forehead and upper eyelid, is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. That syndrome comprises the cutaneous malformation with a leptomeningeal vascular malformation and ipsilateral glaucoma, and it arises from a somatic mosaic GNAQ mutation. Seizures typically begin in the first year and are associated with progressive hemiparesis and developmental impairment if uncontrolled, so early recognition matters. Glaucoma may be present at birth or develop later, which is why ophthalmological surveillance continues throughout childhood rather than being a single assessment.
key_points: A flat vascular lesion fully formed at birth is a malformation, not a haemangioma
Ophthalmic trigeminal distribution, especially forehead and upper eyelid, drives the risk
Leptomeningeal angiomatosis and ipsilateral glaucoma are the two associations to exclude
Propranolol has no role in capillary malformations
Pulsed dye laser is cosmetic and does not alter neurological or ocular risk
explanation.pearls: Early magnetic resonance imaging in an infant can be falsely reassuring because leptomeningeal enhancement may not be apparent before about one year of age, so a normal early scan in a child who later develops seizures should be repeated rather than relied upon.

options.rationale: A capillary malformation involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve carries a substantial risk of leptomeningeal angiomatosis and of ipsilateral glaucoma, so imaging and measured intraocular pressure are both required. Identifying either early allows seizure treatment and sight saving intervention before damage is established. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

Capillary malformations persist lifelong, darken and may thicken with age, so the natural history offered here is that of a different lesion. Deferring assessment to eighteen months would also miss the window for detecting glaucoma. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

Pulsed dye laser does lighten capillary malformations and is best started early, but it is a cosmetic intervention that does nothing about the neurological and ocular risks. Treating the skin before excluding those associations inverts the priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

Seizures occur in most children with leptomeningeal involvement, but an electroencephalogram in an asymptomatic infant is insensitive and prophylactic anticonvulsants are not established practice. The imaging result determines whether neurology involvement is needed at all. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome)

Propranolol treats an infantile haemangioma, which is a proliferative vascular tumour that appears in the weeks after birth, grows and becomes raised, then involutes. A flat lesion present fully formed at birth that has not changed is a capillary malformation, which does not respond to propranolol. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic persisting more than a year with onset before eighteen years of age, and this boy meets those criteria. Tics characteristically wax and wane, worsen with fatigue, stress and excitement, diminish during absorbing activity, and are preceded by a premonitory urge that is relieved by performing the tic. Treatment is driven by functional impairment rather than tic count, and a child who is coping well needs education and school liaison rather than therapy. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics teaches awareness of the premonitory urge and a competing physical response that is incompatible with the tic, plus function based strategies for situations that worsen tics. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder each present in a large minority and often causing more impairment than the tics.
key_points: Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic for over a year defines Tourette syndrome
Treatment threshold is functional impairment, not tic frequency
Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first line where available
Antipsychotics and clonidine are second line and chosen by comorbidity and adverse effect profile
Screen actively for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms
explanation.pearls: Stimulants prescribed for coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder were long avoided in tic disorders, but controlled data show they do not worsen tics on average and treating the attention disorder often reduces overall impairment more than treating the tics.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for tics that do not impair function, but this boy is being socially isolated and is now refusing school, which is the threshold for active treatment. Most tics do improve by late adolescence, which does not help him this school year. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

Serotonin reuptake inhibitors treat the obsessive compulsive symptoms that frequently accompany tic disorders but have no direct effect on tics themselves. This boy has no compulsions or intrusive thoughts, so there is no target for the drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built on habit reversal training with a competing response, is the recommended first line treatment for impairing tics in children and has effect sizes comparable to medication without drug adverse effects. Preserved suppressibility and premonitory urge, both present here, are what make the competing response technique work. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

Antipsychotics reduce tic severity but carry weight gain, metabolic and extrapyramidal burden, so they are reserved for tics that remain disabling after behavioural therapy has been tried or is unavailable. Starting here skips the treatment with the better risk to benefit ratio. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological option, particularly when attention deficit hyperactivity disorder coexists, and has a milder adverse effect profile than antipsychotics. It nevertheless sits behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence for a child whose tics are suppressible and who has no comorbid attention disorder. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

explanation.summary: Equinus gait in spastic cerebral palsy may be dynamic, driven by velocity dependent hypertonia, or fixed, driven by shortened muscle and tendon, and separating the two determines the whole treatment plan. The Silfverskiold test compares ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended and flexed, since gastrocnemius crosses the knee while soleus does not, so a range that improves markedly with knee flexion localises the problem to gastrocnemius and indicates it is not yet a fixed contracture. Focal chemodenervation with botulinum toxin type A produces about three to four months of tone reduction, which is used as a therapeutic window for stretching, strengthening and orthotic tuning rather than as a treatment in itself. Hip surveillance with serial pelvic radiographs runs in parallel throughout childhood because migration percentage rises silently. Escalation to orthopaedic lengthening or neurosurgical procedures follows the emergence of fixed deformity or generalised spasticity that focal treatment cannot address.
key_points: The Silfverskiold test distinguishes gastrocnemius tightness from a combined fixed contracture
Dynamic tone without fixed contracture is the indication for focal chemodenervation
Botulinum toxin effect lasts about three to four months and must be paired with therapy
Oral agents treat generalised spasticity at the cost of weakness and sedation
Surgical lengthening of a dynamic equinus risks iatrogenic crouch gait
explanation.pearls: Overlengthening the triceps surae in an ambulant child with diplegia converts toe walking into a crouch gait with progressive knee flexion and patellar overload, a functional deterioration that is far more difficult to reverse than the equinus it replaced.

options.rationale: Oral baclofen reduces tone across every muscle group, so in a child whose problem is confined to the calves it buys focal benefit at the cost of generalised weakness and sedation. Systemic agents are preferred when spasticity is generalised and painful rather than focal and functional. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Selective dorsal rhizotomy is considered for children with marked generalised lower limb spasticity, good underlying strength and no dystonia, usually after focal treatments have proved insufficient. It is a substantial irreversible neurosurgical procedure for a boy whose problem is currently confined to two muscle groups. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

Serial casting is effective against a developing contracture with restricted passive range, but this boy already achieves dorsiflexion past neutral with the knee flexed. Casting also immobilises and weakens the limb in a child whose gait problem is tone driven rather than range driven. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

Surgical lengthening is for fixed contracture, where the ankle will not reach neutral even with the knee flexed and slow stretch. Operating on a purely dynamic equinus risks overlengthening and a crouch gait that is far harder to treat than the original problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

A dynamic equinus that releases with knee flexion and slow stretch, with no fixed contracture, is the exact indication for focal chemodenervation, and the resulting window of reduced tone is used for intensive stretching and gait retraining. Combining the injection with orthoses and therapy is what converts a temporary tone reduction into a lasting functional gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

explanation.summary: Juvenile dermatomyositis is the commonest inflammatory myopathy of childhood and reflects a systemic small vessel vasculopathy affecting skin, muscle and sometimes gut and lung. The cutaneous signs are highly specific: a heliotrope discolouration of the upper eyelids, Gottron papules over the extensor surfaces of the finger joints, and dilated tortuous nailfold capillaries with dropout. Weakness is symmetrical and proximal, so children struggle with stairs, hair brushing and rising from the floor while distal power remains normal. Muscle enzymes may be raised but a normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis, and magnetic resonance imaging showing muscle oedema has largely replaced biopsy in typical cases. Early aggressive treatment with corticosteroids plus methotrexate is associated with lower rates of calcinosis, contracture and long term functional loss, so referral should not wait on serology or tissue.
key_points: Heliotrope rash and Gottron papules are the specific cutaneous markers
Weakness is symmetrical and proximal with preserved distal power
A normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis
Assess swallow and respiratory muscle strength at presentation for aspiration risk
Early corticosteroid plus methotrexate reduces calcinosis and long term disability
explanation.pearls: Nailfold capillaroscopy performed at the bedside with a dermatoscope and a drop of oil will show dilated loops and avascular areas in juvenile dermatomyositis, and the density of capillary dropout correlates with disease activity well enough to guide treatment decisions.

options.rationale: Dystrophinopathy causes proximal weakness with a very high creatine kinase but affects boys almost exclusively, progresses over years rather than months, and produces no rash or nailfold capillary change. The photodistributed eruption is the finding that excludes it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Heliotrope discolouration with Gottron papules, nailfold capillary change, symmetrical proximal weakness and a raised creatine kinase are diagnostic of juvenile dermatomyositis, and early combined corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy reduces calcinosis and long term disability. Swallow and respiratory muscle assessment identifies the children at immediate risk of aspiration. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Treating the skin alone leaves an active systemic myositis untreated, and delay in this disease is associated with calcinosis and contractures. The rash here is a marker of a systemic vasculopathy rather than a primary dermatosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Myositis specific antibodies help predict phenotype and risk of calcinosis or interstitial lung disease, but the diagnosis here is clinical and treatment should not wait on serology. A negative antinuclear antibody does not exclude juvenile dermatomyositis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile dermatomyositis)

Biopsy remains useful when the presentation is atypical or the rash is absent, but it is no longer required when the characteristic rash, proximal weakness, raised muscle enzymes and typical magnetic resonance appearances coexist. Insisting on it delays treatment without changing the plan. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile dermatomyositis)

explanation.summary: Medium chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency is the commonest inherited fatty acid oxidation disorder and is detected by newborn screening through a raised octanoylcarnitine on the acylcarnitine profile. Affected children are entirely well when fed, because the defect only becomes relevant once hepatic glycogen is exhausted and the body must generate ketones from fatty acids. The characteristic decompensation is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with vomiting, lethargy and encephalopathy, often precipitated by a gastrointestinal illness or a long overnight fast, and it can progress to seizures, cardiac arrhythmia and death. Management is therefore preventive and consists of avoiding prolonged fasting, a written emergency regimen of frequent glucose polymer drinks during illness, and a low threshold for intravenous dextrose in hospital when oral intake fails. Families should carry an emergency letter, because the child looks well until they suddenly do not and the diagnosis is easily missed by clinicians unfamiliar with it.
key_points: Children are asymptomatic when fed; risk arises entirely from fasting
Decompensation is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy, not acidosis from protein
Medium chain triglyceride oil is contraindicated and treats a different chain length defect
The emergency regimen is frequent oral glucose polymer with escalation if feeds fail
Risk persists into adulthood around surgery, fasting and gastrointestinal illness
explanation.pearls: A child with this disorder who presents unwell and vomiting should receive intravenous glucose at about 10 per cent dextrose running at maintenance or above even if the bedside glucose is still normal, because hypoglycaemia is a late feature and waiting for it forfeits the safe window.

options.rationale: Stopping protein is the emergency approach to urea cycle defects and organic acidaemias, where the toxic metabolite derives from protein catabolism. In a fatty acid oxidation defect protein is not the problem and withholding it removes energy without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

Carnitine supplementation is sometimes used where the free carnitine is low, but it is adjunctive and does not prevent decompensation. Waiting for documented hypoglycaemia before presenting is unsafe, because encephalopathy and arrhythmia can develop rapidly once the glucose starts to fall. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Risk is highest in the first two years but persists into adult life, with decompensations reported during gastroenteritis, surgery and prolonged fasting at any age. Standard advice to withhold feeds during vomiting is precisely what precipitates crisis in this condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

This disorder is asymptomatic while the child is fed and becomes dangerous only when fasting forces a switch to fatty acid oxidation that the child cannot complete, so an emergency regimen providing frequent carbohydrate is the entire management. Escalating to hospital when feeds are refused prevents the hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy that cause death. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

Medium chain triglyceride supplementation is the treatment for long chain fatty acid oxidation defects and is exactly the wrong intervention here, since the enzyme that is missing metabolises medium chain substrates. The two disorders are distinguished by chain length, and the therapies do not transfer between them. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration in the neonatal period most often reflects inadequate breast milk intake in the first two weeks, and the clinical signs of dehydration are deceptively mild because water is drawn from the intracellular compartment and the circulating volume is relatively preserved. Doughy skin turgor and a preserved blood pressure alongside a large weight loss should therefore prompt an immediate electrolyte measurement rather than reassurance. Brain cells generate idiogenic osmoles within hours to defend their volume against a hypertonic plasma, and those osmoles clear only slowly, so lowering the plasma sodium quickly draws water into the brain and causes cerebral oedema and seizures. The safe approach is a small isotonic bolus only if perfusion is genuinely compromised, followed by slow deficit replacement over at least 48 hours with an isotonic or near isotonic fluid, with the sodium measured every four hours and the rate adjusted to keep the fall within about 0.5 mmol/L per hour. Feeding support, weighed feeds and lactation review are as important as the fluid prescription, since the underlying problem is a feeding one.
key_points: Clinical signs underestimate the deficit because intracellular water is lost preferentially
Correct the sodium no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour or about 10 to 12 mmol/L per day
Replace the deficit over at least 48 hours using isotonic or near isotonic fluid
Recheck electrolytes every four hours and adjust the infusion rate to the measured fall
Establish the feeding cause with weighed feeds and lactation support before discharge
explanation.pearls: A seizure occurring several hours into treatment of hypernatraemic dehydration is usually caused by the correction rather than the disease, and the immediate response is to slow the infusion and raise the sodium content of the fluid rather than to load an anticonvulsant.

options.rationale: Perfusion is compromised, so a modest isotonic bolus is justified first, but the accumulated deficit in hypernatraemic dehydration must then be replaced slowly because rapid correction shifts water into brain cells that have accumulated osmolytes. A ceiling of 0.5 mmol/L per hour, or about 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, with sodium rechecked every four hours, is the rate that avoids cerebral oedema and seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

Escalating bolus therapy to 60 mL/kg is the paediatric septic shock sequence and delivers the entire deficit within an hour, which in hypernatraemia produces an abrupt osmotic shift into the brain. This infant has compensated perfusion rather than shock, so repeated large boluses are both unnecessary and hazardous. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

This combines a very hypotonic fluid with rapid deficit replacement, which is the fastest route to a dangerous fall in serum sodium. The free water it delivers would lower the sodium far in excess of the safe ceiling. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

Enteral rehydration is preferred in mild to moderate dehydration, but this infant has lethargy, prolonged capillary refill and a sodium of 168 mmol/L, which places him beyond enteral management alone. The route is also too slow to correct a rising urea and creatinine. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

Hypertonic saline treats symptomatic hyponatraemia or raised intracranial pressure, and giving it to a child whose sodium is already 168 mmol/L would worsen the hyperosmolar state. Cerebral oedema in hypernatraemia is a complication of correcting too fast, not of the presenting sodium. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: Children in nephrotic relapse are functionally immunodeficient because they lose complement factors B and D and immunoglobulin G in the urine while ascitic fluid provides a culture medium, and this combination makes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis the signature infection of the condition. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the classical organism, with Escherichia coli and other Gram negative bacilli also common, which is why a third generation cephalosporin is the empirical choice in Australia. The presentation is easily attributed to the oedema itself, to constipation from inactivity, or to corticosteroid gastritis, and fever with diffuse guarding and a raised C-reactive protein is what separates infection from those benign explanations. A diagnostic ascitic tap showing a neutrophil count above 250 cells per microlitre confirms the diagnosis, but treatment is started immediately after sampling rather than after the result. Preventive measures include pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination, varicella immunity checks before immunosuppression, and family education that fever during relapse requires same day assessment rather than watchful waiting.
key_points: Urinary loss of complement and immunoglobulin creates a real infection risk during relapse
