Streptococcus pneumoniae is the classical organism; a third generation cephalosporin is empirical therapy
An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells per microlitre confirms peritoneal infection
Sample the ascites first, but never delay the antibiotic for the result
Thrombosis and appendicitis are the two differentials worth actively considering
explanation.pearls: Albumin infusion during active sepsis in nephrotic syndrome should be reserved for genuine circulatory compromise, because the oncotic pull mobilises fluid rapidly and combining it with furosemide in a hypovolaemic septic child can precipitate both hypotension and thrombosis.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: Corticosteroid related gastric pain is epigastric, is not associated with fever or guarding, and would not produce this neutrophilia and C-reactive protein. Escalating immunosuppression in an undiagnosed sepsis is actively harmful. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

Appendicitis remains possible and surgical review is reasonable, but pain that is diffuse rather than migratory to the right iliac fossa, in a child with tense ascites and profound hypoalbuminaemia, points to infected ascites. Computed tomography also adds radiation without changing the immediate antibiotic decision. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Nephrotic syndrome in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.rationale: Fever, diffuse guarding and a neutrophilia in a child with heavy proteinuria and an albumin of 12 g/L indicate infection of the ascitic fluid, which is the commonest serious infection in nephrotic relapse and is driven by urinary loss of complement and immunoglobulin. Sampling before antibiotics preserves the microbiological diagnosis, but the antibiotic must not wait for the result. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

Albumin with furosemide is the correct treatment for symptomatic tense ascites or respiratory compromise from oedema, but it treats the distension while leaving an infection untreated. Diuresing an intravascularly depleted, septic child also risks precipitating circulatory collapse and thrombosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

Thrombosis is a genuine hazard of nephrotic syndrome and deserves consideration, but it typically causes flank pain with haematuria and a falling urine output rather than fever with diffuse peritonism and a C-reactive protein of 96 mg/L. Deferring antibiotics for imaging in suspected peritoneal sepsis costs time that matters. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

explanation.summary: Roughly a third of Australian children with new type 1 diabetes present in ketoacidosis, but the remainder present with osmotic symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia while remaining well perfused and only mildly ketotic, and the two groups need entirely different pathways. Ketoacidosis is defined by hyperglycaemia with a venous pH below 7.3 or a bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L alongside ketonaemia, and it is that biochemical threshold rather than the absolute glucose value that determines whether an insulin infusion is required. A child who is alert, tolerating oral fluids and not acidotic is treated with subcutaneous insulin, which achieves the same glycaemic control while avoiding the fluid shifts and monitoring burden of an infusion. Mild ketonaemia in the range just above the normal cut off reflects the fasting and insulin deficiency and does not by itself mandate intravenous therapy. In rural settings the decision matters practically, because an unnecessary infusion may trigger a retrieval that the child does not need while still requiring same day specialist discussion for education, dosing and follow up.
key_points: Acidosis, not glucose level, determines whether ketoacidosis treatment is required
A venous pH of 7.3 and a bicarbonate of 15 mmol/L are the operative thresholds
Well perfused, alert children tolerating fluids are treated with subcutaneous insulin
Osmotic symptoms with weight loss in a child indicate insulin deficiency, not insulin resistance
Same day specialist contact is required even when the child is not acidotic
explanation.pearls: Blood ketone measurement of beta-hydroxybutyrate is more reliable than urine ketone dipsticks in this decision, because urine testing detects acetoacetate and can read strongly positive from fasting alone or read falsely low while beta-hydroxybutyrate predominates early in decompensation.

options.rationale: A random glucose of 24.6 mmol/L with four weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss is diagnostic, and a tolerance test in symptomatic hyperglycaemia is both unnecessary and dangerous. A glycated haemoglobin can be sent for information but must not delay insulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

Metformin is used where type 2 diabetes is likely, which would require obesity, acanthosis nigricans or a strong family history without the rapid weight loss seen here. Weight loss with four weeks of osmotic symptoms in a 10-year-old indicates insulin deficiency, which metformin cannot treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

An insulin infusion with the two bag protocol is the pathway for ketoacidosis, defined by a pH below 7.3 or a bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L, and neither threshold is met. Infusing insulin into a child who is not acidotic and is drinking freely lowers the glucose faster than necessary and commits a rural department to a resource intensive protocol without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

A fluid bolus is for impaired perfusion, and this girl has a normal heart rate, normal blood pressure, moist membranes and a capillary refill of 2 seconds. Repeating the gas without starting insulin also delays treatment of an established diagnosis that will not improve on its own. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

New type 1 diabetes without acidosis and without vomiting or dehydration is managed with subcutaneous insulin and oral fluids from the outset, and this avoids the risks of an unnecessary infusion. Same day specialist discussion secures the education, dose regimen and follow up that determine the first year of control. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

explanation.summary: Congenital obstruction of the nasolacrimal drainage system affects up to one in five infants and presents with epiphora and mattering from the first weeks of life. The key clinical task is separating it from the two conditions that need action, namely infective conjunctivitis and congenital glaucoma, which is done on the appearance of the conjunctiva and cornea rather than on the discharge itself. Spontaneous resolution occurs in about 90 per cent by the first birthday, so the default is conservative management with sac massage and lid cleaning. Referral is warranted for persistence past 12 months, for a mucocoele, or for any episode of dacryocystitis. Parents should be told to return if the eye becomes red, the lids swell, or the baby becomes unsettled in bright light.
key_points: Watering with a white conjunctiva and clear cornea points to drainage obstruction, not infection.
Photophobia, corneal clouding or corneal diameter above 12 mm raises congenital glaucoma and needs urgent ophthalmology assessment.
Lacrimal sac massage plus lid hygiene is the management for the first 12 months.
Around 90 per cent resolve spontaneously by 12 months, so probing before that age is premature.
Antibiotic drops treat a red discharging eye, not chronic epiphora.
explanation.pearls: Press over the lacrimal sac: mucoid reflux confirms a patent canaliculus with distal obstruction, and if the overlying skin is red and tender instead, that is dacryocystitis needing systemic flucloxacillin and same-day ophthalmology review.

options.rationale: Probing is reserved for obstruction persisting beyond 12 months of age or for complications such as recurrent dacryocystitis, because more than nine in ten ducts open spontaneously in the first year. Probing this infant would expose her to anaesthesia for a problem likely to resolve without it. (Source: RCH CPG: Blocked nasolacrimal duct)

Topical antibiotic is for bacterial conjunctivitis, which produces a red conjunctiva and purulent rather than clear-mucoid discharge; the white eye here excludes it. Antibiotic drops are appropriate only if this infant later develops conjunctival injection or sac cellulitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Blocked nasolacrimal duct)

Persistent watering from early infancy with a quiet white eye, a clear cornea and mucoid reflux on sac pressure is a patent-but-obstructed drainage system, and conservative management with sac massage plus lid hygiene is correct while spontaneous canalisation occurs. Review at 12 months is the point at which referral becomes appropriate if symptoms persist. (Source: RCH CPG: Blocked nasolacrimal duct)

Congenital glaucoma also presents with watering in infancy but is accompanied by photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and a corneal diameter above 12 mm; a clear cornea of normal diameter with no light sensitivity is the finding that separates the two. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric eye examination)

Chlamydial ophthalmia presents between days 5 and 14 of life with a red, swollen, discharging eye, not with four months of clear watering in a white eye. Systemic azithromycin would be correct if the swab were positive in that neonatal window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Retained fetal lung fluid is the commonest cause of respiratory distress in a term infant and is strongly associated with delivery by caesarean before labour, because the fluid clearance that labour triggers has not occurred. It declares itself within two hours of birth, peaks in the first day and resolves within 72 hours, distinguishing it from surfactant deficiency, which worsens over the first day, and from pneumonia, which is usually accompanied by risk factors or temperature instability. The radiograph is characteristic, showing interstitial fluid and fluid tracking into the fissures with preserved lung volume. Management is observation with feeding support and supplemental oxygen only if saturations fall. Persistent tachypnoea beyond 72 hours should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, including congenital heart disease.
key_points: Tachypnoea from the first hour after caesarean without labour is usually retained lung fluid.
Fluid in the fissures with normal lung volumes is the radiographic signature.
Antibiotics are driven by sepsis risk factors and clinical trajectory, not by tachypnoea alone.
Feeds are usually withheld only once the respiratory rate exceeds about 80 per minute.
Failure to resolve by 72 hours should prompt review for cardiac and other causes.
explanation.pearls: Saturations that sit at or above 94 per cent in room air argue strongly against cyanotic congenital heart disease, but the pre-discharge pulse oximetry screen still applies: a difference of more than 3 percentage points between right hand and foot warrants an echocardiogram before going home.

sources.label: SA Perinatal Practice Guideline: Early onset neonatal sepsis

options.rationale: Retained lung fluid after caesarean without labour produces tachypnoea from the first hour that improves over 24 to 72 hours, and with saturations of 94 per cent in air, settling recession and no sepsis risk factors the management is observation with feeding support. Escalation is triggered by rising oxygen requirement or worsening work of breathing, neither of which is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress)

Empirical antibiotics are indicated when risk factors for early onset sepsis are present, such as maternal fever, prolonged rupture, prematurity or a positive group B streptococcus screen; none applies here and the infant is improving. Antibiotics would be correct if the tachypnoea worsened or the baby became temperature unstable. (Source: SA Perinatal Practice Guideline: Early onset neonatal sepsis)
source_refs: SA Perinatal Practice Guideline: Early onset neonatal sepsis

options.rationale: Continuous positive airway pressure is reserved for a persisting oxygen requirement, grunting at rest or rising carbon dioxide, and this infant's recession is resolving on room air. It is the correct escalation if saturations fall below 90 per cent despite low-flow oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress)

Surfactant treats deficiency, which on radiograph shows low lung volumes with a diffuse ground glass pattern and air bronchograms, not the wet interstitial pattern with normal volumes seen here. The radiographic distinction is what separates the two diagnoses at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress)

Withholding feeds is justified when the respiratory rate is high enough to make aspiration likely, conventionally above 80 per minute with significant work of breathing. At 74 per minute with settling recession, oral feeding with close observation is safe and supports maternal attachment. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress)

explanation.summary: Positional deformation of the skull became far more common after supine sleeping was adopted for sudden unexpected death prevention, and it is a benign condition that does not affect brain growth or development. The single most useful bedside sign separating it from lambdoid suture fusion is the position of the ipsilateral ear and forehead: in positional flattening the whole side is pushed forward, giving a parallelogram, while true fusion pulls the ear backwards and gives a trapezoid with a palpable ridge. Every infant with plagiocephaly should also be examined for neck rotation restriction, since muscular torticollis is the commonest treatable driver. Conservative management works best before 6 months, while skull growth is fastest. Parents need explicit reassurance that supine sleeping must continue.
key_points: Parallelogram shape with the ear and forehead forward indicates positional deformation.
Trapezoid shape, a palpable ridge, and the ear pulled backwards suggest lambdoid suture fusion.
Always test passive neck rotation, as torticollis is the commonest correctable cause.
Repositioning and supervised tummy time are most effective under 6 months of age.
Head circumference crossing centiles or progression despite repositioning warrants referral.
explanation.pearls: Tell parents to place the cot so the interesting side of the room, and the door their parents come through, is on the side that forces the baby to turn away from the flattened occiput; this passive change outperforms instructions to reposition the head after the baby has fallen asleep.

options.rationale: Physiotherapy is indicated when passive neck rotation is restricted or a sternocleidomastoid mass is palpable, because untreated muscular torticollis drives progressive flattening. Full and symmetrical passive rotation here removes that indication. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Imaging is for suspected premature suture fusion, which produces a palpable ridge, a trapezoid rather than parallelogram outline, and posterior rather than anterior displacement of the ipsilateral ear. Open non-ridged sutures with a parallelogram shape make radiation exposure unjustifiable. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Helmet therapy is considered only for severe deformity persisting despite repositioning, and randomised evidence shows no advantage over conservative care for mild to moderate deformity. It also carries skin irritation and pressure complications for a condition that usually improves on its own. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

A parallelogram head shape with the ipsilateral ear and forehead pushed forward, open sutures and unrestricted neck rotation is positional deformation, which responds to repositioning during sleep, alternating the cot orientation, and supervised prone play while awake. Review confirms improvement once the infant sits independently and pressure is taken off the occiput. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Neurosurgical referral is appropriate when sutures are ridged, head circumference crosses centiles, or the deformity progresses despite repositioning. A head circumference that has tracked the 50th centile from birth argues against restricted skull growth. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Tetanus prophylaxis after injury depends on two independent questions: whether the wound is tetanus prone and whether the child has had at least three documented doses of a tetanus containing vaccine. Tetanus prone wounds include deep penetrating injuries, those contaminated with soil or manure, compound fractures, bites, and burns with devitalised tissue. When three or more doses are documented, a booster is given if the last dose was more than five years ago for a tetanus prone wound, and immunoglobulin is not needed. When the history is uncertain or incomplete, immunoglobulin is added because there is no primed memory response to rely on. Children arriving from overseas without records should be treated as unvaccinated and entered into a catch-up schedule, with serology reserved for planning rather than acute care.
key_points: Deep soil-contaminated punctures are tetanus prone wounds by definition.
Fewer than three documented doses, or an uncertain history, means immunoglobulin plus vaccine.
Three or more documented doses means vaccine alone, and only if the last dose was over five years ago for a tetanus prone wound.
Antibiotics treat wound infection and have no role in toxin neutralisation.
Children arriving without records are managed as unvaccinated and started on catch-up.
explanation.pearls: Tetanus immunoglobulin and the vaccine are given at the same visit but at separate injection sites with separate syringes, and for a tetanus prone wound the immunoglobulin dose is 250 IU intramuscularly, rising to 500 IU if more than 24 hours have passed since the injury.

options.rationale: Vaccine alone is correct for a tetanus prone wound when three or more documented doses have been given, because a primed immune system mounts an anamnestic response within days. It is inadequate when priming cannot be confirmed, as antibody will not appear in time. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Tetanus)

A deep, soil-contaminated puncture is a tetanus prone wound, and when the vaccination history is uncertain or fewer than three doses are documented, immunoglobulin is required for immediate passive protection alongside the first dose of a catch-up course for durable immunity. Both components are given at the same visit at separate sites. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Tetanus)

Immunoglobulin provides passive protection lasting only a few weeks and leaves the child unprotected against the next injury, so vaccination must accompany it. Serology is not used to guide acute wound management because results arrive far too late. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Tetanus)

Antibiotics address wound infection and are reasonable for a contaminated plantar puncture, but they do not neutralise tetanus toxin and are not a substitute for immunoglobulin and vaccine. This option treats the wrong risk from this injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Deferring protection ignores an incubation period that can be as short as three days after a heavily contaminated deep wound. Catch-up scheduling alone would be acceptable only for a clean minor wound in a child with an uncertain history. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Tetanus)

explanation.summary: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis occurs in roughly one to two per cent of infants born to mothers with Graves disease and is caused by transplacental passage of thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies rather than by maternal thyroid hormone. The crucial point is that the mother's own thyroid function tells you nothing about the risk, because a woman treated definitively with radioiodine or surgery may be euthyroid or hypothyroid on replacement while still producing high antibody titres. Onset is typically in the first two weeks, and is delayed when the mother has taken a thionamide during pregnancy, since that drug crosses the placenta and suppresses the fetal thyroid for several days after birth. Features are tachycardia, irritability, poor weight gain despite hunger, sweating, goitre, and in severe cases heart failure, craniosynostosis and death. Treatment with a thionamide plus a beta blocker is required until maternal antibodies clear, usually over one to three months.
key_points: The illness is antibody mediated, so a euthyroid mother on replacement can still have an affected infant.
Maternal thionamide treatment during pregnancy can delay onset by several days after birth.
Tachycardia, irritability, weight loss despite hunger and a goitre are the key features.
Untreated disease progresses to heart failure and carries real mortality.
Treatment continues until maternal antibodies clear, usually over one to three months.
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies in every pregnant woman with current or past Graves disease at around 20 to 24 weeks, because a titre more than three times the upper limit identifies the pregnancies that need fetal heart rate surveillance and a planned neonatal review.

options.rationale: Maternal thyroid status and maternal antibody status are separate: stimulating antibodies persist for years after ablation or surgery and cross the placenta even when the mother is euthyroid on replacement. This is the single most common reason the diagnosis is missed. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

Deferred review is unsafe when an infant is losing weight with a heart rate approaching 200 per minute, because untreated disease progresses to heart failure and carries appreciable mortality. Routine weighing would be appropriate for an otherwise well infant with slow weight gain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Sepsis is the standard response to an unsettled neonate who is not gaining weight, but she is afebrile, alert and well perfused with warm peripheries, and sepsis does not produce a goitre. Antibiotics would be appropriate if she were febrile, lethargic or poorly perfused. (Source: RCH CPG: The febrile child)

Beta blockade controls the adrenergic features and is part of treatment, but giving it without confirming the diagnosis and without close monitoring leaves the underlying hormone excess untreated. It is used alongside a thionamide once thyroid function is known. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Tachycardia, irritability, sweating, weight loss and a goitre in the second week of life in the infant of a mother with a history of Graves disease indicate transplacental transfer of stimulating antibodies, and the diagnosis is confirmed by urgent free thyroxine and thyroid stimulating hormone. Admission allows cardiac monitoring and prompt treatment with a thionamide and beta blockade while results are obtained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Recurrent stereotyped vomiting episodes separated by complete wellness form a recognised functional disorder that is strongly associated with a family history of migraine and often evolves into migraine in adolescence. The diagnosis is clinical and requires at least a few identical episodes, normal growth, and a normal examination between and during attacks. The critical safety step is excluding the mimics, which are raised intracranial pressure, intermittent obstruction such as malrotation, and metabolic disease presenting with vomiting and ketosis, so any change in the stereotyped pattern deserves re-evaluation. Acute treatment aims to break the cycle early with dextrose containing fluid and an antiemetic, ideally in a quiet darkened room. Between episodes, identifying triggers such as excitement, infection and fasting, and considering prophylaxis, reduces frequency.
key_points: Identical episodes with complete wellness in between is the defining pattern.
Dextrose containing intravenous fluid interrupts the ketosis that sustains the vomiting.
Ondansetron is the antiemetic of choice in Australian paediatric practice.
A change in the stereotyped pattern, headache on waking or abnormal neurology mandates brain imaging.
Prophylaxis is an outpatient decision after the acute episode has resolved.
explanation.pearls: Treat early rather than waiting for the child to fail oral intake: once blood ketones exceed about 2 mmol/L the vomiting becomes self-sustaining, and families who present in the first few hours with a written plan often avoid admission altogether.

options.rationale: Oral rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration in gastroenteritis, but vomiting every 20 minutes with established ketosis means oral intake will not keep pace and the ketosis itself perpetuates the vomiting. It becomes appropriate once the vomiting has been broken. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyclic vomiting syndrome)

Stereotyped prolonged vomiting episodes with complete wellness between them are managed acutely by interrupting the ketotic cycle with dextrose containing intravenous fluid and by controlling emesis with a 5HT3 antagonist. Dextrose is the component that matters, because ketosis both drives and is driven by the ongoing vomiting. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyclic vomiting syndrome)

Imaging is warranted when vomiting is accompanied by headache on waking, abnormal neurology, papilloedema or a change in episode pattern, since a posterior fossa tumour can mimic recurrent vomiting. A normal neurological examination with a stereotyped pattern over a year makes it unnecessary before treating. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyclic vomiting syndrome)

Prophylactic agents such as propranolol or pizotifen reduce episode frequency and are discussed once the diagnosis is established, but they do nothing for the current episode and starting them in a dehydrated vomiting child is not feasible. This is an outpatient conversation for after recovery. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyclic vomiting syndrome)

Obstruction is suggested by bile-stained vomit, abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds or localised tenderness, none of which is present. A plain film in a soft non-tender abdomen with a year of identical self-limiting episodes would not change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Paroxysmal posturing in infancy is one of the most frequently misdiagnosed presentations in paediatrics, and the great majority of referred events are non-epileptic. Preserved awareness is the most powerful bedside sign: an infant who keeps tracking a parent through the event is not having a tonic seizure. A temporal link to feeds, associated regurgitation and faltering growth point to reflux-associated dystonic posturing, which resolves when the reflux is treated. Recognising it prevents years of unnecessary antiseizure medication and repeated imaging. Conservative management with feed thickening, smaller more frequent volumes and upright positioning is first line, with weight gain as the measure of success and referral reserved for those who fail it.
key_points: Preserved awareness and visual tracking during an event argues strongly against a seizure.
A consistent temporal link to feeding is the second distinguishing feature.
A normal interictal recording never excludes epilepsy, so the clinical description carries the diagnosis.
Faltering growth shifts reflux from physiological to pathological and justifies intervention.
Acid suppression is reserved for proven oesophagitis or failure of conservative measures.
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to film an episode on a phone: a 60 second video showing the infant making eye contact mid-event settles the question faster than any electroencephalogram and is now routine practice in Australian paediatric clinics.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Antiseizure medication is not indicated when awareness is preserved throughout the event, which is the single most useful feature separating it from a tonic seizure. A normal interictal recording does not exclude epilepsy, but preserved visual tracking during the event does argue strongly against it. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Imaging is warranted for focal neurological signs, developmental regression, an abnormal head circumference trajectory or true focal seizures. Normal examination, normal development and a head circumference on its own centile line make a structural lesion unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

Acid suppression has a limited evidence base in infants and is reserved for proven oesophagitis or for failure of conservative measures, and it also carries increased risk of gastroenteritis and lower respiratory infection. It would be the step after thickening and positioning fail, not before them. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Stereotyped dystonic posturing tied to feeds, with preserved awareness throughout and a normal interictal recording, is a reflux-associated movement pattern rather than epilepsy, and the faltering weight makes reflux with feed refusal the likely driver. Feed thickening with upright positioning after feeds is the first line intervention, with growth as the objective measure of response. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: A metabolic cause is suggested by episodes triggered by fasting or intercurrent illness, encephalopathy during the event, or acidosis between episodes, and posturing after feeding fits poorly with that pattern. Newborn screening in Australia would also have detected most disorders presenting this way. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

explanation.summary: Infant botulism follows ingestion of spores that germinate in the immature gut and release toxin locally, with honey the classic identified source, which is why honey is not recommended before 12 months of age. The clinical sequence is characteristic: constipation first, then a weak cry and poor feeding, then descending weakness with bulbar and pupillary involvement, all in an afebrile infant whose conscious state is preserved. The main threat is respiratory failure from a combination of bulbar weakness and inadequate ventilation, so admission to a unit that can intubate is the priority regardless of how well the infant currently looks. Human-derived botulism immune globulin shortens hospital stay substantially and works best when given early, so it is arranged on clinical suspicion. Notification to the public health unit is required.
key_points: Constipation preceding weakness is the early clue and often precedes presentation by days.
Weakness descends from the cranial nerves, with ptosis and sluggish pupils, unlike ascending inflammatory neuropathy.
The infant remains afebrile and alert, which separates it from sepsis and encephalitis.
Immune globulin is given on clinical grounds because faecal confirmation takes days.
Aminoglycosides are avoided because they worsen neuromuscular blockade.
explanation.pearls: Honey should not be given to infants under 12 months in any form, including on a dummy or mixed into food, because spore contamination is not removed by pasteurisation.

options.rationale: Constipation preceding a descending weakness with bulbar signs, ptosis and sluggish pupils in an afebrile alert infant is the recognised pattern of botulism, and management is supportive care in a setting able to intubate plus early human-derived botulism immune globulin, accessed in Australia through the state health department. Treatment is started on clinical grounds because confirmation from faecal testing takes days. (Source: CDNA: Botulism national guidelines)

Sepsis is the reflex answer for a floppy infant, but it does not explain ptosis with sluggish pupils, and this infant is afebrile, alert and haemodynamically stable with normal inflammatory indices. Antibiotics would be justified alongside treatment if the picture were febrile or the diagnosis uncertain. (Source: RCH CPG: The febrile child)

Standard immunoglobulin is the treatment for acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, which classically ascends from the legs and spares the pupils, whereas this weakness descends from the cranial nerves and involves pupillary responses. Specific antitoxin-containing immune globulin, not standard preparations, is what neutralises circulating toxin. (Source: CDNA: Botulism national guidelines)

Deferring assessment is unsafe when the cough is weak and respiration shallow, because respiratory failure in this condition develops over hours and about half of affected infants require ventilation. Electrophysiology supports the diagnosis but must not delay admission or treatment. (Source: CDNA: Botulism national guidelines)

Antibiotics directed at gut organisms are avoided in this setting because bacterial lysis can release further toxin, and aminoglycosides in particular potentiate neuromuscular blockade. The constipation here is the first neurological symptom rather than a primary bowel problem. (Source: CDNA: Botulism national guidelines)

explanation.summary: Spinal muscular atrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder of anterior horn cells caused in most cases by homozygous deletion of the survival motor neuron 1 gene, with severity modified by the copy number of the nearly identical survival motor neuron 2 gene, which produces only a small proportion of functional protein. Two copies predict the severe infantile form, historically fatal or ventilator dependent by two years, while three or four copies predict later onset and milder disease. Australian newborn bloodspot screening now includes the condition precisely because the available disease modifying therapies, an antisense oligonucleotide given intrathecally, a single dose gene replacement therapy and an oral small molecule, transform outcomes when started before weakness appears. Anterior horn cell loss is fastest in the first months of life and is irreversible, so time from screening result to treatment is the variable that matters most. Management is otherwise multidisciplinary, with respiratory, nutritional, orthopaedic and physiotherapy input, and families need genetic counselling because each subsequent pregnancy carries a one in four recurrence risk.
key_points: Most cases are caused by homozygous deletion of the survival motor neuron 1 gene.
Copy number of the second gene predicts severity, with two copies indicating severe infantile disease.
Anterior horn cell loss is fastest in the early months and is irreversible.
Treatment before weakness appears produces far better motor outcomes than treatment afterwards.
Recurrence risk is one in four in each subsequent pregnancy, so genetic counselling is required.
explanation.pearls: Mild head lag with otherwise normal strength is easy to dismiss in a 2-week-old, so treat the screening result rather than the examination: the presymptomatic window for this condition is measured in weeks, and referral within days is what separates a walking child from a ventilated one.

sources.label: Newborn Bloodspot Screening National Policy Framework

options.rationale: Confirmatory diagnostic genetic testing is arranged through the specialist service and runs in parallel with referral, not instead of it, and a month of delay in this condition is measured in motor neurons that cannot be recovered. Repeating the screening assay adds nothing that the diagnostic test does not. (Source: Newborn Bloodspot Screening National Policy Framework)
source_refs: Newborn Bloodspot Screening National Policy Framework

options.rationale: Normal feeding and antigravity movement today are expected in the presymptomatic window and offer no reassurance about what follows, since with this copy number weakness typically declares itself within the first few months. Watchful waiting is precisely the approach screening was introduced to replace. (Source: Newborn Bloodspot Screening National Policy Framework)
source_refs: Newborn Bloodspot Screening National Policy Framework

options.rationale: A screen showing homozygous loss of the survival motor neuron 1 gene with a low copy number of its backup gene predicts severe early onset disease, and disease modifying therapy started before weakness appears produces dramatically better motor outcomes than treatment after symptoms begin. Same week referral allows confirmatory testing and treatment to be arranged within days rather than weeks. (Source: Australian Genomics: Neuromuscular disorders)

Electrophysiology and biopsy were the diagnostic route before genetic testing and are now reserved for cases where genetic testing is negative but the phenotype is convincing. Performing them first delays treatment and subjects the infant to an anaesthetic for information the genetic result already provides. (Source: Australian Genomics: Neuromuscular disorders)

Physiotherapy and multidisciplinary supportive care are essential components of management but do not alter the loss of anterior horn cells that defines the disease course. Offering them alone would withhold the therapy that changes the trajectory. (Source: Australian Genomics: Neuromuscular disorders)

explanation.summary: Alkali ingestion causes liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply and continues after contact, so the oesophagus bears the brunt of injury while the mouth may escape. Three symptoms predict significant injury and drive management: drooling, refusal or inability to swallow, and vomiting, with two or more of these markedly increasing the probability of a high grade burn. The absence of oral burns does not exclude oesophageal injury, because studies consistently show children with normal oral examinations who have grade 2 or 3 oesophageal injury. Endoscopy is performed between about 12 and 24 hours, late enough for the burn to declare itself and early enough to precede the phase of maximal friability and perforation risk. Induced emesis, neutralisation and charcoal are all contraindicated, and all such ingestions warrant discussion with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.
key_points: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis, which penetrates deeper than acid injury.
Drooling, dysphagia and vomiting predict oesophageal injury better than the oral examination.
A normal mouth does not exclude a grade 2 or 3 oesophageal burn.
Endoscopy is timed at 12 to 24 hours to grade the injury before friability peaks.
Neutralisation, induced emesis and activated charcoal are all contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: Grade 2b or 3 injury at endoscopy predicts stricture formation in a large proportion of children, with dysphagia typically appearing between two and eight weeks after ingestion, so every discharged family needs that specific warning and a follow-up appointment.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.rationale: Neutralisation is avoided because the acid base reaction is exothermic and adds thermal injury to chemical injury, and any oral fluid risks provoking vomiting that re-exposes the oesophagus. Small volumes of water immediately after ingestion are sometimes suggested, but not 90 minutes later in a drooling child. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind corrosives, obscures the mucosal view at endoscopy, and carries a significant aspiration risk in a child who is already drooling. It remains the correct decontamination step for many other ingestions presenting within an hour. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.rationale: The absence of oral burns does not exclude significant oesophageal injury, because the liquid passes the mouth quickly and burns are absent in a substantial minority of children with grade 2 or 3 oesophageal lesions. Symptoms, not the oral examination, drive the decision. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.rationale: Contrast swallow has a role weeks later in defining a developing stricture, but in the acute phase it cannot grade mucosal injury and risks mediastinal contamination if there is a perforation. Direct visualisation is what grades the burn and predicts stricture risk. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.rationale: Drooling and refusal to swallow after an alkali ingestion predict oesophageal injury regardless of the appearance of the mouth, so the child is kept nil by mouth, admitted and endoscoped within 12 to 24 hours, the window in which the burn can be graded before tissue friability peaks. Grading determines feeding, the need for dilatation and long term stricture surveillance. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

explanation.summary: Chronic dysphagia in a school-aged child with atopy, particularly when accompanied by adaptive eating behaviours such as drinking with every mouthful, prolonged meal times and avoiding meat and bread, should prompt consideration of eosinophilic disease of the oesophagus. A food bolus impaction is often the presentation that finally brings the child to attention, and it is an indication for endoscopic assessment in its own right. Lack of response to an adequate acid suppression trial strengthens the case but does not define it, since a proportion of patients with the same histology do respond to proton pump inhibitors and are still regarded as having the disease. Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy, with samples taken from more than one level because involvement is patchy and the mucosa may look macroscopically normal. Treatment options are dietary elimination, swallowed topical corticosteroid and acid suppression, with response confirmed histologically.
key_points: Adaptive eating behaviours and food bolus impaction in an atopic child are the classic history.
Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on biopsy.
Biopsies must be taken from proximal and distal oesophagus because disease is patchy.
A macroscopically normal oesophagus does not exclude the diagnosis.
Skin prick testing does not identify the responsible foods in this non immunoglobulin E mediated disease.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically how long the child takes to finish a meal compared with siblings and whether they avoid steak and bread: these two questions identify compensations that children rarely volunteer and that often predate the first bolus impaction by years.

options.rationale: A properly taken eight week full dose trial that produces no change has already answered the question, and escalating it delays diagnosis in a child who has had a bolus obstruction. Acid suppression may still be used later, but as a treatment chosen after histology rather than as a further diagnostic trial. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Dysphagia with compensatory eating behaviours and a food bolus episode in an atopic child that does not respond to acid suppression requires histology, and because the mucosa can look normal and the disease is patchy, multiple biopsies are taken from both proximal and distal oesophagus. The diagnosis rests on eosinophil counts on biopsy, not on the endoscopic appearance. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Contrast studies detect strictures, rings and motility abnormalities but cannot diagnose mucosal inflammation, and a normal study would not exclude the leading diagnosis. It is useful when a tight stricture is suspected and endoscopy needs planning. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Skin prick and specific immunoglobulin E testing correlate poorly with the foods that drive this oesophageal disease, because the mechanism is not immunoglobulin E mediated. Allergy testing guides management of coexisting immediate-type food allergy, not the oesophageal diagnosis. (Source: ASCIA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Elimination diets are an established treatment but are started after histological confirmation, because response is assessed by repeat biopsy rather than symptoms alone and unnecessary restriction harms growth and quality of life. Starting the diet first also risks masking the histology at a later endoscopy. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal herpes simplex infection carries the highest mortality of any neonatal viral infection and presents in three overlapping patterns: localised skin, eye and mouth disease, central nervous system disease, and disseminated disease. Two features make it easy to miss. First, around three quarters of mothers have no history of genital lesions, because most transmission follows asymptomatic shedding during a first episode acquired near term. Second, vesicles are absent at presentation in a substantial proportion of infants with central nervous system or disseminated disease, so their absence carries no reassurance. The combination of seizures in the second week of life, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases is the pattern that should trigger empirical aciclovir, even when the cerebrospinal fluid looks unremarkable. Treatment is intravenous aciclovir at high dose for 14 days in skin, eye and mouth disease and 21 days for central nervous system or disseminated disease, with repeat lumbar puncture at the end of therapy to confirm clearance.
key_points: Most mothers of affected infants have no history of genital herpes.
Absence of vesicles does not exclude central nervous system or disseminated disease.
Bland cerebrospinal fluid early in the illness is common and must not delay antiviral therapy.
Thrombocytopenia with raised transaminases points to disseminated disease.
Treatment is intravenous aciclovir for 21 days in central nervous system or disseminated disease.
explanation.pearls: Send herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction on cerebrospinal fluid, blood and a surface swab from the conjunctiva, nasopharynx and rectum together, and repeat the cerebrospinal fluid test at the end of the 21 day course, because a persistently positive result mandates extending intravenous therapy rather than stepping down.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: A seizure with fever in the second week of life, together with thrombocytopenia and a transaminase in the hundreds, is the disseminated and central nervous system pattern of neonatal herpes simplex infection, and empirical high dose intravenous aciclovir is started while polymerase chain reaction testing of cerebrospinal fluid and blood is pending. Waiting for confirmation is unsafe because mortality rises steeply with delayed treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroid is not recommended in neonatal bacterial meningitis, where evidence of benefit is absent, and it would be actively unhelpful if the cause is viral. Its established role is in older children with Haemophilus influenzae type b or pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

The cerebrospinal fluid does not reassure: a normal cell count, normal protein and negative Gram stain do not exclude herpes encephalitis in the neonate, in whom the fluid is frequently bland early in the illness. Every hour of delay in starting antiviral therapy worsens neurodevelopmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Oral antiviral therapy achieves inadequate central nervous system concentrations for acute disease and is used only as six month suppressive therapy after the intravenous course is complete. Route, not agent, is what makes this option wrong. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Imaging defines the extent of parenchymal involvement and informs prognosis, but early scans are frequently normal and transporting an unstable neonate to the scanner delays therapy. Imaging is arranged after treatment has started. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation follows sudden axial traction on a pronated forearm and is among the commonest upper limb injuries of early childhood, peaking between one and four years while the annular ligament is still lax. The diagnosis rests on the mechanism plus a systemically well child with no bony tenderness who resists supination rather than palpation. Radiographs are reserved for an atypical mechanism, focal bony tenderness, swelling, deformity, or failure to recover after two reduction attempts. Recurrence is common enough that parents should be warned against lifting a child by the hands or wrists. Persistent non-use after an apparently successful reduction should prompt reconsideration of an occult fracture.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated forearm is the mechanism; a fall onto the arm is not.
The child is systemically well, holds the arm pronated, and has no bony tenderness.
Supination with flexion, or hyperpronation, reduces it at the bedside without imaging.
Radiograph for focal bony tenderness, swelling, deformity or failed reduction.
explanation.pearls: After a successful supination-flexion or hyperpronation manoeuvre most toddlers use the arm spontaneously within 5 to 15 minutes; if the arm is still not being used at 30 minutes, radiograph the elbow rather than attempting a third manipulation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: The traction mechanism, the pronated slightly flexed posture, absent bony tenderness and pain confined to attempted supination are the picture of radial head subluxation, and supination with flexion relocates the annular ligament at the bedside. Most children begin using the arm again within minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

A backslab is for a suspected or confirmed fracture, which the absence of swelling, deformity and bony tenderness argues strongly against here. Immobilising an unreduced subluxation simply postpones recovery. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Ultrasound is useful when a septic or inflamed joint is in question, but this child is afebrile and systemically well with a clear traction mechanism. Septic arthritis of the elbow holds the joint in mid-flexion with warmth and swelling and resists movement in every direction, not supination alone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: Imaging is the right first move when the history or examination suggests a fracture, but a pure traction mechanism with no swelling and no bony tenderness does not, and films of a subluxed radial head are almost always reported as normal. Reducing first and imaging only if the arm does not recover spares an unnecessary study. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

A sling treats the pain rather than the problem and leaves the annular ligament interposed, so the child continues not to use the arm for weeks. Slings are also poorly tolerated at this age and delay a reduction that takes seconds at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis affects roughly one in 250 infants and is associated with difficult or instrumental delivery, breech position and intrauterine crowding. The infant tilts towards the shortened sternocleidomastoid and rotates the chin away from it, and a fibrous mass in the muscle belly is palpable in a substantial minority. Deformational plagiocephaly follows because the infant always rests on the same part of the occiput, and it corrects as the neck range is restored rather than requiring separate treatment. The differential that must be excluded clinically is ocular torticollis, posterior fossa or cord pathology, and atlantoaxial abnormality, all of which spare the passive range or add neurological signs. Referral delayed beyond twelve months substantially raises the proportion who go on to need surgical release.
key_points: Tilt is towards the tight muscle and chin rotation is away from it.
A mechanically restricted passive rotation distinguishes muscular from ocular causes.
Plagiocephaly here is secondary and remodels once the neck range is restored.
Abnormal tone, abnormal eye movements or a growing mass change the pathway to imaging.
explanation.pearls: Physiotherapy started before six months of age resolves congenital muscular torticollis in over 90 per cent of infants, while referral after twelve months raises the surgical release rate several-fold, so the referral is made at the visit the tilt is noticed rather than at the next one.

options.rationale: Ocular torticollis is distinguished by a full passive range of neck movement with no palpable muscle mass, the tilt being adopted voluntarily to fuse images. Here the range is mechanically restricted and the eye examination is normal, which points to the muscle rather than the eye. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

A restricted passive rotation with a palpable sternocleidomastoid mass in an otherwise normal infant is muscular in origin, and supervised stretching with positioning and tummy time is the treatment. Started before six months it resolves the great majority and the head shape remodels as the tilt corrects. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

The mass of muscular torticollis is a fibrotic segment of the sternocleidomastoid itself, firm, painless, non-growing and confined to the muscle belly. A mass that is growing, tender, outside the muscle, or accompanied by systemic symptoms would warrant imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Helmet therapy addresses the deformational head shape but not the muscle restriction that is causing it, so the tilt recurs and the flattening returns. Positional plagiocephaly secondary to torticollis is treated by treating the torticollis first. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Plagiocephaly)

Neuroimaging is indicated when the tilt is accompanied by abnormal tone, developmental regression, a bulging fontanelle or abnormal eye movements, none of which are present. A normal neurological examination with a palpable muscle mass makes a posterior fossa or cord lesion very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Nasal foreign bodies are common between the ages of one and five, and because the insertion is frequently unwitnessed or denied the presentation is usually the secondary infection rather than the event. The cardinal sign is unilateral foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge, sometimes with epistaxis or nasal obstruction, and the strict unilaterality is what distinguishes it from rhinitis and sinusitis, which in a young child are bilateral. Removal at the bedside is attempted with a nasal speculum and good illumination using the positive pressure technique, in which the carer blows into the mouth while occluding the unaffected nostril, or with forceps for a graspable object or a curved hook passed behind a smooth one. Blind instrumentation, probing without a clear view and repeated failed attempts all risk pushing the object posteriorly, where it can be aspirated, so two attempts is a reasonable limit before referral. Button batteries and paired magnets are the exceptions that convert this into an emergency, since a battery causes liquefactive necrosis and septal perforation within hours and magnets in opposite nostrils trap and necrose the septum between them.
key_points: Unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a young child means a foreign body until excluded.
Rhinitis and paediatric sinusitis are bilateral, which is the discriminating feature.
Removal needs a speculum and good light; blind probing risks posterior displacement and aspiration.
Antibiotics cannot clear an infection sustained by a retained object.
explanation.pearls: A button battery in the nose causes liquefactive necrosis and septal perforation within hours, so a disc-shaped shiny object or a history of missing hearing aid batteries means immediate ear nose and throat referral for removal rather than a routine outpatient appointment.

options.rationale: Saline is a reasonable adjunct for viral or allergic rhinitis and has already been tried without effect. Strict unilaterality is what separates a mechanical cause from an inflammatory one, and a month of irrigation delays removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

Topical corticosteroid treats allergic rhinitis, which is bilateral, produces clear rather than offensive discharge and is accompanied by sneezing and itch. It will not shift an obstructing object and another four weeks risks pressure necrosis of the septum. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

Unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a young child is a retained foreign body until proven otherwise, and the secondary infection resolves once the object is out. Direct inspection with a speculum and good light both confirms the diagnosis and permits removal at the same visit. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

Antibiotics may briefly reduce the smell but cannot clear an infection that is being sustained by a retained object, which is why the previous course failed. Bacterial sinusitis would also be bilateral in a child of this age and accompanied by fever or facial tenderness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Sinus imaging carries radiation to the developing orbit and lens and is reserved for suspected complications of sinusitis such as orbital or intracranial spread. Most nasal foreign bodies are radiolucent, so a scan can be negative even when an object is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

explanation.summary: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis appears in the first weeks to months of life and is thought to reflect maternal androgen-driven sebum production together with Malassezia colonisation. It is distinguished from atopic dermatitis by the greasy rather than dry scale, the flexural and scalp distribution, and above all by the absence of itch in a settled infant, since atopic dermatitis makes babies miserable and they scratch. It is self-limiting, usually resolving within weeks to a few months, and carries no implication for later atopy. Treatment escalates only if simple measures fail, with hydrocortisone 1 per cent for residual inflammation and a topical antifungal for extensive or recurrent disease. Secondary bacterial or candidal infection is the reason management changes, so parents are told what weeping and golden crusting look like.
key_points: Greasy scale in a settled non-itchy infant separates this from atopic dermatitis.
Scalp vertex and flexural folds are the typical sites and the course is self-limiting.
Emollient softening with gentle mechanical removal is the first-line measure.
Satellite pustules beyond the rash margin indicate candida and change treatment.
explanation.pearls: Itch separates them: infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis leaves the baby comfortable, so a six-week-old who is scratching, waking and rubbing has atopic dermatitis until proven otherwise, whatever the scale looks like.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are for secondary bacterial infection, signalled by golden crusting, weeping, surrounding cellulitis or a systemically unwell infant, none of which are present. Uncomplicated scale carries no indication for a swab. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

Maternal dietary exclusion is considered in proven cow's milk protein allergy, which presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, blood in the stool or poor weight gain rather than with isolated scalp scale in a thriving baby. Unnecessary exclusion risks maternal nutritional deficit. (Source: RACGP: Common infant skin conditions)

Topical antifungal has a place in extensive or persistent disease and in candidal nappy rash, but it is second line to emollient and descaling for uncomplicated scalp involvement. Candidal nappy rash is distinguished by satellite pustules beyond the margin of the main rash, which are absent. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

Greasy adherent scale over the vertex and flexural folds in a thriving infant who is not itchy is infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis, and softening the scale with an emollient before gentle mechanical removal is the first-line treatment. It is self-limiting and usually clears over weeks to a few months. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

A moderately potent steroid is disproportionate for scale on infant scalp skin and is the treatment for inflamed itchy eczema rather than for greasy adherent scale. A brief course of hydrocortisone 1 per cent is reasonable only if erythema persists once the scale has been cleared. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pain, still widely called growing pains, affects up to a third of primary school-aged children and is a clinical diagnosis made on pattern rather than on tests. The defining features are pain that is bilateral, muscular rather than articular, confined to the evening or night, and completely absent by morning in a child whose growth, examination and activity are normal. The conditions that must not be missed all break that pattern in a specific way, with leukaemia producing bone pain, bruising, pallor or organomegaly, osteoid osteoma producing focal unilateral night pain, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis producing morning stiffness with joint signs. Because the diagnosis rests on the absence of red flags rather than on a normal test, safety-netting and planned review carry the clinical weight. A child whose pain migrates into the day, becomes unilateral, or is accompanied by a limp is re-examined and investigated.
key_points: Bilateral, muscular, evening or night pain with a completely normal morning is the pattern.
A limp, unilateral pain, fever, weight loss, bruising or organomegaly are the red flags.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes morning stiffness, the reverse of this timing.
No investigation is required when the pattern is typical and the examination is normal.
explanation.pearls: Pain that wakes a child from sleep is not by itself alarming in benign limb pain, but pain that persists into the following morning or produces a limp has left the benign pattern and warrants a full blood count, film and radiograph of the symptomatic site.

options.rationale: Radiographs are for focal bony tenderness, a limp, or pain that wakes a child and does not settle, since an osteoid osteoma or a malignant bone lesion is focal and unilateral. Bilateral muscular pain with a normal examination does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is distinguished by joint rather than muscle pain, morning stiffness that eases through the day, and objective joint swelling or restriction. The pattern here is the mirror image, with evening pain and a normal morning. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

Regular scheduled anti-inflammatory for six weeks medicalises a self-limiting condition and exposes the child to gastric and renal risk for episodic pain that responds to rubbing. Simple analgesia as needed is all that is warranted. (Source: RACGP: Growing pains in children)

Blood tests are indicated when a red flag is present, such as a limp, unilateral or persistent daytime pain, fever, weight loss, bruising or organomegaly. Investigating a textbook benign pattern generates incidental abnormalities and prolongs parental anxiety rather than resolving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

Bilateral pain confined to the evening or night, in the muscles rather than the joints, in a thriving child who is entirely well and running normally by day, is benign nocturnal limb pain and needs no investigation. Explanation, massage, heat and simple analgesia with planned review is the complete management. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

explanation.summary: Lower limb alignment follows a predictable developmental arc, with physiological varus maximal at around 18 months, a neutral axis at about two years, physiological valgus peaking near three to four years, and adult alignment reached by about seven. Parents and grandparents commonly present a toddler at the varus peak, so recognising the normal trajectory prevents a cascade of imaging and referral. The findings that take a child off the physiological pathway are asymmetry, progression after age two, sharp angulation at the proximal tibia, pain, a lateral thrust at the knee during stance, and short stature. Blount disease and nutritional rickets are the two diagnoses that account for most pathological varus, and each is suggested clinically before any test is ordered. Measuring and recording the intercondylar distance converts a subjective impression into a number that can be compared at the next visit.
key_points: Physiological varus peaks near 18 months and neutralises by about two years.
Symmetry, normal stature and a painless gait define the physiological pattern.
Asymmetry, progression after age two, or a lateral knee thrust suggests Blount disease.
Short stature with wrist or costochondral widening points instead to rickets.
explanation.pearls: Record the intercondylar distance in centimetres with the medial malleoli touching: a physiological varus shrinks at the six month review, whereas a measurement that is unchanged or larger after the second birthday is the trigger for standing alignment radiographs.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Symmetrical genu varum centred at the knees in a child of normal stature who walks without pain is the physiological pattern, which peaks around 18 months and corrects spontaneously. Documenting the intercondylar distance gives an objective measure to compare against at review. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Alignment films are reserved for bowing that is asymmetrical, progressive after the age of two, sharply angulated, painful, or accompanied by short stature. None of those applies, and radiographing physiological varus exposes a toddler to radiation for a normal result. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Nutritional rickets is suggested by short stature or faltering growth, wrist and costochondral widening, delayed dentition or a restricted diet with little sun exposure. A child on the 50th centile with normal wrists and a varied diet does not warrant the panel. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Bracing has no role in physiological varus, which corrects without intervention, and orthopaedic referral is reserved for the patterns that do not correct. Offering a brace treats the grandmother's concern rather than the child's leg. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: A skeletal dysplasia declares itself with short stature, disproportion between limb and trunk length, or a family history, and normal centile tracking argues strongly against one. A skeletal survey is a substantial radiation exposure that this presentation does not justify. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Subgaleal haemorrhage is bleeding into the loose areolar plane between the epicranial aponeurosis and the periosteum, a potential space that extends from the orbital ridges to the nape of the neck and can accommodate the whole neonatal blood volume. It complicates roughly 4 per 10000 spontaneous births and rises sharply with vacuum extraction, particularly after multiple pulls or a failed attempt followed by forceps. The bedside distinction from the two benign mimics is anatomical, since caput succedaneum is superficial and pits while cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal and therefore stops at the suture lines, whereas subgaleal blood crosses them and shifts with gravity. Each centimetre of head circumference increase corresponds to roughly 38 mL of blood, so serial measurement is the monitoring tool while volume replacement is the treatment. Mortality approaches one in five once shock develops, which is why any infant delivered by vacuum has scalp and observation checks scheduled rather than left to chance.
key_points: Blood crossing the suture lines and shifting with position distinguishes it from cephalhaematoma.
Vacuum extraction, particularly multiple pulls or sequential instruments, is the main risk factor.
Tachycardia, pallor and a rising head circumference indicate ongoing loss into the scalp.
Treatment is volume resuscitation and transfusion in a neonatal unit, not imaging first.
explanation.pearls: Each 1 cm rise in head circumference in a subgaleal haemorrhage represents roughly 38 mL of blood, which in a 3.5 kg newborn is about 13 per cent of the circulating volume, so a 2 cm increase over a few hours is a haemorrhagic emergency however well the baby looked at birth.

options.rationale: Serial head circumference is the right monitoring tool but it is not a treatment, and this infant has already declared himself with tachycardia, hypotension, pallor and a falling haemoglobin. Observation on a postnatal ward without venous access is how these babies exsanguinate into the scalp. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

A swelling that crosses suture lines and shifts with position in a shocked infant after instrumental delivery is bleeding into the subaponeurotic space, which can hold the entire circulating volume. Immediate transfer with volume replacement and early red cell transfusion, alongside correction of coagulopathy, is the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

This is a clinical diagnosis made at the cot side, and taking a shocked neonate to a scanner before restoring circulating volume delays the only intervention that changes the outcome. Imaging has a place later for a suspected coexisting intracranial bleed or skull fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

Vitamin K should certainly be confirmed as given and a coagulopathy corrected, but neither addresses the acute hypovolaemia and neither works fast enough to matter in the next fifteen minutes. This is an adjunct to resuscitation, not a substitute for it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

Head wrapping does not tamponade the subaponeurotic space, which communicates widely from orbit to nape, and a tight bandage obscures the serial head circumference that is being used to track ongoing bleeding. It substitutes a mechanical gesture for circulatory support. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal resuscitation)

explanation.summary: Most red umbilical lesions after cord separation are granulomas, which are soft, dull pink, friable, blanching masses of granulation tissue that respond to desiccation with salt or to silver nitrate cautery. An umbilical polyp is the important mimic and it is a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct or urachus lined by heterotopic intestinal or bladder mucosa, which is why it appears bright red, firm, glistening and mucosal and why it is entirely unresponsive to chemical treatment. The practical rule is that failure of adequate topical therapy reclassifies the lesion rather than earning another course. Excision is required both to remove the polyp and to exclude a deeper patent tract to the ileum or bladder, which can present later with faecal or urinary discharge, infection or volvulus around a persistent band. Histology of the excised specimen confirms the mucosal lining and directs any further imaging.
key_points: Granuloma is soft, dull pink and blanching; polyp is firm, bright red and mucosal.
Failure of salt or silver nitrate reclassifies the lesion rather than warranting repeat treatment.
A polyp is a vitellointestinal or urachal duct remnant and requires surgical excision.
A persistent deep tract can later cause discharge, infection or volvulus around a band.
explanation.pearls: Two failed treatments is the decision point: an umbilical lesion that has not shrunk after an adequate course of salt and one silver nitrate application is referred for excision rather than treated a third time, because a polyp has no granulation tissue for either agent to act on.

options.rationale: Salt desiccates the friable granulation tissue of an umbilical granuloma, which is dull pink, soft and blanching, and a lesion that has already failed salt is by definition not behaving like one. Repeating a treatment that has twice failed delays the diagnosis rather than testing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

Silver nitrate works on granulation tissue and does nothing to epithelialised intestinal or urothelial mucosa, and repeated application risks chemical burns to the surrounding abdominal skin. Two failed treatments are the signal to reconsider the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

A firm bright red non-blanching lesion with a mucosal appearance that has resisted both salt and silver nitrate is an umbilical polyp, a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric or urachal duct lined by intestinal or urothelial mucosa. It requires surgical excision with histology and assessment for a deeper persistent tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, induration, tenderness and a systemically unwell infant, and it is a paediatric emergency in the neonatal period rather than a five week outpatient problem. The skin around this lesion is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Omphalitis)

Ultrasound is a reasonable adjunct where a urachal sinus is suspected, particularly with urinary leakage, but it does not distinguish granuloma from polyp at the surface and it does not remove the lesion. Imaging is arranged by the surgical team alongside excision rather than instead of referral. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Umbilical anomalies)

explanation.summary: Pectus excavatum is common and usually isolated, but it is also a systemic feature in the revised Ghent criteria for Marfan syndrome, so its presence obliges a look for the other systemic features rather than a straight referral for repair. The systemic score counts findings such as wrist and thumb signs, reduced upper to lower segment ratio with increased arm span to height ratio, scoliosis, pes planus, a high arched palate and characteristic facial features. Aortic root dilatation at the sinuses of Valsalva is the feature that determines prognosis, since dissection and rupture account for most premature deaths, and it is measured by echocardiography and indexed as a Z score for body surface area. An early diastolic murmur in this setting represents aortic regurgitation from a dilated root and moves the assessment from elective to prompt. Management once confirmed includes beta blockade or an angiotensin receptor blocker, serial imaging, avoidance of isometric and contact sport, and family screening, all of which are unavailable until the echocardiogram is done.
key_points: Pectus excavatum is a systemic feature of Marfan syndrome, not only a cosmetic issue.
Arm span to height ratio, thumb and wrist signs and palate shape build the systemic score.
An early diastolic murmur suggests aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Echocardiography with a body surface area indexed root Z score drives all further management.
explanation.pearls: An aortic root Z score of 2 or more at the sinuses of Valsalva satisfies the aortic criterion in the revised Ghent nosology, and a root diameter approaching 45 mm in an adolescent with Marfan syndrome is the usual threshold for referral to consider prophylactic root replacement.

options.rationale: Waiting is reasonable for an isolated chest wall depression in an otherwise unremarkable adolescent, but it is not reasonable when a diastolic murmur and a family history of unexplained sudden death in a young adult are present. Aortic root dilatation progresses silently during exactly the growth phase he is in. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

The Haller index is derived from cross-sectional imaging rather than a plain film and it grades the severity of the chest wall deformity only. It measures the cosmetic problem rather than the lethal one. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pectus excavatum)

A chest wall repair addresses the deformity the boy has asked about while leaving the systemic condition it is a marker of entirely unassessed. Surgical planning in a connective tissue disorder also requires the aortic dimensions to be known beforehand. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

Tall stature with disproportionate arm span, positive thumb and wrist signs, a high arched palate, chest wall deformity and an early diastolic murmur point to a heritable connective tissue disorder, and the murmur suggests aortic regurgitation from root dilatation. Echocardiography with root measurement indexed to body surface area is the investigation that determines both diagnosis and immediate risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

Lung function quantifies the restriction some deep chest wall deformities cause and is used when surgery is being planned for functional reasons, but it does not assess the aorta. A boy who swims twice a week without breathlessness is unlikely to have physiology that changes management. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pectus excavatum)

explanation.summary: Indirect inguinal hernia in infancy results from a patent processus vaginalis and carries a far higher incarceration risk than in adults, concentrated in the first year and highest in ex-premature infants, which is why repair is arranged promptly rather than deferred. At the bedside, a hernia has no palpable upper border because it extends through the external ring into the abdomen, while a hydrocele transilluminates, has an upper border and does not obstruct, and a torted testis presents with an abnormal tender testis rather than a separate groin mass. Incarceration announces itself with irreducibility, pain, and then bilious vomiting and distension as bowel obstruction develops. Adequate opioid analgesia and sedation allow gentle sustained taxis to succeed in most cases, after which repair proceeds on the same admission once oedema settles, typically within 24 to 48 hours. Failed reduction, peritonism or systemic compromise means immediate operation, and the ipsilateral testis is at risk throughout because the cord structures are compressed at the external ring.
key_points: Inability to define an upper border distinguishes a hernia from a hydrocele or testicular problem.
Prematurity markedly increases the risk of incarceration in the first year of life.
Analgesia with gentle sustained taxis reduces most incarcerated infant hernias.
Repair follows on the same admission, and failed reduction means immediate operation.
