explanation.pearls: In an incarcerated infant inguinal hernia the ipsilateral testis is at risk from cord compression as well as the bowel, so the operation note and the discharge examination both record testicular size, and a testis that is smaller at six week review prompts surgical re-referral.

options.rationale: Elective repair is what should have happened when the reducible lump was first noticed, and it is the correct pathway for a hernia that reduces easily. Once incarceration with obstruction has occurred the timeframe is hours, not weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

Antibiotics are given as part of preparation for theatre when strangulation is suspected, but they are an adjunct and do not relieve the obstruction. An infected or necrotic segment that had already perforated would show peritonism, fever and shock rather than this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Delay is the single most dangerous choice here because incarcerated bowel becomes ischaemic within hours and the testicular vessels sharing the inguinal canal are compressed at the same time. Bilious vomiting with a distended abdomen indicates obstruction that is already established. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

Ultrasound is the right test when the diagnosis is in doubt between a hydrocele, a torted testis and a hernia, but here both testes are normal and separately palpable and there is no upper border to the swelling. Waiting for imaging in an obstructed infant costs the bowel time it does not have. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

An irreducible groin swelling with no upper border, bilious vomiting and abdominal distension in an ex-premature infant is an incarcerated inguinal hernia, and adequate analgesia with gentle sustained taxis succeeds in the majority. Surgical involvement is contemporaneous because failure of reduction mandates immediate operation and successful reduction still requires repair on the same admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

explanation.summary: In-toeing in a toddler is usually one of three benign rotational variants, namely metatarsus adductus in infancy, internal tibial torsion in the second year and increased femoral anteversion from around three years, all of which are symmetrical, painless and self-correcting. The clinical value of a rotational profile is that it localises the level of the problem, with the lateral foot border assessing the forefoot, the thigh-foot axis assessing the tibia, and hip rotation assessing the femur. A unilateral pattern is the finding that takes a child off that pathway, because a dysplastic hip produces compensatory femoral internal rotation along with a Trendelenburg gait, reduced abduction in flexion and apparent femoral shortening. Late-presenting developmental dysplasia is missed by newborn examination and neonatal ultrasound in a meaningful minority, and it presents exactly like this once walking is established. Treatment after walking age generally requires closed or open reduction with femoral or pelvic osteotomy rather than a harness, and outcomes deteriorate with every year of delay.
key_points: Benign rotational variants are symmetrical, painless and leave hip examination normal.
Unilateral in-toeing with a Trendelenburg gait points to the hip, not the foot or tibia.
Restricted abduction in flexion plus a positive Galeazzi sign is dysplasia until excluded.
Ultrasound is accurate only before the femoral ossific nucleus appears; then use radiography.
explanation.pearls: Hip ultrasound loses accuracy once the femoral ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months, so a walking child with suspected developmental dysplasia is imaged with an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph rather than the ultrasound used in the newborn period.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Unilateral in-toeing with a painless Trendelenburg gait, restricted abduction in flexion and a positive Galeazzi sign is late-presenting developmental dysplasia, in which the femur internally rotates to keep the head in a shallow acetabulum. After the femoral head has ossified a plain pelvic radiograph is the diagnostic test. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Derotation devices and twister cables have no evidence of benefit even for the benign rotational variants they were designed for, and they treat the visible foot position rather than the hip driving it. Bracing an undiagnosed dysplastic hip wastes a year of growth. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

Orthotics address the foot and would be considered for a metatarsus adductus, which is excluded here by the normal lateral foot border. They cannot influence acetabular development and the referral delays the radiograph. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

Ultrasound is the imaging of choice for developmental dysplasia but only while the femoral head is still cartilaginous, conventionally under about four to six months of age. After the ossific nucleus appears, the head casts an acoustic shadow and a plain radiograph becomes the accurate study. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Benign rotational variants are symmetrical, involve no limp and leave hip abduction and leg length untouched, whereas this child has unilateral findings with restricted abduction and apparent shortening. Reassurance here would allow a treatable hip to deteriorate through the years when treatment works best. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

explanation.summary: Acute mastoiditis is the commonest suppurative complication of acute otitis media and follows spread of infection from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells, which communicate with it directly through the aditus ad antrum. Incidence has fallen in the antibiotic era but the diagnosis persists and is now often seen in children who have been on oral therapy, so recent antibiotic treatment is no reassurance at all. The clinical triad is postauricular erythema, tenderness and swelling with loss of the postauricular crease, protrusion of the pinna inferiorly and laterally, and signs of middle ear infection such as a bulging drum or sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus are the usual organisms, and treatment is intravenous antibiotics with otolaryngology involvement, proceeding to myringotomy with or without grommet insertion, or cortical mastoidectomy, where there is a subperiosteal abscess or failure to improve. The complications that make this a same-day problem are facial nerve palsy, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, subperiosteal or Bezold abscess, labyrinthitis, meningitis and intracranial abscess, so any new focal neurological sign, altered conscious state or neck stiffness prompts urgent contrast imaging.
key_points: Loss of the postauricular crease with a displaced pinna is the defining physical sign.
Recent or current oral antibiotic treatment does not exclude the diagnosis.
Otitis externa spares the middle ear and does not displace the pinna.
Facial palsy, neck stiffness or altered conscious state signal intracranial extension.
explanation.pearls: Compare the two ears from behind and above with the child sitting up: the loss of the postauricular crease and the forward and downward displacement of the pinna are far more obvious from that angle than from the front, and they are what separate mastoiditis from simple postauricular lymphadenitis.

options.rationale: Swapping one oral agent for another concedes that the first has failed while leaving the child on a route that cannot achieve adequate concentrations in infected bone. Cefalexin also has poorer activity against the pneumococcus and Streptococcus pyogenes that predominate here. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

Postauricular swelling with loss of the crease and a displaced pinna in a febrile child with a bulging drum is acute mastoiditis, a suppurative complication of otitis media involving the mastoid air cells. Admission for high dose intravenous antibiotics with same-day otolaryngology involvement for possible myringotomy or cortical mastoidectomy is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

Topical quinolone drops treat otitis externa and discharging grommets, and otitis externa can mimic this because it also causes canal changes and postauricular tenderness. The distinction is that otitis externa spares the middle ear, gives pain on tragal pressure with a normal drum, and does not displace the pinna or obliterate the postauricular crease. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

Imaging has a definite role in suspected intracranial extension, subperiosteal abscess or a poor response to treatment, but this is a clinical diagnosis and an outpatient appointment introduces a delay of days. Antibiotics are started first and imaging arranged from the ward if needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

Needle aspiration of a postauricular collection without imaging or surgical support risks injuring the facial nerve and the sigmoid sinus, both of which lie in the operative field. Drainage, where required, is a theatre procedure performed by an otolaryngologist. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

explanation.summary: The toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft caused by a low energy twisting force in a newly ambulant child, typically between nine months and three years. Because the periosteum is thick and the fracture line is often hairline and oblique, initial radiographs miss a large proportion of cases and the diagnosis is made clinically. The differential that matters is infection, so the afebrile, systemically well child with a clear mechanism can be immobilised and reviewed rather than investigated further. Persistent refusal to weight bear at review, fever, or a rising inflammatory response should redirect towards osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. Non-accidental injury deserves consideration when the child is not yet walking independently, because the mechanism requires an ambulant child.
key_points: Low energy torsional mechanism in a newly walking child with refusal to weight bear.
Pain reproduced by rotating the foot against the shin, with no focal bony tenderness.
Up to half of initial radiographs are normal; a normal film does not exclude it.
Immobilise and review clinically; reserve advanced imaging for atypical or persistent cases.
A spiral tibial fracture in a child who cannot yet walk should raise safeguarding concern.
explanation.pearls: Healing periosteal new bone appears on radiographs at about 10 to 14 days, so a repeat film a fortnight later confirms the diagnosis retrospectively if it is ever needed, which is why the plaster goes on before the imaging is conclusive.

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance would show the fracture line, but it needs sedation at this age and does not change a management plan that is immobilisation either way. It is reserved for the child whose symptoms persist despite immobilisation or whose picture suggests infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

Hip ultrasound is the move when the hip is the painful joint, but this boy moves both hips through full range without complaint and localises to tibial torsion. Transient synovitis restricts internal rotation of the hip and does not reproduce pain on rotating the foot against the shin. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Analgesia alone is reasonable when the examination is genuinely normal, but reproducible pain on tibial torsion is a positive finding and unprotected weight bearing on an occult spiral fracture prolongs the limp. A normal first radiograph does not exclude the injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

A well child with a torsional mechanism, pain on tibial rotation and no bony tenderness elsewhere has an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture until proven otherwise, and this pattern is invisible on up to half of first films. Immobilisation with clinical review, rather than repeat imaging, is the management whether or not a fracture is later confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

A septic workup belongs to the febrile or systemically unwell limping child, and this boy is afebrile, feeding normally and settles the moment the leg is left alone. Treating him as infected commits him to a cannula and admission for a mechanical injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to one in five infants and arises from a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner at the distal end of the duct. It presents with epiphora and mattering from the first weeks of life, with a white conjunctiva between episodes, and mucoid material that can be expressed from the sac. Two conditions must be excluded before reassurance: infantile glaucoma, which adds photophobia, corneal clouding and enlargement, and acute dacryocystitis, which makes the sac red, tense and tender. Spontaneous resolution occurs in about 90 per cent by twelve months, so probing is deferred until then in the uncomplicated child. Persistent obstruction beyond a year, or recurrent infection of the sac, warrants ophthalmology referral for probing with or without intubation.
key_points: Watering from the first weeks of life with a quiet white conjunctiva suggests duct obstruction.
Expressible mucoid reflux at the punctum supports the diagnosis.
Exclude infantile glaucoma: photophobia, corneal clouding, enlarged corneal diameter.
About 90 per cent resolve by twelve months; massage and hygiene in the interim.
Refer earlier for recurrent dacryocystitis or if signs of glaucoma appear.
explanation.pearls: Crigler massage works by raising hydrostatic pressure in the sac: press firmly over the sac just medial to the inner canthus and stroke downward towards the nose about ten times, twice daily, rather than rubbing the eyelid itself.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are for acute dacryocystitis, in which the sac becomes red, tense and tender with surrounding cellulitis and the infant is often febrile. Expressible mucoid material from a soft non-tender sac is not infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Same day review is for infantile glaucoma, which also waters but adds photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and an enlarged corneal diameter. Clear corneas of equal size and a comfortable child make it very unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

Epiphora from birth with mucoid reflux, a quiet conjunctiva and a normal red reflex is congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and around 90 per cent resolve spontaneously during the first year. Massage and lid hygiene with planned review is the correct conservative course. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

Probing is the correct step, but the timing is wrong: intervention before twelve months treats obstructions that would have resolved on their own and adds an anaesthetic. Probing is reserved for persistence beyond a year or for recurrent dacryocystitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

Topical antibiotic treats bacterial conjunctivitis, which injects the conjunctiva and does not persist for months against a white quiet eye. Repeated courses explain the transient improvement without addressing an anatomical blockage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Clavicular fracture is the commonest fracture of birth, occurring in around one to two per cent of vaginal deliveries and far more often when the birth weight exceeds 4000 g or shoulder dystocia occurs. The critical examination task is to separate the bony injury from an accompanying brachial plexus palsy, because the two often coexist and the management differs entirely. Preserved palmar grasp with spontaneous elbow and wrist movement against an asymmetrical Moro points to pain-limited movement rather than denervation. Uncomplicated clavicular fractures need no imaging, no immobilisation and no orthopaedic follow-up, and parents should be warned that a palpable lump of callus will appear within a week or two. Any baby with a genuine plexus lesion needs early referral because the window for surgical assessment is measured in months.
key_points: Macrosomia and shoulder dystocia are the dominant risk factors.
Grip and distal movement distinguish a painful clavicle from a plexus palsy.
No immobilisation, no imaging and no orthopaedic follow-up are needed.
Warn parents about the callus lump appearing at one to two weeks.
Refer early if grip is absent or the arm is held adducted and internally rotated.
explanation.pearls: An asymmetrical Moro reflex on its own does not distinguish fracture from plexus injury, because pain inhibits the reflex; it is the palmar grasp, which is spared in Erb palsy and absent in Klumpke palsy, that tells you which nerve roots are involved.

options.rationale: Strapping the limb is an adult and older child strategy and offers nothing in a neonate whose clavicle remodels completely within weeks. It also restricts the arm movement that keeps the shoulder supple. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

A mid clavicular fracture after shoulder dystocia with an intact palmar grasp and preserved elbow and wrist movement is a bony injury alone, and these unite rapidly without any intervention. Analgesia and careful handling are all that is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

A skeletal survey investigates unexplained fractures, and this one has a documented obstetric mechanism in a macrosomic baby delivered with shoulder dystocia. Escalating to safeguarding for an explained birth injury exposes the family to unwarranted investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Ultrasound is useful when the shoulder itself is swollen and the humeral epiphysis may have separated, which produces a pseudoparalysis with swelling and no palpable clavicular step. The palpable crepitus over the collarbone already localises the injury. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Birth injuries)

Urgent plexus referral belongs to the baby with a true palsy. Obstetric brachial plexus injury abolishes the palmar grasp in lower root lesions or holds the arm adducted and internally rotated in upper root lesions, whereas this baby grips and moves the elbow and wrist. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

explanation.summary: Most paediatric rhinosinusitis is viral and resolves within ten days, so the diagnostic problem is deciding which child has a bacterial infection worth treating. Three patterns justify antibiotics: persistent symptoms beyond ten days without improvement, severe symptoms with fever above 39 degrees and purulent discharge for three or more consecutive days, or double sickening in which a clearly improving illness worsens again. Australian guidance makes amoxicillin the first line, with amoxicillin and clavulanate reserved for treatment failure or recent antibiotic exposure. The complications that drive urgent referral are orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess and intracranial extension, so eye signs and neurological status must be documented at every assessment. Failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours of starting antibiotics should prompt reassessment rather than a simple repeat script.
key_points: Double sickening after day five is a recognised trigger for antibiotic treatment.
Amoxicillin is first line in Australia; escalate only for failure or recent antibiotic use.
Imaging is for suspected complications or surgical planning, not for diagnosis.
Document eye movements, proptosis and visual acuity to exclude orbital spread.
Reassess rather than repeat the script if there is no response by 72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Orbital cellulitis in a child almost always originates from the ethmoid sinuses through the thin lamina papyracea, so painful or restricted eye movement in a child with sinusitis is a surgical emergency rather than a reason to change oral antibiotic.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Saline and analgesia alone are correct for the uncomplicated viral illness that is steadily improving, or for symptoms under ten days without double sickening. A documented second deterioration with fever changes the probability enough to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Intranasal corticosteroid is an adjunct in chronic and allergic rhinosinusitis rather than a treatment for an acute bacterial episode, and oral decongestants are not recommended in this age group. Neither addresses the bacterial infection. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Double sickening, a clear improvement then deterioration after day five with fever and purulent discharge, is the pattern that identifies acute bacterial sinusitis rather than a prolonged viral illness. Amoxicillin is the first line agent in Australia and review at 48 to 72 hours catches non-response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Intravenous therapy and urgent specialist review are the correct response to orbital or intracranial extension, the complication to fear. Full painless eye movements with no periorbital swelling or proptosis exclude that here. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Sinus imaging is reserved for suspected complications or for surgical planning in recurrent disease, because mucosal thickening is common in well children and does not confirm infection. It would add radiation without changing this plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Paediatric trigger thumb is a mechanical mismatch between a nodular thickening of the flexor pollicis longus tendon, called Notta's node, and the A1 pulley at the base of the thumb. Unlike adult trigger finger it is not an inflammatory condition and is only rarely associated with systemic disease, so it presents painlessly and is usually noticed by a parent rather than the child. Most children present with the thumb already fixed in flexion because the earlier intermittent triggering phase passes unnoticed. Spontaneous resolution is reported in a proportion of cases, particularly under one year of age and when the thumb still extends passively, which is why observation is reasonable early and surgery is preferred once the contracture is fixed. Release of the A1 pulley is a short day procedure with a high success rate and low recurrence.
key_points: Painless fixed flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint in a toddler.
A firm nodule gliding with the flexor tendon at the metacarpophalangeal level.
It is mechanical rather than inflammatory, so corticosteroid injection is not used.
Observation suits the young infant or the passively correctable thumb.
Refer for A1 pulley release once the deformity is fixed.
explanation.pearls: The nodule of paediatric trigger thumb sits at the metacarpophalangeal level rather than at the joint that is bent, so palpating the base of the thumb while passively flexing and extending the tip is what confirms the diagnosis without any imaging.

options.rationale: Sheath injection is an adult treatment for trigger digit and is not used in young children, in whom the pathology is a size mismatch between a thickened tendon and the pulley rather than inflammation. It also requires sedation at this age. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Trigger finger)

A fixed flexion deformity at the thumb interphalangeal joint with a palpable nodule over the flexor tendon is paediatric trigger thumb, and a contracture that has been fixed for weeks is unlikely to resolve without surgical release of the A1 pulley. Referral avoids a permanent deformity. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

Spontaneous resolution does occur, but rates fall sharply once the deformity is fixed rather than intermittently triggering, and this one has been fixed for six weeks. Waiting a further year risks a stiff joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

Splinting and stretching have a role in the intermittently triggering thumb that still extends passively, but they do not reliably correct an established fixed contracture. Six months of therapy delays a definitive procedure without changing the outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

This workup targets juvenile idiopathic arthritis, which can also present with a digit held flexed. Arthritis produces a swollen warm tender joint with morning stiffness rather than a painless nodule that glides with the flexor tendon. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Reflex anoxic seizure, sometimes called a pallid breath holding attack, is a vagally mediated asystolic pause of several seconds triggered by pain, surprise or a minor knock in a young child. The child goes pale first, loses consciousness, and only then develops tonic stiffening or a few clonic jerks, which distinguishes the sequence from a primary generalised seizure where the convulsion comes first and colour change follows. Recovery is rapid with a short period of floppiness rather than the prolonged drowsiness of a true postictal state. The essential investigation is an electrocardiogram, because long QT syndrome and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia can present identically after a fright and carry a risk of sudden death. Iron deficiency is a common associated factor and treatment reduces attack frequency, so ferritin is worth checking once the cardiac assessment is clear.
key_points: Trigger then pallor then collapse then convulsion is the reflex anoxic sequence.
A primary seizure convulses first and changes colour afterwards.
Recovery is within minutes without a prolonged postictal phase.
An electrocardiogram with the corrected QT interval is mandatory in every case.
Treat coexisting iron deficiency, which reduces attack frequency.
explanation.pearls: Ask the witness which came first, the colour change or the jerking, because pallor preceding the convulsion points to a circulatory cause while a convulsion preceding the colour change points to epilepsy, and that single question separates them more reliably than any description of the movements.

options.rationale: Head imaging is driven by the severity of the head injury and by focal neurological signs, and a light knock in a child who is now alert and neurologically normal meets no imaging criterion. The bump was the trigger, not the cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury)

Electroencephalography addresses epilepsy, but the sequence here starts with a trigger and pallor and ends with rapid recovery, which is circulatory rather than epileptic. An incidental abnormality on the trace risks anticonvulsants for a benign condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

The pallor preceding collapse and the trivial provoking stimulus identify this as a reflex anoxic seizure, in which the convulsive movements are secondary to cerebral hypoperfusion. The one condition that mimics it and kills is a long QT syndrome, so an electrocardiogram is the single essential test. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

Iron deficiency is genuinely associated with these episodes and treating it reduces their frequency, so this is a reasonable adjunct. It is not the priority investigation because it cannot exclude the arrhythmic mimic that would be fatal to miss. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding attacks)

Metabolic testing helps when recovery is prolonged or the child is unwell between episodes, neither of which applies to a toddler back to baseline in five minutes. A normal result would not change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is the commonest symptomatic first infection with herpes simplex virus type one and peaks between six months and five years. The feature that separates it from hand, foot and mouth disease is the gingivitis: red, swollen gums that bleed on contact, with ulcers extending onto the anterior tongue, buccal mucosa and hard palate, and no peripheral rash. The illness is self-limiting over ten to fourteen days but the pain regularly causes enough reduction in oral intake to require hospital assessment. Aciclovir gives a modest benefit in symptom duration and oral intake when started within the first three to four days, and after that window it is not worth commencing. Adequate analgesia is the intervention that most often prevents admission, because many children who refuse fluids at triage will drink once the pain is controlled.
key_points: Bleeding swollen gingivae with palatal ulcers and no peripheral rash indicates herpes simplex.
Hand, foot and mouth disease spares the gingivae and adds a rash on hands, feet and buttocks.
Analgesia before a supervised drinking trial is the step that avoids admission.
Oral aciclovir helps only if started within about 72 to 96 hours of symptom onset.
Intravenous therapy is for failed oral intake, immunocompromise or dissemination.
explanation.pearls: Herpetic whitlow on a sucked thumb and herpetic keratoconjunctivitis are the two autoinoculation complications to warn parents about; a red painful eye in a child with gingivostomatitis needs same day ophthalmology review rather than topical steroid.

options.rationale: Intravenous aciclovir is for the immunocompromised child or for disseminated disease, and this boy has moist mucous membranes, normal perfusion and wet nappies. Cannulating before an adequately analgesed oral trial converts a ward avoidable presentation into an admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis)

Gingivostomatitis with bleeding swollen gums and palatal involvement is herpes simplex rather than an enteroviral exanthem, and aciclovir started within 72 to 96 hours of onset shortens the illness and the period of poor intake. Effective analgesia first is what allows a trial of oral fluids to succeed. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis)

Corticosteroid has no role in herpetic gingivostomatitis and may prolong viral shedding, in contrast to its use in croup and some autoimmune oral ulceration. It also does not address the immediate barrier to drinking, which is pain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

This combination treats acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, which produces punched out interdental ulceration with grey slough and halitosis in older children and adolescents. Diffuse shallow ulcers across the tongue and palate in a toddler are viral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Oral and Dental)

Paracetamol alone rarely provides enough analgesia for this degree of mucosal pain, and viscous lidocaine is avoided in young children because of systemic absorption and the risk of impairing the swallow. Discharge without a documented drinking trial risks representation with dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis)

explanation.summary: Pubertal gynaecomastia affects up to 60 per cent of adolescent boys and reflects a transient imbalance between oestradiol and testosterone as puberty proceeds, typically appearing at Tanner stage 3 to 4 and resolving spontaneously within one to two years. The clinical task is to identify the small minority with a secondary cause, and the examination that does most of that work is the testicular examination. Symmetrical volumes appropriate for pubertal stage support the physiological diagnosis, small firm testes suggest Klinefelter syndrome, and an asymmetrically enlarged or irregular testis raises a hormone secreting germ cell or Leydig cell tumour. Drugs are the other major group, with spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, antipsychotics and anabolic steroids among the common culprits, so a medication and supplement history is essential. Firm concentric subareolar tissue distinguishes true glandular gynaecomastia from the diffuse fatty pseudogynaecomastia of obesity.
key_points: Pubertal gynaecomastia is common, symmetrical and resolves within one to two years.
Testicular examination is the highest yield part of the assessment.
Asymmetrical or irregular testes suggest a hormone secreting tumour and need imaging.
Small firm bilateral testes with tall stature suggest Klinefelter syndrome.
Always take a medication and supplement history before attributing it to puberty.
explanation.pearls: Testicular volume measured with an orchidometer is the single most useful sign in adolescent gynaecomastia: under 6 mL bilaterally points to Klinefelter syndrome, a difference of more than 3 mL between sides points to a testicular mass, and symmetrical volumes above 8 mL support physiological puberty.

options.rationale: The asymmetrical testicular volume with a firm irregular area is the finding that overrides the otherwise reassuring picture of pubertal gynaecomastia, because a testicular germ cell tumour secreting beta human chorionic gonadotrophin causes breast tissue. Imaging and the tumour marker are the immediate steps. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Medical therapy is occasionally considered for persistent painful gynaecomastia after a secondary cause has been excluded, not before. Starting it now would treat a symptom while leaving a possible testicular tumour undiagnosed for a further three months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Thyrotoxicosis, chronic liver disease and hyperprolactinaemia are all recognised secondary causes and would be reasonable in a boy with no localising findings. They do not explain a focal testicular abnormality and would delay assessment of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Reassurance and review is right for the boy with symmetrical testes in mid puberty, and pubertal gynaecomastia does resolve in most within two years. An asymmetrically enlarged irregular testis is not part of that picture and must not be observed. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

This panel is aimed at Klinefelter syndrome, which also causes adolescent gynaecomastia but gives small firm testes of less than 6 mL bilaterally with tall stature. The large asymmetrical testes here point the opposite way. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

explanation.summary: Non retractility of the foreskin is normal in the majority of boys through early childhood and separation continues into adolescence, so physiological phimosis is a finding rather than a diagnosis. Balanitis xerotica obliterans, the genital form of lichen sclerosus, is the main pathological phimosis in boys and typically presents between the ages of seven and twelve. The distinguishing features are a firm pale sclerotic ring at the preputial orifice, loss of retraction that had previously been achieved, ballooning with a spraying stream, and recurrent balanoposthitis. It is one of the clear medical indications for circumcision in childhood, and the specimen is sent for histology because the condition can extend to the glans and meatus and needs ongoing surveillance. Untreated disease can progress to meatal stenosis and urethral involvement, so referral should not be delayed for a trial of topical steroid.
key_points: Physiological phimosis is soft, common and improves with topical steroid and time.
A pale sclerotic ring with regression of retraction indicates balanitis xerotica obliterans.
Ballooning with a spraying stream and recurrent balanoposthitis support the diagnosis.
It is a recognised medical indication for circumcision, with histology on the specimen.
Progression to meatal stenosis and urethral stricture follows untreated disease.
explanation.pearls: Meatal involvement occurs in roughly a fifth of boys with balanitis xerotica obliterans, so the meatus should be inspected at the time of circumcision and the boy followed for a spraying or narrowing stream afterwards rather than discharged as cured.

options.rationale: Reassurance suits physiological non retraction, which is normal in most boys until later childhood and is not scarred. A foreskin that has gone backwards in retractability with a visible white ring is pathological and will not improve with time. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

A pale sclerotic ring with loss of previously achieved retraction, ballooning and recurrent balanoposthitis is balanitis xerotica obliterans, a pathological phimosis in which the scarring is irreversible. Circumcision is both the treatment and the way the diagnosis is confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Separating congenital adhesions between the inner prepuce and the glans is a different problem from a scarred narrowed orifice, and forcing a sclerotic ring tears it and worsens the scarring. The two are distinguished by whether the narrowing is at the tip or is adherence to the glans. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Topical corticosteroid with gentle stretching is the correct first line for physiological phimosis and succeeds in most boys, but it cannot reverse established sclerotic scar tissue. Delaying referral for six weeks allows the meatus to become involved. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Imaging and culture would be appropriate if there were recurrent urinary tract infection or a suspicion of upper tract involvement, and this boy has had neither. The diagnosis here is made by inspection of the prepuce. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Non tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis is a disease of immunocompetent children between one and five years, acquired from soil and water and presenting as a slowly enlarging unilateral submandibular or preauricular node. The child remains well, which is the feature that separates it from pyogenic adenitis, and the overlying skin classically thins and takes on a violaceous or parchment appearance before it breaks down. Failure to respond to two courses of conventional oral antibiotics is a common part of the referral history. Complete surgical excision cures around 95 per cent and provides tissue for culture, whereas incision and drainage leaves a chronically discharging sinus. Where the node overlies the facial nerve and excision carries an unacceptable risk, prolonged combination therapy with clarithromycin plus rifampicin or ethambutol is the alternative, accepting a slower and less certain resolution.
key_points: A well preschooler with a painless enlarging unilateral node and normal growth.
Violaceous thinning skin adherent to the node is close to specific.
Non response to two courses of conventional oral antibiotics is typical.
Complete excision is both diagnostic and therapeutic with the highest cure rate.
Incision and drainage causes a chronic sinus and should be avoided.
explanation.pearls: Tuberculin skin testing in non tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis is often weakly positive at 5 to 10 mm because of shared antigens, so an intermediate reaction in a well Australian born preschooler with a single neck node points towards the environmental mycobacteria rather than towards tuberculosis.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Non tuberculous mycobacterial infections

options.rationale: Incision and drainage is correct for a pyogenic abscess, which is hot, tender and rapidly evolving in a febrile child. Opening a mycobacterial node reliably produces a chronically discharging sinus that takes many months to close. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

Combination macrolide based therapy is a genuine alternative when the node sits over the facial nerve or excision is otherwise unsafe, so it is a legitimate second choice rather than a wrong concept. Cure rates are lower and treatment runs for months, so surgery is preferred when the site allows. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This pathway targets tuberculous lymphadenitis, which is suggested by contact history, overseas residence, systemic symptoms or bilateral nodes. Interferon gamma release assays also cross react with some non tuberculous species and can mislead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Malignancy deserves consideration in any persistent node, but lymphoma in this age group usually gives a rubbery mobile node with systemic symptoms or nodes at several sites rather than skin adherence and discolouration. The skin changes are close to specific for mycobacterial disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

A painless enlarging node in a preschooler with violaceous adherent skin and no response to two antibiotic courses is non tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis, and complete excision gives both the highest cure rate and the diagnosis. Incisional approaches risk a chronically discharging sinus. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

explanation.summary: Juvenile recurrent parotitis is the second commonest cause of parotid swelling in children after mumps and presents with repeated episodes of unilateral or alternating parotid inflammation between the ages of three and six. The pathology is non obstructive sialectasis with ductal ectasia, and each attack lasts days to a couple of weeks before settling spontaneously. Three conditions have to be reasoned past: mumps, which is usually bilateral and does not recur in an immunised child; acute suppurative parotitis, which is febrile with purulent ductal discharge; and an autoimmune sialadenitis, which brings sicca symptoms. A raised total amylase is expected and reflects the salivary isoenzyme, so it should not trigger a pancreatic workup. Ultrasound is the imaging of choice and most children outgrow the condition by puberty, with sialendoscopy reserved for frequent disabling attacks.
key_points: Recurrent unilateral parotid swelling in a well immunised child is rarely mumps.
Clear ductal saliva and an afebrile child argue against suppurative parotitis.
Total amylase rises from the salivary isoenzyme and does not indicate pancreatitis.
Ultrasound showing sialectasis confirms the diagnosis without radiation.
Most cases resolve spontaneously around puberty with conservative management.
explanation.pearls: Splitting total amylase into pancreatic and salivary isoenzymes, or simply checking a lipase, resolves the diagnostic confusion in minutes: lipase is normal in salivary disease because the salivary glands do not produce it.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

options.rationale: Mumps remains notifiable and would be the default for parotid swelling, but it is characteristically bilateral or sequential, occurs once, and is very unlikely in a child fully covered by the measles mumps and rubella schedule. A third episode on the same side is not mumps. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia)

Antistaphylococcal therapy treats acute suppurative parotitis, which occurs in dehydrated or debilitated children with a hot erythematous gland and frank pus expressible from the duct. Clear saliva in an afebrile well child argues against it, and two previous courses have already failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Juvenile Sjogren syndrome is the systemic mimic worth remembering and does cause recurrent parotid swelling, but it is far commoner in adolescent girls and is accompanied by dry eyes and a dry mouth. Normal salivary flow and no ocular symptoms make it improbable as a first line test. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren syndrome)

Recurrent unilateral parotid swelling in a well immunised child with clear ductal saliva is juvenile recurrent parotitis, and ultrasound showing multiple small hypoechoic sialectatic areas confirms it without radiation. Management is conservative with hydration, gland massage and sialogogues during attacks. (Source: RCH CPG: Parotitis)

The amylase here is salivary in origin: any inflamed salivary gland raises total amylase without pancreatic disease, and this boy has no abdominal pain or vomiting. Lipase would be normal and the imaging would be negative. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

explanation.summary: A thyroglossal duct cyst is the commonest congenital midline neck swelling in childhood and arises from the embryological tract along which the thyroid descends from the foramen caecum at the base of the tongue to its final pretracheal position. Its attachment to that tract is what produces the diagnostic sign of elevation with tongue protrusion as well as with swallowing, distinguishing it from a dermoid cyst, which is also midline but does not move with the tongue, and from lymphadenopathy, which is lateral. Because descent can arrest anywhere along the tract, a minority of children have no orthotopic gland at all and the cyst contains their entire functioning thyroid, which is why ultrasound is performed before any excision and why normal thyroid function tests cannot substitute for it. These cysts often first present when they enlarge and become infected during an upper respiratory illness. Definitive management is the Sistrunk procedure, removing the cyst with the tract and the central hyoid body, since simple cystectomy has a high recurrence rate.
key_points: Elevation with tongue protrusion as well as swallowing is the discriminating sign
Ultrasound before excision confirms a normally sited gland is present
Normal thyroid function tests do not exclude the cyst containing the only thyroid tissue
Infection during an upper respiratory illness is the usual trigger for presentation
The Sistrunk procedure removes the central hyoid body to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: Removing a thyroglossal cyst that contains ectopic thyroid without preoperative imaging leaves the child permanently athyreotic and dependent on lifelong thyroxine, which is the single reason ultrasound is mandatory even when thyroid function tests are entirely normal.

options.rationale: Excision of the tract together with the central portion of the hyoid bone is the correct definitive operation and it will very likely be the eventual plan, but performing it before imaging risks removing the child's only thyroid tissue. The operation follows the scan rather than replacing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

Imaging before any operation establishes that a normal gland sits in its usual position, because in a small proportion of these children the swelling contains the only functioning thyroid tissue they have and removing it renders them permanently hypothyroid. Normal thyroid function tests do not settle this, since ectopic tissue can maintain euthyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

Drainage is reserved for a genuinely fluctuant abscess that has not settled with antibiotics, and here the inflammation has already resolved. Opening the lesion also risks creating a discharging sinus and makes the later definitive excision considerably more difficult. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

Cytology is used where malignancy is a genuine concern, signalled by a hard fixed mass, rapid painless growth or associated lymphadenopathy, none of which is present in a soft midline lesion that elevates on tongue protrusion. It carries the same risk of establishing a sinus tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

The infective episode has already resolved and the residual swelling is the underlying structural lesion rather than persisting infection. Further antibiotics treat something that is no longer present and delay the definitive pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis presents in the first weeks to months of life with the head tilted toward the affected sternocleidomastoid and the chin rotated away from it, and a firm painless mass within the muscle is present in a proportion of cases and resolves over several months. Difficult instrumental delivery and intrauterine crowding are the usual antecedents. The two associations to check at the same visit are developmental dysplasia of the hip, which shares the crowding aetiology and occurs more often in these infants, and positional plagiocephaly, which develops because the infant persistently rests on the same part of the skull. Physiotherapy with passive stretching and active positioning resolves most cases, with better outcomes the earlier it starts. Features that should redirect the assessment include a tilt without contralateral chin rotation, abnormal tone, limitation that is painful, an eye movement abnormality suggesting ocular torticollis, or failure to improve over several months of an adequate program.
key_points: The head tilts toward the affected muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Start physiotherapy early rather than observing, because outcomes are time dependent
Check the hips at the same visit given the shared association with crowding
Watch for positional plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry developing
Reserve surgery for failure of conservative treatment after about twelve months
explanation.pearls: A head tilt without the expected chin rotation to the opposite side is not muscular torticollis and should prompt assessment for an ocular cause, a posterior fossa lesion or an atlantoaxial abnormality rather than a physiotherapy referral.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Surgical release is considered only after a sustained conservative program has failed, conventionally not before twelve months of age. Operating at seven weeks removes the chance of the spontaneous resolution that most infants achieve. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Imaging is reserved for atypical features such as a tilt that is not accompanied by rotation to the opposite side, abnormal tone or reflexes, developmental regression, or failure to respond to an adequate physiotherapy program. Her examination is otherwise normal and imaging at this age would require sedation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Passive stretching, positioning to encourage active rotation toward the restricted side and parent education resolve the great majority of cases when started in the first few months. Earlier referral produces better and faster correction, which is why this is done now rather than after a period of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Botulinum toxin has been used as an adjunct in resistant cases in older children, but it is not a first line intervention and the evidence in infancy is limited. It would be considered only well after a stretching program had failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Untreated restriction leads to progressive facial asymmetry and positional flattening of the skull, and the window in which stretching works best is the first few months. Reassurance alone forfeits that window. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Inguinal hernia in infancy is almost always indirect and results from a patent processus vaginalis, the same embryological structure whose incomplete obliteration produces a communicating hydrocele. The clinical distinction rests on whether the upper border of the swelling can be felt: a hydrocele confined to the scrotum allows the examiner to palpate normal cord above it and typically transilluminates, whereas a hernia extends up through the inguinal canal so that no upper border is reachable. Prematurity is the strongest risk factor and incidence rises steeply with decreasing gestational age. The clinical urgency comes from incarceration, which is far more common in infancy than in later childhood and threatens both the bowel and the ipsilateral testis through compression of the gonadal vessels. Because of this, hernias in young infants are repaired promptly on an elective list, whereas hydroceles are observed and usually resolve by around two years without intervention.
key_points: A patent processus vaginalis underlies both infant hernia and communicating hydrocele
Inability to palpate normal cord above the swelling indicates a hernia
Prematurity markedly increases both incidence and incarceration risk
Incarceration threatens bowel and the ipsilateral testis within hours
Hydroceles are observed to about two years, hernias are repaired promptly
explanation.pearls: The risk of incarceration in an untreated infant inguinal hernia is highest in the first six months of life and is reported at around 30 per cent in infants under one year, which is why repair is arranged within weeks rather than deferred until the child is older and larger.

options.rationale: Spontaneous closure over the first year is the natural history of a communicating hydrocele, which is why this option is tempting in an infant with a scrotal swelling. A hernia containing bowel does not close spontaneously, and the inability to feel normal cord above the swelling separates the two at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

The diagnosis is clinical and ultrasound adds little when the examination findings are as clear as these. A three month delay in an infant of this age spans the period of greatest incarceration risk. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons)

Emergency operation is required for an irreducible swelling, particularly with tenderness, discolouration, vomiting or abdominal distension, none of which he has. His swelling reduces with gentle pressure and he is feeding and passing stool normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

A reducible groin hernia in early infancy carries a high risk of incarceration, greatest in the first months of life and higher again in babies born preterm, so repair is arranged promptly rather than deferred. Referral while it remains reducible allows an elective operation instead of an emergency one. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

Waiting for pain means waiting for incarceration, which presents with an irreducible tender lump and can progress to bowel and testicular ischaemia within hours. Emergency repair in that setting carries substantially higher complication rates than elective repair. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia describes a lingual frenulum short or anteriorly attached enough to restrict tongue movement, and it is present in a meaningful minority of newborns, though only a fraction of those have any feeding problem at all. This distinction governs practice: the anatomical finding alone is not an indication to operate, and rates of division rose substantially in Australia before that point was re-emphasised. The indication combines a restrictive frenulum on examination with a genuine functional problem, meaning nipple pain and trauma, ineffective milk transfer with poor weight gain, or prolonged unsatisfying feeds, that has not resolved with skilled assessment of positioning and attachment. Weight loss beyond about 10 per cent of birth weight is itself a marker requiring prompt action regardless of cause. Frenotomy is performed without general anaesthesia in young infants, bleeding is usually minimal and the infant can feed immediately, with maternal pain scores improving most consistently in trials.
key_points: The anatomical finding alone is never the indication for division
Combine a restrictive frenulum with a documented functional feeding problem
Skilled attachment review must come first and be seen to fail
Weight loss beyond about 10 per cent of birth weight requires prompt action
Maternal nipple pain is the outcome that improves most consistently after frenotomy
explanation.pearls: A nipple that emerges compressed into a wedge or lipstick shape at the end of a feed indicates a mechanical compression problem rather than infection, and it distinguishes a restrictive tongue tie from candidal nipple pain, which burns between feeds as well as during them.

options.rationale: Abandoning breastfeeding forecloses a problem with an effective and simple treatment. It should be a decision the mother reaches after the remediable cause has been addressed, not a first line clinical recommendation. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

Shields can reduce pain in the short term but often reduce milk transfer further, which is the opposite of what a baby who has lost 11 per cent of his birth weight needs. Waiting a further week without addressing transfer risks continued weight loss. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

Supplementation may well be needed in the short term to protect his weight and would reasonably run alongside the definitive step, but used alone it leaves the mechanical restriction and the maternal pain untreated and predictably ends breastfeeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding)

Candidal infection causes burning nipple pain that characteristically persists between feeds and is often accompanied by oral plaques in the infant, whereas her pain is confined to the feed and the nipple emerges compressed, which indicates a mechanical problem. There are no oral plaques. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A frenulum that restricts tongue elevation, combined with nipple trauma, prolonged ineffective feeding and weight loss that has not responded to two skilled attachment reviews, is the specific situation in which frenotomy improves maternal pain and feeding effectiveness. Division is a brief procedure that allows immediate feeding afterwards. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Amblyopia is reduced vision in an eye that is structurally normal, caused by the developing visual cortex suppressing a degraded or misaligned image during the sensitive period of visual development. The three mechanisms are a difference in refractive power between the eyes, misalignment, and deprivation from an obstruction such as a cataract or a ptosis, and the first two frequently coexist as they do here. It is the leading cause of monocular vision loss in Australian children and is usually asymptomatic, which is the rationale for preschool screening, since a child with one good eye reports nothing wrong. The normal symmetrical red reflex and normal fundus are important because they exclude deprivational causes including cataract and retinoblastoma, either of which would demand urgent rather than routine referral. Treatment begins with spectacles, worn for a period of refractive adaptation, before occlusion or atropine penalisation is added for residual deficit, and outcomes deteriorate steadily as treatment is started later in childhood.
key_points: Amblyopia is reduced vision in a structurally normal eye and is usually asymptomatic
A normal symmetrical red reflex excludes cataract and retinoblastoma as the cause
Correct the refractive error first and allow three to four months of adaptation
Add occlusion or atropine penalisation only for the residual deficit
Treatment response declines steadily with increasing age at presentation
explanation.pearls: Roughly a third of children with anisometropic amblyopia reach normal acuity on spectacles alone within about sixteen weeks of refractive adaptation, so patching started on the day of diagnosis subjects many children to occlusion they never needed.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.rationale: Correcting a large difference in refractive power between the eyes is the necessary first treatment, because a substantial proportion of children recover normal vision on spectacles alone over a period of refractive adaptation lasting about three to four months. Occlusion is added only for the deficit that remains after that. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

Patching the better eye before the blurred image is corrected asks the weaker eye to work through an uncorrected 5 dioptre error, which limits what occlusion can achieve and imposes an unnecessary burden on the child. It is the correct second step once spectacles have been worn and the deficit reassessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

Surgery addresses the cosmetic and sensory consequences of misalignment but does not itself restore vision in the affected eye. In this pattern the deviation is often driven by the uncorrected hypermetropia and improves substantially with spectacles alone. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.rationale: Pharmacological penalisation blurs the better eye and is a recognised alternative to patching with comparable outcomes, particularly where compliance with a patch is poor. Like patching, it belongs after refractive correction rather than before it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.rationale: Visual development is plastic only through the first several years and treatment response falls progressively with age. Deferring for a year in a 4-year-old spends a substantial part of the remaining treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect around one in twenty young children, typically begin between six and eighteen months and resolve by about five years of age. The cyanotic form follows a period of vigorous crying after pain, frustration or fright, with expiratory apnoea, colour change, loss of tone and brief loss of consciousness, while the less common pallid form follows a minor bump or fright and is mediated by a vagally driven asystolic pause. Brief tonic stiffening or a few clonic jerks occur in a substantial minority because of transient cerebral hypoperfusion and are frequently misread as a seizure, so the discriminating features are the invariable emotional or painful trigger, the crying that precedes the event, and rapid complete recovery without a postictal phase. Iron deficiency is associated with more frequent and more severe spells, and randomised evidence shows that iron supplementation reduces their frequency, which makes a full blood count and ferritin part of the standard assessment. Excessive cow's milk intake beyond about 500 mL a day in a toddler is the commonest dietary cause of the deficiency, and parents need explicit advice to maintain normal boundaries rather than avoid triggers.
key_points: Episodes are always preceded by crying after an upset, pain or fright
Brief jerking reflects cerebral hypoperfusion, not epilepsy
Check a full blood count and ferritin because iron deficiency worsens spells
Iron supplementation reduces both frequency and severity
Counsel parents to keep normal limits rather than avoid triggers
explanation.pearls: Cow's milk intake above about 500 mL a day in a toddler displaces iron rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss, and reducing it while giving three months of oral iron is what actually reduces breath holding spell frequency.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Brief jerking at the end of an episode reflects cerebral hypoperfusion rather than a primary seizure, and the constant provoking trigger of crying, the rapid complete recovery and the absence of any drowsy phase afterwards all argue against epilepsy. Investigation is reserved for episodes that occur without a trigger or that are followed by prolonged confusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

These episodes are benign, stereotyped and reliably provoked by crying after an upset, and iron deficiency is a well established association that is present here on the blood film indices and ferritin. Correcting the deficiency reduces both the frequency and the severity of episodes, and excessive cow's milk intake is the usual dietary driver to address alongside it. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

Anticonvulsant therapy treats a condition she does not have and exposes a toddler to hepatotoxicity and other adverse effects for no benefit. These episodes do not respond to anticonvulsants. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Cardiac assessment is warranted when episodes occur during exertion, during swimming, without any provoking trigger, or where there is a family history of premature sudden death. Her electrocardiogram, cardiac examination and femoral pulses are all normal and every episode has followed an emotional trigger. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Parents commonly begin to give in to avoid provoking an episode, and warning against this is an important part of counselling, so the advice is exactly backwards. Abandoning normal limit setting reinforces the behaviour without altering the underlying physiology. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy affects roughly one in 3500 to 5000 boys and follows X linked recessive inheritance, with about a third of cases arising from new mutations so that a negative family history is common. Presentation is typically between two and five years with delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty with stairs and running, and a positive Gowers manoeuvre, and around a third of boys also have global developmental delay or language delay because dystrophin is expressed in brain as well as muscle. A recurring diagnostic detour is referral for liver disease, because damaged muscle releases alanine and aspartate aminotransferase and these are reported on standard liver panels, so a normal gamma glutamyl transferase alongside raised transaminases in a boy with motor difficulty should redirect thinking to muscle and prompt a creatine kinase. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started at the appropriate stage prolongs ambulation, and structured cardiac and respiratory surveillance changes long term outcome. Genetic confirmation also enables carrier testing of female relatives and access to mutation specific therapies.
key_points: Transaminases rise from damaged skeletal muscle and appear on standard liver panels
A normal gamma glutamyl transferase points away from a hepatic source
Creatine kinase in the thousands with a positive Gowers manoeuvre is the key combination
About a third of boys have associated developmental or language delay
Genetic testing on blood confirms most cases and avoids muscle biopsy
explanation.pearls: In any boy under five referred for unexplained raised transaminases, check the gamma glutamyl transferase and a creatine kinase before imaging the liver; a normal gamma glutamyl transferase with a creatine kinase above 2000 U/L redirects the entire workup to muscle.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: Biopsy with dystrophin staining was formerly the standard confirmatory test and retains a role when genetic testing is negative despite a strong clinical picture. Performing it first subjects the child to a general anaesthetic for information that a blood test usually provides. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

This pursues the referral that has already been made in error. A gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits alongside raised transaminases indicates that the enzymes are coming from skeletal muscle rather than from liver, since hepatocellular injury characteristically raises the gamma glutamyl transferase as well. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

Progressive proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy, a positive Gowers manoeuvre and a creatine kinase in the thousands is a dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and genetic testing on blood confirms the diagnosis in around seven in ten boys through deletion or duplication analysis. It avoids an operation and immediately informs carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the family. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

Electrophysiology can demonstrate a myopathic pattern but cannot identify which myopathy, so it does not reach a diagnosis. It has largely been displaced by genetic testing in this situation and is poorly tolerated by young children. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: A further three months of observation delays a diagnosis that carries immediate implications for corticosteroid timing, cardiac and respiratory surveillance and genetic counselling for the family. The abnormality has already been confirmed on repeat testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Klinefelter syndrome, most often a 47,XXY karyotype, affects around one in 600 male births and is the commonest chromosomal cause of primary hypogonadism, yet the majority of affected men are never diagnosed. The reason is that puberty usually begins and progresses normally under adrenal and early testicular androgen drive, so pubic hair, voice change and body habitus develop on schedule, while progressive seminiferous tubule fibrosis prevents the testes from enlarging beyond about 4 to 6 mL. That discordance between advanced pubic hair and persistently small firm testes is the single most useful clinical clue and is easily missed if testicular volume is not measured. Additional features include tall stature with disproportionately long limbs from delayed epiphyseal closure, gynaecomastia, and a characteristic profile of language based learning difficulty with relatively preserved non-verbal reasoning alongside social difficulties. Biochemically the picture is hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, and management involves testosterone replacement from mid puberty, discussion of fertility preservation because sperm retrieval rates fall with age, and educational and psychological support.
key_points: Advanced pubic hair with testes still at 4 mL is the discriminating discordance
Raised gonadotrophins localise the defect to the testis rather than the pituitary
Tall stature with long limbs reflects delayed epiphyseal closure
The learning profile is typically language based with preserved non-verbal reasoning
Discuss fertility preservation early because sperm retrieval rates decline with age
explanation.pearls: Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer in any tall adolescent boy referred for learning or social difficulties; a volume that remains at or below 6 mL once pubic hair has reached Tanner stage 4 should prompt a karyotype rather than reassurance.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Repeating the androgen measurement refines a number that is already consistent with the clinical picture, and the raised gonadotrophins have already localised the lesion to the testis. It delays the test that gives the answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

Pituitary imaging is indicated when gonadotrophins are low or inappropriately normal alongside a low testosterone, which indicates a central cause. Here the gonadotrophins are raised, which places the defect in the testis and makes the pituitary the wrong organ to image. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

Ultrasound would confirm what the orchidometer has already established and is used principally to look for a testicular tumour, which would present with a discrete mass and typically with high oestrogen rather than raised gonadotrophins. It does not explain the tall stature or the learning profile. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Small firm testes that have failed to enlarge despite advanced pubic hair development, tall stature with long limbs, gynaecomastia and raised gonadotrophins with a low testosterone indicate primary testicular failure with a chromosomal basis, and a karyotype is the definitive test. Making the diagnosis opens access to androgen replacement, fertility preservation counselling and educational support. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

Bone age is valuable when the question is the timing of puberty relative to growth, as in constitutional delay or precocity. His puberty has clearly begun and progressed, so the question is why the testes have not grown with it. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

explanation.summary: Occipital flattening in infancy is usually positional and has become much more common since back sleeping was adopted for sudden infant death prevention, but a small proportion represents premature fusion of the lambdoid suture, and the two are separated at the bedside by looking down on the skull from above. Positional deformity produces a parallelogram: the flattened occiput pushes the ear on that side forwards and the forehead on the same side becomes more prominent. Lambdoid synostosis produces a trapezoid: the ear on the affected side is pulled backwards and downwards, there is a compensatory bulge over the mastoid, and the bossing appears on the opposite forehead. A palpable ridge along the suture supports fusion, and the absence of any response to sustained repositioning is further evidence against a positional cause. Positional deformity is managed with repositioning, tummy time and treatment of any associated neck restriction, with helmet therapy for selected moderate to severe cases, whereas fusion requires craniofacial referral and surgical correction, typically within the first year, to prevent progressive asymmetry and to protect brain growth.
key_points: Look down on the skull from above to judge parallelogram against trapezoid
Positional flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear forwards and bosses the ipsilateral forehead
Lambdoid fusion pulls the ipsilateral ear backwards and downwards with a mastoid bulge
Contralateral frontal bossing and a palpable sutural ridge indicate fusion
Failure to respond to sustained repositioning argues against a positional cause
explanation.pearls: The direction of ear displacement is the single most reliable bedside sign in occipital flattening: an ear pushed forward means positional moulding, an ear pulled backward and down means lambdoid synostosis and a craniofacial referral.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Neck restriction commonly drives positional flattening and physiotherapy is central to managing that pathway, which is why this option is plausible. Her neck movement is not described as restricted and the ear displacement here is backwards rather than forwards, which is the opposite of the positional pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Repositioning is the correct treatment for deformation caused by external pressure, and it has already been tried without effect. A fused suture cannot remodel in response to positioning, so two further months would be lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

Helmet therapy is an option for moderate to severe positional deformity in selected infants within a defined age window. Applying a helmet to a skull with a fused suture does not correct the underlying restriction and delays the operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

Plain films are insensitive for sutural fusion in infancy and a normal film would not exclude the diagnosis, while an abnormal one would still be followed by specialist referral and dedicated imaging. The referral is what changes management. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: A palpable sutural ridge with the ear displaced backwards and downwards, a mastoid bulge and bossing of the opposite forehead describes a trapezoid head shape that indicates a fused suture rather than external moulding. Premature fusion requires surgical assessment and operative correction is generally undertaken within the first year. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

explanation.summary: The character and timing of stridor localise the obstruction: inspiratory stridor arises above the vocal cords, expiratory noise arises in the intrathoracic airway, and biphasic stridor indicates a fixed narrowing at the level of the glottis or subglottis where flow is limited in both phases of respiration. Laryngomalacia accounts for the majority of infant stridor and is distinguished by being inspiratory, worse supine and during feeding or crying, better prone, and by improving spontaneously over the first two years. Acquired subglottic stenosis follows prolonged or traumatic endotracheal intubation, which makes ex preterm infants the principal risk group, and it characteristically presents with biphasic stridor unaffected by position that becomes symptomatic during intercurrent viral illness. Recurrent croup, particularly more than twice in a year or in an infant under six months, is a recognised presentation of an underlying fixed narrowing and is an indication for airway assessment rather than for further episodic treatment. Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy establish the grade of stenosis, which determines whether observation, endoscopic dilatation or open reconstruction is appropriate.
key_points: Biphasic stridor indicates a fixed glottic or subglottic narrowing
Laryngomalacia is inspiratory, worse supine and better prone, and resolves by about two years
Prolonged neonatal intubation is the main risk factor for acquired subglottic stenosis
Recurrent croup under six months of age warrants airway assessment
Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy grade the stenosis and direct treatment
explanation.pearls: Two or more episodes of croup before six months of age, or any croup that does not fully settle between episodes, should prompt referral for airway endoscopy rather than another course of dexamethasone, because acquired subglottic stenosis presents exactly this way.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Stridor that is biphasic, unaltered by position and recurrent in an infant with prolonged neonatal intubation points to a fixed narrowing at or below the vocal cords rather than to a dynamic supraglottic collapse. Direct visualisation of the airway under anaesthesia is the only way to establish the site and severity and to plan treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Acid reflux aggravates supraglottic collapse and antireflux treatment is sometimes used as an adjunct in that condition. It does nothing for a fixed structural narrowing, and six weeks of observation in an infant with recession at rest carries a real risk of decompensation during the next viral illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Spontaneous resolution by around eighteen to twenty four months describes laryngomalacia, which is the commonest cause of infant stridor and the reason this reassurance is so tempting. That condition gives inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine, during feeding and when crying, and improves in the prone position, which is the opposite of what is described. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

A chest film may show a vascular ring or a lower airway abnormality and is a reasonable adjunct, but it images below the level where the obstruction almost certainly lies and a normal film would not exclude it. It does not substitute for direct visualisation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: This is the treatment for viral laryngotracheobronchitis and explains why she has transiently improved at each previous presentation, since reducing mucosal oedema temporarily widens an already narrowed lumen. Treating the recurring exacerbation again without investigating the fixed narrowing beneath it repeats the error of the previous two visits. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced at two weeks of age, or at three weeks if preterm and breastfed, needs a split bilirubin, because a conjugated fraction is never physiological and always requires investigation.
