Prader Willi syndrome causes neonatal hypotonia but with preserved reflexes and global developmental delay.
explanation.pearls: Look at the tongue at rest and test the reflexes in every floppy infant, because fine tongue fasciculations with absent reflexes and a normal creatine kinase point to spinal muscular atrophy and justify same week genetic testing, since disease modifying treatment preserves only the motor neurons that have not yet been lost.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Methylation studies diagnose Prader Willi syndrome, which is a leading cause of neonatal hypotonia with poor feeding, but those infants have a weak suck with global developmental delay, characteristic facies and preserved reflexes rather than areflexia with fasciculations. Cognitive and social development here is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Areflexia with tongue fasciculations, a normal creatine kinase and preserved facial and eye movements localise the lesion to the anterior horn cell, and homozygous deletion of exon 7 of the survival motor neuron 1 gene confirms it on a blood sample within days. Urgency matters because disease modifying therapy works by preserving motor neurons that have not yet died, so weeks of delay translate directly into lost function. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Central causes of hypotonia are sought with imaging, and they characteristically produce a depressed conscious state, developmental delay, brisk reflexes or upgoing plantars. A bright socially engaged infant with absent reflexes and fasciculations has a lower motor neuron problem, and anaesthesia carries real respiratory risk in this state. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Metabolic screening is appropriate where hypotonia comes with encephalopathy, regression across multiple domains, organomegaly or acidosis, none of which is present. It is a reasonable parallel test in an undifferentiated floppy infant but not the one that will name this diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Neuromuscular junction disorders are identified this way, and they characteristically involve the extraocular and facial muscles, producing ptosis and a fatigable weak facial expression along with fluctuation through the day. Full facial expression and full eye movements argue strongly against the junction as the site of the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

explanation.summary: Blue episodes triggered by pain or frustration in a toddler, with a short recovery and no episodes during sleep or exertion, describe a hypoxic event rather than a seizure or an arrhythmia. Terminal stiffening is common once the episode lasts long enough to cause cerebral hypoxia and does not change the diagnosis. The feature that should change management here is the combination of pallor and a milk intake that has displaced iron rich solids, because iron deficiency is strongly associated with these episodes and its correction reduces them. Confirming the deficiency before treating avoids committing a child to iron on the basis of appearance alone. A normal corrected QT interval and the absence of exertional or sleep related episodes make cardiac investigation low yield.
key_points: Every episode following a trigger, with recovery in under a minute, argues against epilepsy.
Terminal stiffening reflects cerebral hypoxia and does not warrant an electroencephalogram.
Cow milk above about 500 mL daily in a toddler displaces iron rich foods and impairs absorption.
Correcting iron deficiency reduces the frequency and severity of these episodes.
Episodes during sleep or exertion, or a family history of sudden death, shift the workup to cardiac.
explanation.pearls: Ask the daily milk volume in every toddler presenting with these episodes, because intake above 500 mL a day makes iron deficiency likely, and replacing iron for three months is the one intervention that reduces how often the episodes happen.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.rationale: The episodes are self-limiting within a minute and terminate as breathing resumes, so a rescue anticonvulsant treats nothing and exposes a toddler to sedation and airway risk. Rescue medication belongs with prolonged epileptic seizures, not with hypoxic events of this kind. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.rationale: Reassurance about the benign natural history is correct as far as it goes and is part of the consultation. It is incomplete here because the pallor and the milk intake point to a treatable contributor that reassurance alone will leave in place. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Brief stiffening or a few jerks at the end of a prolonged episode is a hypoxic phenomenon and does not indicate epilepsy when every episode has an emotional or painful trigger. An electroencephalogram in this setting is normal or shows non-specific findings that risk an incorrect diagnosis. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring is directed at episodes occurring without warning, during exercise or during sleep, or where the family history raises the possibility of an inherited arrhythmia. A normal corrected QT interval with a consistent emotional trigger and no relevant family history makes this a low yield test. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.rationale: Iron deficiency is found in a large proportion of children with these episodes and treating it reduces both their frequency and their severity, which is the only intervention shown to change the natural history. Her milk intake of 1.4 litres daily displaces iron rich food and inhibits absorption, and she is pale, so the deficiency is likely and worth confirming before it is treated. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Most childhood nosebleeds arise from the anterior septum, where a superficial vascular plexus sits close to the surface and is easily damaged by picking and by dry heated air. The features that separate this local pattern from a bleeding disorder are the single nostril, the short duration with pressure, the absence of bleeding at other sites, and an uneventful tonsillectomy. Management is mucosal treatment plus correcting the first aid, because families very commonly pinch the bony bridge, which does not compress the bleeding point. Antiseptic ointment reduces crusting and colonisation and is a reasonable first line in Australian practice. Cautery and haematological investigation both sit downstream of this step.
key_points: The anterior septum is the source of the great majority of childhood nosebleeds.
Pressure must be applied to the soft part of the nose, not the bony bridge.
Bleeding from both nostrils or at other sites shifts the assessment toward a haemostatic disorder.
Normal haemostasis at tonsillectomy is strong evidence against an inherited bleeding disorder.
Unilateral obstruction with profuse bleeding in an adolescent boy warrants imaging and endoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to demonstrate how they hold the nose, because most families compress the bony bridge where no bleeding vessel lies, and ten minutes of correctly applied pressure to the soft part settles nearly all anterior bleeds without any prescription at all.

options.rationale: Bleeding from one nostril in a well child with a visible excoriated area on the anterior septum is local in origin, and treatment is directed at the mucosa and at the technique. Pressure belongs on the soft part of the nose rather than the bony bridge, and an antiseptic ointment reduces crusting and staphylococcal colonisation, which shortens the run of bleeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

Cautery is reserved for bleeding that continues despite mucosal treatment and correct first aid, and it carries a risk of septal injury when the mucosa is already excoriated. It is a second line step rather than the opening move in a child having short self-limiting bleeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

Saline addresses dryness from heated indoor air and is a reasonable adjunct, but on its own it leaves the colonised excoriated area untreated and the family still pinching the wrong part of the nose. The technique correction is the part of this consultation that most reliably shortens each episode. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

A haemostatic workup is indicated when bleeding comes from both nostrils, lasts beyond about ten minutes despite correct pressure, involves other sites, or where surgery or family history suggests a disorder. None of those apply, and he bled normally at tonsillectomy, which is a substantial haemostatic challenge. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

Endoscopy is warranted for unilateral obstruction, foul discharge or profuse posterior bleeding, particularly in an adolescent boy where a vascular nasal tumour is a consideration. Short anterior bleeds with a visible septal cause in a 7-year-old do not raise that possibility. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Epistaxis)

explanation.summary: Anterior knee pain in a rapidly growing adolescent athlete, with tenderness localised to the tibial tubercle and pain reproduced by resisted knee extension, is traction apophysitis at the patellar tendon insertion. The absence of night pain, rest pain, systemic features and effusion removes the presentations that require imaging, and full painless hip rotation removes the referred pain from a slipped epiphysis that must always be considered. Treatment is load modification rather than cessation of sport, combined with stretching of the quadriceps and hamstrings, because reduced flexibility during the growth spurt increases traction on the apophysis. The condition resolves as the apophysis fuses, and families need to be told the prominence itself will remain. Persisting symptoms after skeletal maturity are the only situation in which surgery is discussed.
key_points: Tenderness confined to the tibial tubercle with a normal joint line indicates apophysitis, not internal derangement.
Every adolescent with knee pain needs hip rotation examined to exclude referred pain.
Night pain, rest pain or systemic symptoms mandate radiographs to exclude bone tumour.
Load is reduced to a pain tolerable level rather than stopped altogether.
The bony prominence persists after symptoms resolve and does not indicate treatment failure.
explanation.pearls: Tell the family at the first visit that the lump is permanent even though the pain is not, because otherwise they return repeatedly for the unchanged prominence and are offered imaging that was never indicated.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children

options.rationale: Surgery to remove a residual ossicle is confined to skeletally mature patients whose symptoms have persisted well beyond the end of growth despite full conservative treatment. Operating during the growth spurt risks the tubercle and is never the first response. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

Imaging is indicated for night pain, rest pain, systemic symptoms, an effusion or a history of significant trauma, because those raise the possibility of bone tumour or an internal derangement. Focal tenderness over the tubercle with pain reproduced by resisted extension is a clinical diagnosis and radiographs add nothing. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

Corticosteroid placed near a tendon insertion weakens the collagen and risks avulsion of the apophysis, which is precisely the structure already under traction stress. There is no role for injection in this condition at any stage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children

options.rationale: Referred pain from a slipped upper femoral epiphysis genuinely can present as knee pain in this age group, which is why hip rotation must be examined in every adolescent with knee pain. Full and painless internal rotation of both hips makes that diagnosis very unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

Traction apophysitis at the tibial tubercle is a self-limiting overuse condition of the growth spurt, and load modification with a stretching program addresses the tight extensor mechanism that drives it. Complete withdrawal from sport is neither necessary nor helpful, so activity is reduced to a level that does not provoke pain while flexibility improves. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

explanation.summary: Newborn bleeding from vitamin K deficiency has an early form in the first week and a late form at two to twelve weeks that typically presents as intracranial haemorrhage, and the late form is almost confined to exclusively breastfed infants who received no prophylaxis. A single intramuscular dose is the most effective prevention, but when parents refuse it the oral schedule of three doses is the accepted alternative and is markedly better than nothing. Because oral prophylaxis fails more often, especially in infants with unrecognised cholestasis, the later two doses must be arranged explicitly rather than left to chance. Accepting outright refusal, giving the injection covertly and relying on maternal supplementation are all unsafe responses in different ways. The conversation and the residual risk belong in the record.
key_points: Late bleeding occurs at two to twelve weeks and often presents as intracranial haemorrhage.
Exclusively breastfed infants who receive no prophylaxis carry the highest risk.
The oral alternative is three doses, at birth, at three to five days and at four weeks.
Oral prophylaxis fails more often than intramuscular, particularly with undiagnosed cholestasis.
Treating a child over an explicit parental refusal without legal authority is unlawful.
explanation.pearls: When parents accept the oral route, book the four week dose before they leave the ward, because the third dose is the one families forget and it is the dose that covers the window in which late intracranial bleeding actually occurs.

sources.label: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K
RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.rationale: Notification is reserved for refusal of treatment for an established life threatening condition, not for declining prophylaxis where a reasonable alternative is accepted. Escalating at this point damages a relationship these parents have engaged with and would not change the outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.rationale: Maternal supplementation raises breastmilk concentrations only modestly and unpredictably, and breastmilk is inherently a poor source, which is why exclusively breastfed infants carry the highest risk of late bleeding. It cannot be relied on as the infant prophylaxis. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

options.rationale: Where an injection is refused, the oral schedule of three doses given at birth, at three to five days and at four weeks is the recognised alternative for a breastfed infant and preserves most of the protection. It is less effective than the single intramuscular dose, particularly against late bleeding, so the discussion and the residual risk are recorded and the parents are told the later doses are essential. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

options.rationale: Treating a child against an explicit parental refusal without legal authority is an assault and destroys the trust on which every subsequent conversation depends. The strength of the clinical case for the injection does not create consent. (Source: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.rationale: Surveillance does not prevent bleeding, and late haemorrhagic disease presents as intracranial bleeding without warning signs in a previously well infant. Declining the injection is the parents right, but leaving the infant with no prophylaxis at all when an oral alternative is available is not an equivalent plan. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

explanation.summary: The two questions that decide the management of a swallowed metallic disc are where it is and what it is. An object still in the oesophagus needs removal because it causes pressure necrosis and cannot be expected to pass, whereas a blunt object that has reached the stomach passes spontaneously in almost all children. The appearance on the film distinguishes a coin from a button battery, which shows a double ring on the frontal view and a step at the edge on the lateral, and a battery in the oesophagus is a surgical emergency because it burns through the wall within hours. This child has a smooth uniform disc below the diaphragm and no symptoms, so she can go home with return advice. Repeat imaging has a role only if the object has still not passed after several weeks.
key_points: A blunt object that has reached the stomach passes spontaneously in the great majority of children.
A button battery shows a double ring on the frontal film and a step on the lateral.
A battery lodged in the oesophagus causes mucosal burns within two hours and needs immediate removal.
Sharp objects, elongated objects and multiple magnets warrant retrieval even from the stomach.
Laxatives do not speed transit and serial same day films change nothing.
explanation.pearls: Look for the double ring on the frontal film before you call anything a coin, because a 20 mm lithium battery and a coin are the same size and shade, and mistaking one for the other costs the child an oesophageal perforation within hours.

options.rationale: Urgent removal from the stomach is reserved for a button battery, for a sharp or elongated object, and for multiple magnets, each of which causes injury while it sits there. A single smooth coin in the stomach of a well child does none of that. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

Coins of 20 mm and above do lodge more often in a small child, which is why the oesophagus must be imaged, but this one has already passed the narrow points and lies in the stomach. The site on the film, not the diameter alone, determines the risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

Laxatives do not accelerate the passage of an ingested foreign body and fasting a toddler for days is both unnecessary and unkind. Normal diet encourages normal transit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal foreign bodies)

A blunt object that has reached the stomach in an asymptomatic child of this size passes without intervention in the great majority of cases, so management is observation at home with clear return advice. The radiograph excludes the two appearances that would change this, a lodged oesophageal position and the double ring that identifies a battery. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

Serial films are used when an object remains in the stomach on a repeat film taken after some weeks, which is the point at which retrieval is considered. Imaging a well child again the same day exposes her to radiation without any decision depending on the result. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance is that all infants should be given the common allergenic foods, including peanut and egg, in the first year of life and preferably by around six months, once solids have begun. Infants with eczema have the highest risk of food allergy and therefore stand to gain the most, so eczema is a reason to introduce earlier rather than to delay. Screening tests before a first exposure are counterproductive because sensitisation without clinical allergy is common and a positive result leads to unnecessary avoidance. Whole nuts are a choking hazard at this age, so peanut is given as a smooth paste thinned into food the infant already takes. Regular ongoing intake matters, because tolerance is maintained by continued exposure rather than by a single successful feed.
key_points: Introduce common allergenic foods in the first year, preferably around six months.
Eczema raises the risk of food allergy and argues for earlier, not later, introduction.
Screening tests before a first exposure detect sensitisation and cause unnecessary avoidance.
Whole or chopped nuts are a choking hazard until about four years of age.
Regular continued intake is needed to maintain tolerance once the food is introduced.
explanation.pearls: Tell the family to keep peanut in the diet at least twice a week after the first successful feed, because a single tolerated exposure followed by months of avoidance does not maintain tolerance and allergy can still develop.

sources.label: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Testing before introduction in a child who has never reacted generates positive results that reflect sensitisation rather than clinical allergy, and acting on them delays or prevents an introduction that would have been tolerated. Testing is indicated after a reaction, not before a first exposure. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Maternal avoidance during breastfeeding is unnecessary and her diet can return to normal, but exposure through breastmilk is not the mechanism that induces tolerance. The infant needs to eat the food herself in a form she can manage. (Source: NHMRC: Infant Feeding Guidelines)

Waiting for clear skin postpones introduction past the window in which it is protective, and moderate eczema in infancy often persists for years. Eczema raises the risk of allergy, which is a reason to introduce sooner rather than later. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Introducing peanut in the first year and continuing it regularly reduces the development of peanut allergy, and the benefit is greatest in infants with eczema because they carry the highest baseline risk. She has already tolerated other solids and has no history of reaction, so the introduction happens at home in the usual way with a smooth form appropriate to her age. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.rationale: Supervised introduction is reserved for an infant who has already reacted to that food or who has a sibling with anaphylaxis and a positive test. Routine referral for every infant with eczema would delay introduction by months and is not what the risk justifies. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

explanation.summary: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis are both common in the first year and are frequently confused, but they separate cleanly on three features. Seborrhoeic dermatitis appears in the first weeks to months, produces greasy adherent scale on the scalp, face and flexures including the nappy area, and above all does not itch, so the infant is comfortable. Atopic dermatitis appears later, itches intensely enough to disturb sleep, spares the nappy area and favours the cheeks and extensor surfaces. Getting this right matters because it determines whether the family leaves with reassurance and an emollient or with a corticosteroid, a formula change and an unnecessary interruption to breastfeeding. Referral is reserved for the infant whose scalp rash is petechial or purpuric, fails simple treatment, or comes with organomegaly or faltering growth.
key_points: Seborrhoeic dermatitis in infancy does not itch and the infant is comfortable.
It involves the nappy area and flexures, which atopic dermatitis characteristically spares.
Atopic dermatitis appears later in infancy and disturbs sleep through itch.
Treatment is emollient softening and gentle washing, and it resolves by around a year.
Petechial scale with organomegaly or faltering growth warrants urgent assessment.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the baby scratches or wakes because of the rash, because a comfortable infant with a florid scaly scalp has seborrhoeic dermatitis and needs paraffin, while an infant who rubs his face on the sheets has atopic dermatitis and needs a steroid.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial belongs to suspected cow milk protein allergy, which presents with blood or mucus in the stools, vomiting, poor weight gain or an itchy eczema that fails standard treatment. Advising a thriving breastfed infant to stop breastfeeding for a rash of this appearance causes real harm for no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

Greasy adherent scale on the scalp and face with flexural involvement in a comfortable infant who does not scratch is a self-limiting condition of the first months that resolves without active treatment. Loosening the scale with an emollient such as white soft paraffin or a bath oil before gentle washing is all that is required, and the parents need to know it settles by around a year. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.rationale: Urgent referral is warranted when a scaly scalp rash is petechial or purpuric, fails to respond to simple measures, or occurs with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or faltering growth, because Langerhans cell histiocytosis can present this way. A thriving infant with typical greasy scale and none of those features does not need a biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

Bacterial infection complicating an infant rash produces honey coloured crusting, weeping, surrounding erythema and often fever, none of which is present. Greasy scale without any of those features is not an infection and antibiotics treat nothing. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.rationale: A topical corticosteroid is the treatment for atopic dermatitis, which itches intensely, spares the nappy area and appears later in infancy on the cheeks and the outer limbs. This infant does not scratch and has flexural and nappy involvement, so the diagnosis is different and a moderately potent steroid on facial and flexural skin risks atrophy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

explanation.summary: Hairs broken off a few millimetres above the scalp identify an infection inside the hair shaft rather than on the skin surface, and that anatomical fact drives the entire management. Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the shaft, so scalp disease requires an oral agent for six to eight weeks, and the four weeks of failed cream in this history is the expected outcome rather than a sign of resistance. Samples for microscopy and culture are taken before treatment because the responsible species influences the drug choice and because a long course should not rest on a clinical guess. Reactive occipital nodes are typical and do not indicate bacterial infection, while a boggy pustular mass represents the inflammatory form that additionally risks scarring alopecia. Antifungal shampoo is an adjunct that reduces transmission to household and school contacts.
key_points: Hairs broken close to the scalp indicate infection within the shaft.
Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the hair shaft and reliably fail on the scalp.
Oral treatment runs six to eight weeks and samples are taken before it starts.
Reactive occipital lymphadenopathy is expected and does not mean bacterial infection.
A boggy pustular mass is the inflammatory form and risks permanent scarring alopecia.
explanation.pearls: Any scalp scale with broken hairs and palpable occipital nodes gets an oral antifungal and a specimen, never a cream, because every week of topical treatment is a week the shaft infection keeps spreading and the culture takes up to four weeks to come back.

options.rationale: Psoriasis produces thick silvery scale on a well demarcated plaque and characteristically spares the hair, whereas hairs broken off close to the scalp indicate the shaft itself is infected. A corticosteroid without an antifungal allows a dermatophyte to spread more widely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

Potency is not the problem, penetration is. No topical preparation reaches the fungal elements within the hair shaft, which is why four weeks of cream produced nothing and why another eight weeks would do the same. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

Fungal infection of the scalp sits within the hair shaft, where topical agents cannot reach, so systemic treatment for several weeks is required and topical therapy alone predictably fails. Samples are taken before treatment starts because the course runs for six to eight weeks and the species identified guides the choice and duration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

Reactive occipital nodes are an expected part of scalp fungal infection and do not by themselves indicate bacterial disease. A tender boggy mass with pustules would suggest the inflammatory form, which still needs an antifungal and is treated with an added corticosteroid rather than an antibiotic alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

Shampoo reduces surface spores and is a useful adjunct that limits spread to others, but it does not cure the infection within the shaft. Exclusion from school is not required once systemic treatment has started. (Source: RCH CPG: Skin infections)

explanation.summary: Night predominant itch with linear tracks in the web spaces and on the flexor wrists is the classic distribution of this infestation, and involvement of the soles is characteristic in infants and toddlers. The single most common reason treatment fails is that asymptomatic household contacts are not treated, because itch is a hypersensitivity phenomenon that takes four to six weeks to develop after a first infestation. Everyone in the household is therefore treated on the same day, whether or not they itch, and the application is repeated a week later to kill mites that hatch from eggs surviving the first treatment. In children under two the cream is applied to the scalp and face as well as the body, and to the palms and soles at every age. Bedding and clothing from the preceding days are washed hot or sealed for several days.
key_points: Itch develops four to six weeks after a first infestation, so contacts are infested before they are symptomatic.
All household members are treated on the same day regardless of symptoms.
Application is repeated after seven days to cover eggs surviving the first treatment.
In infants and toddlers the scalp, face, palms and soles are all treated.
Itch persisting up to two weeks after treatment does not indicate failure.
explanation.pearls: Warn the family before they leave that the itch will continue for up to two weeks after successful treatment, or they will return convinced it has failed and be tempted into a third and fourth application that only causes irritant dermatitis.

options.rationale: Itch arises from a delayed hypersensitivity response that takes four to six weeks after a first infestation, so an asymptomatic contact is very often already infested. Waiting for symptoms is what produces the cycle of repeated treatment failures families describe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

Oral treatment is reserved for crusted disease, for outbreaks in institutions and for people in whom topical treatment has failed or cannot be applied. It is not used as first line for ordinary infestation in a small child, where topical treatment is effective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

A corticosteroid may be added after the infestation has been treated, because itch commonly persists for a fortnight once the mites are dead. Given alone it suppresses the inflammatory response, allows the mites to multiply and produces the widespread crusted form in a vulnerable child. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

Treating only the symptomatic child guarantees reinfestation, because contacts carry mites for weeks before itch begins, which is why the father and brother being well does not exclude them. Simultaneous treatment of the whole household with a second application a week later covers eggs that survive the first, and permethrin is applied to the whole body including the scalp and soles in a child of this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

Secondary bacterial infection does complicate scratched lesions and is treated when honey coloured crusting, surrounding erythema or systemic features appear. This child has excoriation without any of those signs, so antibiotics address nothing and leave the cause untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

explanation.summary: Physiological bowing is symmetrical, painless and improves after the second birthday, and it is not accompanied by changes elsewhere in the skeleton. Widening at the wrists, prominences along the costochondral junctions, a delayed fontanelle and height crossing centiles all point instead to failure of mineralisation at the growth plate. The risk factors here are prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation beyond six months, minimal dietary intake and almost no ultraviolet exposure, which together deplete vitamin D stores. Baseline biochemistry confirms the metabolic picture and separates nutritional deficiency, in which parathyroid hormone rises and phosphate falls, from the inherited phosphate wasting disorders that require a different treatment. Treatment follows the results and is high dose vitamin D with adequate calcium, since replacing vitamin D alone in a child with poor calcium intake gives an incomplete response.
key_points: Wrist widening and costochondral prominences distinguish metabolic bone disease from physiological bowing.
Physiological bowing is symmetrical and improves after about two years of age.
Prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation plus minimal sun exposure depletes vitamin D stores.
A raised alkaline phosphatase with low phosphate and raised parathyroid hormone indicates the deficiency state.
Calcium intake must be adequate or vitamin D replacement alone gives an incomplete response.
explanation.pearls: Run your thumb along the costochondral junctions of any toddler with bowed legs, because a palpable row of beads turns an orthopaedic referral into a blood test and a treatable deficiency that also affects the mother and the next baby.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.rationale: Wrist widening and costochondral prominences are the signs of unmineralised growth plate rather than of physiological bowing, and this biochemical panel confirms the metabolic pattern and shows how far it has progressed. A raised alkaline phosphatase with a low phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone identifies the deficiency state and distinguishes it from the inherited phosphate wasting forms. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Malabsorption is a genuine cause of this bone disease and coeliac serology belongs in the workup if the first line biochemistry is abnormal and the dietary history does not explain it. Here the combination of prolonged breastfeeding with minimal solids and near complete sun avoidance explains the deficiency directly, and his stools are normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Densitometry in a toddler is difficult to interpret because results must be corrected for bone size and skeletal maturity, and it does not distinguish the cause. The diagnosis here is biochemical and radiographic, not densitometric. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Treatment is indeed high dose vitamin D with adequate calcium intake, but starting before baseline biochemistry removes the ability to confirm the diagnosis and to detect the inherited phosphate wasting forms that will not respond. Baseline results also allow the response to be measured. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Alignment films are used when bowing is the only abnormality and the question is physiological bowing against a growth plate disorder of one side. Wrist widening, rib changes and height crossing centiles have already moved this beyond an alignment problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Effortless posseting of unchanged milk in an infant who feeds willingly, settles afterwards and grows along a centile is physiological and needs explanation rather than treatment. The feed volume matters: 180 mL every three hours in a baby of this age is well above the usual requirement of about 150 mL per kilogram per day, and overfeeding is one of the few reversible contributors. Acid suppression has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for crying and vomiting in infants and carries a real infection risk, so it is reserved for proven oesophagitis or for reflux with faltering growth. Features that should redirect the assessment include bile or blood in the vomit, faltering growth, feed refusal, blood in the stools and fever. Side or prone sleeping is never recommended because the risk of sudden unexpected death outweighs any reduction in reflux.
key_points: Effortless vomiting with normal growth and settled behaviour needs explanation, not treatment.
Requirement is about 150 mL per kilogram per day and exceeding it worsens posseting.
Acid suppression does not outperform placebo for infant crying or vomiting.
Bile, blood, faltering growth, fever or feed refusal each redirect the assessment.
Supine sleeping is maintained regardless of reflux because of sudden death risk.
explanation.pearls: Work out the millilitres per kilogram per day before you write anything, because a baby taking over 200 mL per kilogram daily will keep vomiting on any dose of any acid suppressant, and reducing the volume per feed usually settles it within a week.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial is reasonable where vomiting occurs with blood or mucus in the stools, eczema, faltering growth or marked feed refusal, since cow milk protein allergy can mimic reflux. None of those features is present and a formula change adds cost and complexity without a target. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Effortless vomiting of unchanged milk in a thriving infant who feeds happily is a normal developmental phenomenon that resolves as the infant spends more time upright and takes solids. He is being offered around 200 mL per kilogram per day, well above requirement, and overfeeding is the reversible driver here, so reducing the volume per feed while keeping the frequency is the intervention that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Positional measures reduce measured reflux episodes but any sleep position other than supine increases the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy, so the trade is not acceptable. Cot elevation has not been shown to reduce symptoms and can cause the infant to slide into an unsafe position. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

Pyloric stenosis presents with forceful vomiting during or straight after a feed in a hungry infant who loses weight, and it declares itself between two and eight weeks. Effortless vomiting with steady growth at three months does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting in infants)

Trials in infants show acid suppression does not reduce crying or vomiting more than placebo, and it is associated with increased gastrointestinal and respiratory infection. Its place is in proven oesophagitis or in reflux with faltering growth, neither of which describes a settled infant on the 75th centile. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

explanation.summary: Brief arousals between sleep cycles happen in every young child several times a night, and whether they become a presenting problem depends on what the child needs in order to fall back asleep. A child who falls asleep at bedtime with a parent beside her requires that same parent at each arousal, which converts normal physiology into repeated calls for help. The effective intervention therefore targets bedtime rather than the night waking itself, teaching the child to fall asleep independently through graduated settling with progressively longer intervals before responding. Snoring only during colds, a clear nasal airway and small tonsils argue against obstructive sleep apnoea, which is the differential that would require a very different pathway. Parental exhaustion of this degree deserves acknowledgement in its own right and makes deferral an unsatisfactory answer.
key_points: Night waking becomes a problem when the child cannot return to sleep unaided.
The conditions present at sleep onset must be recreated at each normal arousal.
Graduated settling targets bedtime and has the strongest evidence at this age.
Habitual snoring, witnessed pauses or mouth breathing indicate assessment for obstructive sleep apnoea.
A single early afternoon nap remains developmentally appropriate at two years.
explanation.pearls: Ask exactly what is happening in the room at the moment the child first falls asleep, because that detail predicts what she will demand at two in the morning better than anything else in the history, and changing it is what fixes the nights.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.rationale: Learned sleep associations of this kind persist for years without intervention rather than resolving on their own, and the maternal sleep deprivation described is itself a safety issue at work and on the road. Reassurance without a plan leaves a treatable problem in place. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.rationale: She wakes normally between sleep cycles as every toddler does, but she can only return to sleep by recreating the conditions present when she first fell asleep, which is a parent lying beside her. Changing what happens at bedtime is therefore the intervention that changes the night waking, and graduated settling with progressively delayed responses has the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.rationale: Melatonin shortens the time taken to fall asleep and has a place in neurodevelopmental conditions where the sleep phase is genuinely delayed. It does not address a learned sleep association and does not reduce night waking of this type, and it is not first line in an otherwise well toddler. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.rationale: A sleep study is directed at habitual snoring, witnessed pauses, mouth breathing, restless sleep with sweating or daytime behavioural change. Snoring only with intercurrent colds and a clear airway on examination does not meet that threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

One early afternoon nap is developmentally appropriate at two years and removing it usually produces an overtired child who settles worse. Nap timing matters if the nap runs late into the afternoon, which is not the case here. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

explanation.summary: The decision to treat a sore throat with antibiotics in Australia depends on where the child lives rather than on the appearance of the throat. In most urban settings sore throats are managed symptomatically because rheumatic fever is rare and antibiotics shorten symptoms by less than a day. In communities with a high incidence of acute rheumatic fever, every sore throat in a child of school age is treated empirically and immediately, because the aim is preventing a disease that follows untreated infection weeks later. Oral penicillin for ten days is the standard course, with the long-acting injection used when adherence to a ten day oral course is uncertain, and a macrolide reserved for genuine penicillin allergy. Treatment is not stopped if the swab later returns negative in a high risk setting.
key_points: Background rheumatic fever incidence, not throat appearance, determines whether to treat empirically.
The aim of treatment is preventing rheumatic fever rather than shortening the sore throat.
Ten days of oral penicillin is required, since shorter courses do not prevent rheumatic fever.
The long-acting intramuscular injection is an option when oral adherence is uncertain.
Secondary prophylaxis applies to children who have already had rheumatic fever or have rheumatic heart disease.
explanation.pearls: In a high incidence community, treat the sore throat the day it walks in and finish all ten days, because the rheumatic fever that follows arrives two to four weeks later in a child who has long since felt better and stopped the tablets.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.rationale: Waiting for a result is the correct approach in a low risk urban setting, where most sore throats are viral and rheumatic fever is rare. Here it leaves a child in a high incidence community untreated for four days during the window in which treatment prevents rheumatic fever. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.rationale: The long-acting injection is the mainstay of secondary prophylaxis, given four weekly to a child who has already had rheumatic fever or has established rheumatic heart disease. A single dose is also an option for treating this episode if adherence to oral treatment is doubtful, but calling it prophylaxis misplaces it, since he has had no previous episode. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.rationale: The organism responsible remains uniformly susceptible to penicillin, so broadening the spectrum adds adverse effects and selection pressure with no gain. A seven day course would also fall short of the duration needed to prevent rheumatic fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)

A macrolide is the alternative for a child with genuine penicillin allergy, and shorter courses are attractive for adherence. Macrolide resistance among these organisms is rising and the shorter course has not been shown to prevent rheumatic fever, so it is a second line choice rather than a convenience option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)

Where rheumatic fever is common, every sore throat in a child of school age is treated as streptococcal from the moment it presents, because the purpose of treatment is preventing rheumatic fever rather than shortening the illness. A full ten day course is required for that purpose, and stopping early on a negative swab is not recommended in a high risk setting. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset because that determines the likely organism and therefore the route of treatment. Presentation within the first few days with marked chemosis suggests gonococcal infection and is a sight threatening emergency needing parenteral therapy. Onset towards the end of the first week or in the second week suggests chlamydial infection, which requires oral macrolide therapy because the organism also colonises the nasopharynx and can produce an afebrile pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks. Diagnosis of either in a neonate is also a diagnosis in the parents, so contact testing and treatment are part of the management.
key_points: Day of onset is the main clue to the organism in neonatal conjunctivitis
Chlamydial infection needs oral not topical therapy because of nasopharyngeal carriage
Untreated chlamydial carriage can cause an afebrile pneumonitis weeks later
A swab for nucleic acid testing is taken before treatment starts
Parental testing and treatment are part of managing the neonate
explanation.pearls: Chlamydial conjunctivitis typically declares itself between day five and day fourteen, and the oral macrolide is given to prevent the pneumonitis that can follow at four to twelve weeks, not merely to clear the eye.

options.rationale: Onset at the end of the first week with copious discharge and lid oedema points to a genitally acquired organism, which needs systemic rather than topical therapy because it also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause pneumonitis. Treating the parents prevents reinfection and addresses their own untreated infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Topical therapy does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage and so does not prevent the later respiratory complication. It would be reasonable for an uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis in an older infant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Saline toilet alone is appropriate for a blocked tear duct, which presents with watering rather than this degree of purulent discharge and lid swelling. Withholding treatment here risks progression. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

This intensity of treatment is reserved for the hyperacute presentation of a different genital organism, which characteristically appears in the first days of life with marked chemosis and corneal risk. The timing and corneal findings here do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antiviral therapy is directed at a vesicular or dendritic presentation, and the fluorescein stain here shows no dendritic ulcer. Copious purulent discharge is not the expected pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the classic driver, displacing iron rich solids and causing occult gut blood loss. The diagnosis rests on a microcytic hypochromic picture with a low ferritin, remembering that ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal during inflammation. Treatment is oral elemental iron with a deliberate continuation phase after the haemoglobin corrects, because haemoglobin recovery precedes store repletion by months. Failure to respond should prompt review of adherence, of ongoing losses, and of alternative diagnoses such as thalassaemia trait.
key_points: Cow milk intake above about 500 mL daily in toddlers displaces dietary iron
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal with inflammation
Haemoglobin corrects within weeks but stores need months of continued therapy
A reticulocyte rise within a week supports the diagnosis
Persistent failure to respond prompts review for thalassaemia trait or blood loss
explanation.pearls: Continue oral iron for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation: stopping the day the count is normal is the single commonest reason a toddler is back with the same microcytic anaemia six months later.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.rationale: Stopping at haemoglobin normalisation leaves stores depleted and the anaemia predictably recurs. The haemoglobin recovers well before ferritin does. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Diet alone is too slow to correct an established deficiency of this degree, though it is essential to prevent recurrence. It would be appropriate for borderline iron status without anaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Parenteral iron is reserved for failed or not tolerated oral therapy, malabsorption, or ongoing losses, none of which has been established here. Oral therapy has not yet been tried. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.rationale: Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic severe anaemia, and this child is stable with a haemoglobin well above that threshold. It would also delay the diagnostic value of the response to iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

Replacement corrects the haemoglobin within weeks but the stores take far longer, so treatment continues past normalisation to refill ferritin and prevent early relapse. Reducing milk volume and increasing iron rich solids is given alongside the supplement. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis means bedwetting with a normal daytime voiding pattern and no other urinary symptoms, and it is distinguished from non-monosymptomatic enuresis because the two are managed differently. Constipation must be excluded and treated first because it is a common reversible contributor. The alarm and desmopressin both work but differ in what they achieve: the alarm conditions arousal and gives the best chance of dryness that persists after treatment ends, while desmopressin acts only while it is taken and is best used for short term cover of specific events. Choosing between them therefore depends on whether the family wants a durable cure or immediate cover, and on their capacity to persist with a device that wakes the household.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis requires a normal daytime voiding pattern
Treat coexisting constipation before starting enuresis specific therapy
The alarm gives the highest sustained dryness after treatment stops
Desmopressin suits short term cover such as camps and sleepovers
Imaging is reserved for daytime symptoms or abnormal examination
explanation.pearls: Alarm training needs a minimum of six to eight weeks of consistent nightly use before it is judged to have failed, so it is the wrong choice when a family needs dryness for an event only days away.

options.rationale: The alarm produces the highest rate of sustained dryness after treatment stops, which matches this family's stated goal and their capacity to persist. The timeframe before camp comfortably allows a full alarm course. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

Desmopressin suppresses wetting while it is being taken but relapse on stopping is common, so it suits short term cover such as a single camp rather than a durable cure. Here there is ample time for definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

Lifting a sleeping child does not teach the arousal response and simply empties the bladder, and severe evening fluid restriction is not effective as sole therapy. These measures support but do not replace definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

Anticholinergic therapy targets detrusor overactivity, which typically shows as daytime urgency and frequency, and this boy has an entirely normal daytime pattern. It would be considered where alarm and desmopressin have both failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, abnormal examination, or treatment resistant cases, none of which applies to uncomplicated monosymptomatic bedwetting. His assessment is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened clinically in every newborn, but clinical examination detects instability rather than dysplasia and therefore misses a proportion of affected hips. Selective ultrasound is added for recognised risk factors, principally a first degree family history and breech presentation in later pregnancy. The timing of the scan matters as much as the decision to order it, because maternal hormone mediated laxity in the first weeks produces immature appearances that resolve spontaneously and generate false positives. A frankly dislocated or dislocatable hip on examination is a different situation and needs urgent orthopaedic referral rather than a routine scan.
key_points: Clinical examination detects instability but can miss dysplasia without instability
First degree family history and breech presentation prompt selective ultrasound
Ultrasound is deferred to around six weeks to avoid physiological false positives
Radiography is unhelpful until the femoral head ossifies at four to six months
An abnormal examination needs orthopaedic referral rather than routine imaging
explanation.pearls: A positive Ortolani or Barlow test at the newborn check bypasses the six week ultrasound pathway entirely and goes straight to orthopaedic referral, because a dislocatable hip is a treatment decision rather than a screening question.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Newborn hip screening

options.rationale: Scanning in the first days of life commonly shows physiological immaturity from maternal hormones and generates false positives with unnecessary follow up. The examination timing, not the modality, is what is wrong here. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: A first degree family history is a risk factor that warrants imaging even when the examination is normal, because dysplasia can be present without instability. Scanning is deferred to about six weeks so that normal neonatal laxity has resolved and the study is interpretable. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: The femoral head is not ossified at this age so radiography cannot assess the joint reliably, and ultrasound is the modality of choice. Radiography becomes useful once the ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Double nappies are not an effective treatment or substitute for imaging and may falsely reassure the family. Clinical review alone will miss dysplasia without instability. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Relying on serial examination alone misses the dysplastic but stable hip, which is exactly the pattern that a family history predicts. Risk factors change the screening pathway even when examination is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Deciding whether a fracture is accidental rests on whether the injury, the explanation, and the child's developmental stage are congruent, not on the fracture configuration alone. The spiral tibial fracture of early walking, sometimes described as a toddler's fracture, is produced by a twisting force through a planted foot and is a common accidental injury once a child is independently mobile. The features that should raise concern are a fracture in a child who is not yet mobile, an absent or changing explanation, delayed presentation, injuries of differing ages, or associated bruising in sites that do not take the impact of ordinary falls. Every child under two with a suspicious fracture warrants a skeletal survey, and inflicted injury should be considered alongside metabolic bone disease rather than instead of it.
key_points: Congruence of injury, explanation and developmental stage drives the assessment
Spiral tibial fractures are a recognised accidental pattern in walking toddlers
A fracture in a pre-mobile infant is the strongest single red flag
Skeletal survey is indicated under two years when the account is inconsistent
Metabolic bone disease is considered alongside, not instead of, inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: The developmental question that reframes a toddler fracture is whether the child walks independently: the same spiral tibial fracture that is unremarkable at sixteen months demands a skeletal survey in a 6-month-old who cannot yet cruise.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

options.rationale: Notification is driven by a mismatch between injury and explanation rather than by fracture type alone, and no such mismatch exists here. A spiral configuration is not by itself an indicator of inflicted injury in a mobile child. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

A skeletal survey is indicated for children under two when the injury is unexplained or inconsistent, which is not the case with this witnessed and congruent account. It would be correct had he been pre-mobile. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

A spiral fracture of the distal tibia in an independently walking toddler is a recognised accidental pattern produced by rotation on a planted foot, and the mechanism, mobility and consistent history fit it. There are no other injuries and no features that would make the account implausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Metabolic bone investigation is prompted by multiple fractures, blue sclerae, wormian bones or a family history, none of which is present. A below knee cast also fails to control rotation at this level. (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

options.rationale: This fracture needs immobilisation to control rotational forces and to provide pain relief, so symptomatic management alone is inadequate. It would suit an undisplaced buckle fracture of the distal radius. (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

explanation.summary: The vomiting neonate presenting in the second week of life is a high stakes presentation because the common benign diagnoses and the lethal ones share a surface appearance. The electrolyte pattern does most of the discriminating work: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis indicates gastric outlet obstruction, whereas hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and acidosis indicates adrenal insufficiency. Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically declares itself between day seven and day twenty one, after the newborn check and often after discharge, and virilisation may be obvious in an affected girl but absent in a boy, so normal looking genitalia offer no reassurance. Treatment is fluid resuscitation with immediate hydrocortisone, and the diagnostic sample is drawn before the first steroid dose so that confirmation remains possible.
key_points: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia in a neonate suggests adrenal insufficiency
Gastric outlet obstruction produces the opposite acid base and potassium picture
Salt wasting crisis typically presents after the newborn check in the second week
Normal appearing genitalia do not exclude the diagnosis in a male infant
Take the diagnostic sample before the first hydrocortisone dose
explanation.pearls: A male infant with salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia has no virilisation to give the diagnosis away, so the second week presentation of vomiting with a potassium above 6 mmol/L and a sodium below 130 mmol/L is the finding that must trigger hydrocortisone.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.rationale: This is the pathway for gastric outlet obstruction, which produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis and a palpable mass rather than this electrolyte pattern. The acid base and potassium findings here point the opposite way. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Sepsis is a reasonable parallel consideration and cultures should be taken, but antibiotics alone do not address the hormone deficiency that is driving the electrolyte derangement. Treating only for sepsis risks a fatal outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a collapsing neonate indicates mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency, which needs fluid resuscitation and immediate steroid replacement. Taking the diagnostic sample first preserves the ability to confirm the diagnosis without delaying treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or coma attributable to hyponatraemia, and rapid correction in a chronically adapted neonate risks osmotic injury. The sodium here will correct as the underlying deficiency is treated. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia)

Cow milk protein allergy causes vomiting and poor feeding but does not produce hyperkalaemia with hypoglycaemia and acidosis. The metabolic picture excludes it as the explanation. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

explanation.summary: Viral croup follows a predictable course in which dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline produce reliable improvement, with adrenaline wearing off over two to three hours rather than forty minutes. Departure from that course is the signal to reconsider the diagnosis, and the specific combination of high fever, a toxic appearance and poor or short lived response to adrenaline suggests bacterial tracheitis. This is a bacterial infection of the trachea, most often staphylococcal, that produces adherent purulent membranes and can obstruct the airway abruptly. Management is urgent airway inspection by anaesthetics and ENT in a controlled environment with antistaphylococcal antibiotics, since these children frequently require intubation and toilet of the airway. Epiglottitis remains in the differential but is now rare in immunised children and classically produces a muffled voice with marked drooling rather than a hoarse voice and barking cough.
key_points: Nebulised adrenaline should give two to three hours of improvement in croup
A toxic appearance with high fever is not part of uncomplicated viral croup
Bacterial tracheitis is most often staphylococcal and may need intubation
Airway inspection belongs in theatre, not in the radiology department
Epiglottitis gives a muffled voice and drooling rather than a barking cough
explanation.pearls: Recurrence of stridor within an hour of nebulised adrenaline, rather than at the expected two to three hours, alongside a rising fever is the combination that should move bacterial tracheitis ahead of croup and trigger a call to anaesthetics.

options.rationale: Repeat adrenaline is appropriate for recurrent stridor in an otherwise well child with viral croup, but here the fever and toxic appearance signal a different pathology. Repeating it treats the symptom while the underlying process progresses. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Corticosteroid has already been given and a further dose does not address a bacterial process, while ward admission without airway assessment misjudges the risk. Steroid dosing is not the limiting factor here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Sending a child with a compromised airway to the radiology department removes them from immediate help and delays definitive assessment. Imaging does not change the need for inspection under controlled conditions. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

High flow therapy does not relieve a fixed upper airway obstruction and may delay recognition of deterioration, and the steroid route is not the issue. Neither addresses the likely bacterial cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

A toxic child with rising fever whose stridor recurs rapidly after adrenaline has moved outside the expected course of viral croup and suggests bacterial infection of the trachea. Definitive assessment is airway inspection in a controlled setting with antistaphylococcal cover started. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Bone pain in adolescents is common and almost always benign, so the discriminating features matter: pain that wakes the child from sleep, pain that persists beyond the expected course of an injury, systemic symptoms such as weight loss, and a palpable mass all argue against a mechanical cause. Osteosarcoma has a peak incidence during the adolescent growth spurt and arises most often in the metaphyses around the knee and proximal humerus. The radiographic hallmarks are an aggressive periosteal reaction, either lamellated or spiculated, with cortical destruction and a soft tissue component. The single most consequential management point is that biopsy must be planned and performed by the unit that will carry out the definitive resection, because a poorly sited tract contaminates tissue planes and can cost the patient their limb.
key_points: Night waking pain and weight loss are the features that reframe adolescent bone pain
Osteosarcoma favours the metaphyses around the knee during the growth spurt
Aggressive periosteal reaction with cortical destruction suggests malignancy
The biopsy tract is excised at definitive surgery and must be sited by that unit
Osteomyelitis usually produces fever and markedly raised inflammatory markers
explanation.pearls: Refer a suspected primary bone tumour before biopsy rather than after: a tract placed outside the sarcoma unit crosses compartments that the definitive resection would have spared and is a recognised reason limb salvage becomes impossible.

options.rationale: A locally placed biopsy tract can cross compartments that the definitive resection would otherwise spare and may convert a salvageable limb into an amputation. The diagnosis is not what determines where the biopsy happens. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

Osteomyelitis is the main alternative but would be expected to produce fever with markedly raised inflammatory markers rather than this indolent four month course with weight loss. Treating empirically would delay oncological staging. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

Magnetic resonance imaging is part of staging but a six week wait is far too long given an aggressive radiographic appearance and progressive symptoms. Timeliness is the problem rather than the modality. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

Marked relief with a non-steroidal agent suggests osteoid osteoma, which produces a small sclerotic lesion with a lucent nidus rather than cortical destruction. A therapeutic trial here would waste critical time. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

Night pain, weight loss, a soft tissue mass and an aggressive periosteal reaction indicate a primary bone malignancy, and the biopsy tract itself becomes part of the tissue that must later be resected. Performing it outside the treating unit can compromise limb salvage, so referral precedes biopsy. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

explanation.summary: Prolonged neonatal jaundice is defined as jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant or twenty one days in a preterm infant, and it mandates fractionation of the bilirubin rather than reassurance. The purpose of that single test is to separate the common and benign unconjugated causes, principally breast milk jaundice and hypothyroidism, from conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, which is always pathological. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that drives the urgency, because the success of the Kasai portoenterostomy falls substantially once the infant is beyond about sixty days of age, and an infant who looks well and is feeding normally can still have it. Pale stools and dark urine are the classic accompanying features and should never be attributed to breast milk jaundice. Other conjugated causes include neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, metabolic disease and sepsis.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term infant requires bilirubin fractionation
A raised conjugated fraction is always pathological and needs urgent workup
Pale stools with dark urine exclude breast milk jaundice
A well looking, thriving baby can still have biliary atresia
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes deteriorate sharply beyond about sixty days
explanation.pearls: The Kasai portoenterostomy achieves far better bile drainage when performed before sixty days of age, which is why a 3-week-old with pale stools needs the conjugated fraction measured the same day rather than at the next routine visit.

options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires an unconjugated picture with normally pigmented stools, and pale stools exclude it outright. Reassurance here would delay a time-critical diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days requires the bilirubin to be fractionated, because a raised conjugated fraction indicates cholestasis and demands urgent investigation. Pale stools with dark urine make this imperative, since the outcome of biliary atresia surgery deteriorates sharply with age. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

A total level without fractionation cannot distinguish cholestasis from unconjugated jaundice, and phototherapy charts do not apply beyond the early neonatal period. Fractionation is the step that changes management. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Interrupting feeding to observe a fall in bilirubin is an outdated approach that risks undermining breastfeeding and wastes time. It does not address the possibility of an obstructive cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Haemolytic disease presents in the first days of life with an unconjugated picture and anaemia, not at three weeks with pale stools. The stool colour points to an obstructive rather than haemolytic mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity is a proliferative retinal vascular disease of preterm infants whose natural history is time critical, because the treatable stage occupies a narrow window and untreated progression causes retinal detachment and irreversible blindness. Australian screening criteria select infants by gestation below 31 weeks or birthweight below 1250 g, and deliberately do not use oxygen exposure as an entry criterion because disease occurs without it. The first examination is timed at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later, which protects the most immature infants from being examined before disease could plausibly appear. Examinations then repeat at one to two week intervals, with the interval determined by the zone and stage found, until vascularisation reaches the periphery.
key_points: Screening eligibility is gestation below 31 weeks or birthweight below 1250 g
Supplemental oxygen exposure modifies risk but is not an entry criterion
First examination at four weeks postnatal or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later
Examinations repeat every one to two weeks until peripheral vascularisation completes
Screening continues after discharge and must be handed over explicitly
explanation.pearls: The later of four weeks postnatal age and 31 weeks postmenstrual age sets the first examination, so a baby born at 24 weeks waits until 31 weeks postmenstrual age while a baby born at 30 weeks is examined at four weeks of age.

sources.label: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity
Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

options.rationale: The first examination is timed to four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever falls later, so waiting until 36 weeks would step over the window in which treatable disease usually declares itself. A 36 week timing belongs to a more mature infant being checked for late structural sequelae rather than for evolving disease. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: Oxygen exposure modifies risk but does not define eligibility, and disease occurs in preterm infants who never receive supplemental oxygen at all. Eligibility is set by gestation and birthweight, which she meets on both counts. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: She was born below 31 weeks with a birthweight below 1250 g, so she qualifies for screening, and the first examination falls at four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later. At 33 weeks and 4 days corrected the four week point governs, which is today. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: Screening is a serial process with examinations every one to two weeks until the retina is fully vascularised, not a single snapshot. A single examination tied to a discharge date would miss disease that progresses after she goes home. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

options.rationale: The birthweight threshold for screening is 1250 g rather than 1000 g, so a weight of 1180 g sits inside the criteria rather than outside them. Her gestation below 31 weeks would qualify her independently in any case. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

explanation.summary: Neonatal herpes simplex infection is acquired around the time of birth and presents in three overlapping patterns: disease limited to skin, eye and mouth, central nervous system disease, and disseminated disease with hepatitis and coagulopathy. The absence of a maternal history and the absence of vesicles are both common, because most transmission comes from asymptomatic shedding during a first infection the mother never recognised. Any neonate with fever, seizures, an unexplained transaminitis or a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid should receive empirical high dose aciclovir alongside antibacterial cover while testing proceeds. Delay is the main determinant of death and of neurological disability among survivors.
key_points: Most mothers of affected babies have no history of genital herpes
Vesicles are absent in a large proportion at presentation
Unexplained transaminitis with thrombocytopenia suggests disseminated disease
Empirical aciclovir is started on suspicion, not after confirmation
Antibacterial cover continues until bacterial sepsis is excluded
