explanation.pearls: Neonatal herpes needs 20 mg/kg of intravenous aciclovir every eight hours, which is well above the dose used in older children, and disseminated or central nervous system disease is treated for at least 21 days.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: A lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid with a negative Gram stain, marked transaminitis and thrombocytopenia points away from a pyogenic bacterial cause that antibiotics alone would cover. Waiting for cultures wastes the interval in which antiviral therapy changes outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus, which in the congenital form presents at birth with growth restriction, microcephaly and a positive urine test in the first three weeks, not with an acute febrile encephalopathy at day nine. The acute disseminated picture here fits a different virus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroid is used in older children with proven or suspected Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis and is not recommended in neonates, where evidence of benefit is absent. It would not address the viral process suggested by these results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Disseminated neonatal herpes presents in the first two weeks with seizures, hepatitis and thrombocytopenia, and fewer than half of affected babies ever develop a rash or have a mother with a known history. Empirical high dose aciclovir is started on suspicion because mortality rises steeply with every hour of delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.rationale: Cerebrospinal fluid viral testing can be falsely negative early in the illness and takes time to return, so a negative or pending result does not justify withholding therapy. Treatment is started empirically and stopped later if testing and the clinical course exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced beyond 14 days of age needs a split bilirubin, and a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total defines cholestasis that requires urgent investigation. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that sets the clock, because the Kasai portoenterostomy restores bile drainage in most infants operated before about 60 days but in far fewer after 90 days, and those who fail drainage need transplantation in infancy. Pale stools and dark urine are the classic combination but are frequently missed because parents are not asked to look, and the baby otherwise thrives. The broader cholestasis workup for infection, metabolic and endocrine causes proceeds alongside referral rather than before it.
key_points: Jaundice beyond 14 days needs a split bilirubin, not reassurance
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total is always pathological
Kasai outcomes deteriorate sharply beyond about 60 days of age
Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and cannot explain pale stools
Other cholestasis investigations run in parallel with urgent referral
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to photograph a nappy rather than describe the stool colour, because pale stools are reported as normal by most parents who have never been shown a comparison chart.

options.rationale: A conjugated fraction this high is already abnormal and never physiological, so repeating it adds no information while consuming the operative window. Watchful repetition is appropriate for unconjugated jaundice in a thriving breastfed baby, which is a different problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Pale stools with a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total demand same day specialist referral, because the outcome of portoenterostomy falls sharply once the infant passes about 60 days of age and she is already 49 days old. Definitive assessment is an intraoperative cholangiogram, so referral is to a unit able to proceed to surgery on the same admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Ursodeoxycholic acid is an adjunct for cholestatic symptoms once a cause is known and does nothing for an obstructed biliary tree. Starting it here creates the appearance of treatment while the operative window closes. (Source: GESA: Paediatric liver disease)

Cystic fibrosis and metabolic disorders do belong in the wider cholestasis workup, but they are pursued in parallel with urgent referral rather than ahead of it. Sequencing them first delays the one diagnosis whose treatment is time critical. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and by definition has a normal conjugated fraction, so it cannot explain a conjugated bilirubin of 92 micromol/L or pale stools. Attributing conjugated jaundice to breastfeeding is the classic reason these infants present too late. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease in Australian children is diagnosed on the combination of positive serology and duodenal histology obtained while the child is still consuming gluten. The single most common preventable error is starting the diet before biopsy, because villous architecture recovers quickly and the family is then left choosing between an unconfirmed lifelong restriction and a gluten challenge that nobody wants to undertake. Tissue transglutaminase IgA is the screening test of choice but must be paired with a total IgA, since selective IgA deficiency is over ten times more common in coeliac disease and produces a falsely negative result. Associated autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, raise the pre-test probability and appear frequently in the family history.
key_points: Biopsy is taken while the child is still eating gluten
Total IgA must accompany tissue transglutaminase IgA to exclude IgA deficiency
HLA typing excludes rather than confirms the diagnosis
Faltering growth and iron deficiency are common presenting features
Serology is used after diagnosis to monitor dietary adherence
explanation.pearls: If a family has already removed gluten before testing, a formal challenge of at least four weeks of gluten daily is needed before serology and biopsy become interpretable again.

options.rationale: Histological confirmation remains the standard in Australian paediatric practice, and the mucosal changes begin to heal within weeks of gluten withdrawal, so removing gluten before biopsy can make the diagnosis impossible to secure. A lifelong dietary restriction warrants a firm diagnosis before it is imposed. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

Symptomatic improvement on withdrawal is not diagnostic, because many children without coeliac disease feel better on the diet, and the change forecloses confirmatory biopsy. An empirical trial is reasonable only where coeliac disease has already been formally excluded. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

Antibody titres fall with gluten withdrawal in both affected and unaffected children, so a falling level after four weeks discriminates nothing. Serial titres have a role in monitoring adherence once the diagnosis is established. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

The genetic test is useful for its negative predictive value, since absence of both alleles effectively excludes the disease, but roughly half the general population carries one and a positive result confirms nothing. It cannot substitute for histology. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

Faltering growth with iron deficiency and a strongly positive antibody is an indication to complete the diagnostic pathway rather than to observe. Six months of further growth failure would be difficult to recover. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

explanation.summary: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents in the third to sixth week with non bilious forceful vomiting in a baby who remains hungry, and the diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound by muscle thickness above about 3 mm with a channel longer than 15 mm. The metabolic consequence is the part that kills: loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, which the kidney perpetuates by exchanging hydrogen for sodium once chloride is unavailable, generating the paradoxical aciduria. Pyloromyotomy is therefore never an emergency, and operating before correction exposes the infant to postoperative apnoea from a centrally depressed respiratory drive. Resuscitation with sodium chloride and potassium typically takes 24 to 48 hours, and surgery follows once the chloride exceeds about 100 mmol/L and the bicarbonate has fallen below about 30 mmol/L.
key_points: The vomiting is non bilious and the infant remains hungry afterwards
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria is the signature
Pyloromyotomy is elective and follows biochemical correction
Chloride replacement is what allows the kidney to excrete bicarbonate
Uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea
explanation.pearls: Aim for a chloride above 100 mmol/L and a bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L before pyloromyotomy, which usually takes 24 to 48 hours of sodium chloride with added potassium once the infant is passing urine.

options.rationale: The obstruction is mechanical but not strangulating, so there is no ischaemic emergency and nothing is gained by operating on an alkalotic infant. Anaesthesia in uncorrected metabolic alkalosis carries a recognised risk of postoperative apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Dextrose without sodium and chloride does not replace the losses that generated the alkalosis and risks worsening the hyponatraemia. Correction requires chloride specifically, which this fluid lacks. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Persistent vomiting of gastric contents strips hydrogen and chloride, producing a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that the kidney sustains until chloride is replaced. Pyloromyotomy is an elective procedure performed only once the chloride and bicarbonate have normalised, because uncorrected alkalosis depresses the central respiratory drive under anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

There is no infective process here, and continuous nasogastric drainage removes yet more gastric chloride and worsens the alkalosis. Free drainage is used for a distal obstruction with bilious aspirates, which is a different clinical problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Oral fluid will not be retained past a mechanically obstructed pylorus, so the deficit persists while the delay accumulates. Oral rehydration is the route of choice in gastroenteritis, where the gut remains patent. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome follows the rapid breakdown of a large tumour burden, releasing potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids that are metabolised to urate, with acute kidney injury the feared endpoint. Risk stratification in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia rests on the white cell count, the baseline urate and renal function, and this child is high risk on all three. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts existing urate to the far more soluble allantoin and is the agent of choice for high risk disease, but the reaction liberates hydrogen peroxide, which red cells lacking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase cannot detoxify. The result is brisk haemolysis with methaemoglobinaemia, so the enzyme deficiency converts the preferred drug into a contraindicated one and allopurinol with aggressive hydration becomes the fallback.
key_points: High white cell count, raised baseline urate and renal impairment define high risk
Rasburicase degrades existing urate; allopurinol only prevents new formation
Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended and worsens phosphate deposition
Hydration underpins every regimen regardless of the agent chosen
explanation.pearls: Screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before rasburicase in any patient of African, Mediterranean or Southeast Asian ancestry, because the resulting haemolysis with methaemoglobinaemia does not respond to methylene blue in these patients.

options.rationale: The risk profile does argue for aggressive urate control, but rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide as it degrades urate and precipitates severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in enzyme deficient patients. His deficiency makes this an absolute contraindication rather than a relative one. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

The haemolytic reaction is not dose dependent in a way that makes reduction safe, and monitoring detects the injury rather than preventing it. Dose reduction is a strategy for renal clearance issues, not for an enzymatic contraindication. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Hydration is the backbone of prophylaxis but is insufficient by itself when the urate is already elevated with this blast burden. Hydration alone suits a low risk tumour with a normal baseline urate. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate deposition in the tubules while the patient is already hyperphosphataemic, and it is redundant alongside effective urate lowering. The rasburicase component remains contraindicated regardless. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase and prevents further urate formation without any oxidative stress on red cells, making it the safe choice when rasburicase cannot be used. Combined with high volume intravenous hydration it protects renal function while the blast burden falls, accepting that existing urate is cleared more slowly than with the enzyme. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: A slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and classically presents with knee or thigh pain rather than hip pain, which is why a limping adolescent needs the hip examined and imaged regardless of where the pain is felt. Treatment is in situ screw fixation, since attempting to reduce the slip strips the posterior retinacular blood supply and causes avascular necrosis. The contested decision is the opposite hip: baseline contralateral slip rates sit near 20 per cent and most units accept clinical follow up, but prophylactic fixation becomes the recommended course when the risk is markedly elevated. The recognised high risk groups are children with endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency or renal osteodystrophy, and those presenting at a young chronological age relative to their skeletal maturity.
key_points: Knee or thigh pain with a limp requires hip imaging in an adolescent
Fixation is performed in situ because reduction risks avascular necrosis
Contralateral slip occurs in about one in five otherwise healthy children
Endocrinopathy or young age at presentation justifies prophylactic fixation
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the classic examination finding
explanation.pearls: Suspect an underlying endocrinopathy when a slip occurs below ten years of age or in a child whose height is well below the weight centile, and check thyroid function before discharge.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions

options.rationale: Clinical surveillance alone is the default for an otherwise healthy adolescent with a unilateral slip, where the contralateral risk is roughly one in five and presentation is usually symptomatic. It underprotects a child whose endocrinopathy raises that risk substantially. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: An underlying endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism raises the rate of a subsequent contralateral slip towards and beyond half, which is the accepted threshold for prophylactic fixation. Doing both hips under one anaesthetic avoids a second operation and prevents a slip that could present late with avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Imaging the asymptomatic side can identify a pre slip but does not alter the decision in a child who already meets the criteria for prophylactic fixation on endocrine grounds. It adds cost and a further anaesthetic in a young child without changing the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Forceful reduction of a stable slip disrupts the retinacular vessels and is the principal iatrogenic cause of avascular necrosis in this condition. Fixation is performed in situ, accepting the existing deformity. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.rationale: Non operative management allows progression of the slip and does not stabilise the physis, so it is not used for a diagnosed slip. Traction has no role once the diagnosis is radiologically confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest congenital infection and the leading non genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, which is why a failed newborn hearing screen should prompt consideration of it. Diagnosis must be established on urine or saliva nucleic acid testing within the first three weeks of life, because a positive sample after that point cannot distinguish congenital infection from postnatal acquisition through breast milk or saliva. Treatment is reserved for symptomatic disease, defined by features such as growth restriction, microcephaly, petechiae, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification or sensorineural hearing loss. Six months of oral valganciclovir started within the first month improves both hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes, while asymptomatic infants are followed with serial audiology rather than treated.
key_points: Confirmation requires urine or saliva testing within the first three weeks of life
Only symptomatic infants are treated with antivirals
Six months of oral valganciclovir beats six weeks of intravenous therapy
Therapy must begin within the first month to achieve benefit
Neutropenia is the dose limiting toxicity and requires scheduled counts
explanation.pearls: A positive cytomegalovirus test after 21 days of age cannot distinguish congenital from postnatally acquired infection, so retrieve the stored newborn screening card for testing if the diagnosis is raised later.

options.rationale: Observation is the correct course for asymptomatic infection detected incidentally, where treatment has not been shown to help and carries toxicity. This baby has multisystem disease, which is precisely the group in whom treatment improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

Six weeks of intravenous ganciclovir was the older regimen and is now used only for the initial phase when oral therapy is not tolerated, because six months of oral treatment produces better hearing and developmental outcomes. Stopping at six weeks forfeits that additional benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

The treatment benefit depends on starting within the first month of life, so deferring until progression is documented moves therapy outside the window in which it works. Later deterioration is managed with amplification and implantation rather than with antivirals. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

Symptomatic congenital infection confirmed within the first three weeks of life is treated with six months of oral valganciclovir begun before one month of age, which improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes compared with shorter or later therapy. Neutropenia is the dose limiting toxicity, so the full blood count is monitored weekly at first and then monthly. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

Hyperimmune globulin has been studied mainly as an antenatal intervention to prevent transmission and has not shown benefit as postnatal treatment of established disease. It does not replace antiviral therapy in a symptomatic newborn. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

explanation.summary: Epileptic spasms present between three and twelve months as clusters of brief symmetrical flexion or extension, typically on waking, and are far too often mistaken for colic or reflux until developmental regression brings the child back. The triad of spasms, the chaotic high amplitude electroencephalogram pattern called hypsarrhythmia and developmental arrest defines West syndrome, and time to treatment is the main modifiable determinant of cognitive outcome. First line therapy is hormonal, usually high dose oral prednisolone in Australian practice, except where tuberous sclerosis complex is identified, in which case vigabatrin is clearly superior. Every infant with spasms therefore needs a careful skin examination under ultraviolet light, since the hypopigmented macules of tuberous sclerosis may be the only external clue and they directly change the drug chosen.
key_points: Clusters on waking with developmental regression suggest epileptic spasms
Hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram completes the West syndrome triad
Hormonal therapy is first line except in tuberous sclerosis complex
Vigabatrin is the preferred first agent when tuberous sclerosis is present
Time from onset to effective treatment predicts developmental outcome
explanation.pearls: Vigabatrin causes an irreversible concentric visual field constriction in roughly a third of treated patients, so baseline and serial ophthalmological assessment is arranged and the duration of therapy is kept as short as the response allows.

sources.label: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

options.rationale: The hypopigmented macules indicate tuberous sclerosis complex, and vigabatrin is markedly more effective than hormonal therapy for spasms in that specific setting, with response rates well above those achieved in other causes. It is therefore chosen first rather than as a second line agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

Hormonal therapy with prednisolone is the first line choice for spasms without an identified structural or genetic cause, and it would be right had the skin examination been normal. The neurocutaneous findings here shift the preferred agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

Valproate is a later option with substantially lower rates of spasm cessation and carries hepatotoxicity risk in infants with undiagnosed metabolic disease. An outpatient timeframe also underestimates the urgency of stopping the spasms. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

Conventional anticonvulsants including levetiracetam are relatively ineffective against epileptic spasms, and a four week delay allows continued developmental regression. The distinction from focal or generalised seizures matters because the drug classes that work are different. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

Spasms do eventually remit but at the cost of permanent developmental loss, and the duration of untreated spasms is the strongest predictor of poor cognitive outcome. Observation is never appropriate once the diagnosis is made. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

explanation.summary: A painless abdominal mass in a well preschool child, often discovered by a parent during bathing, is a Wilms tumour until proven otherwise, and the key clinical feature is that it arises within the kidney and does not cross the midline. The main differential is neuroblastoma, which characteristically does cross the midline, encases rather than displaces vessels, produces a child who looks unwell and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites. Hypertension occurs in roughly a quarter of children with Wilms tumour through renin mediated mechanisms, and microscopic haematuria is common. The most important management principle is that percutaneous biopsy is avoided, because tumour spill upstages the disease and adds radiotherapy to the treatment burden of a child who is otherwise highly curable.
key_points: Wilms tumour arises within the kidney and does not cross the midline
Neuroblastoma crosses the midline and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites
Hypertension and microscopic haematuria are common accompanying features
Percutaneous biopsy seeds the track and upstages otherwise curable disease
Australian units proceed to upfront nephrectomy for resectable unilateral tumours
explanation.pearls: Handle the abdomen as little as possible once a Wilms tumour is suspected and document that in the notes, because repeated deep palpation risks capsular rupture with the same staging consequence as a biopsy.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass in children

options.rationale: Needle sampling breaches the tumour capsule and seeds the track, which upstages the disease and commits the child to flank radiotherapy she would otherwise avoid. Biopsy is reserved for unresectable or bilateral disease or when imaging suggests a different tumour type. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

This sequence combines the staging penalty of biopsy with delayed surgery and is not used for a resectable unilateral tumour. It carries the same track seeding problem as biopsy alone. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

Imaging showing an intrarenal mass with a claw sign of surrounding renal parenchyma in a preschool child, with normal catecholamine metabolites excluding the main alternative, is sufficient to proceed to upfront radical nephrectomy, which provides both the diagnosis and the staging. Australian practice follows the North American approach of immediate surgery for resectable unilateral disease, with chemotherapy then guided by the operative stage and histology. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

Preoperative chemotherapy without histology is the European protocol approach and is a defensible strategy internationally, but it is not the pathway followed in Australian units for resectable unilateral disease, where upfront surgery preserves accurate staging. The two approaches differ mainly in whether stage is assigned before or after chemotherapy. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

A solid renal mass of this size in a child of this age requires definitive management rather than surveillance, and delay allows local progression and metastatic spread. Interval imaging has no role once a solid intrarenal tumour is identified. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy typically declares itself between three and five years with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and a Gowers manoeuvre, and a markedly raised creatine kinase should trigger genetic testing rather than a muscle biopsy in the first instance. Corticosteroids remain the only intervention shown to prolong independent ambulation, and the decision that matters clinically is when to start rather than whether to start. Australian and international consensus times initiation to the plateau phase, identified on serial timed function testing as the point at which motor skills stop improving but have not yet declined, which usually falls between four and six years of age. Treatment brings a predictable burden of weight gain, growth suppression, reduced bone mineral density and behavioural change, so bone health, blood pressure, glucose and immunisation status are addressed before and during therapy.
key_points: Serial timed function tests identify the plateau phase that triggers treatment
Corticosteroids prolong ambulation and delay scoliosis and cardiac decline
Starting during the improving phase adds toxicity without added benefit
Bone density, growth, glucose and behaviour need scheduled monitoring
Live vaccines should be completed before immunosuppressive doses begin
explanation.pearls: Check varicella immunity and complete live vaccines before starting corticosteroids, because daily prednisolone at these doses makes subsequent live vaccination unsafe and varicella exposure then requires immunoglobulin.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: Waiting until walking is lost forfeits the main benefit, which is prolonging ambulation and delaying scoliosis. Steroids started after loss of ambulation still have a role for respiratory and cardiac function but no longer preserve walking. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: Respiratory decline occurs years after the ambulatory phase, so using it as the trigger would delay treatment well past the window in which walking can be preserved. Spirometry guides later respiratory management rather than steroid initiation. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: Weight gain, growth suppression, reduced bone density and behavioural change are real and require active monitoring, but the evidence for prolonged ambulation, delayed scoliosis and preserved cardiorespiratory function is strong enough that steroids are standard care. The adverse effects are managed rather than used as a reason to withhold. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: Starting during the phase when a young boy is still gaining motor skills exposes him to years of additional toxicity without added benefit, since the gains continue regardless. The genetic diagnosis defines who will need treatment, not when it begins. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: The accepted trigger is the plateau phase, when motor skills have stopped improving but have not yet begun to decline, which his serial timed testing demonstrates across three visits. Starting at this point maximises the years of preserved ambulation and delays scoliosis and cardiorespiratory decline. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

explanation.summary: Measles is among the most transmissible infections known, with airborne spread persisting in a room for up to two hours after an infectious person leaves, which is why shared waiting room exposure counts as significant contact. Post exposure prophylaxis is chosen by the interval since exposure and by the susceptibility of the contact. A measles containing vaccine is preferred for immunocompetent contacts aged six months and over when given within 72 hours, while normal human immunoglobulin covers the period up to six days and is also used for infants under six months, pregnant women without immunity and immunocompromised contacts regardless of timing. Measles is notifiable in every Australian jurisdiction, and contact tracing is run by the public health unit. Infants who receive a measles vaccine before twelve months of age still require the routine doses at twelve and eighteen months, because early vaccination produces a less durable response.
key_points: Airborne spread persists for up to two hours after the case leaves a room
Vaccine works as prophylaxis only within 72 hours of exposure
Immunoglobulin extends the prophylaxis window to six days
Immunoglobulin is preferred for infants under six months and immunocompromised contacts
A dose given before twelve months does not replace the routine scheduled doses
explanation.pearls: A measles vaccine given to an infant under twelve months for outbreak control does not count towards the schedule, so both routine doses at twelve and eighteen months must still be given.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles national guidelines

options.rationale: Vaccine provides protection only when given within 72 hours of exposure, and at four days that window has closed, leaving immunoglobulin as the effective option up to six days after contact. Measles is a notifiable disease, so the public health unit coordinates contact management alongside the clinical decision. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Vaccine is the preferred option for an immunocompetent contact aged six months or older, but only within 72 hours of exposure, because it must generate immunity faster than the wild virus replicates. At four days it is too late to prevent disease. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Transplacental maternal antibody wanes over the first six to nine months and its presence depends on the mother's own immunity, which is unknown here. Infants in this age band are among the most vulnerable to severe measles. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Vitamin A is given as an adjunct to treatment once measles is established, particularly in young children admitted to hospital, and has no prophylactic role. Waiting for a rash forfeits the prophylaxis window entirely. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Serology at this point reflects his pre exposure status rather than infection, and the turnaround time would push him beyond the six day limit for immunoglobulin. The decision must be made on exposure history and immunisation status. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
